title: DHS pushes through billions for deportations, border projects | CNN Politics
authors: Priscilla Alvarez, Audrey Ash, Annie Grayer
description:
At DHS, it’s been business as usual, and officials have continued to ink contracts at a pace similar to the one before the elections.
Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, told CNN he’s exploring how to put curbs on how the funds are used.
That includes placing some restrictions on ICE and providing more funds to the Homeland Security inspector general for oversight.
Democratic lawmakers already have plans to scrutinize who DHS struck contracts with — and how they did it — in a series of oversight measures.
A $100 million contract in August went to supporting the 287(g) program in Texas, which deputizes local law enforcement to perform some immigration law enforcement actions.
text:
On a recent Tuesday afternoon, Deputy Homeland Security Secretary Troy Edgar stood before dozens of contractors and industry leaders and boasted of his department’s multibillion-dollar budget, claiming that it was bigger than that of American Airlines.

The message — described by two people who were in attendance — was clear to those in the room: DHS was eager as ever to spend money to advance President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign promise. The department needs more detention space, more airlines, more of everything to solve for what Edgar described as a supply chain issue, the people said.

It’s the latest example of how DHS is taking advantage of the billions of dollars in its coffers despite waning public support for the president’s immigration crackdown. And the effort comes as Democrats, flush from massive midterm victories, prepare to use their majorities to conduct tough oversight of the department’s spending and look for ways to rein it in.

In recent months, DHS has awarded a nearly $1.3 billion contract for Immigration and Customs Enforcement deportation flights, at least $1.5 billion for border infrastructure, a multimillion-dollar contract to transport ICE detainees, and nearly $13 million for a canine facility.

“They want to use their spending authority that they’ve got to do what they want to do before there is a new sheriff in town,” GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who oversees the DHS budget in the House for the remaining weeks of the Republican majority, told CNN.

A Homeland Security spokesperson said in a statement that the department is using the funds “to strengthen border security, hire more ICE officers, fully fund the 287(g) program, and expand detention space,” adding that thanks to legislation passed this year, “ICE and CBP are FULLY FUNDED through the rest of President Trump’s term — ensuring our mission to protect the homeland continues undeterred.”

Democrats hope to build ‘guardrails’

In the immediate days after the midterms, Trump appeared to briefly waver on his immigration policy, acknowledging that it was “too tough” in a “60 Minutes” interview. He later defended his policy and has elevated Stephen Miller — the administration’s staunchest advocate for mass deportations — to White House chief of staff. At DHS, it’s been business as usual, and officials have continued to ink contracts at a pace similar to the one before the elections.

Last year, Republicans passed the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, providing $75 billion for ICE to spend over the next four years, and $65 billion for Customs and Border Protection. In June, Congress approved a roughly $70 billion immigration enforcement package — the Secure America Act — meant to fund ICE and CBP through the end of the second Trump administration.

A CNN analysis of government records found that in fiscal year 2026, which ran from October 2025 through September 2026, ICE and CBP signed new contracts valuing at over $41.7 billion — with the potential to increase to $63.7 billion. That’s more than three times the amount from the year before: In the twelve months prior, which includes three months of the Biden administration, the two agencies only awarded $12.3 billion worth of contracts.

Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the ranking member on the House Appropriations Homeland Security subcommittee, told CNN he’s exploring how to put curbs on how the funds are used.

“Once we have control, then there’s a lot more we can do on guardrails,” he said, referring to bringing the funds under his committee’s oversight. That includes placing some restrictions on ICE and providing more funds to the Homeland Security inspector general for oversight.

Democratic lawmakers already have plans to scrutinize who DHS struck contracts with — and how they did it — in a series of oversight measures. But pulling back the billions in funding is likely to be an uphill battle given that Democrats would need Trump to agree, or assemble an unlikely veto-proof majority.

“The only thing stopping (DHS) is the Congress or the public pressuring the president to put limitations on it,” said Claire Trickler-McNulty, a former senior ICE official.

Even before Democrats take over, Amodei, who is retiring, told CNN he is keeping track of how DHS is making spending decisions to monitor whether the agency is veering into politically unpopular territory.

“We’re keeping an eye on what they’re doing. But it appears to be a bit of a far cry on the earlier days of warehouses and airplanes and whatever the heck,” he said.

As of September, ICE has already set aside $22.2 billion using funds from the pair of bills passed by Republicans, with $91 billion left to spend, while CBP had obligated $45.2 billion from those same funds with $45 billion left to spend, according to data compiled by Senate Budget Committee Democratic staff.

Some of the department’s largest contractors, meanwhile, have been proceeding with their plans.

In a quarterly earnings call this month, CoreCivic — one of the largest private prison and immigration detention operators in the US — told investors that they don’t expect DHS to slow down post-election and anticipate detention population to continue to increase.

“There’s nothing that would cause us to think otherwise. They have the secure funding to do so, and that goes through 2029, and they can continue to enter contracts and utilize bed capacity through that funding up until then. We believe that they’ll continue to do so,” said CoreCivic President and CEO Lucibeth Mayberry.

Some Homeland Security officials told CNN the pace of spending has been steady since Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin scrapped his predecessor Kristi Noem’s policy of signing off on contracts that surpassed the $100,000 mark and now they simply have more money and contracts to distribute.

Other officials have shared with contractors that they’re accelerating contracting, particularly with companies that have historically worked with the department.

“They went into overdrive,” a source familiar with the contracting process told CNN. “It’s the fear of the unknown.”

Billions to buy detention facilities, planes

In Front Royal, Virginia, the agency’s canine division facility is getting a $12.8 million revamp; in Georgia, the Federal Law Enforcement Training Center is getting a new ammo storage facility valued at $2.2 million.

A $100 million contract in August went to supporting the 287(g) program in Texas, which deputizes local law enforcement to perform some immigration law enforcement actions. The contract pays for 24/7-armed support for the transportation of detainees from local law enforcement to ICE custody. While only $100 million has been obligated so far, the contract has the potential to increase to $382.3 million.

Several of the 2026 contracts are for construction at aging CBP facilities. Some of the highest CBP contracts, all valued at more than $100 million apiece, are for designing, building, or maintaining structures in Texas, California, Florida and New Mexico.

That’s in addition to border wall spending. CBP Commissioner Rodney Scott said in June that border wall construction is “ahead of schedule and below budget,” citing previous wall money appropriated by Congress and the president’s “big beautiful bill” which allocated $46.5 billion for construction.

The Supreme Court also recently allowed Trump to continue border wall construction in the Big Bend region of Texas – including Big Bend National Park – pausing a lower court ruling that temporarily blocked that work while it considers whether the administration had the authority to bypass environmental requirements.

This week, Rep. Veronica Escobar of Texas, alongside other Democratic lawmakers, urged the Homeland Security inspector general to investigate the contracting process behind an award of nearly $7.5 billion for border infrastructure projects in the Big Bend region.

One of the largest contracts in the last two years was signed this October with CSI Aviation, a flight charter company that’s held lucrative contracts with DHS in the past. Valued at $1.28 billion, the contract is for on-demand flight services for “enforcement and removal operations under the ICE Air program.” At least $885 million has been paid to CSI through that contract, indicating some services have already been provided.

DHS was already under intense scrutiny over the purchase of the planes CSI Aviation is contracted to fly. In 2025, DHS spent hundreds of millions of dollars on contracts and 10 planes to create a mini deportation airline for ICE. CNN previously reported the majority of those planes remained parked in a hangar in Louisiana, with no firm plan in place to fly them.

ICE has also been spending heavily on purchasing detention facilities from two of its largest contractors.

Private contractors own and operate 34 detention facilities nationwide, GEO Group CEO George Zoley told investors this month. Of those, GEO Group owns and operates 20, while CoreCivic is responsible for 12.

CoreCivic announced the sale of four facilities to DHS this year for a total of around $2.2 billion, according to company filings with the SEC. Mayberry told investors that company officials “continue to have discussions with ICE about the potential acquisition of additional CoreCivic detention facilities,” though she cautioned that talks are in preliminary stages. CoreCivic is charged with the care of more than 60,000 ICE detainees.

In a report released this week, the Government Accountability Office found that ICE’s current plans indicate that the agency expects to obligate remaining detention funds from the president’s “big beautiful bill” by the end of next year.

This article has been updated with additional information.

text:
A federal judge said that the US Immigration and Customs ⁠Enforcement agency (ICE) “made a mockery of court orders” in Colorado and that the court found government officials in contempt ⁠for instantly re-arresting a ⁠man whom ​the judge had ordered released.

US district judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to take any further action because she ⁠said the officials had “cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue” as sworn by an official in court.

“ICE’s new ‘policy’ of ⁠immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ ​immediate release,” the judge wrote on Wednesday, ‌according to court records in ‌the US district court for the district of Colorado.

At least 18 people ‌in Colorado have been held in detention longer than they should have been or have been re-arrested within minutes of their judge-ordered release in the past six weeks, CPR News, the news division of Colorado Public Radio, reported.

The report said that immigration attorneys estimated the number may be ‌higher given that some immigrants represented themselves.

The phenomenon of immigration detainees being released and then quickly re-detained has been noticeable in recent months and legal advocates say the trend is on the rise.

Sometimes a person is re-arrested days later, sometimes without even leaving the detention center and, according to advocates, often in violation of a federal court order.

ICE, which is part of the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), has been the face of ​Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free speech and due process rights.

Human rights groups also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised ⁠concerns about racial profiling.

The Trump administration has maintained that ​its actions aim to ​improve domestic security and are ​in compliance with the law. ICE and the DHS did not ​immediately respond to ‌a request ​for comment on what ​the judge said on Wednesday.

Democrats, who won majorities in the House and Senate in the midterm elections, now aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

text:
A Princeton University doctoral student was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after attending a neuroscience conference in Washington, D.C., according to the university and members of her research lab.

Eva Yi Xie, a third-year Ph.D. student at the Princeton Neuroscience Institute, was detained by ICE on Thursday at an airport near Washington, D.C. and is believed to be being held in Chantilly, Virginia, according to The Daily Princetonian, the university's student newspaper.

The Brody Lab, a neuroscience research group at Princeton University, said in a post on X that Xie was detained at Ronald Reagan National Airport while returning from the Society for Neuroscience conference, where she had presented a research poster.

Read More on News

Princeton has arranged legal representation for Xie, university spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss told The Daily Princetonian.

Trump’s push for mass deportations has transformed ICE into a central force in the administration’s immigration crackdown, dramatically expanding arrests and removals across the country. ICE deported 483,200 people and made more than 491,000 immigration arrests in fiscal year 2026, the highest annual totals in the agency’s history, according to DHS data.

Although the administration says its campaign is aimed at enforcing immigration law and removing dangerous offenders, federal data and independent analyses show that many of those arrested have no criminal convictions, while students and immigrants who entered through legal pathways have also been caught up in the crackdown.

Xie emigrated from Shanghai, China, to the United States in 2016 and attended the Bronx High School of Science in New York, according to a 2020 profile in The Science Survey, the school's student newspaper. The profile said Xie initially struggled with English, but went on to become a finalist in the Regeneron Science Talent Search for research focused on using genomics to improve treatments for heart disease.

Newsweek has contacted Princeton University, ICE, and the Department of Homeland Security for comment via email outside office hours. The offices of New Jersey Senators Cory Booker and Andy Kim, as well as the government of New Jersey, have also been contacted for comment. Kim’s office and Princeton University declined to comment further on the case.

The Brody Lab said Xie sent a message to her lab colleagues on Slack asking for help on November 19 before they lost contact with her. The lab said her lawyers were working to secure her release.

Carlos Brody, a Princeton neuroscience professor who advises Xie, criticized her detention in a statement to The Daily Princetonian, describing her as a “law-abiding student.”

"Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot," he said.

Xie graduated from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology in 2024, with degrees in computer science and mathematics and a concentration in economics, according to her portfolio.

Princeton Graduate School Dean Rodney Priestley told neuroscience graduate students that the university would remain in contact with Xie’s family, legal team and colleagues as the situation developed, according to an email obtained by The Daily Princetonian.

It remains unclear what immigration status Xie held at the time of her detention.

title: 'Traumatizing': hunger striker in ICE detention tells of force-feeding ordeal - The Guardian
description:
The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez.
Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out.
On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas.
The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone.
In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.
text:
The text message that came from inside the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention center was stark: “I have spent five days eating regular food. If I don’t eat it, they put the tube in me to feed me.”

A Cuban asylum seeker, Luis Alejandro Cora Pérez, 32, said in messages to the Guardian this month that he was still weak and dizzy after three months without eating, but that he had broken his hunger strike because being force-fed was just too painful.

The Trump administration responded to requests for comment by denying it had force-fed Cora Pérez. But the detainee sent more details – and his is far from an isolated case.

Cora Pérez was one of two men on hunger striker at a Texas facility for whom ICE sought and received a federal judge’s permission to force-feed in recent weeks, a Guardian investigation found.

Cora Pérez and the other man were locked up inside the Port Isabel service processing center, an ICE detention facility in south Texas, just a few miles from the US-Mexico border, on the coast near where Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches rockets. Cora Pérez began a hunger strike in August to protest against his prolonged detention by federal immigration officials while his case plays out. At first he only drank water, then after three weeks, he says he began to drink one Ensure nutritional shake per day.

On 30 October, court records show ICE received permission to forcibly feed and hydrate him, and to restrain him while doing so.

The next day he says six guards at the center held him down, while medical staffers inserted a feeding tube through his nose and down his throat, and pumped nutritional liquid into his stomach – a process he called “traumatizing, both physically and psychologically”.

On 3 November, ICE then received permission from a federal judge to force-feed another hunger striker at Port Isabel, from Uzbekistan, federal court records show. The DHS says the Uzbek man has not been subjected to the practice, however.

On Wednesday night, after weeks of communications, Cora Pérez was suddenly transferred to another detention center in Texas. His relative says neither of them were alerted to any plans to transfer him, or a reason for it.

The DHS did not specify why Cora Pérez was transferred, adding that ICE makes custody determinations on a “case-by-case” basis based on “various factors”.

The revelations come as ICE’s detention practices continue to come under fire amid allegations of mistreatment, and as an increasing number of sporadic hunger strikes have been breaking out in ICE facilities across the country.

The two men’s cases in Texas, revealed here for the first time, are some of the most recent instances of government lawyers seeking a federal judge’s permission, as required by ICE policy, and receiving the go-ahead to force-feed detained hunger strikers. The Guardian’s reporting is based on court records, interviews, dozens of messages exchanged and an interview conducted with Cora Pérez via a facility phone. It further reveals how the Trump administration is increasingly obtaining such court orders to force-feed detained immigrants, a secretive practice widely condemned as torture by human rights organizations and medical ethics groups.

Detainees driven to hunger strike are typically using it as a last resort to protest against poor conditions and the Trump administration’s preference for arrest and prolonged detention while their civil immigration cases proceed through the system.

Cora Pérez said detention center staff inserted the feeding tube and left it in his body, a not uncommon practice, according to experts, and introduced nutrition – first a “clear liquid”, followed by a “milky liquid”, he recalled – through the tube twice more that day, before he cracked and said he broke his hunger strike, citing what he called “horrific torture”. He began voluntarily drinking nutritional shakes the following day, he said.

“ICE does not hold back on anything, and they do anything they want, like we have seen, even killing their own US citizens,” he wrote to the Guardian, referring to the fatal shootings of Renee Good by an ICE officer and Alex Pretti by a border patrol officer in January of this year during Trump’s pivotal immigration crackdown on Minneapolis.

Detained hunger strikers subjected to involuntary medical procedures, including force-feeding, have rarely spoken out about their cases or revealed their identities, much less while still detained. Cora Pérez’s messages offer a rare glimpse at conditions inside a detention center’s restricted medical unit where hunger strikers and suicidal detainees are held.

“They just took [the Uzbek man] in an ambulance after [him] fainting in front of the medical lobby where they take our vitals, our weight and our temperature,” Cora Pérez said in an alarmed message last Monday morning.

The Uzbek man was returned the following day to the facility, Cora Pérez said.

“I see him every day because I see him in the room in front of me, but they don’t let us talk to each other,” he added.

The Guardian independently confirmed the Uzbek’s man identity but is not publicly naming him, because efforts to contact him have been unsuccessful. The man arrived at the Mexico-US border in April 2022 and was released into the country while navigating his immigration case. He was arrested by border patrol officials in April of this year and placed in detention. The man does not appear to have any criminal record and the DHS did not point to any criminal history.

In a statement, DHS said that after they received the court’s permission to force-feed the Uzbek man, he “has voluntarily taken in fluids and there has been NO force-feeding or forced hydration”.

Security operations at the sprawling Port Isabel facility in Los Fresnos, Texas, are run by a private prison company, Akima Global Services, while healthcare is primarily handled by government workers.

“ICE respects detainees’ rights to exercise self-expression and medical autonomy by refusing nourishment and medical care,” the DHS said in a statement. “ICE Health Services Corps may provide involuntary medical treatment only to prevent imminent life-threatening harm or death. Medical staff may provide treatment only to medically stabilize the patient, bringing the detainee outside the imminent harm, incapacitation, or death.”

The US attorney’s office in the southern district of Texas, which represented ICE in its force-feeding request, did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Virginia-headquartered Akima Global Services, and its parent company Nana Regional Corporation, based in Alaska, did not respond to a request for comment.

Force-feeding cases are shrouded in secrecy. After a detainee launches a hunger strike, ICE often sequesters them in medical isolation cells for monitoring, according to ICE’s detention standards. The DHS said that ICE continues to offer hunger strikers three meals per day.

After a certain period of not eating, which varies per case, ICE will request a federal judge’s permission to force-feed the hunger striker. Many court records, and sometimes entire court dockets, are sealed and hidden from public view. In Cora Pérez and the Uzbek man’s cases, like in others, they did not have any legal representation to challenge the force-feeding requests.

The Guardian found at least five instances in which ICE requested permission to force-feed hunger strikers in Port Isabel since January 2025. The federal judge who ruled on Cora Perez and the Uzbek man, Rolando Olvera, has similarly ordered in at least three other cases, records show. Olvera’s judicial assistant said the court had no comment for this article.

ICE is known to have requested permission to force-feed at least 21 detainees across the US since January 2025, the Guardian found, but the number is probably higher since an unknown number of records and dockets remain sealed, unsearchable and not feasible to locate. Most of the cases coinciding with the second Trump administration and tracked by the Guardian are in Texas and Florida, with others in Georgia, Arizona and Washington state. Under the Biden administration, ICE force-feeding requests were also made in Louisiana and California.

Amy Zeidan, an emergency medicine physician based in Atlanta and an expert on healthcare in immigration detention, said force-feeding hunger strikers can amount to “torture”, and lead to significant psychological distress. She also said it was a violation of medical ethics.

“Essentially it’s like inserting a straw into your nose,” Zeidan said. “You have a gag reflex, so most times people will gag, and that’s really uncomfortable. And people will even vomit repeatedly if it continues to irritate their gag reflex.”

Zeidan added that the forceful insertion of a feeding tube can lead to the swelling of the nostrils and the throat, and even tear them, leading to bleeding.

“It is like torture – somebody is doing a painful procedure to you that you don’t consent to,” Zeidan added. “Autonomy is a fundamental principle of medical ethics. We can’t do something to patients if they don’t want to, even if we think it’s good for them.”

There are numerous cells and rooms inside the Port Isabel medical unit, including isolation cells and shared rooms for ill detainees, according to Cora Pérez. In recent weeks, there were five people in the Port Isabel medical isolation cells used for hunger striking or suicidal detainees, he added. He described the cells as “practically freezing”, constantly surveilled with a security camera, and with just a bed, toilet and sink. As well as himself, he says he observed the Uzbek man, a Middle Eastern man, a “tall” eastern European man and a Black man of unknown nationality in the isolation cells. Unit detainees are escorted by facility staff to showers and sometimes receive yard and television access, he said.

Cora Pérez worries for the other detainees. The Black man, whose identity or nationality he does not know, seems to have “serious mental health problems”, Cora Pérez observed.

“He harms himself and spends the night yelling and hitting the door, and does not let anyone sleep,” he said.

The Guardian has independently confirmed the eastern European and Middle Eastern men’s identities, but is not publicly naming them because efforts to contact them have been unsuccessful. The DHS did not comment on the other men inside the medical isolation unit, saying they could not comment without the Guardian providing their identities.

Cora Pérez had left his son and parents in Cuba and requested asylum at the Mexico-US border in 2023, according to a relative who spoke to the Guardian on condition of anonymity due to fear of retaliation by immigration authorities. Cora Pérez went to live with the relative in Florida, where he worked in maintenance at a hotel and as a food delivery worker, he said.

In March 2025, Cora Pérez was arrested by local police and later convicted of two misdemeanors, including “breach of peace” and “obstructing an officer without violence”, according to local records. He was sentenced to two months in jail, his relative said. But ICE placed a hold on him and as he was being released in June 2025, immigration officials took him into custody – a common system – and soon transferred him to the Adelanto detention center, a privately-run facility in California.

Days in Adelanto turned to weeks, then months, then a over year, according to a federal court order denying one of his petitions requesting his release. His multiple requests to immigration and ordinary federal courts for release from detention, while he fights his asylum case, have been unsuccessful.

“All his claims will be heard by an immigration judge, and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law,” DHS said. “Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the US.”

In August, he stopped eating to protest against his protracted detention.

“I have spent two birthdays behind ICE’s bars,” he wrote. “The reasons I did the hunger strike in Adelanto are for my political asylum, for the time I have spent detained, [and] because I have a 14-year-old son who is starving to death in Cuba because he does not have my help.

“Also due to the mistreatment by the officials,” he added.

Cora Pérez did not tell his family about the hunger strike, so as not to further worry them. It was not until he was transferred to Port Isabel in late September that he confessed to his relative he had been on a prolonged hunger strike.

“He doesn’t share details so that I won’t get upset or worry,” the relative said in a phone interview.

Cora Pérez’s mother, who is in Cuba, “does not know anything, because she is sick, and with his detention she has gotten worse”, the relative added, between tears. “I don’t want her nor his grandmother to know anything about it,” the relative added.

On 30 October, the federal prosecutors requested permission for ICE to forcibly feed and hydrate Cora Pérez. Hours later, a federal judge approved the procedures without hearing from Cora Pérez. Cora Pérez told the Guardian in various instances he felt it was unfair he was not given the opportunity to present his case to the judge before the judge approved his force-feeding.

“It’s very disturbing because the judge is basically making a decision on information that is only provided by one side,” said Linus Chan, a professor of clinical law and the director of the detainee rights clinic at the University of Minnesota law school. “That just seems ridiculous.”

Cora Pérez was force-fed the following day, he said in his messages and in a phone call, adding that he did not physically resist because he “had seen a lot of mistreatment of others detained”.

“[ICE does] what they want with us, whatever they want, because a federal judge gave them permission,” he added. “I have suffered on the island [of Cuba] and now at the hands of ICE.”

After asking Cora Pérez about the DHS’s denials that he was force-fed, he repeated that he was. “Brother, ICE says and does whatever they want. They deny, punish, retaliate and do everything at their own will. They have even sent Cubans to Africa,” he said.

The number of people detained by ICE has soared under the Trump administration. And due to policy and legal changes, tens of thousands of people are forced to stay in detention for long periods while they fight their immigration cases.

Chan, from the University of Minnesota, says prolonged detention and delays in their cases lead to logical conclusion. “That’s exactly when people protest,” he said.

“And the only form of protest, for many of these people, is a hunger strike,” he said.

As Trump’s hardline immigration crackdown continues and people are detained as a first resort while their cases play out, Chan said: “Hunger strikes will become more common.”

text:
ROANOKE, Va. (WDBJ) - A father and grandfather who says he has lived in the United States for decades is afraid to leave for work after seeing friends and coworkers detained.

The man spoke with WDBJ7 in Spanish outside his home. He did not share his name, country of origin or immigration status.

During the interview, a car pulled up to drop off food. Before he knew why it was there, he appeared visibly shaken and knocked on the wall of his home to alert people inside.

Despite his fears, he wanted to speak about what he and others in his community are experiencing.

The man said he came to the United States seeking a better life after leaving a country affected by crime. Now, he said, he is troubled by how he sees people being treated here.

He said he no longer wants to go to work after seeing videos on his phone of people being detained, including friends and coworkers. He said he is worried about expenses but would rather lose his job than be detained.

He said people should be treated as human beings, not animals.

He also said a neighbor he had known for about 20 years was detained for three months. He described the neighbor as a good person and said the detention brought sadness to the neighborhood.

The man has three children and seven grandchildren, and young children were inside the home during the interview. He expressed concern about how witnessing detentions could affect children.

Addressing those he believes are responsible for the treatment he described, he said they would one day have to answer to God.

WDBJ7 again reached out to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement for comment and to ask how many people have been detained in Roanoke this week. WDBJ7 also reached out to Congressman Ben Cline and has not received a response.

text:
iPost wins FOIL lawsuit against Orchard Park

Investigative Post sued Orchard Park over its refusal to release police reports involving calls to immigration agencies. Supreme Court Judge Dennis Ward this week ruled in our favor.

Share on

Orchard Park town hall. Image via WKBW.

In September 2025, Orchard Park police conducted a traffic stop of a vehicle that contained migrants. The encounter led to a call to a federal immigration agency, and criminal charges filed against the driver.

In January, Investigative Post filed a Freedom of Information request with the Orchard Park Police Department for any arrest or incident reports where officers responded to a scene and then called a federal immigration agency, be it ICE, Border Patrol or Customs and Border Protection. Arrest and incident reports are generally considered public records.

But Orchard Park denied the request — and a subsequent appeal — arguing that releasing the documents would “interfere with present or future judicial proceedings.” Investigative Post then sued.

On Tuesday, a Supreme Court judge ruled that Orchard Park can no longer keep details about that incident secret.

Investigative Post reported in December that local law enforcement in the Buffalo suburbs and Niagara County regularly contacts federal immigration agencies. Such contacts have resulted in multiple local ICE detentions, Investigative Post found, effectively turning local police into an arm of the Trump administration’s crackdown on migrants.

We followed up on that reporting by requesting records from Orchard Park.

During an October hearing, an attorney representing the town — Michael Perley of the firm Hurwitz Fine — argued that releasing and publishing the incident report would alert the driver and the other passengers that police and prosecutors know who they are. That might encourage them not to show up at future court hearings, or not to cooperate in the case with police, Perley argued.

Supreme Court Judge Dennis Ward, after reviewing the incident report in question, didn’t buy it.

“Those witnesses already know that the prosecution has their names,” he wrote in his Tuesday ruling. “The claim that the publication of their names would increase the likelihood of their lack of cooperation with the prosecution or the court is speculative, at best.”

Ward wrote that if he ruled in Orchard Park’s favor, the public hypothetically could be denied access to every police report that names someone who isn’t a criminal defendant.

“To provide a blanket shield on the disclosure of such documents would eliminate the availability to the public of such information in every case where the name of any witness was included,” Ward wrote. “That would defeat the intent of the FOIL statute. At that point, the exception would swallow the rule.”

Ward ordered Orchard Park to release the records by this coming Sunday.

Investigative Post was represented in the case by Kyle Clauss and Heather Murray of the Cornell Law School First Amendment Clinic. In a statement, Clauss called the ruling “a win for government transparency.”

“Rather than promptly disclosing the record as FOIL required, the Town of Orchard Park fought for months to keep it hidden without any valid basis for doing so,” Clauss said.

“The Erie County Supreme Court recognized that agencies must provide a specific justification for withholding records from public scrutiny, and the Town of Orchard Park failed to meet this burden.”

Perley did not respond to a request for comment.

Ward ordered Orchard Park to release the report by the end of the week. He denied a request to award attorney’s fees to the Cornell Law School. Clauss said he’s considering appealing that part of the ruling.

text:
New York Attorney General Letitia James sued Holiday Inn parent IHG Hotels & Resorts, a Rochester hotel owner and a renovation contractor, on November 19, 2026, alleging that dozens of immigrant workers were forced to work without pay and threatened with deportation while renovating the property.

Workers allegedly endured schedules totaling as many as 112 hours a week and lived with their families in abandoned hotel rooms without heat, electricity, or running water. The state accuses IHG of continuing to benefit from the renovations after its managers learned about the conditions during a June 2024 inspection.

The dispute stems from renovations that began in spring 2023 at a downtown Rochester hotel owned by Nayan Patel and his company, Horizon Edge Hospitality. The property operated under a Holiday Inn franchise agreement that required improvements overseen by IHG.

Attorney Advertising

On June 14, 2024, IHG managers inspected the hotel's seventh floor, photographed the rooms and spoke with workers who said they had gone at least eight months without wages and faced threats of deportation, according to the complaint.

The managers relayed their findings to an IHG regional vice president. Four days later, the executive emailed Patel describing the workers as "squatters" who posed security and reputational risks to the Holiday Inn brand and instructed the owner to remove them.

IHG subsequently offered to restore the hotel's access to its reservation system, extended a deadline for Patel to pay more than $96,000 in overdue fees, and waived over $13,000 in interest. Company officials allegedly failed to investigate the workers' accounts or report them through IHG's internal reporting system.

Under the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act, businesses can face civil liability for knowingly benefiting from ventures they knew or should have known involved forced labor. James is invoking that provision against IHG over its alleged knowledge of the Rochester workers' treatment.

Attorney Advertising

IHG disputes the accusations. In a statement reported by Reuters, the company condemned human trafficking and said the hotel owner and contractor should be held responsible for any violations of the law. It also emphatically denied having knowledge of the serious misconduct alleged in the lawsuit.

Contractor Roman Petrik and his company, Exterior Hotel Improvement, recruited workers from several states and countries, promising hourly wages and housing at the property. Payments allegedly stopped after the first two weeks, although employees continued working long hours to meet renovation deadlines.

One worker who was promised $18 an hour spent approximately 29 weeks working an average of 68 hours per week. State investigators calculated that he should have received about $30,506 but was paid only $2,200.

When workers demanded their wages or stopped working, Petrik allegedly threatened to have them deported. Patel is accused of making similar threats, claiming connections to immigration authorities and warning that workers could be removed from the country without receiving their earnings.

Living conditions deteriorated after workers and their children were moved to the hotel's abandoned seventh floor in September 2023 to accommodate paying guests. Rooms lacked functioning toilets, showers, heating, and electricity, while pests and vermin infested much of the floor. Some workers became ill, and at least three were allegedly evicted after demanding payment.

State investigators also accuse Petrik of repeatedly sexually assaulting a female worker after threatening to withhold her wages unless she complied with his demands. The woman eventually fled the hotel without receiving her pay and became homeless, according to the filing.

Additional claims against Patel, Petrik and their companies involve alleged violations of New York labor and human rights laws, including wage violations, retaliation and sexual harassment.

The Rochester property was rebranded as a Wyndham in January 2025. City officials closed the hotel in June 2026 following fire code and other violations.

text:
Sen. Elissa Slotkin is firing back at the Justice Department for threatening to prosecute her for recent comments she made about the need for congressional oversight.

In a letter to Slotkin publicly shared last week, U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz of Texas wrote that Slotkin’s recent “deterrence message” urging young people to think twice about working for the Trump administration may be “unlawful.” Reitz also told her she could be subject to sanctions and other “significant legal consequences” if she does not preserve all communications relevant to her “intent to weaponize congressional investigations.”

Slotkin, who serves on the Senate’s Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, is among the lawmakers who have made clear their plans to hold the Trump administration accountable for possible misconduct once the party takes control of Congress next year.

She hit back in a letter of her own to Reitz on Wednesday, noting that “in addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility,” and telling Reitz, “Your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

More articles

Slotkin is also one of the six Democratic lawmakers who cited military law in a 90-second video last year, reminding those in the defense and intelligence sectors to “refuse illegal orders” amid President Donald Trump’s deployment of troops to major U.S. cities for crime and immigration enforcement operations.

In the face of continued threats from the Trump administration, the lawmakers doubled down on their message in a press conference Thursday.

“It was important for us to come together a year later to say: number one, we stand behind the video we made. Number two, we won’t be intimidated out of calling out threats to our democracy,” Slotkin said Thursday. “We stand behind our men and women in uniform for the amazing work that they do, and I think we feel strongly that if this is the thing we need to do to stand up for the country we love, we have no problem doing that.”

In response to the video, Trump nicknamed the lawmakers — including Slotkin, Sen. Mark Kelly of Arizona, Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado, Rep. Chris Deluzio and Rep. Chrissy Houlahan of Pennsylvania, and Rep. Maggie Goodlander of New Hampshire — the “Seditious Six” and in social media posts called for their executions.

The fallout from the video was immediate.

Slotkin said she received threatening messages and that her father’s house was swatted shortly before his death. Other lawmakers also spoke about their family’s fear for their safety.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth attempted to censure Kelly, demote his military rank and decrease his pension as punishment for his involvement in the video, which Hegseth argued was “conduct unbecoming an officer and a gentleman.” A federal judge in February blocked the Pentagon’s punishment of Kelly, which Hegseth has appealed.

Trump continues to rail against the lawmakers and the video. As recently as last week, the president again called for their prosecution in a social media post.

text:
TALLAHASSEE, Fla. (WCTV/Gray Florida Capital Bureau) - Florida’s capital city is threatening to end its cooperation with ICE. But state officials have a warning: Becoming a sanctuary city is illegal here.

Florida’s attorney general said a city does not have to sign a 287(g) agreement with ICE, but if one is already signed, like the city of Tallahassee has, backing out could come with consequences.

In the shadow of the state capitol, Tallahassee’s city commission voted 5-0 on Wednesday to consider ending their agreement with ICE, signed by the police chief without the input of the commission.

In response, Florida Governor-elect Byron Donalds said he won’t allow Tallahassee to become a sanctuary city.

Attorney General James Uthmeier echoed that sentiment.

“I’ve heard rumblings that there’s some localities that are looking at their 287 obligations here in Florida. I don’t write the law, I enforce it,” Uthmeier said. “We are always going to be a rule of law state.”

Florida politics:

Uthmeier sent a letter to the City of Doral, saying that if a city tears up an agreement with ICE without “extenuating circumstances,” they “likely” violate the law against becoming a sanctuary city.

“Local governments around the state do have Florida law statutory obligations to engage in best efforts to support the federal government in its mission,” he said.

Florida CFO Blaise Ingoglia said state law enforcement agencies might step in to conduct immigration enforcement in the capital city, like they did during a major raid in 2025.

The chair of Florida’s Republican party posted on social media that Tallahassee’s Democratic commissioners went “too far” and that the reconsideration might “end poorly.”

“And now, they have placed Amendment 3 on us to reduce our budgets, even further straining our budget to have an unfunded mandate to provide federal civil immigration services. I don’t think it’s tenable,” Tallahassee Mayor Jeremy Matlow said.

title: Narratives That Kill: On ICE, Emergency Rooms, and Medical Racism - Literary Hub
description:
It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable.
It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable.
In just one night, ICE amplified the narrative that seeking medical care can cost you the ultimate health penalty: arrest, possible deportation, and separation from your loved ones.
When racism and access to medical care collide, it is not only the actual subpar care that kills people, it is also the narratives that then affect people’s behavior.
Maybe as Senators they can help write a new narrative—one where racism and access to medical care are no longer intertwined, but ripped apart.
text:
On November 7th, ICE agents in Los Angeles took a man in their custody to Adventist Health White Memorial Medical Center in Boyle Heights, a neighborhood which is more than 90 percent Hispanic and Latino.

ICE, the hospital, and local activists dispute much of what happened that day. On social media, some activists alleged that ICE, when not given free rein of the hospital, purposefully retaliated against the community. Regardless of which combination of actions happened and with what intent, three things occurred which no one really disputes.

First, ICE agents blocked access to the Adventist Health White’s Emergency Room for approximately two hours. According to the hospital:

Federal agents brought a person in their custody to our emergency department, and we cared for that patient with dignity and privacy, as we do for every patient. When agents formed a line across our ambulance entrance, which we did not request nor authorize, we diverted ambulances to nearby hospitals for about two hours to ensure every patient received timely care.

“White Memorial,” the hospital spokesperson insisted, “does not participate in immigration enforcement. We know last night frightened our neighbors. No matter what happens outside our doors, everyone who comes inside is our patient, and our focus will only be on that patient, and it will not change.”

Second, around the same time, local residents got word that ICE was at the hospital. As has happened across Southern California, Minneapolis, and around the nation in recent years, rapid response community defense measures kicked in. As Boyle Heights Beat reported, activists on the scene included Abraham Zavala of the group Union del Barrio. Zavala, who was born at Adventist Health White (as were his children), described it as “sacred ground.” At least two protesters, both of whom are U.S. citizens, were then detained by ICE, according to the Boyle Heights Immigration Rights Network.

And third, the intended damage was done: ICE wanted people to be frightened and they are, understandably, frightened. We will never know if any (or how many) people died during those two hours when the ER was not available at Adventist Health White. We will never know if someone’s life will be shortened by months or years because they couldn’t access emergency care that Saturday night. And we certainly won’t ever know who didn’t seek care at all that night because they saw on TikTok or on the local news that ICE had blocked access to their neighborhood hospital.

It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable.

ICE blocking that ER is a very tangible example of how medical racism manifests: armed agents of the state not only threatened to arrest anyone seeking care in the hospital, but they physically blocked access to all medical care in a Latino neighborhood. Such nasty work is rarely done so brazenly, and ICE’s harm that night is just a beginning.

How that harm will manifest is unpredictable. It may make Latinos think twice about getting medical care, or possibly forgo it entirely—especially if their immigration status makes them vulnerable. It may make undocumented family members less likely to accompany their ill relatives to the hospital, resulting in potentially substandard care. If racism is, as Ruth Wilson Gilmore writes, “the state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death,” the seed planted that one night will likely result in medical health disparities and in needlessly premature deaths.

Narratives entwining health and racism are powerful. I grew up not too far from Boyle Heights, in the city of Oxnard, another majority-Mexican American community. The threat of raids and the occupation of a hospital ER will, no doubt, make worse an ongoing problem. Too many children in my hometown are not going to school because their parents fear some member of their family will be abducted en route. When I talk to Latinx medical providers—from a dentist in Oxnard to an eye doctor in Queens, New York—they tell me how empty their once-full calendars have become. Many of their Latinx patients are simply forgoing teeth cleanings or eye exams (or pap smears or mammograms) because the narrative is working: ICE can grab you anywhere, so you better stay put as much as possible. (Similarly, a recently deported gay immigrant told me that when he was cooped up for months avoiding ICE, he stopped taking the HIV-prevention medication PrEP, and then became HIV-positive.) In just one night, ICE amplified the narrative that seeking medical care can cost you the ultimate health penalty: arrest, possible deportation, and separation from your loved ones.

This is not a new situation in America, and it reminds me of a narrative born from the too-short life and tragic death of Dr. Charles Drew. Despite only living about 46 years. Dr. Drew was one of the most accomplished African American physicians in history. The narrative of his death also bloomed in predictable ways.

Like many Black children of my age, I learned about the mythology of Dr. Drew as a child, and was wowed and chilled by the irony of his death.

Prior to enrolling in medical school at McGill in the late 1920s, young Drew had already worked teaching biology and chemistry at the university level. Upon completing his MD, he joined the faculty of Howard Medical School and became a surgeon at Freedman’s Hospital in D.C., where he dedicated himself to the health of Black people. He then pursued a Doctor of Science at Columbia, where he wrote his dissertation, Banked Blood: A Study on Blood Preservation. While blood banks existed, they were not very effective. Medical science and the lay public had long imagined different races of people to have different types of blood. Even though the four major blood types (A,B, AB and O) had been discovered at the turn of the 20th century, many scientists and scientific organizations nonsensically segregated blood by race. Primitive blood banks had been used in World War I, but not knowing what blood type the wounded possessed (“dog tags” didn’t start listing blood type until the 1940s), combined with the crude storage techniques, made shock and infection common, which rendered transfusions of limited use.

Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

In the 1930s, Dr. Drew made a major breakthrough which broadly benefited all of humanity: he discovered how to separate blood plasma from the red and white cells of blood, and how to store it safely in such a way that it could be used for up to two months. Because anyone could be given plasma in an emergency, regardless of their blood type, his findings exponentially increased the life-saving capacity of blood transfusions. He also invented the “bloodmobile,” expanding how donations could be collected. Thus, Dr. Drew became the “father of the modern blood bank,” and the Allied Powers used his techniques to save countless lives in WWII.

Yet, despite his enormous achievements, racism haunted Drew throughout his career and—through the power of narrative—long after his death.

Drew was appointed the first director of the American Red Cross’s blood bank program in 1941. However, when the powers that be insisted that blood from “Negro donors” be rejected unless it was stored separately, he resigned in 1942.

Every year for more than a decade, Dr. Drew would travel to a free clinic in Tuskegee, Alabama, providing free surgery for poor Black people. In 1950, he and three other Black doctors drove more than 700 miles from D.C. to perform this service. On the last night of the clinic, he worked overnight in the operating theater. Then, he got into his car, drove home, and fell asleep at the wheel. After flipping several times, the car crashed in a field.

The other three doctors in the car with him that night suffered minor injuries, but Dr. Drew was in a bad way. And here, many Black children my age likely heard some version of the following myth:

Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and was denied a blood transfusion…even though he had invented the process for using plasma in this way.

Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, and they had his blood type…but the hospital wouldn’t give it to him, because it was “white blood” and they didn’t have any “Negro blood.”

Or, Dr. Drew was taken to the nearest hospital, which was segregated…and they were out of “Negro beds,” and while being transported to a Negro hospital, he died in the ambulance.

In truth, according to the three other doctors who were with him that night, Dr. Drew received immediate and competent care at the nearest hospital. Dr. John Ford, his friend who survived the crash, said Drew’s injuries were so severe that nothing could have saved him.

But the myths were born because they revealed much that was true (in the manner that “myths” are not false stories, but stories which reveal broad truths about history and society). Dr. Drew had been pushed out of the American Red Cross because of the segregation of “Negro blood” (a policy the organization continued until after his death). Black people routinely did die in the Jim Crow south because there weren’t “Negro beds” available, because the best resourced hospitals were segregated, and because of longer ambulance ride times. And Dr. Drew himself was a victim of the “state-sanctioned or extralegal production and exploitation of group-differentiated vulnerability to premature death” at least in part because of racism. Consider that he traveled to Tuskegee (a city synonymous with another horrific instance of medical racism) because there was not sufficient healthcare there for Black Americans, that he had to work all night because of this paucity of care, and that he was forced to drive home exhausted because there were few or no motels for Black people on his segregated driving route.

Narratives play a huge role in revealing fundamental truths, regardless of the exact incident which may incite them. Whether or not individual ICE agents meant to intimidate Latinos on November 7th is irrelevant; care was suppressed and people were made to feel intimidated in ways that will resonate in lethal ways for years to come. Similarly, how exactly Dr. Drew died did not stop African Americans, hearing of the death of the most prominent Black doctor of his time, from understanding that racism played a role in it. When racism and access to medical care collide, it is not only the actual subpar care that kills people, it is also the narratives that then affect people’s behavior. This manifests as the person who doesn’t call 911 because they’re worried the first responder might arrest their undocumented mother. Or the Black person afraid they have a sexually-transmitted infection who doesn’t trust going to a clinic. Or a would-be patient too frightened to approach a hospital because they have good reason to believe they may be made to feel unwelcome (or turned away entirely) if they are transgender, immigrant, or Black.

Narratives are powerful. One I have been suspicious of is the story that the Democratic Party is the anti-ICE party. Many mid-term voters cast their ballots for Democrats seemingly under the belief that ICE was the creation of Republicans while Democrats are the anti-ICE party. (Seeing people place “I Voted” stickers on the death sites of Rene Goode and Alex Pretti seemed especially egregious considering that for decades, Democrats have repeatedly funded the kinds of immigration agents who killed them.)

Then, on election night, I saw the Democratic U.S. Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan promise to “rip ICE apart.”

Godspeed to her and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed. Maybe as Senators they can help write a new narrative—one where racism and access to medical care are no longer intertwined, but ripped apart.

title: AG Letitia James sues former Rochester Holiday Inn, alleging forced labor and trafficking
description:

text:
State authorities claim one of the nation's largest hospitality companies overlooked human trafficking during renovations of a downtown Rochester hotel, allegedly labeling the unpaid workers "squatters" and pledging incentives if the hotel owner evicted them from the property.

New York Attorney General Letitia James is suing Nayan Patel, the former downtown Rochester Holiday Inn owner and operator; its renovation contractor Roman Petrik; and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts. The lawsuit accuses them of knowingly benefiting from what the Attorney General's Office argues was a forced labor scheme involving dozens of immigrant workers.

The lawsuit, filed in state Supreme Court, alleges workers were recruited with promises of hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but went months without pay, worked as many as 112 hours a week, and faced threats of deportation, eviction from the floor they were living on and arrest when they demanded their wages.

The allegations overlap the timeline when the former Holiday Inn on State Street downtown began taking in asylum seekers from New York City. That program brought aid workers into the hotel who learned of the problems and alerted authorities.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans said in a statement that he is appalled by the allegations.

"The City of Rochester engaged these same owners in an attempt to bring that facility up to City Code and ensure the safety of hotel guests and employees – and ultimately forced its closure due to continued concerns," Evans wrote. "We will support Attorney General James as she proceeds with this lawsuit and remain committed to working with the foreclosing mortgage holder to get this important Downtown hotel property in the hands of a new owner."

The city ordered the hotel closed in June, citing multiple fire and building code violations. The building has been tied up in foreclosure proceedings since September.

In an email to WXXI News, a spokesperson from IHG said it condemns trafficking in any form and that the company denies that they had any knowledge of serious misconduct by Patel or Petrik.

WXXI News reached out to Patel and Petrik for comment but did not immediately hear back.

Lawsuit accuses IHG of knowing about workers' conditions

The lawsuit accuses IHG of knowingly benefiting from the alleged exploitation despite being informed of the workers' situations.

IHG required the renovations as a condition of the hotel’s Holiday Inn license. It dictated the scope of the work and conducted periodic inspections, according to the complaint.

During a June 14, 2024, visit, IHG officials inspected the seventh floor where the workers were living, photographed the rooms, and spoke directly with workers who allegedly told them they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in uninhabitable conditions, and had been threatened with deportation, according to the lawsuit.

Four days later, IHG Regional Vice President George Hall allegedly emailed Patel that the people living on the seventh floor, who are described in the email as squatters, posed security and reputational risks to the Holiday Inn brand and that Patel was responsible for removing them, the lawsuit complaint said.

James alleges that IHG made no effort to find out whether the workers had been paid, and that none of the IHG employees involved reported the situation to the company’s own reporting hotline.

The following month, IHG told Patel that it was glad the issue involving "squatters" had been resolved and told him he would need to complete the company’s anti-human trafficking training, according to court filings.

The complaint states that IHG thought it was important for Patel to complete the anti-trafficking training because they were concerned that the workers at the hotel had been subjected to human trafficking.

"IHG did not hire the renovation contractor or its workers, and we did not know they were subject to forced labor as alleged by the Office of the Attorney General," a company spokesperson wrote in an email to WXXI News. "We did not own or operate the hotel and did not manage the construction project."

The spokesperson said the former Holiday Inn was removed from IHG's system in 2024 due to concerns about safety issues, the property's conditions, among other things.

"We never allowed the hotel to reopen to guests, and we terminated its license to operate as a Holiday Inn in January 2025," the email said.

Denied wages, and alleged threats of deportation

The lawsuit complaint alleges workers regularly worked 10- to 13-hour days, six days a week, totaling approximately 60 to 80 hours per week. At times, particularly ahead of IHG inspections and renovation deadlines, workers were required to put in as many as 98 to 112 hours a week.

One worker, promised $18 an hour, worked about 68 hours per week for 29 weeks. He should have received approximately $30,506; but Petrik allegedly paid him just $2,200 over the entire period, according to the Attorney General's Office.

When workers demanded their wages and staged work stoppages between October 2023 and February 2024, Petrik allegedly laughed at them, told them immigration officials were regularly at the hotel and said he could have them deported at any time, according to court filings.

Some workers were unable to purchase food for themselves or their families because they were receiving little to no pay. The lawsuit complaint alleges at least three workers were illegally evicted after seeking their wages.

Workers and families allegedly living in uninhabitable conditions

The lawsuit also alleges that workers and their families, including children, were forced to live in dangerous conditions on the hotel's abandoned seventh floor in September 2023 to make room for paying guests.

The floor, which had been decommissioned since at least 2016; lacked electricity, running water, functioning toilets or showers, and working heating and cooling systems. The rooms had no door locks, and most were infested with pests and vermin, the lawsuit alleges.

Workers and their children spent the winter without heat. Some workers became ill from the living conditions and because of the exposure to construction dust, paint, and extreme cold. Workers were also denied legally required sick leave, the lawsuit alleges.

Irene Sanchez, executive director of Enlace Services Inc., said the organization's outreach team alerted the attorney general's office after workers shared their experiences.

"Our advocates have helped families put food on the table, get medical care, and find other support in the community," Sanchez said. "Workers need to know they can count on that support long after they first speak up. That’s why we urge local agencies to keep their services separate from ICE enforcement. Every worker should feel safe reporting abuse or asking for help without fear of deportation.”

Lawsuit seeks damages, unpaid wages

Petrik, Patel, and their companies are also accused of violating the federal Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act by trafficking workers and obtaining their labor through threats of deportation, eviction, and financial harm.

A worker also claims to have been sexually assaulted, but it is unclear if authorities will pursue criminal charges.

James is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages, and penalties for the workers, as well as repayments for each defendant that was made from their work.

The Trump administration moved Thursday, November 19, 2026, to end its lawsuit challenging Democrat Mary Peltola's victory in Alaska's U.S. Senate race while asking a federal appeals court to VacaturVacatur is a court order setting aside or nullifying an earlier judgment or ruling. An appellate court may consider vacatur when a case becomes moot before appellate review is completed, although vacatur is an equitable remedy and is not automatically granted.Read more → an earlier ruling against the Justice Department.

Federal prosecutors told the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit that the completed election had made their case Mootness DoctrineThe mootness doctrine generally requires courts to stop deciding a case when later events eliminate the live dispute between the parties. If a court can no longer provide meaningful relief, the case may be dismissed as moot.Read more →. The department had sought to delay certification of the results while investigators examined whether voters confused Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan with an independent candidate sharing his name.

Peltola secured more than 50% of first-choice votes in the November 3 election, winning the race without additional rounds of ranked-choice counting. Her victory was confirmed November 17, leaving the Justice Department's proposed investigation unable to affect the outcome.

Attorney Advertising

Prosecutors acknowledged that ballots cast for independent candidate Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. had already been mixed with other votes, preventing investigators from determining whether some voters intended to support the Republican senator.

The department is asking the Ninth Circuit to vacate U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason's November 1 dismissal and return the lawsuit to the district court for dismissal as moot. Gleason had ruled that prosecutors lacked standing because their proposed investigation offered no workable remedy for alleged voter confusion.

The Justice Department sued Alaska on October 22, seeking to block certification if the Republican incumbent lost by a margin smaller than the number of votes cast for Sullivan Jr., a retired teacher from Petersburg. Prosecutors alleged that his candidacy was intended to confuse voters and divert Republican support toward Peltola.

Gleason dismissed the case two days before the election, finding that federal officials had failed to establish how a court could provide the requested relief while protecting Ballot SecrecyBallot secrecy is the principle that a voter's choices on a completed ballot should remain private and should not be traceable back to that individual. Election systems use procedures designed to separate a voter's identity from the voter's selections while still maintaining records showing whether the person participated in the election.Read more →. Alaska officials also opposed the federal challenge, arguing that the Justice Department lacked authority to interfere with the state's certification process.

The League of Women Voters of Alaska and Common Cause, which intervened in the lawsuit, have asked the Ninth Circuit to affirm the dismissal and consider SanctionsSanctions are penalties or other corrective measures a court may impose for violating court rules, disobeying court orders, filing improper claims or papers, abusing the litigation process, or engaging in other prohibited conduct.Read more → against federal attorneys involved in the case. The organizations argue that the government's legal claims lacked a valid basis and that its pursuit of the appeal warrants judicial scrutiny.

President Donald Trump and Sen. Sullivan have accused Democrats of orchestrating the retired teacher's candidacy to split Republican support. Peltola has denied involvement in recruiting Sullivan Jr., who maintains that his campaign was legitimate.

Federal and state investigators continue examining allegations surrounding Sullivan Jr.'s entry into the race, including reported efforts to recruit candidates with names resembling Republican incumbents. The FBI and Alaska Bureau of Investigation are conducting inquiries separate from the civil litigation.

text:
Will Venezuelan TPS Be Restored on November 20?

No automatic reinstatement is scheduled for November 20, 2026.

On November 18, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit extended a temporary stay preventing enforcement of a lower court’s decision that would restore Venezuelan TPS protections.

That stay will remain in place until seven days after the appeals court publishes its judgment, unless another court order changes the situation.

On November 19, the federal government withdrew its latest emergency application to the U.S. Supreme Court following the appeals court’s decision.

Importantly, this withdrawal does not mean TPS has been restored or that the underlying legal dispute has been resolved.

The litigation primarily concerns the termination of Venezuela’s 2023 TPS designation. Venezuela’s separate 2021 designation was also terminated, effective November 7, 2025.

Is Your TPS Work Permit Still Valid?

This was one of the most important questions Carolina raised during our interview.

Some Venezuelans have employment authorization documents displaying expiration dates that differ from the dates on which their TPS protections ended.

However, the expiration date printed on a work permit does not always establish whether that authorization remains valid.

Its validity depends on several factors, including the TPS designation, the employment authorization category, applicable court orders, and official government notices.

Someone who has lost TPS-based employment authorization may still have a valid work permit obtained through another immigration category.

A pending asylum application, however, does not automatically authorize employment. Eligible asylum applicants must obtain employment authorization under the applicable rules.

What If You Have a Pending Asylum Application?

Borja raised a question that affects many families: What happens if you lose TPS but still have an asylum application pending?

A pending asylum application may have important legal consequences, but it is essential to understand what it does—and does not—provide.

Under federal immigration law, a person with a bona fide pending asylum application generally does not accumulate unlawful presence for purposes of the three- and ten-year inadmissibility bars during the qualifying period, provided the statutory conditions are met.

One important exception involves unauthorized employment while the asylum application is pending.

This protection also does not erase unlawful presence that may have accumulated before the asylum application was filed.

A pending asylum application does not automatically grant lawful immigration status.

It also does not guarantee that a person cannot be detained or placed in removal proceedings. The applicable procedures and protections depend on the individual’s circumstances and the status of the asylum case.

What Should Venezuelans Who Lost TPS Do?

My recommendation is to review your immigration situation individually rather than assume that losing TPS eliminates every possible option.

Your prior immigration status, pending applications, employment authorization, and immigration court history may all affect your legal position.

As the litigation continues, it is especially important to follow official court decisions and USCIS announcements instead of relying on rumors or outdated information.

I thank Borja Voces and Carolina Sarassa for inviting me to Noticiero Univision Edición Digital and for giving our community an opportunity to better understand these developments.
