text:
By: Jagan Tamirisa | November 19, 2026

On November 17, 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) published a final rule (Department of Justice, Appellate Procedures for the Board of Immigration Appeals, 91 Fed. Reg. 73876 (Nov. 17, 2026)) introducing significant changes to appeals before the Board of Immigration Appeals (BIA), which reviews certain decisions made by Immigration Judges and immigration authorities.

Effective December 17, 2026, the rule generally reduces the deadline for filing many immigration appeals from 30 days to just 10 calendar days. It also introduces procedures allowing the BIA to dismiss many appeals without issuing a detailed written decision. The changes are intended to reduce the BIA's growing backlog and speed up immigration appeal decisions.

Importantly, the new procedures generally apply to decisions issued on or after December 17, 2026, and do not apply retroactively to appeals involving earlier decisions.

Which Immigration Cases Are Affected?

The new rules primarily affect appeals before the BIA, including Immigration Judge decisions involving removal proceedings, adjustment of status (Form I-485), cancellation of removal, certain immigration waivers, and other immigration relief. The rules do not generally apply to USCIS decisions on H-1B, L-1, O-1, or other nonimmigrant visa petitions, which follow separate administrative appeal procedures. However, individuals holding these visa classifications may be affected if they are placed in removal proceedings and appeal an Immigration Judge's decision to the BIA. Certain asylum appeals and other specified cases are subject to different procedural requirements.

Appeal Deadline Reduced from 30 Days to 10 Days

Previously, individuals generally had 30 days to appeal an Immigration Judge's decision. Under the new rule, many appeals must be filed within just 10 calendar days.

For example, if an Immigration Judge denies a Form I-485 application for adjustment of status (green card) in removal proceedings, the individual generally will have only 10 calendar days to appeal that decision to the BIA, rather than the previous 30 days.

Certain asylum appeals will continue to have a 30-day deadline. However, the shorter deadline applies to some asylum-related decisions, including cases involving certain statutory bars to applying for asylum. The applicable deadline depends on the type of case and the reasons for the Immigration Judge's decision.

BIA May Dismiss Appeals Within 15 Days

Another significant change concerns how the BIA reviews appeals. Under the new rule, the BIA generally will not conduct a full review of every appeal. For most covered cases, further review will occur only if a majority of permanent BIA members votes to consider the appeal. Otherwise, the appeal may be dismissed without a separate, detailed written opinion. These summary dismissals generally must be issued within 15 days after the appeal is filed.

This means an individual may receive a final administrative decision without the opportunity to submit additional written arguments. Certain categories of appeals, including specified custody and detention matters, are excluded from these procedures.

All Appeal Issues Must Be Identified in the Notice of Appeal

Individuals filing an appeal must identify the specific legal or factual issues they are challenging in the Notice of Appeal (Form EOIR-26). For example, if an individual believes that the Immigration Judge incorrectly evaluated evidence, applied the wrong legal standard, or improperly denied immigration relief, those issues must be identified when filing the appeal. Issues not identified in the Notice of Appeal will generally be considered waived, meaning the individual may lose the opportunity to raise them later in the appeal.

Although identifying appeal issues has long been required, the new rule expressly reinforces this requirement. With the shorter filing deadline and expanded dismissal procedures, preparing a complete and accurate Notice of Appeal becomes particularly important.

Changes to Written Arguments and Briefing

When the BIA accepts an appeal for further review, both sides generally have 20 days to submit their written arguments, rather than receiving separate briefing deadlines. Extensions will be limited to exceptional circumstances, and reply briefs generally will not be permitted unless the BIA authorizes additional briefing. Some of these procedural changes were already implemented under the earlier February 2026 interim rule and are retained in the final rule.

Why Is This Rule Being Finalized Now?

DOJ initially introduced these changes through an interim final rule published in February 2026. However, in March 2026, a federal district court set aside several provisions, including the shorter appeal deadline, expanded summary dismissal procedures, and the express waiver requirement for issues omitted from the Notice of Appeal.

Following a public comment period, DOJ issued the November 17 final rule adopting these provisions with certain modifications. DOJ maintains that the final rule addresses the procedural concerns raised in the earlier litigation. However, further court proceedings may affect its implementation.

What Should Individuals Facing Immigration Proceedings Know?

Individuals facing removal proceedings should carefully review the applicable appeal deadlines and seek appropriate legal guidance before an Immigration Judge issues a decision. The shorter filing period may leave very little time to identify legal errors, prepare the Notice of Appeal, and arrange representation.

An unfavorable BIA decision may also make a removal order administratively final. Although federal court review may be available in certain cases, filing a petition for review generally does not automatically prevent removal.

Rochester, N.Y. (WHAM) — New York Attorney General Letitia James has sued the former operators of a downtown Rochester hotel, a renovation contractor and Holiday Inn parent company IHG Hotels & Resorts, alleging dozens of immigrant workers were trafficked and forced to renovate the property without pay.

The lawsuit, filed in Monroe County Supreme Court, alleges workers at the Holiday Inn on State Street were threatened with deportation, eviction and arrest when they demanded payment. It also accuses contractor Roman Petrik of sexually assaulting a worker. The allegations have not been proven in court.

Enlace Services Executive Director Irene Sanchez said the organization began working with the workers in 2024, after its outreach team encountered them while providing case management to migrant families relocated from New York City to the hotel.

“We started spotting them in the service elevators and started engaging with them and inviting them to attend some of our activities and events,” Sanchez said. “And slowly gained their trust. That’s how we identified them and started working with them.”

Sanchez said Enlace alerted the Attorney General’s Office and the Worker Justice Center of New York to the workers' concerns in 2024.

The Attorney General’s Office says workers were promised hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but most stopped receiving pay after their first two weeks. The lawsuit alleges they routinely worked 10- to 13-hour days, six days a week, sometimes logging 98 to 112 hours in a single week ahead of inspections and renovation deadlines.

One worker, promised $18 an hour, worked approximately 68 hours a week for 29 weeks, according to the complaint. The state alleges the worker earned about $30,506 but received just $2,200.

Sanchez said the workers’ families, including children, were also affected. The lawsuit alleges they were housed on the hotel's abandoned seventh floor, which lacked heat, electricity, running water and functioning bathrooms. The floor had been out of service since at least 2016, according to the state.

“It was a large group of workers that was impacted,” Sanchez said. “Workers were talking about families and children also being involved, living in inhumane conditions where nobody should have been living.”

The lawsuit alleges Petrik and hotel owner Nayan Patel threatened workers with immigration enforcement when they demanded wages. At least three workers were also allegedly evicted after seeking payment.

“It was a very scary time for them,” Sanchez said. “They were working so often without pay and in those conditions because they literally had no money to go nowhere else.”

The state further alleges IHG knew workers were being exploited but continued to benefit from the renovation. According to the Attorney General’s Office, IHG managers spoke with workers during a June 2024 visit and were told they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in poor conditions and had been threatened with deportation. **The company allegedly failed to investigate the wage complaints.

Sanchez said Enlace and partner agencies helped relocate workers to safer housing. Many have since found jobs and are receiving health care and mental health support.

“They are being treated with respect and with dignity,” Sanchez said. “Some of them got married, some have children, some are really learning English now. They are being part of the community now.”

The Attorney General’s Office is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages and penalties, along with profits the defendants allegedly earned from the workers' labor. The lawsuit also asks the court to bar Petrik and his company from the renovation business, and Patel and his company from the hotel business in New York.

13WHAM could not reach Petrik or Patel for comment.

Rochester Mayor Malik Evans condemned the alleged treatment of workers and said the city previously sought to address code violations at the property.

The City of Rochester is appalled by the allegations announced today against former operators of the hotel at 70 State St. The lawsuit brought by New York State Attorney General Letitia James brings attention to the scourge of human trafficking, and we applaud the OAG for investigating these serious allegations and bringing justice to victims.

The City of Rochester engaged these same owners in an attempt to bring that facility up to City Code and ensure the safety of hotel guests and employees – and ultimately forced its closure due to continued concerns. We will support Attorney General James as she proceeds with this lawsuit, and remain committed to working with the foreclosing mortgage holder to get this important Downtown hotel property in the hands of a new owner.

Sanchez said Enlace continues to provide free, confidential case management and support services. Workers or members of the public who believe someone may be facing similar circumstances can contact Enlace at 585-566-2559.

title: Broader Boundaries, Greater Risks: California Expands Immigration-Related Retaliation Protections
description:
Employers operating across jurisdictions face an increasingly complex patchwork of requirements affecting immigration enforcement, employment verification, worker protections, and employer communications involving immigration status.
California continues to expand its rules in this area, including through recent legislation addressing workplace immigration enforcement and employee notice requirements.
In addition to those who formally assert rights, the legislation protects individuals who: Make good-faith workplace complaints; Seek information regarding legal compliance; Inform others regarding workplace rights; Encourage others to exercise workplace rights; or Assist another individual in asserting workplace protections.
Protection does not require a formal complaint: asking about workplace rights, assisting a coworker, or seeking compliance information may suffice.
Those actions should be supported by documented business and compliance considerations and should not appear to discourage employees or applicants from exercising workplace rights.
text:
The Reach of Immigration-Related Retaliation Expands: California Amends Labor Code Section 1019

Immigration compliance is increasingly becoming a state-law issue as well as a federal one. Employers operating across jurisdictions face an increasingly complex patchwork of requirements affecting immigration enforcement, employment verification, worker protections, and employer communications involving immigration status.

California continues to expand its rules in this area, including through recent legislation addressing workplace immigration enforcement and employee notice requirements. Effective January 1, 2027, Assembly Bill 2495 (AB 2495) significantly broadens Labor Code Section 1019, expanding the rights protected, individuals covered, and immigration-related conduct that may give rise to liability.

This state legislative activity also comes against a backdrop of increased federal scrutiny of immigration-related recruiting and hiring practices. Recent Department of Justice and Department of Labor activity involving the PERM labor certification program reflects heightened attention to whether recruitment processes provide U.S. workers a genuine opportunity to apply and receive consideration. Although the federal and California legal frameworks address different conduct and protect different interests, together they reinforce the importance of carefully designed and consistently administered recruiting, sponsorship, and employment-verification practices.

The California changes are particularly significant as employers take a closer look at sponsorship requests, foreign-national hiring, work authorization, and workforce planning. Decisions and communications that employers may view primarily as immigration or business matters may increasingly be examined through a retaliation lens under California law.

Expanding the Range of Protected Conduct

Historically, Section 1019 focused largely on rights under the Labor Code or applicable local ordinances. Beginning January 1, 2027, it will cover the exercise or attempted exercise of rights under virtually any federal, state, or local law applicable to employees. Immigration-related conduct connected to wage-and-hour complaints, discrimination concerns, safety complaints, leave requests, accommodations, whistleblower activity, or other statutory rights may therefore give rise to claims.

In addition to those who formally assert rights, the legislation protects individuals who:

Make good-faith workplace complaints;

Seek information regarding legal compliance;

Inform others regarding workplace rights;

Encourage others to exercise workplace rights; or

Assist another individual in asserting workplace protections.

Protection does not require a formal complaint: asking about workplace rights, assisting a coworker, or seeking compliance information may suffice.

A New Focus on Conduct That May “Dissuade” Employees

A significant change is the statute’s focus on conduct that may discourage individuals from exercising workplace rights before any complaint is made. The amended law prohibits conduct related to actual or perceived immigration status that would reasonably tend to dissuade a person from exercising a legal right or induce an action the person has a legal right to decline.

The focus thus extends beyond whether retaliation occurred to whether comments or conduct could reasonably discourage protected activity, creating litigation risk from interactions not previously viewed as actionable.

Although each situation is fact-specific, employers should be mindful of communications such as:1

Referencing an employee’s immigration or visa status during a workplace dispute;

Suggesting that raising concerns could affect future sponsorship opportunities;

Asking unnecessary immigration-status questions unrelated to a legitimate business need;

Making statements that could be interpreted as discouraging employees from reporting workplace concerns; or

Linking work authorization to complaints about wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other protected rights.

Claims may arise even if an employee never files a complaint or exercises the underlying right.

Coverage Now Extends Beyond Current Employees

AB 2495 also expands the definition of “employee” to include:

Applicants;

Current employees; and

Former employees.

Coverage of applicants may affect recruiting and hiring. Liability turns not on actual immigration status but on whether conduct related to actual or perceived status could be viewed as retaliatory or as discouraging the exercise of workplace rights. The law does not prohibit lawful questions about work authorization or future sponsorship needs. Employers generally remain free to decide whether to sponsor employment-based visas and to ask whether applicants are authorized to work in the United States and need sponsorship now or in the future. Those questions, and decisions based on the responses, should be grounded in legitimate business considerations and administered consistently. Employers should also evaluate how sponsorship-related screening interacts with their broader recruiting practices and applicable federal anti-discrimination requirements.

Questions about work authorization and sponsorship, including follow-up questions, should serve a legitimate business purpose, be asked consistently, and avoid statements that could discourage the exercise of workplace rights. Coverage of former employees also extends potential exposure beyond active employment.

Where Employers May Face Increased Exposure

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Employers should continue to follow federal Form I-9 and E-Verify requirements while ensuring that employment-verification practices are applied consistently and are not used, or perceived as being used, in response to protected workplace activity. Requests for additional documentation, unnecessary immigration-status inquiries, or changes in verification practices involving an employee who has raised workplace concerns may receive particular scrutiny.

The potential exposure, however, extends beyond the employment-verification process. Even employers that do not intend to retaliate may face liability arising from routine decisions and conversations about sponsorship, work authorization, immigration status, or compliance.

Areas to review include:

Recruiting channels, application processes, and applicant screening practices;

Layoffs, reductions in force, and workforce restructuring affecting sponsored positions or related occupations;

Questions regarding current work authorization and future sponsorship needs;

Communications regarding sponsorship decisions;

Form I-9 and E-Verify practices;

Internal complaint and investigation procedures;

Manager and supervisor training;

Responses to employee concerns regarding wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other workplace rights; and

Communications involving immigration status, visa sponsorship, or future employment authorization.

As employers reassess sponsorship strategies, recruiting practices, layoffs, hiring priorities, and long-term workforce planning against a changing federal immigration landscape, immigration-related decisions and communications may receive increased scrutiny from multiple directions. Employers generally retain discretion over sponsorship, but discussions should remain tied to legitimate business considerations and separate from workplace complaints or other protected activity.

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Routine employment-eligibility verification, document review, and immigration-status communications may give rise to claims. Actions that appear to single out employees based on actual or perceived immigration status may receive heightened scrutiny, particularly when connected to workplace complaints or disputes.

Section 1019 does not diminish employers’ federal immigration obligations or ability to make lawful hiring and sponsorship decisions. Employers must continue to verify employment authorization, evaluate sponsorship needs, and plan their workforces consistent with business objectives and legal requirements. Those actions should be supported by documented business and compliance considerations and should not appear to discourage employees or applicants from exercising workplace rights.

Significant Penalties Remain Available

The amendments are more than technical. Individuals subjected to an unfair immigration-related practice may already sue under Section 1019 for equitable relief, damages, and available penalties. Existing law authorizes civil penalties of up to $10,000 per employee or person per immigration-related violation. Employers may also face injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees in certain circumstances, and other remedies under California law.

Looking Ahead

Before January 1, 2027, employers should review recruiting practices, sponsorship communications, complaint procedures, manager training, and employment-verification processes to confirm they are applied consistently and serve legitimate business and compliance objectives. Managers, recruiters, talent acquisition teams, and human resources professionals should understand how to discuss immigration-related issues lawfully and recognize that comments about immigration status, sponsorship, or work authorization may receive heightened scrutiny when connected to workplace rights.

Proactive compliance may reduce litigation risk. Given the law’s focus on conduct that may “dissuade” workers from exercising legal rights, employers should review not only formal decisions but also everyday communications during hiring, onboarding, investigations, and employee-relations matters. Because these issues intersect with immigration, employment, and anti-discrimination laws, employers should consider consulting experienced counsel on complex or high-risk situations.

description:
A lawsuit filed by Attorney General Letitia James alleges dozens of immigrant workers were exploited during the renovation of a now closed downtown Rochester hotel.
James alleges the contractor routinely delayed and withheld wages.
The suit also alleges IHG Hotels & Resorts knew about the exploitation but continued to benefit financially from the renovation project.

text:
A lawsuit filed by Attorney General Letitia James alleges dozens of immigrant workers were exploited during the renovation of a now closed downtown Rochester hotel.

The suit, filed against the owners and operators of the former Holiday Inn, the renovation contractor and Holiday Inn's parent company, IHG Hotels & Resorts, claims workers were forced to work up to 112 hours a week, often without being paid. It also alleges they were left to live in dangerous and uninhabitable conditions with no heat, electricity or running water.

James says the contractor allegedly recruited workers from multiple states and countries for the project. According to the suit, workers were promised hourly wages and housing at the hotel, but after their first two weeks, the pay largely stopped. James alleges the contractor routinely delayed and withheld wages.

According to the AG's office, workers who demanded their wages were threatened with deportation, eviction or arrest. One worker was even allegedly sexually assaulted repeatedly by the contractor and he threatened to refuse to pay her if she didn't comply, James' office says.

The suit also alleges IHG Hotels & Resorts knew about the exploitation but continued to benefit financially from the renovation project. James' office says its investigation revealed that IHG Hotels & Resorts visited the site in June 2024, inspected living conditions and spoke with workers who told IHG managers that they had not been paid for at least eight months, were living in intolerable conditions and had been threatened with deportation when they asked for their wages.

After that, Attorney General James says IHG did not follow up to find out whether the workers had been paid, and she alleges none of the IHG employees involved reported the situation to the company’s own reporting hotline.

“A company that calls itself a leader in the fight against human trafficking cannot look away when workers inside its own hotel ask for help,” said James. “These workers came to New York to do an honest job. Instead, they were cheated out of their pay, left without heat through a brutal Rochester winter and threatened with deportation for speaking up. My office will hold each of these defendants accountable and fight to get these workers every dollar they earned.”

AG James says her office is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages and penalties for the workers, as well as requiring the defendants to surrender profits made from the workers' labor. The lawsuit also asks the court to ban the contractor and his company from the renovation business and the hotel owner and his company from the hotel business in New York.

The Rochester Holiday Inn eventually became the Wyndham Rochester Downtown before the city closed the hotel for code violations over the summer this year.

text:
Dozens of protesters gathered outside Ocean Knoll Elementary School Thursday morning where less than 24 hours earlier a mother was taken by immigration enforcement agents after dropping off her kindergartener at school, according to a city official.

Encinitas City Council Member-elect Brad Lefkowits (Dist. 4) said in a Facebook reel multiple immigration enforcement vehicles were parked outside the elementary school where the mother, who has not been named, had just dropped off her child and participated in the school's food drive.

"When that mom left the campus, they followed her, pulled her over, broke her window and arrested her," Lefkowits said in the video. "It's hard to put into words the chaos and fear this puts into our community when this happens."

Lefkowits said inside the abandoned vehicle were photographs of the Ocean Knoll kindergartener as well as the food and target gift card from the drive.

The Encinitas Union School District confirmed the arrest near its elementary school and said in a statement district personnel were working with the family to provide support.

"The presence of immigration enforcement officers near our schools creates fear and uncertainty for many of our families. It is unacceptable that they are being confronted with the fear of immigration enforcement while simply trying to get their children to school," A statement from EUSD said, in part.

Local

NBC San Diego has reached out to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security regarding the incident and has not yet heard back.

Incidents near schools over the last few months have urged local political and school leaders to demand change from federal authorities.

The San Diego Unified School District this week penned a letter to DHS after a Fay Elementary third grader was detained by ICE at an immigration appointment. The letter demanded an end to family separations, enforcement near schools, and several other policy changes to "prevent this trauma from ever happening again."

The boy was held for weeks and ultimately taken to a facility in Texas. He has since been released to family in San Diego.

The OUSD meanwhile said its had to expand its immigration support services because at least 20 families have been impacted by immigration enforcement efforts.

"Our families are telling us that there is a lot of fear right now in our communities," OUSD board member Nancy Lincona said. "We serve families as they come forward and so we're constantly identifying new families that need support as they reach out for help."

title: Body camera footage shows how police responded when ICE called for help in North Long Beach
description:
When neighbors surrounded ICE agents who’d injured a man in North Long Beach last month, local police cleared the roadway to help them leave, newly released body camera video shows.
The Long Beach Post has repeatedly requested all relevant body camera footage and 911 audio from that Oct. 17 confrontation, but the LBPD has refused to release most of it.
The body camera footage released by Long Beach police Thursday provides a fuller view of the aftermath but does not show officers’ initial arrival on scene.
The officer wearing the body camera even says in the footage he was delayed in activating it.
In a statement, LBPD Chief Wally Hebeish said he decided to authorize the release of footage from this one body camera.
text:
When neighbors surrounded ICE agents who’d injured a man in North Long Beach last month, local police cleared the roadway to help them leave, newly released body camera video shows. It was the quickest way to safely diffuse the tense situation, according to the Long Beach Police Department, even as some neighbors accused officers of helping immigration officials, something they are banned from doing in most cases.

The 17-minute video shows LBPD officers at a chaotic scene where neighbors are yelling angrily at ICE agents and blocking agents’ cars, including one vehicle holding a person they said was wrongfully detained.

Police begin clearing cars and people out of the streets so ICE agents can leave before an LBPD officer says a supervisor has ordered officers to leave the scene.

“We’re being ordered to pull out, so you guys are going to be on your own,” the LBPD officer wearing the body camera tells an ICE agent. “I’m sure you’re used to it. Good luck.”

When asked about why officers were ordered to leave, LBPD spokesperson Allison Gallagher said they departed “once there was no longer a public safety need.”

The footage shows only a portion of what happened and from a single perspective.

The Long Beach Post has repeatedly requested all relevant body camera footage and 911 audio from that Oct. 17 confrontation, but the LBPD has refused to release most of it.

Neighbors who spoke to the Post gave a broader perspective. They said several ICE vehicles had been parked in the neighborhood since the early morning.

That afternoon, a U.S. citizen named Ricardo Gonzalez was riding an e-bike near Elm Avenue and 56th Street when an agent jumped out of an unmarked car and took him to the ground, according to four residents who spoke to the Post.

Surveillance video showed the agents’ vehicle veering toward Gonzalez, but it’s unclear if they hit him. Neighbors said agents tased Gonzalez twice, and one agent knelt on his back while Gonzalez yelled in pain and said his arm was broken.

Neighbors said agents also detained two women during the ensuing confrontation, but they were ultimately freed before agents left.

An ICE spokesperson said Gonzalez was among a group of “anti-ICE agitators” who tried to “impede operations, threaten officers, and damage government vehicles.”

The spokesperson said agents took Gonzalez into custody after he “smashed the mirror of a government vehicle.” They said agents did not hit him with their vehicle.

Residents began confronting federal agents while Gonzalez was handcuffed on the ground. Cell phone video of that confrontation quickly went viral.

The body camera footage released by Long Beach police Thursday provides a fuller view of the aftermath but does not show officers’ initial arrival on scene.

The officer wearing the body camera even says in the footage he was delayed in activating it.

In a statement, police said officers showed up because ICE agents made an emergency call for help to the city’s communications center “due to vehicle vandalism taking place and a subject in need of medical attention.”

Gonzalez was bleeding on the ground when police arrived, according to the LBPD, and officers drove him to a nearby fire station so he could be taken to the hospital.

Officers also tried “to de-escalate the situation and keep the peace by directing everyone to clear the area.”

In the body camera footage, one LBPD officer walks up and down the street ordering drivers to move their cars to clear an exit for the unmarked federal vehicles.

He tells drivers, “We’re trying to de-escalate” and asks one driver to “help me help out.”

While he’s doing this, one driver asks him, “What about you cooperating with ICE? Because that’s what you’re doing.”

The officer responds by saying she can move her car or have it towed.

Near the end of the video, another neighbor yells at the officer while he’s walking by.

“This is our neighborhood. Our kids live here. What are you going to do to protect that?” she asks.

The Long Beach Police Department emphasized that officers did not participate in any immigration enforcement and quickly got medical help for Gonzalez.

“The officers prioritized de-escalating the situation and keeping the peace, which included clearing the street so that ICE agents could leave the area,” Gallagher said.

When some of the ICE agents followed police to a private parking lot at the police station, they were told to leave, LBPD said.

The video’s release comes more than a month after the incident, which grabbed national headlines and sparked calls for a federal investigation from Long Beach’s mayor and congressional representatives.

LBPD initially completely denied the Post’s request for a release of all relevant body camera footage and 911 audio, claiming the department was not required to release them because the video and audio were collected as part of an investigation.

In a statement, LBPD Chief Wally Hebeish said he decided to authorize the release of footage from this one body camera. He said it showed officers “complied with local and state law and acted in accordance with department policy.”

A public records expert disagrees with police’s justification for keeping secret other evidence of what happened that day.

David Loy, a lawyer for the First Amendment Coalition, said the LBPD was not legally justified in withholding any footage or audio.

The investigatory exemption of the California Public Records Act does not apply because LBPD was not investigating a crime that day, Loy said.

“Police departments do many things that are not about investigating crimes,” Loy said. “It’s not enough to simply say police officers responded and therefore they were automatically investigating a crime.”

text:
Eva Yi Xie GS, a third-year Ph.D. student in neuroscience, has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at an airport near Washington, D.C. She is believed to be held in a detention center in Chantilly, Va. Xie is the first known Princeton student to be reported to be detained by ICE.

“The University has arranged for legal counsel to represent the student,” University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss wrote in a statement to The Daily Princetonian Thursday night.

The Society for Neuroscience annual conference was held in Washington, D.C., from Saturday through Wednesday. Xie presented a poster at the conference on Wednesday titled “Entorhinal grid-like coding generalizes to jointly organize physical and cognitive dimensions.”

Xie is a member of the Brody Lab. She is advised by neuroscience professor Carlos Brody and coadvised by neuroscience professor Nathaniel Daw and computer science professor Benjamin Eysenbach.

“It seems wildly unfair,” Brody wrote in a statement to the ‘Prince.’ “Eva is a brilliant law-abiding student and wonderful person who has many talents to contribute to the United States. Detaining her, with the intent of deporting her, makes no sense whatsoever. It is cruel, and it is our country shooting itself in the foot.”

Dean of the Graduate School Rodney Priestley emailed graduate students in the Princeton Neuroscience Institute about the incident at 11:01 p.m. Thursday evening.

“We hope she is able to soon resume her studies at Princeton,” the email, obtained by The Daily Princetonian, read. “Please be assured that we will stay in close contact with the student’s family, her legal team, and her PNI colleagues as this situation is resolved.”

Wynne Stagnaro GS, a fellow PNI graduate student in the Brody Lab, shared specifics of the incident in a message on the Graduate Student Government Slack. According to Stagnaro, Xie sent a “call for help” to her lab mates via Slack Thursday afternoon. The lab mates have since lost contact with her.

“Eva is a brilliant computational and experimental systems neuroscientist. She is also a valued colleague, mentor, and friend, and we are privileged that she chose our lab for her thesis research,” Stagnaro wrote in her message. “She went to a conference to present her work, and now she’s in a detention center. She should be home.”

An X post from the Brody Lab shared similar sentiments.

Stagnaro shared that members of the Brody Lab have been in touch with the office of Sen. Andy Kim, D-N.J., other elected officials, and members of the media. Stagnaro did not add anything beyond the Slack post in a statement to the ‘Prince.’

text:
HOUSTON – The Texas Attorney General’s Office has renewed its April lawsuit against the City of Houston after Mayor John Whitmire implemented an executive order changing how Houston Police Department (HPD) officers interact with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

“I took the bold step, the legal step to implement an executive order, which is working,” Whitmire said.

The executive order states HPD will no longer contact ICE during a routine traffic stop, doing so only when someone commits a crime that requires jail time.

Council members push for permanent ordinance

Shortly afterward, three council members moved to make the order more permanent by introducing it as a city ordinance: Alejandra Salinas of at-large Position 4, Edward Pollard of District J and Tiffany Thomas of District F. City Attorney Arturo Michel said the proposed ordinance conflicts with state law.

“I’m just fulfilling my duties to pass on the lawfulness of an ordinance,” Michel said. “The way the ordinance is written is unlawful.”

Some council members say the fight is worth taking on.

“I think the real risk is being able to stand up for Houstonians and make this law, because we know the legal system will be on our side,” Thomas said.

Mayor stands by executive order

Michel said risks exist with the executive order as well, though he is not required by law to approve its legality — something he said Whitmire understands. At the same time, Whitmire said he sees no need for an ordinance to reinforce his order.

“What is broken with my executive order? It went into immediate effect. I used the most expeditious plan to use HPD to go after the worst of the worst,” Whitmire said.

Thomas said the community’s voice is clear on the issue.

“Houstonians have already said they want to separate ICE’s involvement from our local law enforcement,” Thomas said.

WASHINGTON – A federal judge said on Wednesday that the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency “made a mockery of court orders” in Colorado and that the court found government officials in contempt for instantly re-arresting a man whom the judge had ordered released.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to take any further action because she said the officials had “cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue” as sworn by an official in court.

“ICE’s new ‘policy’ of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release,” the judge wrote, according to court records in the U.S. District Court for the District of Colorado.

At least 18 people in Colorado have been held in detention longer than they should have been or have been re-arrested within minutes of their judge-ordered release in the past six weeks, CPR News, the news division of Colorado Public Radio, reported.

The report said that immigration attorneys estimated the number may be higher given that some immigrants represented themselves.

ICE, which ​is part of ​the Department of Homeland Security, has been ⁠the face of Republican President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free ​speech and due process rights.

Human rights groups also say ​the ⁠crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

The Trump administration has maintained that its actions aim to improve domestic security and are in compliance with the law. ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment on what the judge said on Wednesday.

⁠Democrats, ​who won majorities in both chambers of ​Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for ​its immigration policies.

Attorneys in the South Bay fear criminal justice may take a hit with people too afraid to show up to court due to an increased presence in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents.

In the name of justice, La Raza Lawyers Association, a powerful attorneys group, called Thursday for an end to ICE enforcement around the Hall of Justice and neighboring Santa Clara County Main Jail in San Jose. The association is made up of prosecutors, public defenders and private attorneys in Santa Clara County.

"The way that they framed the Constitution, everyone has access to justice, everyone has a right to due process," La Raza Lawyers Association President Felipe Romero said.

Fear ramped up last week after David Oyer, a deputy public defender, was pepper-sprayed by ICE. Video footage of the incident showed ICE agents arresting a man just steps from the Hall of Justice. Oyer, who said he just happened to be walking by at the time, recorded the arrest. Then he got pepper-sprayed.

"I am OK," Oyer said. "A little shaken up mentally, but physically OK."

Oyer filed a police report, claiming the ICE agents assaulted him. At the same time, Oyer said he fears the agents also assaulted the criminal justice system. Some clients have told Oyer that they’re now too afraid to show up to court.

"That’s certainly something I worry about," Oyer said. "It's something I’ve heard from clients. I'd imagine it’s happening as well with the victims and witnesses of crimes."

Some prosecutors shared the same concerns.

"It could be potentially pretty detrimental in terms of prosecuting cases, but more specifically, it's detrimental to the community because then they can’t seek that justice," Romero said.

In a statement to NBC Bay Area about the pepper-spray incident, the Department of Homeland Security said the man they were detaining had a history of drug possession and delivering drug paraphernalia.

"During the incident, approximately eight agitators obstructed their path…After the agitators began physically assaulting officers, officers relied on their training to deescalate the attack," the statement read.

Texas officials face blowback from Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin after signaling they plan to limit local law enforcement cooperation with Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

In a Nov. 18 statement to Fox News, Mullin argued that ICE operations in the state have been successful and said that if Texas cities and officials stopped cooperating with ICE, it "would be one of the worst derelictions of duty we’ve seen in a very long time."

"We are calling on Governor-elect (Gina) Hinojosa and other leaders throughout the state to continue cooperating with us. If they do not, then crime and violence will plague the Lone Star State, and innocent Americans will suffer as more sanctuary politicians put illegal alien criminals over their own constituents," he wrote.

The statement comes as Democrats are set to take control of several statewide offices starting in January, ending Republicans' control. Democrats will also control the state House, while Republicans will maintain the Senate majority.

It also comes at a time when ICE operations in the state have faced both public and elected officials' scrutiny following two shootings — one in Austin in September and another in Houston in July

Here is what Texas officials are saying about allowing local law enforcement to cooperate with ICE.

Hinojosa to scrutinize Texas' collaboration with ICE

In an interview with The Texas Tribune published on Nov. 18, incoming Democratic Gov.-Elect Hinojosa responded to a question asking whether she should rescind outgoing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott's executive order allowing state agencies to help federal immigration officers investigate, arrest and detain unauthorized migrants.

"What ICE is doing is making us less safe. We should not facilitate that. So I’d have to read the specifics of that executive order, but I do not think we should be facilitating the chaos that ICE has wrought in Texas. That is something that we’ll make sure to do what we can to stop that," she told the Tribune.

Houston mayor orders police to limit work with ICE

Democratic Houston Mayor John Whitmire told The New York Times days after the midterm elections that he was directing local police to limit their cooperation with ICE by not alerting the agency to an unauthorized migrant during traffic stops or in connection with other low-level infractions.

Instead, officers would alert ICE only when they arrested someone and brought them to, or the person had already arrived at, a county jail.

Texas sees 2 ICE officer-involved shootings in 2026

Texas has seen two officer-involved shootings involving ICE agents in 2026 — one in Houston and another in Austin.

Houston fatal July ICE-involved shooting

On July 7, Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, 52, was driving a white van in Houston on July 7 when ICE agents pursued the vehicle, USA TODAY reported.

ICE agents said they were conducting a targeted enforcement operation and that Salgado Araujo attempted to evade arrest, with federal officials saying he rammed an ICE vehicle, refused commands, and used his vehicle in an attempt to hit an officer.

The agency said that the shooting happened after Salgado tried "to run over" an agent who was trying to detain Salgado Araujo. He was taken to a hospital, where he died.

Austin September ICE-involved shooting

An ICE officer shot and injured Wilber Rafael Garces Perez, 28, in North Austin on Sept. 20, USA TODAY reported.

The incident happened in the middle of a DoorDash delivery Garces Perez was trying to complete after ICE agents pulled him over after they saw him leaving a restaurant and identified him as having a final order of removal.

The agents then instructed Garces Perez to put the car in park and step out, but "he ignored the request and engaged in a conversation in Spanish about moving the car and parking it," the federal complaint alleges.

Garces Perez then drove off, allegedly striking one of the officers in the torso with the driver’s side-view mirror.

During a brief vehicle chase, Garces Perez allegedly attempted to hit an officer with his car, and the officer fired into the vehicle's back right window, striking Garces Perez in his upper back, according to the complaint.

text:
Back in January, Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) announced two deaths at Camp East Montana, the nation’s biggest immigrant detention center. At the time, the facility at Fort Bliss in El Paso, Texas, was operated by a tiny contractor most people had never heard of.

The agency reported that Geraldo Lunas Campos, a 55-year-old from Cuba, had been found “in distress” and died after “lifesaving measures.” Victor Manuel Diaz, a 36-year-old from Nicaragua, had been found with “a ligature around his neck”—likely suicide.

ICE, it turns out, didn’t share the full story. By the end of January, a medical examiner had determined that Lunas Campos actually died by homicide—guards asphyxiated him while restraining him to stop him from self-harm. Now, records obtained in a Freedom of Information Act request show that ICE privately blamed its contractor for failing to stop Diaz’s death—so much so, that the agency cited it as one of multiple reasons for ending the company’s roughly $1.3 billion contract.

The records are communications between ICE and the contractor, Acquisition Logistics, a small Virginia-based company that went from relative obscurity to the subject of national headlines after the Trump administration asked it to build and manage Camp East Montana in 2025. At the time, it had no prior experience in incarceration and was so small it operated out of a single-family home. Archived screenshots of its website—whose header simply said “Site maintenance in progress”—showed it had once specialized in supply chain management.

When ICE ended its contract in March, a year and a half early, the agency didn’t elaborate publicly on the reason, simply saying a bigger company would possess the “size, maturity and pedigree” to implement “higher standards of medical care, more thorough case processing and intake procedures, and delivery of performance requirements according to well-defined accountability measures.” The records Mother Jones obtained include “Contract Discrepancy Reports” and other documents that outline, in more detail, exactly what standards were not met—and the deadly consequences.

Acquisition Logistics’ relationship with ICE soured quickly, the records show. In the beginning, its main point of contact for Camp East Montana was not the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), but the Pentagon: Even though the camp would detain immigrants, the Navy had awarded the contract. “It’s weird,” Charles Tiefer, a professor emeritus of government contracting at the University of Baltimore law school, told me at the time.

“It seems messy,” added Claire Trickler-McNulty, who served as an ICE official in the Obama, Biden, and first Trump administrations.

As I reported then, DHS had tried to award the contract before the Navy did, to a firm called Deployed Resources, but canceled the deal days later “for convenience,” according to a government website that cited an executive order about “wasteful spending.”

This was an extremely unusual move, and some current and former ICE officials speculated that ­Deployed lost the job for political reasons. The Washington Free Beacon reported in 2023 that Deployed had snagged no-bid contracts for immigrant detention under President Joe Biden, and that a member of its board was married to the former chief of staff for Kamala Harris’ husband, Doug Emhoff. (The DC Enquirer called it “Kamala’s cronyism.”) A DHS spokesperson dismissed this as speculation, saying the contract was canceled due to an “inability to meet the specialized needs of the facility.”

Not long after ditching Deployed, ICE put the Fort Bliss contract out for bids again, and then quickly pulled it a second time, without explanation. The job went to Acquisition Logistics in the summer of 2025 under a Navy special contracting program in which only small businesses could apply. “If you want a detention center run by people who know what they’re doing, you hold serious competition, but that takes time,” Tiefer, the contracting expert, told me. “This is the third time they’re trying to make a procurement, and they’re under the gun—gotta get those detention centers up and running, gotta meet the quota. They were just betting [Acquisition Logistics] would have the minimum competence to hold the thing together, join in picking the subcontractors, and supervise them.”

It was “an absolute rush,” says Congresswoman Veronica Escobar, an El Paso Democrat whose district includes the camp. “Donald Trump and Stephen Miller wanted to do it the easiest, quickest way possible.”

Things went about as smoothly as one might expect. Although Camp East Montana was up and running in impressive time—ground broke in July 2025 and new detainees were arriving by August—a worker died during construction and, by September, journalists were documenting horrific conditions inside. ICE’s own inspectors found 60 violations of federal detention standards in 50 days, the Washington Post reported. “That was somewhat shocking,” recalls Michelle Brané, who led the Biden administration’s Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, the main oversight body for ICE detention.

It’s not unusual for a new detention facility to have problems, so the best practice is to open it slowly—but that didn’t happen here, says former ICE official Trickler-McNulty, who has worked on contracts and detention standards. “None of it sounds like good governance,” she told me.

In October 2025, after Camp East Montana was operational, the administration transferred oversight of Acquisition Logistics’ contract from the Pentagon to ICE, according to emails I obtained. Later that month, an ICE contracting officer wrote CEO Ken Wagner to say that the funding wasn’t officially locked in yet, but that the company should proceed anyway because the work was “mission-essential.”

Wagner agreed, but by November 2025, emails show that his firm was desperate for cash. (Many federal contractors have struggled to be reimbursed promptly on Trump’s watch, according to Brané.) “As a small business, ALC and subs cannot continue to perform at such a high risk. Payrolls have to be met, vendors have to be paid, and it really is a crisis situation,” a company rep wrote to ICE.

Some funding came through soon after, but the relationship remained strained. On December 11, Wagner explained in a letter that ICE’s communications with his team had been “ineffective and, at times, perceived as threatening.”

“This has created an environment of uncertainty, hindered productive dialogue, and is creating significant concerns between ALC and our subcontractors,” he wrote. With discussions “eroding,” Wagner added, he was seeking “assistance in resetting our relationship to move forward in a more productive fashion.”

He provided excerpts from the allegedly threatening communications—all redacted in the documents I received. But other records show that ICE had expressed concerns over Acquisition Logistics’ lapse of liability insurance, a detainee’s escape, and problems with medical care. The agency had even sent a “Show Cause Notice” to the company in early October, days after taking control of the contract. “[Y]ou are hereby provided the opportunity to present any facts or explanations that demonstrate why the contract should not be terminated,” an ICE officer had written.

It had been complicated, Wagner said in his letter, for his company to transition from Pentagon to DHS control and navigate the agencies’ different expectations. He remained worried about a “lack of payment 75 days into the Option Period,” which posed “unnecessary and significant risks” to his business.

“Despite our repeated efforts to seek clarification and guidance, ALC has not received a government response to our concerns, leading to resource inefficiencies in our operations,” Wagner wrote. He requested a meeting with ICE officials to discuss solutions and figure out how to stop “de-railing productive hours” to messy back-and-forth.

Little seemed to improve. In February, an ICE contracting officer sent Acquisition Logistics another “Show Cause Notice” threatening to end the partnership. The CEO likely understood what this meant, Tiefer told me: “He can hear they’re clicking the rifle bolts on the firing squad. He’s writing his will at this point.”

The camp’s security protocols were not up to standard either, ICE said. In January, an officer’s firearm had gone missing, along with the spare key to the locker where it was stored. Transportation delays resulted “in significant operational disruptions” and janitorial services were inadequate. Housing units were supposed to be cleaned daily by staff, but an inspection found they were cleaned only once a week—and that guards had, on occasion, convinced detainees to clean for them by offering cookies.

Some of these allegations appeared in a Government Accountability Office report over the summer and received media coverage, but the records I obtained from ICE went into greater detail.

For one, in February, subcontractor Amentum Services “unilaterally” decided to cut detainees’ food intake below the contractual minimum of 3,000 calories a day. This deprivation resulted in “active hunger strikes” and “threats of riots,” ICE wrote. (Neither Amentum nor Acquisition Logistics and ICE responded to requests for comment for this story.)

Another subcontractor, Akima, let its guards track daily operations at the facility in a damaged logbook with missing pages—which became a problem, ICE wrote, after Geraldo Lunas Campos died. A witness told the Associated Press that Lunas Campos was handcuffed, tackled by guards, and put in a chokehold until he went unconscious. ICE’s report offered new details: Lunas Campos was restrained on the ground by four officers after he’d tried to hang himself, it said. One officer placed an arm around the man’s neck and another around his armpits with clasped hands, and all four officers were on top of him. When they eventually turned Lunas Campos on his side, he was unresponsive, with vomit on the floor.

“Lack of timely and complete information regarding the destruction of the logbook impeded the [Detainee Death Review] panel’s ability to establish an accurate timeline and conduct a thorough review,” ICE wrote, and also to assess officers’ compliance with use-of-force standards.

Lunas Campos’ family is suing Acquisition Logistics, Akima, and the guards for wrongful death, according to an attorney representing them, Will Horowitz, who told me it’s unclear whether the incident was adequately investigated by the government. “There’s so little that has been said in public about this.”

Another serious allegation involved the case of Victor Manuel Diaz, who was shipped to Camp East Montana after ICE arrested him on January 6 in Minnesota.

Eight days later, ICE wrote in its notice to Acquisition Logistics, custody officers moved Diaz from his dormitory to a medical holding room after he said he’d experienced harassment and “possible sexual abuse”—a detail that hadn’t been publicly reported, according to Rep. Escobar. (ICE has only cited the alleged harassment.) Diaz was scheduled for a Prison Rape Elimination Act interview. A behavioral health provider wrote that he had a “disheveled appearance, depressed mood, flat affect, and low, quiet speech,” though he’d denied that he was contemplating suicide.

ICE’s detention standards require placing at-risk detainees in suicide-resistant cells with “constant or close monitoring”—specifically, at irregular intervals no more than 15 minutes apart. But Diaz was put in a holding room with less frequent monitoring “despite risk indicators,” the agency wrote. He was observed awake at 2 p.m. and asleep at 2:30 p.m. and 3 p.m., the log indicated. Half an hour later staff found him hanging from a sheet he’d removed from his bed.

Staffers took Diaz’s body down and placed it on the bed. Failing to find a pulse, camp medical personnel began CPR and other emergency measures. He was officially pronounced dead at 4:09. Although the “medical response was initiated promptly after discovery,” ICE noted, “the timeline indicates a possible delay in recognizing the emergency and notifying ICE”—and CPR should not have been performed on a soft surface like the bed. “The incident suggests a lack of staff vigilance and possible gaps in suicide prevention training, as staff failed to identify and respond to risk factors and did not maintain required observation protocols.”

ICE wrote that it had reviewed several cases of suicidal detainees at Camp East Montana in which officers hadn’t checked in at staggered 15-minute intervals as required—this problem has plagued ICE detention under past administrations as well, Brané told me. “Detainees on suicide watch are being placed in cells that contain objects and elements that can be used for self-harm,” ICE officials wrote, citing metal benches in holding cells, pony walls around toilets, and instruments affixed to the walls of medical bays.

Camp East Montana, the officials noted, also lacked policies to safely remove a person from suicide watch—one detainee, name redacted, was taken off watch despite suicidal ideation and a plan to act on it. And though detainees are supposed to receive mental health screening within 12 hours of admission, at least one wasn’t screened for about a month, despite indications of mental illness, the agency wrote.

Months before Diaz’s death, ICE also had raised concerns with Acquisition Logistics because the facility’s medical holding rooms lacked “vision panel doors” that would allow officials to monitor the people inside; the company had promised to install the panels but hadn’t. The “failure to promptly address a previously identified and documented security deficiency,” its notice said, “represents a significant lapse in corrective action and facility safety management, and is a material contributing factor in the inability to prevent or timely intervene in the suicide of Mr. Diaz.”

“This incident resulted in the loss of life and exposes the facility, staff, and detainees to increased risk,” ICE added.

“This was a known screw-up,” Tiefer says of the vision panel doors. It seems “the suicide was the straw that broke the camel’s back and led ICE to dump Acquisition Logistics.”

Diaz had entered the United States in 2024 and was working to send money home to his family in Nicaragua, to help them save for a house. “Victor was law-abiding. He had never been in trouble in Nicaragua and, as we understand, was detained by ICE for missing an immigration court date—not for any crime,” his family said in a statement after his death.

In late February, 24 members of Congress wrote to DHS, citing safety concerns and calling for Camp East Montana to be “shut down.” On March 3, ICE sent another notice of “non-conforming performance” that again highlighted Diaz’s death and the infrequent cleaning of housing units, along with a detainee’s escape in October. Ten days later, it announced publiclythat the contract would be terminated and that Amentum, the subcontractor that had cut meals to less than 3,000 calories, would take over. Amentum was a much bigger firm, with a long history of federal contracting. But conditions at the facility remained dire afterward, according to a lawsuit against ICE that cites, among other problems, medical neglect, staff violence, and inadequate food.

ICE apparently wasn’t “seeking a huge change if they just signed a contract with a vendor that was already running parts of the facility they were ostensibly unhappy with,” says Trickler-McNulty, the former ICE official, when I asked about the inadequate meals. But the administration “wants this facility; they likely didn’t want disruption in detention services, so they signed the agreement.”

Brané views the contract swap as a sign of just how bad conditions had become under Acquisition Logistics: worse than even ICE could tolerate. But “it’s probably gotten just as bad at a lot of facilities,” she says, noting that DHS shut down the independent oversight office she used to lead. “We are hearing more and more of these kinds of things, and there is no place to file a complaint and have it addressed, and so conditions have deteriorated across the board.”

Rep. Escobar told me she is glad Acquisition Logistics was fired and that she wants the company to be investigated. But she says it’s not the only entity that should be held accountable. For months, detainees had told her about poor conditions, but the career ICE personnel working at the facility brushed her off. They were “saying, ‘It’s all a lie,’ and it wasn’t,” she says. “They know better. There should have been alarm bells screaming up and down the chain.”

The administration should have forced Acquisition Logistics to address deficiencies immediately—or fired the company quicker, she says. Normally, Trickler-McNulty adds, ICE would use financial sanctions to hold a company accountable for problems early on, but the records we obtained show no signs of that. “There’s blame to be laid not just at the contractor’s feet,” Escobar says. “We have an obligation in Congress to look at the enablers.”

text:
Government is moving to restore approximately 2 400 bad and hijacked buildings across South Africa’s major metros by fast-tracking court litigation, developing a national funding model for temporary emergency accommodation and establishing a uniform national reporting framework.

During an Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Migration media briefing on Thursday, committee chairperson and Minister of Justice and Constitutional Development, Mmamoloko Kubayi, set out government’s plan to tackle the challenge of derelict and overtaken buildings.

“The IMC [has] tasked the Department of Cooperative Governance (DCOG) to lead the development of a phased Program of Action for eight metros, supported by a multi-sectoral National Technical Task Team to undertake this important work.

“The Committee recognises that enforcement must be accompanied by lawful processes and appropriate arrangements for affected occupants.

“Government will not allow unsafe buildings, criminal property syndicates and regulatory failures to continue undermining the safety, dignity and stability of our communities,” Kubayi stated.

She reiterated government’s prioritisation of tackling “bad, unsafe and hijacked buildings, which present serious risks to public safety, undermine municipal governance and, in some instances, provide opportunities for criminal activities”.

Enforcing business compliance

Alongside urban renewal, Kubayi reiterated that all spaza shops and small businesses must adhere strictly to municipal by-laws, licensing rules, health standards and labour and immigration laws, regardless of the owner's nationality.

“Government remains committed to restoring compliance, fairness and accountability within the informal economy, particularly in relation to spaza shops and other small businesses,” she emphasised.

As such, coordinated interventions involving municipalities, the Department of Small Business Development, the Department of Employment and Labour and law-enforcement agencies are central to the programme of strengthening regulation of the informal economy.

The objective of the programme is to:

Strengthen business registration and regulatory compliance.

Prevent unlawful business practices and exploitation.

Protect consumers and promote food safety.

Ensure compliance with labour and immigration legislation.

Support legitimate small enterprises and fair economic participation.

“In this regard, the Department of Small Business Development has finalised the process of recruiting 56 Business Registration Officers (BROs) for deployment across all Provinces by mid-November 2026.

“The informal economy cannot operate outside the law. Government is determined to ensure that business opportunities are pursued within a properly regulated environment that protects consumers, workers and legitimate businesses,” Kubayi said.

Strengthening cooperation

Kubayi stated that migration challenges cannot be “resolved through enforcement measures alone”.

She highlighted that for migration challenges to be resolved, cooperation is required from government, communities, business, labour, civil society, traditional leaders and international partners.

“Government continues engaging stakeholders to address concerns, promote social cohesion and strengthen understanding of immigration laws and procedures. These engagements are essential to preventing misinformation, reducing tensions and encouraging lawful participation in resolving migration-related challenges.

“Internationally, the Department of International Relations and Cooperation, working with Home Affairs and other departments, continues strengthening cooperation with countries of origin and regional partners,” Kubayi said.

Areas of cooperation include:

Identification and documentation of foreign nationals.

Deportation and voluntary repatriation arrangements.

Information-sharing and border management.

Combating transnational organised crime and human trafficking.

Promoting safe, orderly and regular migration.

Protecting diplomatic relations and regional stability.

Kubayi highlighted that the Southern African Development Community (SADC) has resolved to convene a multi-sectoral Regional Dialogue on Migration Governance in Southern Africa envisaged to take place early next year.

“South Africa welcomes this important regional initiative and looks forward to participating in the Dialogue, which will provide an opportunity for Member States to exchange perspectives, assess progress and strengthen cooperation on migration governance across the region.

“The Regional Dialogue is expected to assess progress in the implementation of existing regional policy and legal frameworks governing migration, particularly the SADC Regional Migration Policy Framework and Action Plan (2022–2030).

“Particular attention will be given to strengthening coordination and implementation of existing instruments addressing refugee protection, asylum, trafficking in persons and border management, with a view to advancing a more coherent and coordinated regional approach to migration governance,” the Minister said.

Kubayi emphasised that migration management cannot be addressed through “fragmented interventions, sporadic enforcement or unlawful community action”.

“Government will continue acting decisively against violations of immigration legislation, criminal exploitation of migration systems and conduct that threatens public safety.

“At the same time, all interventions will remain firmly anchored in the Constitution, the rule of law and respect for human dignity.

text:
WASHINGTON – U.S. Senate Democratic Whip Dick Durbin (D-IL), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee, today led the release of the Government Accountability Office’s (GAO) newly-completed report examining the cost of immigration detention under the Trump Administration’s U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) entitled, “ICE Should Determine Cost Effectiveness of New Initiatives Before Continuing”.

ICE received $45 billion in immigration detention funding in July 2025 through Republicans’ One Big Beautiful Bill Act. According to GAO’s report: “In addition to maintaining existing facilities with these funds, ICE began implementing an initiative to buy and renovate a collection of warehouses to use as new detention facilities. However, after acquiring 11 warehouses for about $1.07 billion, ICE scaled down the initiative significantly and plans to sell seven of them. In July and August 2026, ICE also bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion total. However, the scope, time frames, and estimated costs for further acquisitions remain undetermined. In addition, ICE did not update its spending plan for detention funding to reflect the shifting status of the warehouse initiative or other planned acquisitions, as required by its internal guidance. As a result, the spending plan includes an inflated estimate of planned obligations, which affects oversight efforts and ICE’s ability to assess long-term budget needs.”

“This report has uncovered more of what we’ve come to expect from the Trump Administration—rushed and wasteful spending of taxpayer dollars without any benefit to the American people. Remember when Donald Trump promised to get rid of ‘waste, fraud, and abuse’? Well, GAO continues to expose a shocking pattern of waste within the Administration’s unconscionable mass deportation campaign,” said Durbin. “The midterm elections showed that the American people are sick and tired of the Trump Administration’s cruel immigration tactics. It is time to hold DHS and ICE responsible.”

GAO’s key findings include:

Warehouses bought, then abandoned. From January to March 2026, ICE bought 11 warehouses for about $1.07 billion. It paid at least 50 percent above assessed tax value for nine of them and at least double for seven. After DHS paused the initiative, the DHS Secretary testified that the department “had not conducted appropriate due diligence and planning.” ICE now plans to sell seven of the properties, and GAO warns the sales could lose the government money.

$2.2 billion more in facility purchases, with no expected savings. In July and August 2026, ICE bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion. ICE officials told GAO they do not expect these purchases to save money because the goal is to keep operating where ICE faces pushback from state governments. ICE is considering buying up to seven more but gave GAO no timeline or cost estimates.

Paying for empty beds. ICE has committed to pay for 46,688 beds at 64 facilities whether or not they are used. From October 2025 to April 2026, an average of 9,733 of those beds sat empty each day. At just four facilities, GAO estimates ICE paid about $13 million a month for empty beds.

Guantánamo Bay at more than $110 million. ICE and the Department of Defense obligated about $111 million for immigration detention at Guantánamo Bay, where the average daily population was fewer than 30. ICE officials told GAO that cost did not factor into the decision and that conserving costs is not a goal there.

An outdated, inflated spending plan. As of June 2026, ICE’s spending plan still projected about $38 billion in fiscal year 2026 obligations. Through July, ICE had obligated $9.1 billion. GAO called it unrealistic that ICE would obligate another $29 billion in two months.

Overstretched oversight staff. The staff who validate facility invoices are short-handed, with 55 of 87 positions vacant while the number of detention facilities roughly doubled.

A copy of the GAO report can be found here.

text:
The U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts has issued a preliminary injunction and a stay prohibiting U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from enforcing or applying its new interpretation of the requirements for designated school officials (DSOs) to authorize Curricular Practical Training (CPT). ICE announced the interpretation in Student and Exchange Visitor Program (SEVP) Broadcast Messages issued on August 12 and August 24, 2026.

Background

The Broadcast Messages told DSOs that CPT may be authorized only where the training is an integral part of an established curriculum. They also suggested that CPT tied to optional or elective coursework may not qualify, and many schools paused new authorizations in response. On October 5, 2026, several higher education associations challenged the Messages in Association of American Universities v. DHS, Case No. 26-cv-14520 (D. Mass.). They alleged that the Messages violate the Administrative Procedure Act.

The Court’s Order

The preliminary injunction and stay bar ICE from enforcing or applying the new interpretation. The relief is interim: It remains in place while the case continues, and the order may be appealed or modified.

What This Means for Students, Schools, and Employers

F-1 students: Students whose CPT was paused or denied may be able to seek authorization again, subject to school policy. CPT still requires DSO authorization, an updated Form I-20, and a SEVIS update before work begins.

Schools and DSOs: DSOs should not apply the new interpretation while the order is in effect. We expect schools to issue their own guidance on resuming CPT.

Employers: Employers hosting F-1 interns or student employees may see start dates restored or delayed, depending on how quickly schools respond.

Conclusion

The court’s order is a significant, but temporary, development for F-1 students, schools, and employers that rely on CPT. Because the injunction and stay are interim and may be appealed or modified, affected parties should confirm CPT eligibility with the school’s DSO before relying on the ruling. Clark Hill will continue to monitor the case and will report on any further developments.
