title: Corey Ruiz: After the No-Charge Decision, What Legal Paths Remain in - Kohen Avocats
description:
Wisconsin also regulates how deaths caused by officers are investigated, and that statute gives families a concrete document to obtain.
Under subsection (5)(a), the investigators must provide a complete report to the district attorney of the county where the death occurred.
Wisconsin gives the district attorney the primary charging power, but not an exclusive one.
Officers may also raise qualified immunity; in Mendez the district court relied on it in the alternative, and in Biegert the court found no constitutional violation and did not reach it.
Our earlier guide on what Wisconsin law says about a family’s claims after a homicide investigation explains how these wrongful-death rules work when no criminal trial will occur.
text:
The district attorney’s November 19, 2026 decision is a public document, and it is the starting point for any next step. It describes the office’s function narrowly: “The role of the District Attorney’s Office is limited to a review of the facts to determine whether further investigation is merited and, after all available evidence is obtained, whether criminal charges could be merited for any individual who has survived the incident.” It lists the evidence reviewed as officer statements, scene diagrams, video from squad cameras, citizens’ phones and evidence collection, and it adds: “There were no body worn cameras utilized in this incident.” Its conclusion reads: “I conclude it was reasonable for the officer to use deadly force when this person resisted officers, produced a knife, and was not affected by multiple attempts to use Tasers while officers attempted to take him into custody.” The release records that the office decided on Thursday, November 19, 2026, that there is no potential criminal court liability for the City of Madison police officers involved in the July 22, 2026, shooting incident at the intersection of S. Baldwin Street and Williamson Street.

The legal test the release applies is Wisconsin’s self-defense and defense-of-others privilege, which it reproduces verbatim. Under Wis. Stat. § 939.48, a person may use force to prevent or terminate what the person reasonably believes to be an unlawful interference, but “The actor may not intentionally use force which is intended or likely to cause death or great bodily harm unless the actor reasonably believes that such force is necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily harm to himself or herself.” Subsection (4) extends the same privilege to the defense of a third person. In the release, the district attorney states that the law “applies equally to members of law enforcement and to those who are not,” and that “Responding to that threat with deadly force is permitted under the law.” For anyone reading the decision, the useful exercise is to separate three layers: the facts the release says the evidence shows, the statute it applies, and the conclusion it draws. A later reviewer, whether a judge or a civil court, will look at the same three layers but with different rules about who carries the burden.

That burden matters. In criminal cases the prosecutor must be able to prove the offense, and the § 939.48 privilege, where it applies, is a defense to criminal liability. The Wisconsin Supreme Court has described the charging standard in these terms: “A district attorney generally should not bring a charge unless he or she believes the evidence can sustain a finding of guilt beyond a reasonable doubt.” A decision not to charge is therefore not a finding that nothing wrong happened in any legal sense; it is a judgment that a criminal case could not be sustained under the criminal standard and the criminal privilege. Civil claims, discussed in Part II, use a different framework.

Wisconsin also regulates how deaths caused by officers are investigated, and that statute gives families a concrete document to obtain. Wis. Stat. § 175.47 requires each law enforcement agency to have a written policy calling for an investigation by at least two investigators, neither of whom is employed by an agency that employs an officer involved in the death. Under subsection (5)(a), the investigators must provide a complete report to the district attorney of the county where the death occurred. Subsection (5)(b) then governs what happens after a decision like the one announced on November 19: “If the district attorney determines there is no basis to prosecute the law enforcement officer involved in the officer-involved death,” the investigators must release the report, except that they “shall, before releasing the report, delete any information that would not be subject to disclosure” under the state public records law. The district attorney’s release confirms that the Division of Criminal Investigation conducted the investigation in this case.

In practice, the released report is the document that allows anyone to test the summary in a charging decision. A careful review compares the report’s timeline with the press release, identifies every video source it mentions, notes which witness statements were taken and when, and lists any redactions. The statute does not make the report complete in every respect, because it authorizes deletions, but it does require release once the prosecutor finds no basis to prosecute. A family that later decides to pursue either a judicial review of the charging decision or a civil claim will need that report, and it is usually the first record to request.

Wisconsin gives the district attorney the primary charging power, but not an exclusive one. Under Wis. Stat. § 968.02, a complaint charging a person with an offense “shall be issued only by a district attorney of the county where the crime is alleged to have been committed,” except as otherwise provided in the section. Subsection (3) supplies the exception: “If a district attorney refuses or is unavailable to issue a complaint, a circuit judge may permit the filing of a complaint, if the judge finds there is probable cause to believe that the person to be charged has committed an offense after conducting a hearing.” If the district attorney has refused, he or she must be informed of the hearing and may attend, and “The hearing shall be ex parte without the right of cross-examination.” The statute therefore asks a judge two questions, refusal and probable cause, and then leaves the final step to judicial discretion through the word “may.”

The Wisconsin Supreme Court explained this procedure in State ex rel. Kalal v. Circuit Court for Dane County, 2004 WI 58, decided by the Wisconsin Supreme Court on May 25, 2004, in a case that also arose in Dane County. A Madison attorney had reported an alleged theft of retirement funds by her former employer to the Madison Police Department and to the district attorney; after the office told her that she “was free to proceed legally in whatever manner she believed necessary,” a circuit judge found a refusal and probable cause, permitted the complaint, and ordered a special prosecutor at the deputy district attorney’s request. The Supreme Court held that a refusal “can be open and explicit, as in a statement to that effect, or it can be indirect and inferred,” while “inaction alone will ordinarily not support an inference of a refusal to prosecute.” It described the procedure as one that “operates as a limited check upon the district attorney’s charging power and by its terms may be invoked only when a complainant can demonstrate that the district attorney has in fact refused to charge, or is unavailable to do so.” It also held that the person named in the proposed complaint has no right to be heard at the ex parte hearing or to seek reconsideration, although that person may later challenge the complaint in circuit court like any other defendant. Applied to a written, public no-charge decision, Kalal means the refusal element is likely to be satisfied by the announcement itself, so the real questions become whether a judge finds probable cause and chooses to exercise the discretion the statute confers.

Kalal is still part of the court’s working vocabulary. In Wisconsin Elections Commission v. LeMahieu, 2025 WI 4, decided by the Supreme Court of Wisconsin on February 7, 2025, the unanimous majority opinion quoted Kalal, 2004 WI 58, for the rule that statutory language is given its common, ordinary, and accepted meaning when it interpreted a state election statute. That recent citation concerns Kalal’s method of reading statutes rather than § 968.02(3) itself, and a citation search is not a complete citator, so anyone relying on the refusal analysis should begin with the current text of the statute quoted above.

The second route is the John Doe proceeding in Wis. Stat. § 968.26. For this section, the definition of “crime” expressly includes “Any conduct that is prohibited by state law and punishable by fine or imprisonment or both if the individual who allegedly participated in the conduct was a law enforcement officer,” provided the officer was engaged in official duties at the time. The procedure begins with a private complaint to a judge: “If a person who is not a district attorney complains to a judge that he or she has reason to believe that a crime has been committed within the judge’s jurisdiction, the judge shall refer the complaint to the district attorney,” or to another prosecutor if the complaint may relate to the district attorney’s own conduct. The district attorney “shall, within 90 days of receiving the referral, issue charges or refuse to issue charges.” A refusal triggers a duty to forward the law enforcement reports, the office’s records and case files, and a written explanation of the refusal to the judge, who then decides whether a proceeding is necessary.

If the judge convenes a proceeding, the statute requires the judge to subpoena and examine under oath the complainant and the witnesses the judge considers necessary, and to weigh the credibility of testimony on both sides. At the end, “the judge may issue a criminal complaint if the judge finds sufficient credible evidence to warrant a prosecution of the complaint.” The statute limits the proceeding to six months from the day the district attorney forwards the files and explanation, unless a majority of the chief judges of the judicial administrative districts find good cause for an extension, with each judge’s vote made public. Secrecy orders are possible only on the district attorney’s showing of good cause and bind only listed participants. Compared with § 968.02(3), the John Doe route is slower and more formal, but it gives a judge investigative tools, including sworn testimony, and it ends with a decision on a written record.

Several practical checks follow from these two statutes. A complaint or petition should state facts, not conclusions, because the John Doe statute speaks of “reason to believe that a crime has been committed” and § 968.02(3) speaks of probable cause. It should identify the specific Wisconsin offense alleged and address the privilege in § 939.48, since a judge will ask why the privilege would not apply on the evidence. It should rely on the record the statutes make available, beginning with the § 175.47 report. And it should anticipate the next stage: even if a judge permits a complaint, the case proceeds like any prosecution, the defendant may challenge the complaint, and in Kalal the court noted the appointment of a special prosecutor. Neither procedure guarantees charges, and both leave the outcome to a judge’s discretion.

Federal law adds a separate criminal statute. Under 18 U.S.C. § 242, “Whoever, under color of any law, statute, ordinance, regulation, or custom, willfully subjects any person in any State” to the deprivation of federal rights commits a federal crime, and the statute provides for imprisonment for any term of years or for life, or a death sentence, “if death results from the acts committed in violation of this section.” The statute requires that the deprivation be willful, and the decision whether to bring such a case belongs to federal prosecutors. As Kalal recalls in discussing prosecutors generally, “the decision whether or not to prosecute, and what charge to file or bring before a grand jury, generally rests entirely in his discretion.” A state no-charge decision is made by a county prosecutor applying Wisconsin law; it does not apply this federal statute.

The principal civil remedy for unconstitutional police force is 42 U.S.C. § 1983, which makes liable “Every person who, under color of any statute, ordinance, regulation, custom, or usage, of any State” deprives a person of rights “secured by the Constitution and laws.” In a fatal case, the claim is brought for the person who died: in Barnes and in Biegert, both discussed below, the mother of the deceased sued on behalf of the estate. The constitutional question is not whether a crime could be proven but whether the force was objectively reasonable under the Fourth Amendment, and the plaintiff, not a prosecutor, decides whether to file. Readers who want a parallel example involving federal agents can compare our guide on what a federal shooting claim must prove after a charge was dismissed.

The governing framework comes from Barnes v. Felix, No. 23-1239 (May 15, 2025), now reported at 605 U.S. 73, decided unanimously by the Supreme Court of the United States on May 15, 2025. A Texas officer had stopped Ashtian Barnes for suspected toll violations; when the car began to move, the officer jumped onto its doorsill and fired two shots, and the lower courts examined only the two seconds before the shooting under the Fifth Circuit’s moment-of-threat rule. The Court rejected that rule. It held that deadly force violates the Fourth Amendment when it is not objectively reasonable, that the totality-of-the-circumstances inquiry has no time limit, and that “earlier facts and circumstances may bear on how a reasonable officer would have understood and responded to later ones.” In its words, “A court deciding a use-of-force case cannot review the totality of the circumstances if it has put on chronological blinders.” The direct consequence for a family weighing a claim is that the whole encounter, from the first call to the final shot, is part of the record a federal court must weigh, so evidence about every stage matters. The Court expressly declined to decide whether, or how, an officer’s own creation of a dangerous situation factors into the analysis.

The Seventh Circuit, which hears appeals from the federal courts in Wisconsin, has already applied Barnes. In Mendez v. City of Chicago, No. 24-3110 (7th Cir. December 3, 2025), decided by the United States Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit on December 3, 2025, officers responding to a gunshot alert chased a man on foot; he fell, got up, and turned with an object in his hand, and an officer fired three times, leaving him paralyzed. The court affirmed summary judgment for the defense, finding probable cause to believe he posed a threat of serious physical harm under the totality of the circumstances, citing Barnes. The body-camera video was too unclear to show a gun being pointed, but the court explained that “a video can be unclear for one purpose and clear for another,” and that “video evidence enjoys no special status in law by virtue of being video evidence.” It also held that the related Illinois battery claim fell with the Fourth Amendment claim. The practical lesson for a family is that every recording, whether squad, surveillance or bystander video, should be obtained early and reviewed in detail, because a court will ask what each recording clearly shows and what it leaves open.

On a struggle that turns into a knife threat, the Seventh Circuit’s reference case is Estate of Biegert v. Molitor, 968 F.3d 693 (7th Cir. 2020), decided July 31, 2020, on appeal from the Eastern District of Wisconsin. Green Bay officers performing a welfare check tried to pat down Joseph Biegert; a struggle followed, fists, Tasers and a baton failed to restrain him, and he armed himself with a kitchen knife and stabbed one officer before both officers fired. His estate argued that the officers created the danger by failing to plan, failing to secure a knife block and questioning him aggressively. The court affirmed summary judgment for the officers: “Even if the defendants’ actions exacerbated the danger, Biegert’s actions were an intervening cause of the deadly force.” It cautioned that “Having a weapon is not the same thing as threatening to use a weapon,” and it stressed that the officers had escalated force step by step. In Mendez, decided December 3, 2025, the Seventh Circuit cited Biegert again for the rule that deadly force is not constitutionally unreasonable when an officer has probable cause to believe a suspect poses a threat of serious physical harm. Because Barnes left open whether an officer’s own creation of danger counts, a family arguing that a pursuit or takedown created the danger should expect the defense to rely on Biegert, and should build the factual record that distinguishes it.

These decisions show how civil cases are usually won or lost: at summary judgment, on the evidence. In Biegert the estate’s theory of a pause in the shooting rested on garbled dash-camera audio, and the court held that a factual dispute is not genuine when the supporting evidence does not rise above speculation or conjecture. In Mendez the court relied on what the video clearly showed, while acknowledging what it did not. Officers may also raise qualified immunity; in Mendez the district court relied on it in the alternative, and in Biegert the court found no constitutional violation and did not reach it. A family’s early work therefore consists of locating every recording, every witness and every forensic finding, and of reading them against the full timeline that Barnes requires a court to consider.

State-law claims against a city and its officers are governed by Wis. Stat. § 893.80, which sets conditions that are easy to miss. No action may be brought or maintained against a governmental subdivision or its officers for acts in their official capacity unless “Within 120 days after the happening of the event giving rise to the claim, written notice of the circumstances of the claim signed by the party, agent or attorney is served” on the entity and on the officer. The statute measures that period from the event itself, not from any later charging decision. It contains a safety valve: “Failure to give the requisite notice shall not bar action on the claim if the fire company, corporation, subdivision or agency had actual notice of the claim” and the claimant shows that the delay or failure has not prejudiced the defendants. A separate itemized claim must then be presented and disallowed; failure to disallow within 120 days counts as a disallowance, and no action may be brought more than six months after service of a notice of disallowance.

The same section limits what state-law tort claims can achieve. Subsection (3) caps the amount recoverable in tort actions covered by the section at $50,000 and bars punitive damages in such actions, and subsection (4) provides that no suit may be brought against the governmental subdivision itself for the intentional torts of its officers or employees. Subsection (5) adds that when another statute provides rights or remedies for injury, damage or death, that statute applies and the subsection (3) limits do not. Anyone assessing a state claim after a police shooting should map each theory against these subsections before relying on it, because they can narrow both the defendants and the recovery.

Federal law changes that picture for the civil-rights claim. In Felder v. Casey, 487 U.S. 131 (1988), a man allegedly beaten by Milwaukee police officers sued in a Wisconsin court under § 1983 nine months after the incident, and the Wisconsin Supreme Court ordered dismissal for failure to comply with the notice-of-claim statute. On June 22, 1988, the Supreme Court of the United States reversed, holding that Wisconsin’s notice requirements are pre-empted when a § 1983 action is brought in a state court, because the statute conflicts in purpose and effect with the federal remedy and would make outcomes depend on the choice of court. The Court noted that the Wisconsin Supreme Court had already held the statute’s damages limits pre-empted in federal civil rights actions, and it agreed with the near-unanimous view of lower federal courts that notice-of-claim provisions do not apply to § 1983 actions in federal court. It also recalled its instruction that federal courts in § 1983 cases borrow the state-law limitations period for personal-injury claims, which means the limitations question for a federal claim must be answered under Wisconsin law with current Wisconsin authority; this article does not compute it.

The Supreme Court reaffirmed that principle in Williams v. Reed, No. 23-191 (February 21, 2025), decided by the Supreme Court of the United States on February 21, 2025, by a 5-4 vote. Unemployed Alabama workers had sued in state court under § 1983 over delays in processing their benefit claims, and the Alabama Supreme Court dismissed because they had not exhausted the state administrative process. The Court reversed, quoting Felder for the rule that “a state law that immunizes government conduct otherwise subject to suit under §1983 is preempted, even where the federal civil rights litigation takes place in state court.” It held that state courts may not deny such claims on failure-to-exhaust grounds where the state rule “in effect immunizes state officials from §1983 claims challenging delays in the administrative process,” and it described its holding as narrow. For a Wisconsin family, the application is that Wisconsin’s notice-of-claim conditions cannot be enforced against a federal civil-rights claim, while the state-law claims remain subject to every requirement of § 893.80, including the 120-day notice.

Wisconsin’s wrongful-death statute supplies the state-law framework for a death claim. Under Wis. Stat. § 895.04, “An action for wrongful death may be brought by the personal representative of the deceased person or by the person to whom the amount recovered belongs,” and the statute sets the order in which a spouse or domestic partner, lineal heirs and siblings receive the recovery. Subsection (4) caps damages for loss of society and companionship at $350,000 per occurrence for a deceased adult, and settlements involving surviving minor children are void unless a court approves them. Under Wis. Stat. § 893.54, an action “to recover damages for death caused by the wrongful act, neglect or default of another” must be commenced within three years or be barred, with a two-year period when the death arises from a motor vehicle accident. Our earlier guide on what Wisconsin law says about a family’s claims after a homicide investigation explains how these wrongful-death rules work when no criminal trial will occur.

Putting these pieces together produces a short list of checks for any family in a comparable position. First, calendar the § 893.80 notice period from the date of the event and decide promptly whether to serve a notice for the state-law claims, while remembering that Felder removes that condition for the federal claim. Second, request the investigation report that § 175.47 requires to be released after a no-charge decision, and compare it with the prosecutor’s summary. Third, identify every recording the summary mentions, such as squad cameras, surveillance cameras and phones, and ask whether any recording was not mentioned; Mendez shows how much depends on what a video clearly shows. Fourth, have someone appointed to act for the estate, since § 895.04 and the federal cases both proceed through a representative. Fifth, decide whether a request to a judge under § 968.02(3) or a John Doe petition under § 968.26 fits the evidence, recognizing that both are discretionary and that a civil claim can proceed regardless of how either turns out.

One more distinction helps readers keep the timelines straight. For the criminal-review procedures in Part I, the statutes discussed here set a 90-day referral window and a six-month limit once a John Doe proceeding begins; they do not address other time limits, which should be checked separately. The civil timelines are different: the 120-day notice for state claims runs from the event, the itemized claim has its own disallowance and six-month suit periods, the wrongful-death action has a three-year period under § 893.54, and the federal claim borrows a state limitations period that should be confirmed for the specific claim. Mixing these timelines is the most common way a valid claim is lost.

name: Human Rights
title: USA: cruelty towards migrants challenged at the ballot box - CIVICUS LENS
description:
The Trump administration’s cruelty towards migrants is intentional and performative.
Its policies have a silencing effect, making migrants less visible and more afraid to take part in public life.
ICE is also targeting Chinese dissidents who came to the USA to escape authoritarianism, believing they’d be safe in a democracy.
Under Trump, the USA has selectively withdrawn from global bodies it sees as going against its interests or that might hold it to account.
Migrants’ rights groups have challenged third-country deportations in court.
text:
The humbling of Donald Trump’s Republican Party in the midterm elections offers a rare moment of hope in a grim year for the many migrants and refugees who’ve sought a safe home in the USA.

A slew of progressive politicians promising fairer treatment of migrants and refugees have won seats. Polls suggest Latinx and Asian American voters swung sharply towards the Democrats compared to 2024, with violent raids to capture migrants by militarised Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers likely a factor. After his party’s defeat, Trump conceded his deportation policy ‘might be too tough’ and said he was prepared to strike a deal with Democrats to allow more undocumented migrants to stay.

This acknowledgement offers an opportunity to push for changes to an intentionally cruel anti-migrant regime and bring justice for the many victims of abuses, among them the eight-year-old Haitian boy in San Diego, California, whom armed officials snatched from his uncle at an immigration appointment earlier this month, reportedly putting him in restraints before detaining him for 11 days. But whether Trump, more unpredictable than ever, will moderate his anti-migrant policies in practice remains to be seen. His decision to promote Stephen Miller, the architect of the policies, to White House Chief of Staff casts doubt on his post-election comments.

Intentional cruelty

In two separate incidents in July, ICE agents shot dead Colombian man Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine, and Mexican man Lorenzo Salgado Araujo in Houston, Texas. In October in New York, ICE agents shot and wounded Oscar Bengal as he sat in his car with his five-year-old child. A few days later in Texas, an ICE vehicle ran over Miguel Parra-Hernández, causing serious injuries.

These weren’t isolated incidents. Immigration raids are routinely violent and form part of a broader pattern of abuse. Authorities have detained record numbers of people in crowded and dangerous conditions. Detainees face fast-track proceedings designed to thwart immigration lawyers and speed up deportations, including of severely ill people and children who came to the USA without parents or guardians.

Courts are a key line of defence, but the Trump administration is rigging the system, firing many immigration judges and replacing them with others more likely to deny asylum and order deportations. In April, for example, it fired two immigration judges after they ruled in favour of two university students facing deportation for protesting in solidarity with Palestine. Even when people secure their release from detention, they risk ICE immediately detaining them again.

The US government has also closed off accountability routes. In May, it shut down the Office of the Immigration Detention Ombudsman, an independent office within the Department of Homeland Security that heard complaints about treatment in detention. Civil society groups are pursuing legal action.

The Trump administration’s cruelty towards migrants is intentional and performative. It wants to look tough because, until recently, it was convinced this played well with its supporters. It also believes its harshness will have a deterrent effect, discouraging people from coming to the USA and encouraging some already there to remove themselves, an approach it calls ‘self-deportation’. Its policies have a silencing effect, making migrants less visible and more afraid to take part in public life. The result is that some will stay away from services such as education and healthcare, work informally and avoid joining protests or speaking out online.

The Trump administration makes one exception. It claims white Afrikaner people from South Africa are experiencing race-based discrimination from their government, picking up on racist claims spread by Elon Musk that a ‘white genocide’ is taking place. For the fiscal year that ended in September, the government accepted 16,292 refugees. Apart from five from Afghanistan, all were white South Africans. It plans to accept more in the current fiscal year and is considering an ad campaign to encourage more white South Africans to apply. In a world scarred by conflicts, violent state repression and accelerating climate breakdown, these are the people it chooses to prioritise. This is what white supremacism looks like in practice.

No safe return

The conservative-dominated Supreme Court continues to remove protections. In June, it ruled that the administration could strip temporary protected status from Haitians and Syrians living legally in the USA, who until then had been safe from deportation. Some 360,000 people could be returned to countries the US government considers so dangerous it warns its citizens not to travel to them. Last year the court did the same for over 300,000 Venezuelans.

A group of Afghans, including relatives of people who worked with US forces and are at risk of being killed by the Taliban, is now threatened with deportation to Afghanistan. Court documents recently unsealed due to a lawsuit reveal that the government held secret talks with Iran, a country it’s at war with, on potentially deporting Iranians via another country. Those returned to Iran would be at risk of execution.

ICE is also targeting Chinese dissidents who came to the USA to escape authoritarianism, believing they’d be safe in a democracy. In September, ICE also detained Nicaraguan journalist Luis Galeano, stripped of citizenship by his country’s authoritarian regime in 2023, holding him for 12 days before releasing him on bail. Just months before, the government had imposed sanctions on over 100 Nicaraguan officials and called the country’s leadership an ‘enemy of humanity’.

Deportation deals

Third-country deportations have become the cornerstone of the administration’s architecture of cruelty. The USA pays governments to receive people who have no connection with their countries. It has bussed some 20,000 people to Mexico and sent around 5,000 people to other countries, including people who’ve lived most of their lives in the USA. Deportees report not being told where they’re going and being sent to countries where they don’t understand the language.

Striking these deals has become a leading foreign policy goal. Leveraging its global economic and political power, the USA has reached agreements with a reported 35 governments. They include more countries the US government deems too dangerous for its citizens, such as the Central African Republic and South Sudan, and others experiencing conflict, such as the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The list includes El Salvador, whose mass incarceration programme holds people in appalling conditions. Many of the countries have scant respect for basic freedoms. Burundi, Equatorial Guinea and Eswatini all have closed civic space, which means deportees will struggle to speak out about their conditions, and there are also few safeguards against US funding fuelling corruption.

The US government claims it’s deporting people with criminal records, but many have no such history. It also claims it’s meeting its legal obligation not to return people to countries where they’re likely to face persecution. But there is no control over where people end up, as receiving countries are free to deport people onwards to countries where they face grave danger. Those deported include Iranian protesters and LGBTQI+ people from African countries where their identity is criminalised. In May, United Nations (UN) human rights experts appealed to the government of Equatorial Guinea to stop its plans to return deportees to home countries where they face state violence.

The US government has earmarked at least US$410 million for these deals. Around US$81 million of the funding is for receiving governments, and they also gain political capital, since the USA is unlikely to criticise their human rights records. Other sweeteners may come as part of the package, such as the five-year healthcare cooperation programme the US government agreed last December with Eswatini, an absolute monarchy. Having destroyed its international aid programme, the Trump administration is making clear that whatever funding it still provides is there to serve its interests.

Most of the rest of the funding is going to the International Organization for Migration and the UN High Commissioner for Refugees to support people on arrival. Under Trump, the USA has selectively withdrawn from global bodies it sees as going against its interests or that might hold it to account. Its funding for UN humanitarian agencies to receive deportees shows the other side of the coin. It seeks to instrumentalise parts of the international system to pursue its goals. In doing so, it exploits the humanitarian missions of UN institutions while putting their credibility at risk, opening them up to accusations of complicity.

Migrants’ rights groups have challenged third-country deportations in court. In March 2025, they filed a lawsuit arguing the policy was illegal because of the risk of harm to deported people. The following month, a judge issued a preliminary injunction to pause deportations, but in June 2025, the Supreme Court suspended it, allowing deportations to resume. In September 2026, a federal appeals court ruled that the policy was unlawful because people didn’t have a proper chance to raise safety risks before deportation. The Supreme Court again quickly suspended the ruling.

Resistance in the face of cruelty

Civil society is leading the resistance to this assault on rights, shaping the political debate in ways that progressive politicians have been able to capitalise on.

Immigration lawyers are working tirelessly to defend their clients, and their interventions have stopped many deportations. Human rights groups are bringing lawsuits to challenge detention conditions, such as one highlighting the risk of death or serious injury at Camp East Montana in Texas, where guards reportedly use physical and verbal violence as a matter of routine. Despite an increasingly skewed judicial system, litigation is having an impact. Following a court order obtained by a free-speech group, the government has recently agreed to drop its attempts to pressure Apple and Meta to restrict platforms that track ICE officials and operations.

Here, we take a closer look at how Plyler protects undocumented children under the Trump administration today.
On top of that, the Constitution does not establish public education as a right to begin with.

The case set a new precedent: Undocumented children in K-12 public schools would now be protected under the Constitution.
text:
Nearly 50 years ago in Tyler, Texas, Rosario Robles walked her children to school on their first day. Robles and her husband Jose, a pipe factory employee, had lived in Tyler for five years. They were undocumented, but they owned their own home and paid taxes that went to schools.

But when they arrived at Bonner Elementary, the principal told them, “No birth certificates, no school.” He then placed Robles and her children in his car and drove them home.

Robles learned that she would have to pay $1,000 per student per year for her children, who were undocumented, to go to school. With five children, Robles would have to pay $5,000 each year. Today, that amounts to $30,000.

In our latest episode of “Let the Record Show,” the ACLU’s new history podcast, hosts Matt Beat and Shereen Marisol Meraji broke down Plyer v. Doe, a Supreme Court case that ensured undocumented children can access public education for free — and without fear. Today, the Trump administration has used mass deportations and a national policing force as an assault on our rights and liberties. Part of its agenda includes challenges to Plyler from the Trump administration and its allies. Here, we take a closer look at how Plyler protects undocumented children under the Trump administration today.

The issues in Plyler v. Doe arise after Texas amended its state education code in 1975, authorizing public school districts to charge undocumented students tuition fees or exclude them altogether. This led the school board in Tyler to implement a $1,000 tuition fee for each student that could not establish citizenship. Many of these students were Mexican but had spent most of their lives in Texas. If their families couldn’t afford the fees, the children were sent home, like the Robles.

By September 1977, the Mexican American Legal Defense and Educational Fund (MALDEF) filed a lawsuit against James Plyler, the superintendent of the Tyler Independent School District for excluding undocumented students. Representing four families, MALDEF argued that Texas’s new code was unconstitutional because it violated the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment, which says no state shall “deny to any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.”

In response, the state of Texas backed up their revised code. Their most contentious argument was that undocumented students do not have the right to claim equal protection because they aren’t considered people under the Constitution. On top of that, the Constitution does not establish public education as a right to begin with.

Judge William Wayne Justice heard the case in 1977. He ruled that children in Texas should be able to attend public school regardless of their immigration status. Texas appealed twice, and the case went up to the Supreme Court, but in both cases, the courts ruled in favor of the families.

Ultimately, the Supreme Court ruled that Texas’ revised education code was unconstitutional. The case set a new precedent: Undocumented children in K-12 public schools would now be protected under the Constitution.

Despite dissenting, even Supreme Court Justice Warren Earl Burger noted the importance of a robust education system: “Were it our business to set the nation’s social policy, I would agree without hesitation that it is senseless for an enlightened society to deprive any children, including illegal aliens, of an elementary education.”

On its very first day in office, the Trump administration rescinded a longstanding policy that generally protected certain areas, including schools, from immigration enforcement. ICE arrests at and near schools, bus stops, and routes to and from school have made children and parents afraid to go to school. Schools across the country have seen the impact in lowered enrollment rates and the detrimental effect that extends beyond their undocumented students. Last month, the ACLU released “76 Ways Mass Deportation Is Breaking Our Democracy,” a report that outlines the impact mass deportations are having on our democracy and public spaces, such as schools.

In Minnesota, Ryan Doxsey observed ICE operations at a school during morning drop-off. There, he was approached by immigration agents who told him that he would be added to a list of domestic terrorists. Situations like these have spread across communities as federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies have begun carrying out arrests under immigration charges, conducting traffic stops, and setting up checkpoints for “fishing expeditions” or to look for individuals to deport.

If parents keep their kids at home because immigration authorities are patrolling campuses or transit systems that take children to schools, that undermines Plyler.

In order to ensure the rights in Plyler are meaningfully upheld, schools have a responsibility to keep immigration officials out of their buildings. States across the country, like Kansas, Minnesota, and Florida, have proposed laws to limit immigration enforcement’s access to public schools. No parent should have to choose between their child’s education or their family’s safety.

text:
Washington, D.C. (November 19, 2026)—Rep. Jamie Raskin, Ranking Member of the House Judiciary Committee, Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations Ranking Member Richard Blumenthal, and Sen. Adam Schiff demanded records from nine law firms after their investigation uncovered that the law firm Kirkland & Ellis LLP (Kirkland) provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to federal agencies and federal entities after being threatened with an Equal Employment Opportunity Commission investigation and retributive Executive Orders that the Trump Administration had leveled against other firms. The probe also uncovered that Kirkland balked at helping the Trump Administration rename the Kennedy Center and build the President’s triumphal arch, raising questions about whether other firms that struck deals with the Administration took on those projects.

The lawmakers sent follow-up letters to Latham & Watkins LLP (Latham); Simpson Thacher & Bartlett LLP (Simpson Thacher); Willkie Farr & Gallagher LLP (Willkie); Sullivan & Cromwell LLP (S&C); Hogan Lovells Cadwalader LLP (Cadwalader); Allen Overy Shearman Sterling US LLP (A&O Shearman); Milbank LLP (Milbank); Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison LLP (Paul, Weiss); and Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP (Skadden Arps).

“We have recently received substantial and profoundly troubling information that this corrupt bargain went much further than originally understood. Kirkland & Ellis LLP provided at least $11.8 million in free legal services to numerous federal agencies and entities engaged in questionable activities, including approximately $4 million to the U.S. Department of Commerce, $2.2 million to the U.S. Department of Defense, $1.6 million to the U.S. Postal Service, $2 million to the U.S. International Development Finance Corporation, and $1.8 million to represent an investment entity negotiated between the Trump Administration and Japan to create a $550 billion slush fund. The Trump Administration also unsuccessfully tried to involve Kirkland & Ellis in work supporting the President’s political vanity projects, such as the renaming of the Kennedy Center or supporting the illegal construction of his triumphal arch in Washington, D.C.—raising serious questions of whether other firms acceded to these demands,” the lawmakers wrote.

The lawmakers received this information from Kirkland just two days after the November midterm elections. Since April 2025, the lawmakers have repeatedly demanded answers about the ten firms’ dubious multimillion-dollar deals with President Trump. However, to date, the vast majority of the firms still have yet to provide any substantive answers or turn over a single responsive document.

The lawmakers renewed their demands for all outstanding records about the Executive Order and directed the firms to prioritize records of requests for free or discounted legal services from the White House, any executive branch agency, or any public or private associate of the President. They are seeking the nature of each request, who made it, what services each firm agreed to provide, and the hours and billable value of any work performed.

Today’s letters are the latest salvo in an investigation Ranking Members Raskin and Blumenthal launched in April 2025 into Trump’s unprecedented official coercion of major law firms(link is external) and the deals firms struck to avoid retaliation. Joined by Sen. Schiff, they subsequently scrutinized firms’ free legal work for the Commerce Department, sought records of Epshteyn’s role in Kirkland’s deal and pressed Skadden over potential conflicts involving its work for Intel and the Commerce Department. In October, the lawmakers rejected Kirkland’s claims of privilege and renewed their demands for records on its $125 million deal after the firm failed to produce a single responsive document and refused to meet with congressional staff.

The lawmakers warned that they will use every tool at their disposal to pursue the investigation in this Congress and the next. As the initial phases of this investigation make clear, the President of the United States abused the power of the federal government to extract nearly $1 billion in free legal services from some of the nation's largest law firms. Worse, the agreements announced on Truth Social effectively made the President the sole judge of whether those firms were complying with their obligations—putting these firms at the political mercy of the Administration and the personal mercy of the President, driving major firms away from both existing and potential clients and causes that could put them at odds with the mercurial shakedown artist in the White House. For people and communities who rely on pro bono lawyers to defend their rights, that could mean facing the full power and intensifying fury of the federal government alone.

description:

Following media coverage and the work of members of Congress and attorneys, , the planned deportation flight carrying Afghans was suspended.
October marked the first use of DHS-owned aircraft for ICE Air deportation flights, with flights predominantly to Mexico, as well as Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador.
About ICE Flight Monitor ICE Flight Monitor uses publicly available aviation data to track U.S. immigration enforcement flights operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and partner agencies.
Our public interactive ICE Flight Monitor Dashboard enables users to visualize common routes and patterns, track historical deportation flight trends, and look up recent deportation flights to specific countries.
text:
Washington, D.C. — Despite the Trump administration’s efforts to limit visibility into ICE Flight operations, ICE Flight Monitor, housed at Human Rights First, released its latest monthly report today, revealing that the administration carried out 365 removal flights to 39 countries. Under the second Trump administration, immigration enforcement flights have steadily increased, totaling at least 2,112 flights in October, including 10 removal flights operated on U.S. military planes and 10 flights on the newly-operating DHS-owned plane. These flights subject people, including individuals who won refugee protections in the United States, to untold harm in profoundly insecure places (including places that the U.S. government has warned citizens against travelling to), violations of due process rights, and dangerous conditions aboard long ICE Flights, including the pervasive use of shackling.

Beginning in early November 2026, ICE Flight Monitor’s work has been impacted by the administration’s efforts to block flight information on aircraft involved in ICE operations. In September, the government moved to keep ICE aircraft off of public flight-tracking websites. The absence of this vital flight information makes it more challenging to provide attorneys and family members with early indications that a transfer or deportation may be underway. Nevertheless, our project has adapted to these limitations and continues to comprehensively document and monitor all ICE flights, using all available methods to track third country removal flights and other flights of concern in real time.

ICE Flight Monitor has continued to track the administration’s escalating use of forced third country transfers, with 18 flights to 12 countries in October, including a first-time transfer flight of third country nationals to Jamaica. ICE Air flights carried third country nationals, including individuals granted withholding of removal and protections under the Convention Against Torture, to seven African countries. Through this policy, the administration is disappearing people, including people who have lived in the United States for decades, to unknown locations before family members and lawyers can help them, sending them to face arbitrary detention, torture, forced return to their country of origin even after fleeing persecution there, and other serious harms.

Between late October and early November, ICE Flight Monitor also worked with partners and attorneys to track two potential ICE Flights forcibly removing people, including those who sought safety here, to Afghanistan and Iran via Pakistan. Following media coverage and the work of members of Congress and attorneys, , the planned deportation flight carrying Afghans was suspended. A planned flight to Iran via Pakistan was also diverted when Pakistan refused to accept people on board. Human Rights First continues to work with partners to ensure that people fleeing persecution and harm are not returned to the very harm that they fled.

“The ICE Flight Monitor project was spearheaded to bring transparency and accountability to a shadowy system of ICE removal flights that subject people to untold harm. People across the United States deserve to know what their tax dollars are enabling, as well as the devastating extent of the harm caused by these flights. But the Trump administration is attempting to obfuscate their cruel and lawless deportation and disappearance campaign, and violate our right to information and visibility into these processes, ” Savi Arvey, Director of Policy, Refugee and Immigrant Rights at Human Rights First. “It is telling that the same month the Trump administration attempted to inhibit visibility into these flights, they also attempted to carry out two deportation flights to Afghanistan and Iran via Pakistan – subjecting people, including those who helped our own government, to well-documented harms and persecution. ICE Flight Monitor is committed to continuing to shine a light in the darkness, bringing people vital information about these abuses.”

Key Findings from October Include:

In October, the administration’s cruel and lawless deportation campaign continued with a monthly record of 365 removal flights to 39 countries, largely driven by a persistent surge in removal flights to Mexico as land border deportations of Mexican nationals have dramatically declined.

Notably, October saw the second removal flight to Ethiopia since at least 2020 when independent tracking began, following the first in April 2026. A removal flight to Tanzania was also tracked in October, marking the first such flight since at least June 2024.

The Central African Republic and Equatorial Guinea—which have received monthly ICE Air flights carrying third country nationals from the United States since June 2026—each saw ICE Air flights in October, removing nationals of the respective countries and marking the first such flights since at least 2020 when independent tracking started.

October marked the first use of DHS-owned aircraft for ICE Air deportation flights, with flights predominantly to Mexico, as well as Guatemala, Honduras and El Salvador. Removal flights operated on DHS-owned planes started on October 28, with a B-737 plane conducting a total of four deportation flights to Mexico through the end of the month.

IFM recorded a greater expansion of forced third country transfers, with 18 flights tracked to 12 countries in October, including a first-time transfer flight of third country nationals to Jamaica. There were also repeated flights to Burundi, Cameroon, Central African Republic (CAR), Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, Eswatini, Ghana, Liberia, Panama, Saint Kitts and Nevis, and Sierra Leone.

In the Caribbean, an ICE Air flight carried the first group of 22 third country nationals to Jamaica on October 13. The transfer occurred pursuant to a U.S.-Jamaica Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) signed in June 2026, under which Jamaica will serve as a “transit country,” receiving up to 25 third country nationals every two weeks from the United States. The Dominican Republic also received third country nationals on three ICE Air flights, taking place on October 14, 21, and 28. Additionally, an ICE Air flight on October 14 removed five third country nationals to Saint Kitts and Nevis, marking the second such transfer to the country.

October saw three ICE Air flights to the Guantanamo Bay naval base (GTMO), with two flights continuing on to conduct removals in Kenya and Cuba, and the other transferring individuals to and from U.S. detention centers.

Read the October 2026 report and explore the dashboard here.

About ICE Flight Monitor

ICE Flight Monitor uses publicly available aviation data to track U.S. immigration enforcement flights operated by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and partner agencies. Founded on the methodology pioneered by researcher Tom Cartwright, the project provides transparent, data-driven reporting to strengthen accountability and inform the public about the human and democratic costs of mass deportation policies. Our public interactive ICE Flight Monitor Dashboard enables users to visualize common routes and patterns, track historical deportation flight trends, and look up recent deportation flights to specific countries.

text:
An investigation published by 404 Media on 19 November 2026 revealed that United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is paying telecommunications company AT&T millions of dollars to provide access to telephone records and analytical services for federal investigations. The findings are based on an internal ICE procurement document obtained through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request, public contracting records, and interviews with surveillance experts.

According to the internal document, ICE contracted AT&T to provide access to its raw telecommunications data and specialised analysts who process and interpret the information for Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), ICE’s criminal investigative division. The services are intended to support a broad range of investigations and agency priorities, although the document redacts the specific investigative activities for which the data will be used.

The arrangement, described in procurement records as Data Analytics and Support Services, appears to be connected to the earlier Data Analytical Services (DAS) programme, previously known as Hemisphere. Under that programme, AT&T provided federal, state, and local law enforcement agencies with the ability to search extensive collections of telephone metadata, including telephone numbers, call times, contact relationships, and potentially location information. These records do not include the contents of telephone conversations.

The programme’s capabilities were previously documented in materials released by US Senator Ron Wyden in 2023. They include identifying multiple telephone numbers associated with an individual, detecting changes in SIM cards, and determining whether devices associated with international investigative targets have entered the United States. Earlier investigations and legal challenges indicated that Hemisphere could search records involving more than one trillion telephone calls, including communications routed through AT&T’s infrastructure on behalf of other telecommunications providers. Consequently, the programme’s reach may extend beyond AT&T’s direct customers.

According to the procurement records examined by 404 Media, ICE paid AT&T more than US$2.1 million in 2025 and awarded a further contract worth more than US$2.2 million in August 2026. The arrangements could result in payments exceeding US$10 million over the coming years. The internal document also indicates that demand for the services increased during fiscal year 2025, with further growth anticipated.

The findings raise questions about the continuation of surveillance capabilities associated with Hemisphere, whose federal funding was reportedly discontinued in September 2024. Although the earlier programme was described as having been shut down, the newly disclosed records indicate that ICE continues to procure similar data analysis services directly from AT&T.

AT&T told 404 Media that it provides information to government agencies in response to lawful orders and verifies that requests comply with applicable legal requirements. However, surveillance experts noted that some requests for telephone records can be made through administrative subpoenas, which federal agencies may issue without prior judicial approval. Senator Wyden criticised the arrangement, questioning its compatibility with constitutional privacy protections and the adequacy of oversight. ICE did not respond to 404 Media’s requests for comment.

Why does it matter?

The findings raise concerns about the scale of telecommunications surveillance available to US immigration authorities and the legal safeguards governing access to such information. Although the records do not contain the contents of communications, analysing telephone metadata can reveal individuals’ relationships, movements, and patterns of activity. Because AT&T also processes calls for other telecommunications providers, the arrangement may involve information about people who have no direct contractual relationship with the company.

A federal judge stated on Wednesday that the United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency "made a mockery of court orders" in Colorado, finding government officials in contempt for instantly re-arresting a man whom the court had ordered released.

U.S. District Judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to pursue additional measures, stating that officials had "cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue" based on sworn testimony delivered in court.

"ICE's new 'policy' of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners' immediate release," the judge detailed in court records.

Over the previous six weeks, at least 18 people in Colorado were held in custody beyond their required duration or re-arrested minutes after their court-ordered release, CPR News, the news division of Colorado Public Radio, reported.

Legal experts estimated the true figure could be higher since some immigrants acted without attorneys.

Operating within the Department of Homeland Security, ICE has spearheaded Republican President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown and deportation campaign.

Rights organizations contend that the effort violates due process and free speech rights, while creating hazardous conditions and sparking racial profiling concerns, particularly for ethnic minority communities.

The Trump administration maintains its actions align with legal standards and target improved domestic security. ICE and DHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment regarding the judge's statements on Wednesday.

Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they intend to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration practices.

description:
Assuming immigration is a priority item in the new Congressional majority’s agenda, what kind of reforms should proposals include?
Delayed or inaccurate release of immigration data, concerns about due process for immigrant detainees, and sharp declines in immigration application processing deserve scrutiny.
And finally, Congress should still consider border security improvements.
America’s immigration policy should be both lawful and welcoming.
What I’m Reading More In Common has an excellent piece, with charts, on American attitudes about immigration and enforcement.
text:
Congress will look fundamentally different when it convenes for a new session in January. Democratic gains in both the House and the Senate change the math on immigration, and recent comments by President Trump and Secretary Markwayne Mullin indicate a potential willingness to work on immigration reform.

Assuming immigration is a priority item in the new Congressional majority’s agenda, what kind of reforms should proposals include? I think the changes needed are in three broad categories: oversight, the economy, and security.

Accountability matters. Delayed or inaccurate release of immigration data, concerns about due process for immigrant detainees, and sharp declines in immigration application processing deserve scrutiny. Congress should undertake bipartisan oversight to restore trust in the immigration system.

Immigrants work, and America needs workers to continue to power the economy as our society ages and population growth slows. Workers who have been contributing for years need a permanent legislative solution, and Congress should keep the economy top of mind if it tackles future legal migration flows.

And finally, Congress should still consider border security improvements. Trade and travel are vital to our border regions. Irregular migration is low now, but it could return if there is an economic or security crisis in the Western Hemisphere. Congress should continue to appropriate funding to ensure our ports of entry can securely and efficiently move people and goods, while building the appropriate capacity to compassionately handle the next humanitarian crisis.

America’s immigration policy should be both lawful and welcoming. I hope the next Congress works with the Trump Administration to deliver this.

Figure of the Month

1,900

That’s the number of immigrant children held in shelters as of September.

Data Dive

Despite being one of the country’s youngest states, Utah faces an aging population and falling birth rates, making immigrants increasingly important to its workforce. International migration accounted for nearly 21% of Utah’s population growth from 2024 to 2025, according to comments by Olivia Whiteley at a roundtable event covered by the Utah News Dispatch.

A Pew Research Center analysis found that about one in 10 people eligible to vote in the recent midterm elections are naturalized citizens.

What I’m Reading

More In Common has an excellent piece, with charts, on American attitudes about immigration and enforcement. The takeaway? Balance.

The Supreme Court will hear arguments in Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services in the spring. The case is about the January 2025 executive action declaring an invasion at the border and denying any noncitizens from applying for asylum. The challengers assert that this policy violates federal immigration law.

Thousands of immigrants in detention have been suing to force their release. In Washington state, the number of cases is so high that the Department of Justice has begun declining to challenge these petitions in court.

The Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) released the 50th edition of the International Migration Outlook. The report analyzes migration trends in OECD countries and specifically looks at the change in international student destinations and how immigrants are filling labor shortages in long-term care services.

Border barrier construction is set to resume in the Big Bend region of West Texas, including in the national park, after the Supreme Court temporarily paused a lower court’s ruling. The Trump Administration was sued last spring over its plans to build border barriers through the remote terrain, which sees a mere 1.6% of migrant apprehensions at the southwest border.

Some Ukrainians welcomed to the United States after Russia’s illegal full-scale invasion starting in 2022 are being arrested and detained. At least 12 Ukrainian refugees working as truck drivers were detained in Oklahoma and Indiana, according to The New York Times. These arrests are part of broader enforcement efforts targeting immigrant truck drivers across states. Some were deported to Ukraine, others to third countries.

Marketplace reports on the economic reality of immigration enforcement in communities and industries that rely on foreign-born labor. In south Texas, immigration enforcement impacts even legal workers, who fear harassment and detention.

Diadié Camara fled slavery in Mauritania and crossed the U.S.-Mexico border seeking protection. The U.S. deported him to Equatorial Guinea, a country with a poor human rights record. Equatorial Guinea forced him to return to Mauritania, where he is now in hiding. He is one of over 100 people documented who have been returned to their home countries to face persecution despite U.S. court orders.

Upcoming Events

Dec. 1 – University of Oxford: Building Local Capacity for Immigrant Inclusion: The Role of Foundations in Implementing DACA Across U.S. Cities

Dec. 16 – SUNY Institute on Immigrant Integration Research & Policy: When Federal Policy Changes, Can Local Institutions Hold the Line?

Bush Institute Insights

I spoke to Fox News about why a potential legalization for undocumented immigrants could benefit the U.S. economy.

My Bush Institute colleague, Global Policy Director Natalie Gonnella-Platts, and I explain how free countries can address migration and security concerns without legitimizing the Taliban. European countries trying to remove Afghans who are national security risks must do so, but the process doesn’t need to involve rolling out the red carpet for totalitarians.

text:
Batavia, N.Y. (WHAM) — The last few weeks have been "extremely hard" for Iris Davila after her husband, Alaa Duisat, was detained by federal agents while pumping gas at a Rochester gas station.

Davila said Duisat was detained two weeks ago. She spoke with 13WHAM while visiting him at the federal immigration detention center in Batavia.

According to Davila, Duisat is a Swedish citizen who moved to the United States in 2022. The couple married in October 2023.

Davila acknowledged her husband entered the country under a visa waiver program that allowed him to stay for 90 days and remained beyond that period. However, she said he has been working toward obtaining a green card.

"Really, he got a lot of anxiety. He got a lot of depressed anxiety for the situation. Really, it's not OK inside," Davila said.

His detention comes amid growing scrutiny of federal immigration enforcement in the Rochester region, including the recent arrests of Mount Morris restaurant owner Din Zhao Lin and SUNY Brockport IT worker German Machado.

BACKGROUND: Union, students call for SUNY Brockport employee to be released from ICE custody | Petition for release of Mount Morris restaurant owner held by ICE tops 7,000 signatures | Millions await asylum decisions as cases can take years, Rochester attorney says

Gov. Kathy Hochul said she has raised concerns about those arrests with federal officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

"I had a very serious conversation with Secretary Mullin about this exact individual, and it is so sad what has happened to this, you know, someone working in IT at Brockport," Hochul said. "I mean, this is not what you expect when you show up to work."

Hochul added that ICE shouldn't "be picking up innocent people."

"Go after the worst of the worst. But the vast majority of people who've been detained have been law abiding their entire time here," she said. "Many have been here for 30 years, and we're just really challenging this whole proposition."

Hochul has also raised concerns about an expansion of the ICE detention facility in Batavia, where Duisat is being held. The governor is demanding more information about the project following reports that temporary structures could house up to 100 women as winter approaches.

"There's no reason for ICE to expand any facility in New York state. Full stop," Hochul said.

ICE says it is working to expand detention capacity as part of President Donald Trump's immigration enforcement efforts.

Davila said she recognizes her husband overstayed his authorized visit but remains hopeful they can be reunited.

"He's in a lot of pain, my husband inside, and not only for me," she said. "It's a situation for a lot people like my husband here. He's got a lot of family."

Davila said her husband has not been in trouble with the law.

13WHAM reached out to the Department of Homeland Security for information about Duisat's detention but has not received a response.

title: DOJ Attorney Sanctioned After False Claims in LGBTQ Iranian Asylum Case
description:
Last month, federal judge Diane Humetawa formally sanctioned a Department of Justice attorney for making unsupported declarations in written court documents.
He told us that there were two witnesses who could corroborate his case — but that both had already been ordered deported.
When we looked into Abed and Ali’s case files, we discovered that neither of them had really had a fair chance to present their asylum claims.
Both Ali and Abed were ordered deported to Iran after their hearings.
The way I’ve told this story doesn’t do justice to Abed, Ali, and Zain’s strength in standing up for themselves and each other.
text:
Last month, federal judge Diane Humetawa formally sanctioned a Department of Justice attorney for making unsupported declarations in written court documents. He was ordered to an hour of classes on “the special role of U.S. attorneys” and another hour on the need for “evidentiary support” for things you say in court.

This might not seem like a huge deal. But it’s very rare for judges to formally call out government attorneys for not doing the most basic part of their jobs: making sure something is true before asserting it.

It’s also ironic, because the statement he made that turned out to be untrue was accusing me of lying to ICE about my client Abed’s case.

Abed is one of the LGBTQ Iranian clients that I, the director of the Immigration Justice Campaign, have been representing for the past year. During that time, IJC has had to fight to keep Abed and his partner Ali off several flights bound for Iran — even after the U.S. went to war there this spring.

Representing Abed and Ali (as well as Ali’s spouse Zain, a trans man, who married Ali in Iran so they could present as a straight couple to avoid persecution) has been a kind of whirlwind tour in just how many ways the Trump administration has rigged immigration courts against immigrants — and how vigilant lawyers need to be in order to keep their clients safe, much less seek justice for them. The fact that this attorney accused me of obstructing official business, based on a lie, and was himself sanctioned for making assertions without having any facts to back them up instead, is a small victory. But it’s just one of several times we’ve found the government to be dishonest in trying to send Abed and Ali back to Iran.

Some quick background: Abed and Ali were arrested by the “morality police” in Iran and charged with sodomy. Zain had to put up the house he owned with Ali as collateral for the loan he took out to pay their bond. (All three of these names are pseudonyms.) The three of them fled to Turkey, but were outed there, too. On their way to the United States, they were kidnapped and assaulted in Mexico; Ali still has medical issues stemming from the attack. They fled to the U.S. for safety in early January 2025 — days before Trump took office for the second time.

IJC was connected with Zain that summer, in preparation for his case before an immigration judge. He told us that there were two witnesses who could corroborate his case — but that both had already been ordered deported.

When we looked into Abed and Ali’s case files, we discovered that neither of them had really had a fair chance to present their asylum claims. Both had told the court that they had witnesses — which, legally, means the government needed to make those witnesses available from detention to testify. But ICE didn’t do that, and the judges in each case didn’t order it.

The judge in Ali’s case expressed skepticism during the hearing that Ali — who had been charged with sodomy by the Iranian government – had actually been persecuted based on his sexual orientation. He asked, rhetorically, whether “everyone” gay in Iran is hanged.

Both Ali and Abed were ordered deported to Iran after their hearings. Furthermore, Abed’s removal order was unknowingly edited after the fact to designate his asylum claim as “frivolous,” severely limiting his options for appeal.

By the time IJC took on their cases, both men had missed their deadlines to appeal the denials of asylum. That’s because they’d been told they were unlikely to win, and decided to wait six months instead to file petitions for habeas corpus in federal court, asking federal judges to order them released from detention. They figured they could wait the six months because the U.S. wasn’t deporting anyone to Iran, and hadn’t for years.

The problem is that last summer, the U.S. made a deal with Iran to start accepting deportees.

We successfully kept Abed and Ali off the first two deportation flights. But in early December, both Abed and Ali were told they would be on the third one. We had already filed an appeal of Abed’s asylum denial with the Board of Immigration Appeals, but filed a new one on December 2, along with a request for them to officially pause — or “stay” — his deportation while his appeal was pending. Once we filed the appeal, I emailed ICE to notify them that he had a pending appeal. When ICE loaded detainees onto the plane, Abed wasn’t among them. Neither was Ali — his health had deteriorated to the point of needing a wheelchair, and he was physically incapable of sitting on the bus to the airport.

In February of this year, with the assistance of the National Immigrant Justice Center, Abed filed his habeas petition before Judge Humetawa. In its response, the government argued that Abed couldn’t claim he’d been detained for six months or longer after getting ordered deported (a benchmark that the Supreme Court found back in 2001 suggests that the person is unlikely to be deported anytime soon), because the clock had been reset each time he had “obstructed” ICE’s efforts to deport him. One of the examples of “obstruction” they used was that in December, ICE had left him off the manifest after getting a communication from his attorney — me.

The DOJ’s filing said that it was “unknowable” what I had told ICE in December, but because they took him off the deportation flight, it seemed “likely” I had told ICE that Abed had been granted a stay – which “would have been untrue.”

It would have been, had I said that! But it wasn’t. In response, Abed’s legal team produced the email I’d sent ICE at the time, which simply said, “There is now an appeal pending.”

Judge Humetawa was not impressed with the DOJ attorney’s behavior and ordered Abed released.

Meanwhile, we were still fighting for Ali’s release from detention. In May, he was told that even though he’d been granted a stay of removal from the BIA, something that almost never happens, he was going to be deported to Iran after all. (Yes, this is after military action began.) When he got moved to a facility in Arizona in preparation for a removal flight, we sprung into action again on another habeas motion. This time, we got the DOJ to agree that it was unlikely Ali would actually be removed to Iran anytime soon.

Ali was then released from detention, finally reuniting with Abed and Zain.

The way I’ve told this story doesn’t do justice to Abed, Ali, and Zain’s strength in standing up for themselves and each other. And it’s by no means the only horror story we have from the last two years of how difficult it is for asylum seekers to get a fair day in court: just ask me about the client who got ordered deported because the government handed him the wrong form. But it’s rare that we handle a case not only where our clients all end up together and free, but where the government is actually held to account for the stunts it pulls to deny people’s claims and put them on removal flights. This remarkable story is worth sharing with the world.
