Press Releases

Attorney General Tong Encourages New Congressional Majorities to Hold Hearings on Immigration Enforcement Abuses

Joins coalition AGs in recommending inquiries into accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and DHS waste and corruption

(Hartford, CT) —Attorney General William Tong joined a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump administration’s abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Tong and the coalition call on Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Tong and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through truth councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“Trump has terrorized communities with error-riddled warrantless and meritless arrests that have caused serious harm to families and communities. We urge the incoming majorities in Congress to exercise their authority to investigate the Trump administration’s hyper aggressive, lawless, and chaotic immigration enforcement and hold accountable those responsible for needless pain, death and injuries,” said Attorney General Tong.

Trump abuses in immigration enforcement, corruption

Donald Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of terror across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was nearly a fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in sixteen cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

In the letter, Attorney General Tong and the coalition write, “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has also wasted significant sums of money in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course. Now, DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.

Joining Attorney General Tong in the letter to Congressional leaders is Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison, who led the coalition, and the attorneys general of Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, the District of Columbia, Hawai’i, Illinois, Maine, Massachusetts, Michigan, Nevada, New Mexico, New York, Oregon, Rhode Island, Vermont, Virginia, and Washington.

In The Know is your daily briefing on Oklahoma policy-related news. OK Policy encourages the support of Oklahoma’s state and local media, which are vital to an informed citizenry. After air quality report finds little risk from Inola smelter, opponents raise doubts: The proposed Oklahoma Primary Aluminum smelter at the Port of Inola would have little to no impact on air quality, a 336-page report filed last week with the Oklahoma Department of Environmental Quality says. Controversial appointments could signal where Mazzei is headed on education: The governor-elect’s appointment of Lindel Fields as his chief of staff drew bipartisan praise because of the interim superintendent’s apolitical leadership style. Mazzei names economic transition team, includes Stitt’s former COO [The Oklahoman]

Mazzei administration growing; Choctaw Nation chief to join transition team members [Tulsa World]

Paxton wants voters to move Medicaid expansion into state law: Senate President Pro Tem Lonnie Paxton says he’ll try again next session to put a constitutional amendment on the ballot. Lawsuit challenges SNAP restrictions on sugary drinks, food in Oklahoma, 17 other states [Oklahoma Voice]

Gov. Stitt backed Trump’s deportation push. Then it came for Hai Nguyen.: Despite Hai Nguyen holding active work authorization, federal authorities used a two-decade-old marijuana charge to categorize him as the type of criminal the Trump administration had vowed to expel. First child flu death reported in Oklahoma as cases surge statewide [The Oklahoman]

From OK Policy: Policy Matters: Oklahoma needs to make housing affordability a top economic priority

Activists explain pushback against data center projects across Oklahoma [Fox 23]

[The Oklahoman]

KATT 100.5 DJ on OKC layoffs: ‘The warning signs were there’: Local layoffs are part of widespread staffing cuts by KATT owner Cumulus Media, an Atlanta-based company that owns nearly 400 radio stations in 80-plus markets. Dozens of on-air personalities and executives at stations across the country have seen their jobs eliminated since last week. [The Oklahoman]

As the agreements have expanded, so has the number of immigration arrests in Oklahoma. Tulsa’s immigrant community faces heightened fears of deportations, with some reporting firsthand experiences of detainment and arrest to deportation. [La Semana via Tulsa Flyer]

When Tulsa no longer feels like home: Immigrants face mental health challenges [La Semana via Tuylsa Flyer]

Mayo joins Oklahoma County jail trust, signals shift in first meeting [The Oklahoman]

OKC debuts $42M Louisa McCune Animal Welfare Center funded by MAPS 4 [The Oklahoman]

Lack of customers, lingering COVID struggles force three downtown Tulsa closures [The Oklahoma Eagle]

Quote of the Day

“People who, regardless of their status, are afraid sometimes to even go to the grocery store or go to the doctor’s office or go pick up a prescription or go to work. It’s a cultured fear in everyday life activities.”

– Jennifer “Jenny” Franklin, behavioral health director for Tulsa’s Community Health Connection, speaking about the increased enforcement of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. Ramped-up federal immigration enforcement has resulted in higher mental health struggles among immigrants. [La Semana via Tulsa Flyer]

Number of the Day

139

The second Trump administration is using a legal tool to create an immigration dragnet that will blanket the country with law enforcement officers who are willing and able to impose and enforce immigration law on everyone, regardless of immigration status, based on dangerous assumptions about race and nationality. text:
The Reach of Immigration-Related Retaliation Expands: California Amends Labor Code Section 1019

Immigration compliance is increasingly becoming a state-law issue as well as a federal one. Employers operating across jurisdictions face an increasingly complex patchwork of requirements affecting immigration enforcement, employment verification, worker protections, and employer communications involving immigration status.

California continues to expand its rules in this area, including through recent legislation addressing workplace immigration enforcement and employee notice requirements. Effective January 1, 2027, Assembly Bill 2495 (AB 2495) significantly broadens Labor Code Section 1019, expanding the rights protected, individuals covered, and immigration-related conduct that may give rise to liability.

This state legislative activity also comes against a backdrop of increased federal scrutiny of immigration-related recruiting and hiring practices. Recent Department of Justice and Department of Labor activity involving the PERM labor certification program reflects heightened attention to whether recruitment processes provide U.S. workers a genuine opportunity to apply and receive consideration. Although the federal and California legal frameworks address different conduct and protect different interests, together they reinforce the importance of carefully designed and consistently administered recruiting, sponsorship, and employment-verification practices.

The California changes are particularly significant as employers take a closer look at sponsorship requests, foreign-national hiring, work authorization, and workforce planning. Decisions and communications that employers may view primarily as immigration or business matters may increasingly be examined through a retaliation lens under California law.

Expanding the Range of Protected Conduct

Historically, Section 1019 focused largely on rights under the Labor Code or applicable local ordinances. Beginning January 1, 2027, it will cover the exercise or attempted exercise of rights under virtually any federal, state, or local law applicable to employees. Immigration-related conduct connected to wage-and-hour complaints, discrimination concerns, safety complaints, leave requests, accommodations, whistleblower activity, or other statutory rights may therefore give rise to claims.

In addition to those who formally assert rights, the legislation protects individuals who:

Make good-faith workplace complaints;

Seek information regarding legal compliance;

Inform others regarding workplace rights;

Encourage others to exercise workplace rights; or

Assist another individual in asserting workplace protections.

Protection does not require a formal complaint: asking about workplace rights, assisting a coworker, or seeking compliance information may suffice.

A New Focus on Conduct That May "Dissuade" Employees

A significant change is the statute's focus on conduct that may discourage individuals from exercising workplace rights before any complaint is made. The amended law prohibits conduct related to actual or perceived immigration status that would reasonably tend to dissuade a person from exercising a legal right or induce an action the person has a legal right to decline.

The focus thus extends beyond whether retaliation occurred to whether comments or conduct could reasonably discourage protected activity, creating litigation risk from interactions not previously viewed as actionable.

Although each situation is fact-specific, employers should be mindful of communications such as:[1]

Referencing an employee's immigration or visa status during a workplace dispute;

Suggesting that raising concerns could affect future sponsorship opportunities;

Asking unnecessary immigration-status questions unrelated to a legitimate business need;

Making statements that could be interpreted as discouraging employees from reporting workplace concerns; or

Linking work authorization to complaints about wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other protected rights.

Claims may arise even if an employee never files a complaint or exercises the underlying right.

Coverage Now Extends Beyond Current Employees

AB 2495 also expands the definition of "employee" to include:

Applicants;

Current employees; and

Former employees.

Coverage of applicants may affect recruiting and hiring. Liability turns not on actual immigration status but on whether conduct related to actual or perceived status could be viewed as retaliatory or as discouraging the exercise of workplace rights. The law does not prohibit lawful questions about work authorization or future sponsorship needs. Employers generally remain free to decide whether to sponsor employment-based visas and to ask whether applicants are authorized to work in the United States and need sponsorship now or in the future. Those questions, and decisions based on the responses, should be grounded in legitimate business considerations and administered consistently. Employers should also evaluate how sponsorship-related screening interacts with their broader recruiting practices and applicable federal anti-discrimination requirements.

Questions about work authorization and sponsorship, including follow-up questions, should serve a legitimate business purpose, be asked consistently, and avoid statements that could discourage the exercise of workplace rights. Coverage of former employees also extends potential exposure beyond active employment.

Where Employers May Face Increased Exposure

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Employers should continue to follow federal Form I-9 and E-Verify requirements while ensuring that employment-verification practices are applied consistently and are not used, or perceived as being used, in response to protected workplace activity. Requests for additional documentation, unnecessary immigration-status inquiries, or changes in verification practices involving an employee who has raised workplace concerns may receive particular scrutiny.

The potential exposure, however, extends beyond the employment-verification process. Even employers that do not intend to retaliate may face liability arising from routine decisions and conversations about sponsorship, work authorization, immigration status, or compliance.

Areas to review include:

Recruiting channels, application processes, and applicant screening practices;

Layoffs, reductions in force, and workforce restructuring affecting sponsored positions or related occupations;

Questions regarding current work authorization and future sponsorship needs;

Communications regarding sponsorship decisions;

Form I-9 and E-Verify practices;

Internal complaint and investigation procedures;

Manager and supervisor training;

Responses to employee concerns regarding wages, leave, discrimination, safety, or other workplace rights; and

Communications involving immigration status, visa sponsorship, or future employment authorization.

As employers reassess sponsorship strategies, recruiting practices, layoffs, hiring priorities, and long-term workforce planning against a changing federal immigration landscape, immigration-related decisions and communications may receive increased scrutiny from multiple directions. Employers generally retain discretion over sponsorship, but discussions should remain tied to legitimate business considerations and separate from workplace complaints or other protected activity.

Compliant employment-verification practices remain essential. Routine employment-eligibility verification, document review, and immigration-status communications may give rise to claims. Actions that appear to single out employees based on actual or perceived immigration status may receive heightened scrutiny, particularly when connected to workplace complaints or disputes.

Section 1019 does not diminish employers' federal immigration obligations or ability to make lawful hiring and sponsorship decisions. Employers must continue to verify employment authorization, evaluate sponsorship needs, and plan their workforces consistent with business objectives and legal requirements. Those actions should be supported by documented business and compliance considerations and should not appear to discourage employees or applicants from exercising workplace rights.

Significant Penalties Remain Available

The amendments are more than technical. Individuals subjected to an unfair immigration-related practice may already sue under Section 1019 for equitable relief, damages, and available penalties. Existing law authorizes civil penalties of up to $10,000 per employee or person per immigration-related violation. Employers may also face injunctive relief, attorneys' fees in certain circumstances, and other remedies under California law.

Looking Ahead

Before January 1, 2027, employers should review recruiting practices, sponsorship communications, complaint procedures, manager training, and employment-verification processes to confirm they are applied consistently and serve legitimate business and compliance objectives. Managers, recruiters, talent acquisition teams, and human resources professionals should understand how to discuss immigration-related issues lawfully and recognize that comments about immigration status, sponsorship, or work authorization may receive heightened scrutiny when connected to workplace rights.

Proactive compliance may reduce litigation risk. Given the law's focus on conduct that may "dissuade" workers from exercising legal rights, employers should review not only formal decisions but also everyday communications during hiring, onboarding, investigations, and employee-relations matters. Because these issues intersect with immigration, employment, and anti-discrimination laws, employers should consider consulting experienced counsel on complex or high-risk situations.

In January, a new Congress arrives with new majorities, dozens of new members and a historic mandate to rein in ICE’s cruelty and lawlessness. Here are three ways they can act

For nearly two years, Donald Trump and Stephen Miller have run their mass deportation machine without accountability. Then the American people spoke loud and clear in the November election. Their message to Congress about the mass deportation machine: things must change come January, when a new majority steps up to the plate with the gavel, the subpoena and the power of the purse. This new Congress has the historic mandate and tools to rein in ICE, hold the architects of this agenda accountable, end the blank check fueling it, and begin delivering humane solutions for immigrant families. Millions of our neighbors are counting on it. Voters are demanding it.

THE GAVEL: PUT THE HUMAN TOLL ON THE RECORD

Since the start of the second Trump administration, at least 62 people have died in federal immigration custody, with ICE’s own investigators finding that 23 of 29 immigrants who died in detention between January 2025 and January 2026 received medical care the agency itself deemed deficient. Mass deportation agents killed U.S. citizens Ruben Ray Martinez, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, and immigrant dads Lorenzo Salgado Araujo and Johan Sebastián. Children have also borne the brunt of mass deportation, with Brookings estimating that 205,000 kids – including roughly 145,000 U.S. citizens – have had a parent torn from them. Mass deportation agents have also detained more than 500 U.S. citizens, including at least 70 children and teens – and that’s likely an undercount.

But instead of the outgoing Congress holding ICE accountable, Trump’s allies in the Republican-controlled Congress stood by and did nothing as ICE changed its own rules so that it could avoid reporting the deaths of recently released individuals. And in just the past few days alone, armed agents in California brutalized a pregnant U.S. citizen and detained an eight-year-old Haitian boy. While he has since been released to his loved ones, it is undeniable that detention can hurt children in the long-term.

This must stop. U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), the incoming chair of the House Oversight Committee, has named these abuses a top priority, while Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS), the top Democrat on the House Homeland Security Committee, has promised to prioritize investigations into these senseless deaths. Public hearings must center the families who have buried loved ones and the children who watched a parent stolen away from them, placing their testimony alongside the officials responsible for their pain.

THE SUBPOENA: MAKE MILLER AND HIS MASS DEPORTATION ACCOMPLICES ANSWER FOR THEIR ACTIONS

Trump officials seem to be under the belief that Congressional oversight is optional, including violating federal law by blocking members from inspecting detention camps, declining to appear when House Democrats have invited them to testify, and even refusing to answer basic questions about human beings in their custody. This too must change. As Rep. Thompson put it: “In the majority, they will not have that choice.”

The questions that they have the obligation to answer are urgent, starting with Miller’s arrest quotas. “Stephen Miller wants everybody arrested. ‘Why aren’t you at Home Depot? Why aren’t you at 7-Eleven?’” one official recounted about a June 2025 meeting with the mass deportation architect. Since then, ICE leadership has instructed officers to target around 19,000 arrests per week, and officials have said Miller’s promotion to White House Chief of Staff signals this anti-immigrant dragnet will not relent. These quotas are playing out on the ground: in the days following the election, masked officers blocked a hospital emergency room driveway in a Latino neighborhood in California, and authorities in Alabama arrested 19-year-old triplets. The young men are currently financially supporting their mom amid cancer treatment.

“It is painful that my children are in detention. They are the ones who are covering the expenses for my illness,” she said. “It’s not fair when we are good, hardworking people.” Miller and other mass deportation officials paid by the taxpayers must answer to the taxpayers for this cruelty, as America’s Voice and 17 Latino, immigrant and civil rights organizations recently wrote to incoming Congressional leaders. “On November 3, voters from coast to coast rejected this cruel, lawless, and costly agenda and handed you a mandate for change,” the letter states.

THE POWER OF THE PURSE: FOLLOW THE MONEY

ICE still has an astounding $91 billion remaining from two pieces of harmful legislation passed by the outgoing Congress – and the incoming Congress must use the power of the purse to claw back this exorbitant amount of money, as well as freeze any new ICE spending and contracts until Congress receives a full accounting of how the agency has used its funds. Already, the administration has been racing to spend this money before accountability arrives in January.

DHS awarded a $31.8 million contract to convert a warehouse in Roxbury, New Jersey, into a detention center – despite a court order barring the move – and completed the environmental review needed to move ahead with a second warehouse in Arizona. Days after the election, CoreCivic’s CEO urged ICE to “move quickly” on new detention deals. “They have a need for capacity. We have the capacity,” said Lucibeth Mayberry, discussing the for-profit imprisonment of human beings as casually as a linens sale. “There’s no reason to wait.”

And as America’s Voice has documented, mass deportation imposes an ICE tax on everyone no matter their legal immigration status, driving up costs for families and businesses and costing U.S.-born workers up to 297,000 jobs. Oversight exists to stop this human and economic waste. Likely House Speaker Hakeem Jeffries has promised Democrats will not give “a dime” to Trump’s “violent mass deportation machine.” The new majority must make good on that promise.

WHAT COMES NEXT

In January, a new Congress arrives with new majorities, dozens of new members, and a historic mandate to act. Accountability is the essential first step toward common-sense solutions that strengthen our economy and reflect our values as a nation. Those solutions can start now, including the American Dream and Promise Act, which Jeffries has committed to moving in the new year if an ongoing discharge petition is unsuccessful in this Congress:

Democrats can and should build on that commitment by outlining a way forward to reform our immigration system – centered on providing an earned pathway to citizenship for long-established immigrants. It is time to refocus the conversation on permanent solutions for Dreamers, farm workers, healthcare workers and others who are part of our families, communities, and workplaces.

America’s Voice stands ready to work alongside the new Congress, bringing the stories of affected families, the evidence of what this agenda has cost, and the full strength of our partners to the work of reining in ICE and taking us in a new direction on immigration reform.

text:
DOJ, DOL & EEOC Intensify PERM Compliance Enforcement With Multi-Million-Dollar Settlements and Employer Debarment From the PERM Program

The U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ), Department of Labor (DOL) and Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) have announced two significant enforcement actions highlighting increased federal scrutiny of employer recruitment practices under the Permanent Labor Certification (PERM) program. The settlements, announced in October 2026, involve allegations that employers discriminated against U.S. workers by creating barriers to their participation in PERM recruitment.

On October 16, 2026, the DOJ and DOL announced a settlement with Cloudera, Inc., a California-based technology company, following allegations that the company discriminated against qualified U.S. workers during PERM recruitment. According to the government's investigation, Cloudera failed to advertise PERM positions on its public careers website and instead directed applicants to a separate email address that was unable to receive messages from external accounts, effectively preventing U.S. workers from being considered. The settlement includes a two-year debarment from the PERM program, $1.4 million in back pay for affected U.S. workers, and $600,000 in civil penalties. procedures and reporting requirements.

Just days later, on October 20, 2026, the DOJ and EEOC announced a $5 million settlement with Instacart involving similar allegations of discriminatory PERM recruitment practices. The agencies alleged that Instacart required U.S. workers to submit applications by physical mail for PERM-sponsored positions, despite ordinarily accepting electronic applications for other job openings. This additional application requirement resulted in many U.S. applicants not being timely considered for the PERM-sponsored positions. The settlement includes up to $4 million in compensation for affected applicants and $1 million in civil penalties. Instacart must also revise its recruitment procedures, permit electronic applications for PERM positions, provide employee training, and comply with monitoring and reporting obligations.

These enforcement actions underscore that employers must conduct recruitment in good faith and ensure that their procedures do not unlawfully disadvantage U.S. workers. Importantly, the DOJ has emphasized that employers cannot impose additional application burdens or otherwise treat U.S. applicants less favorably simply because recruitment is being conducted in connection with a foreign national's permanent residence sponsorship. Employers should carefully review their PERM recruitment practices, including application procedures, accessibility of job postings, consideration of applicants and documentation of recruitment outcomes. Noncompliance with PERM regulations can result in substantial financial penalties, back-pay obligations, heightened oversight, and employer debarment from the PERM program.

Trump Administration Suspends PERM Adjudications for Major Technology and IT Consulting Employers

On October 8, 2026, Trump Administration officials, led by Vice President JD Vance, U.S. Department of Labor (DOL) Secretary Keith Sonderling and Attorney General Todd Blanche, announced a sweeping enforcement action targeting employment-based immigration programs. The Administration suspended participation in the PERM labor certification program for eight major technology and IT consulting companies: Adobe, Capgemini, Cognizant Technology Solutions, HCL Technologies, Infosys, Microsoft, Tata Consultancy Services and Wipro.

Administration officials stated that the action was based on allegations that these employers relied excessively on foreign labor while reducing opportunities for U.S. workers through layoffs and workforce reductions. The companies will remain subject to ongoing government review and investigation.

The PERM labor certification process is the first step in most employment-based green card cases. Before sponsoring a foreign national for permanent residence, an employer must conduct a prescribed recruitment process and demonstrate that there are no able, willing, qualified, and available U.S. workers for the position and that hiring the foreign worker will not adversely affect the wages and working conditions of similarly employed U.S. workers.

According to DOL Office of Foreign Labor Certification disclosure data, the employers targeted by the suspension have collectively filed tens of thousands of PERM applications over the past several years:

Employer PERM Cases Filed(FY2020-FY2026 Q3)

(10/01/2019 to 06/30/2026) Approval Rate PERM Cases Filed During Current Trump Administration

(01/20/2025-06/30/2026) Approval Rate Adobe Inc. 2,747 98.0% 32 93.7% Capgemini America, Inc. 2,235 91.6% 65 0% Cognizant Technology Solutions US Corp. 2,291 99.9% 0 0% HCL Technologies 1,882 98.6% 21 90.4% Infosys 1,756 96.2% 0 0% Microsoft Corporation 18,189 94.0% 976 89.0% Tata Consultancy Services 7,574 97.9% 0 0% Wipro Limited 1,695 84.9% 0 0%

Immediate Impact

The announcement has significant implications for both employers and foreign national workers:

New PERM labor certification applications may not be filed by the affected employers.

DOL has suspended processing of pending PERM applications involving the named companies.

Current H-1B employees are not immediately affected, and the H-1B visa program remains unchanged.

However, many H-1B workers rely on the PERM process to obtain extensions beyond the standard six-year H-1B limit. Delays or an inability to file PERM applications could jeopardize eligibility for those extensions if statutory green card milestones cannot be met.

The announcement did not expressly affect previously approved I-140 immigrant petitions, adjustment-of-status applications, or completed employment-based green card cases.

Workers whose employers are subject to suspension may need to evaluate alternative immigration strategies, including transfers to other employers able to continue the green card process.

This action represents one of the most consequential restrictions on employment-based immigration since the beginning of the second Trump Administration. By halting PERM filings and processing for several of the nation's largest technology employers and IT consulting firms, the Administration has disrupted a primary pathway through which highly skilled foreign nationals transition from temporary work visas to U.S. permanent residence.

Proposed Fees for Universities Recommending Off-Campus Employment Authorization for Foreign Students

Citing what it describes as “egregious cases of abuse” and “schemes to exploit the current OPT regulations for fraudulent purposes,” the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) has proposed a new fee structure that would require colleges and universities to pay substantial government fees when recommending certain forms of off-campus employment authorization for F-1 students.

Under a Proposed Rule published on October 8, 2026, DHS would impose a $70,000 fee each time a university recommends a foreign student for Optional Practical Training (OPT) and a $30,000 fee for each recommendation for a 24-month STEM OPT extension. The proposal represents a significant departure from the current system, under which universities certify student eligibility through their Designated School Officials (DSOs) but do not pay government fees for OPT recommendations.

OPT is a long-standing benefit available to F-1 students that allows them to gain practical work experience directly related to their field of study. Most foreign students are eligible for up to 12 months of post-completion OPT following graduation. Students who earn degrees in qualifying science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) fields may obtain an additional 24 months of work authorization through the STEM OPT extension program, resulting in a total of up to 36 months of employment authorization.

If finalized, the proposed fees could have a substantial impact on universities with large international student populations, particularly research institutions that enroll significant numbers of STEM students. Critics argue that the proposal could discourage schools from recommending students for OPT, increase administrative costs and reduce the attractiveness of U.S. universities to international students. Supporters contend that the fees are necessary to strengthen program integrity and deter abuse of employment authorization programs.

The proposal is currently subject to the federal rulemaking process, including a public comment period, and has not yet taken effect. As drafted, however, it signals increased scrutiny of student employment authorization programs and the role educational institutions play in facilitating them.

Comments may be submitted until November 9, 2026, at Regulations.gov (https://www.regulations.gov/commenton/ICEB-2026-0100-0001). As of this writing, more than 3,000 public comments have been submitted.

New Investigations of University

On October 8, 2026, the Trump Administration announced investigations into nine universities regarding alleged misuse of the J-1 Exchange Visitor Program. The institutions identified include Harvard University, Stanford University, Yale University, Arizona State University, Brown University, the University of Pittsburgh, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) and the University of California, Davis (UC-Davis).

The administration alleges that these universities may have used the J-1 program in ways that exceed its intended cultural and educational exchange purpose, potentially displacing U.S. workers, or circumventing employment-based immigration pathways. The investigations are part of a broader effort to increase scrutiny of temporary visa programs utilized by higher education institutions and research organizations.

The J-1 Exchange Visitor Program is widely used by universities and teaching hospitals to sponsor a range of foreign nationals, including students, visiting professors, research scholars, short-term scholars, specialists, and physicians participating in graduate medical education and residency programs. Many universities rely heavily on the program to support academic research, international collaboration, and the training of foreign medical graduates.

While the investigations do not currently alter the availability of J-1 visas or program participation, they signal heightened federal oversight of university-sponsored exchange programs. Universities with significant international scholar populations may face additional compliance reviews, documentation requirements, and scrutiny regarding program administration, recruitment practices, and adherence to the program's educational and cultural exchange objectives.

Current State of TPS Designations and Parole Programs

As discussed in our July Business Immigration Monthly, Temporary Protected Status (TPS) has ended or is scheduled to end for many countries. Employers may wish to identify affected employees, monitor work authorization expiration dates, and ensure timely updates to their Form I-9 Employment Eligibility Verification records. Employees losing TPS-based work authorization should evaluate alternative immigration options as soon as possible.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Congressman John Garamendi (CA-08), Congresswoman Lateefah Simon (CA-12), Congresswoman Zoe Lofgren (CA-18) and Congressman Juan Vargas (CA-52) today announced the introduction of the Protect Our Neighbors Act, bicameral legislation to protect long-term immigrant residents who have lived and contributed to their communities for over 10 years.

This legislation was inspired by the story of Congressman Garamendi’s and Congresswoman Simon’s constituent, Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old grandmother who, despite living in the United States for over thirty years, was cruelly detained and later deported by ICE.

“President Trump promised to go after the ‘worst of the worst’ in his immigration policy. Yet his administration has repeatedly decided to cruelly deport residents who have been working, paying taxes, and raising families in their communities for decades,” said Rep. Garamendi (CA-08). This is exactly what happened to one of our constituents. Nearly one year ago, ICE cruelly detained and deported Harjit Kuar, a 73-year-old grandmother with no criminal record — who faithfully reported to ICE every six months for more than 13 years. Her cruel and unreasonable detention and deportation is just one more example of the thousands of individuals across the country whose lives and families have been upended by Trump’s ICE. Unfortunately, this has become far too common under Donald Trump’s mass deportation agenda, which is exactly why I’m proud to introduce this commonsense and humane fix to our immigration system with Representatives Simon, Lofgren and Vargas.”

“No one should have to live in constant fear of being torn away from their family and community after spending years building a life in this country. I am sick of the Trump Administration targeting our neighbors and threatening the lives they have worked so hard to build. These are people who have spent years contributing to our communities, working hard, and putting down roots,” said Congresswoman Simon (CA-12). “The Protect Our Neighbors Act would provide people, like Ms. Kaur who worked in my district for decades, with a fair opportunity to move beyond a final order of removal and continue building futures here in the U.S where they have made their homes and families. I am incredibly grateful to Congressmembers Garamendi, Lofgren, and Vargas for standing with me and partnering on this important legislation.”

“We need a sensible immigration policy for those who have resided peacefully for a long time in America and have been upstanding members of their communities,” said Congresswoman Lofgren (CA-18), a senior member of the House Judiciary Committee and a former immigration lawyer. “Detaining and deporting folks with no criminal record is not what Donald Trump campaigned on, and it’s not what the American people want. The Protect Our Communities Act provides long-term residents who have built their lives here with a fair opportunity to resolve outdated removal orders and earn lawful permanent status.”

“The Trump Administration’s anti-immigrant agenda is destroying lives. Trump isn’t going after the ‘worst of the worst,’” said Congressman Vargas (CA-52). “He’s terrorizing our communities and ripping families apart. I’m proud to introduce this legislation alongside Representatives Garamendi, Simon, and Lofgren to bring a commonsense fix to our immigration system. We need comprehensive immigration reform and an end to Trump’s mass deportation agenda.”

“We are still traumatized and horrified by the cruel treatment of our grandmother one year ago,” said Harjit Kaur’s family. “Harjit was a pillar to our family and our community. She spent over thirty years in the United States, raising her children and later her grandchildren, and became a grandmother figure to our whole community. What was worse about her treatment was how unnecessary it was. We tried to work with ICE to bring her back to India, but at every turn the agency chose the more violent and cruel path — denying her food, moving her in the middle of the night without letting us know, and sending her back without letting us say goodbye. The pain that we still feel today remains with the knowledge that Harjit is one of thousands who’ve experienced the same situation. We thank Congressman Garamendi, Senator Schiff, and Congresswoman Simon for their continued advocacy, and we hope that some good could come from Harjit’s story with this bill and others like it.”

BACKGROUND:

A final order of removal is a formal legal order requiring a noncitizen to leave the U.S., but it doesn’t always mean immediate removal. Removal can be delayed through deferred action, a stay, ongoing litigation, or other circumstances.

According to the American Immigration Council, roughly 1.19 million people with removal orders remain in the U.S., many having spent years building lives, raising families, and working here. Under President Trump, DHS and ICE have aggressively pursued individuals with final removal orders, regardless of how long the case had been deferred, putting long-term residents who have routinely complied with check-ins at renewed risk of detention and deportation.

The Protect Our Communities Act aims to protect these long-standing immigrants by:

Establishing a 10-year expiration on final orders of removal for individuals who have been continuously present in the U.S. and have not been convicted of a crime.

Amending the Immigration and Nationality Act to create a pathway to lawful permanent residency (green card) for individuals with expired orders of removal. This pathway includes an application fee and requirement to confirm an individual’s taxpaying status.

HARJIT KAUR BACKGROUND

Harjit Kaur, 73, had lived in the U.S. since the early 1990s and was a constituent of Congressman John Garamendi. After her asylum case was denied in 2012, she complied with ICE check-ins every six months for over 13 years.

On September 8, 2025, she was detained during a routine check-in and held at an ICE facility in Bakersfield. At around 2:00 am on September 19, she was transported in handcuffs to Los Angeles, flown to Georgia without notice to her family or attorney, and then placed on a charter flight to India — deported before her family, who had arranged to travel with her, could say goodbye.

Kaur had sought travel documents from the Indian Consulate but was reportedly turned away multiple times; she had not refused to return but couldn’t depart without valid documents. During her detention, she was held without a bed, forced to sleep on the floor, shackled during transfers, denied vegetarian meals for her religious beliefs, and denied adequate food, water, and medication.

Since her return to India, she has remained in contact with family but continues to face health issues without relatives nearby to help her.

text:
Immigration – and especially the White House’s focus on mass deportations – was a top issue for voters and candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

And the results are clear. Voters want a change. In exit polling published by NBC News, 59 percent of voters polled said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts had gone too far.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement say the agency arrested more than 491,000 people and deported more than 483,000 in the fiscal year 2026. That’s the most in the agency’s history – and more than last year’s record number of around 442,000.

And in a departure from the high-profile operations in urban areas that we’ve seen in the past, ICE’s presence is being felt in rural communities as well.

In September, an ICE crackdown in Kansas swept through the state’s agricultural heartland. About 110 people were arrested by ICE in southwest Kansas in the week of Sept. 22. And the economic effect was immediate – beef processing plants shortened and cancelled shifts as employees didn’t show up for work. Restaurants and hotels were unable to service guests without workers.

How did Trump’s efforts influence the election? And what will Congress do about immigration in the near future?

text:
Immigration and Customs Enforcement is paying telecommunications giant AT&T millions of dollars to have AT&T’s analysts sift through mountains of raw AT&T data for a wide variety of investigations, according to an internal ICE document obtained by 404 Media, other procurement records, and experts who reviewed those records. Civil liberty experts have called it a mass surveillance program, and they say the data can include trillions of phone records and location data.

The AT&T product, interchangeably called Data Analytics and Support Services or Data Analytical Services, appears to be related to an earlier surveillance program called Hemisphere, in which AT&T provided U.S. authorities at state, local, and federal levels access to AT&T user data. Though that program shut down, ICE is still paying for access to raw data under this new arrangement with AT&T, according to the restricted ICE procurement document obtained by 404 Media. The program likely affects more than just AT&T customers because the company connects phone calls for other phone companies, meaning non-customers are likely swept up too, according to a surveillance expert.

“This requirement provides ICE access to AT&T’s raw data and experienced analysts,” the document obtained by 404 Media reads.

AT&T told 404 Media the data is made available under a valid legal order, but experts point out it requires an administrative subpoena, which agencies can issue themselves and don’t require a judge’s approval, raising concerns that ICE can use the data for essentially whatever it wants. The document also shows how financial incentives play a part in providing data to ICE.

“The Biden administration shut down Hemisphere after I and Rep. Biggs repeatedly questioned this warrantless mass phone surveillance program. 404 Media’s reporting shows that the Trump-Vance administration has created a zombie version of Hemisphere surveillance, and given it to their chosen enforcers at ICE,” Senator Ron Wyden told 404 Media in a statement.

Christopher Soghoian, a surveillance expert who worked for Senator Wyden for a decade until September, told 404 Media, “It’s bad enough that AT&T is mining its customers’ private phone records as a paid service for ICE, but because AT&T is also mining the records of other wholesale telecom companies, consumers can’t vote with their wallets and switch carriers to protect their privacy.”

Last September, ICE posted a procurement record saying it awarded a contract to AT&T for access to its Data Analytics and Support Services. When ICE announced the purchase, an attached document to the listing was marked as “controlled” and not available to the public. 404 Media subsequently obtained the document through a Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) request with ICE. The Financial Times previously reported on the public procurement records but did not report on the restricted document at the time.

“OAQ [the Office of Acquisition Management] intends to procure, on a sole source basis, access to raw data and analytical services from a telecommunications company,” the restricted document reads. It says AT&T analysts will transform the AT&T data “into a suitable format” while “ensuring accurate technical interpretation to accomplish HSI’s investigative mission.” HSI is Homeland Security Investigations, the criminal investigative arm of ICE, which has traditionally focused on things like cybercrime and child abuse cases, but under the Trump administration has dramatically refocused on immigration violations and investigating voter fraud.

The document says the AT&T data will be used to support “a wide range of HSI investigations and agency priorities,” but the specific sorts of investigations, taking up several lines of the document, are redacted.

Another document previously obtained by Senator Wyden’s office lays out the sort of data collected by AT&T and the capabilities available under the Data Analytical Services program. Those services include linking multiple devices or phone numbers to an identified target; identifying devices that have had their SIM cards replaced; determining whether phones associated with an international investigation target have entered the U.S.; and deconflicting international phone numbers associated with targets. That document was provided by the Office of National Drug Control Policy (ONDCP), an obscure White House-affiliated entity that previously funded the Hemisphere program, and which 404 Media reported is behind a growing nationwide network of automatic license plate readers (ALPRs). According to documents previously obtained by the EFF and EPIC, the AT&T program contains more than a trillion phone records.

Soghoian added AT&T also provides “wholesale service to other phone companies, helping them to deliver calls.” Through that, “AT&T is able to collect, save, and mine records of calls by customers of other companies, even conversations in which both callers use non-AT&T phone companies.”

The restricted document 404 Media obtained says that during Fiscal Year 2025, there was a higher demand for data provided by this AT&T system, and “further significant increase in use is anticipated.”

“AT&T is the only vendor who possesses the ability to access AT&T owned raw data,” the document continues. “The requirement is data and analytical services provided by AT&T. If AT&T does not execute the analytical work, the capability will be lost, as no other company has access to the data required.”

Public procurement records show ICE paid AT&T more than $2.1 million in 2025 for access to the service, and more than $2.2 million this August, with the possibility to pay up to more than ten million dollars over the coming years.

“ICE appears to have contracted for access to the same data and service AT&T provided for the Data Analytical Services (DAS) Program, formerly known as the Hemisphere Project, which is the largest telephone record collection program reported to date. ICE using DAS or something akin to it would potentially come with access to trillions of phone records and location data,” Jeramie Scott, senior counsel at EPIC and director of EPIC's Surveillance Oversight Program, told 404 Media. “This program is ripe for abuse and is being used by an agency known for the abuse of its authority.”

“This is AT&T continuing to leverage its phone service to conduct mass, indiscriminate surveillance to sell to law enforcement,” Scott added. “ICE is now taking advantage of AT&T’s surveillance as a service model while likely evading any judicial oversight and conducting no privacy impact assessment prior to using the service to determine whether it should be used in the first place. Spoiler alert: It shouldn’t!”

Scott pointed out the data likely includes location information too, and this raises the question whether the program violates the law given Supreme Court rulings Carpenter and Chatrie. The former ruled that law enforcement needed a warrant to obtain phone location data. The latter made a similar judgment around location data and geofence warrants.

“Americans are pushing back on government surveillance, from Flock cameras to FISA, all across the country and will be rightfully outraged that AT&T is allowing ICE to search through its customers' phone records without a warrant or court oversight,” Senator Wyden added.

An AT&T spokesperson told 404 Media in an email, “For decades, we have been a trusted partner to provide reliable connectivity to federal agencies as well as state and local governments. We are required by law to provide information to government and law enforcement agencies when it is demanded under lawful order. We ensure that these requests are valid, and that our responses comply with the law.”

ICE did not respond to multiple requests for comment, but previously told the Financial Times, “Nothing new here. For years law enforcement across the nation has leveraged technological innovation to fight crime. ICE is no different.”

The precursor to Data Analytical Services was a program called Hemisphere. The New York Times first revealed Hemisphere in 2013, in which AT&T employees sat alongside Drug Enforcement Administration agents and supplied them with phone data going as far back as 1987. Authorities said they stopped federal funding for Hemisphere in September 2024 and shut the program down. But Data Analytical Services is essentially a continuation of that program. The document Senator Wyden’s office previously obtained says that Data Analytical Services was previously called Hemisphere.

“Hemisphere is a surveillance program that refuses to die and keeps coming back with different names and different forms,” Soghoian added. “It is now clear that the Biden White House misled Congress when it said that Hemisphere had been shut down. The White House drug office funded program used by state and local law enforcement may be gone, but federal agencies are continuing to pay AT&T for the same services.”

description:

Immigration and Customs Enforcement say the agency arrested more than 491,000 people and deported more than 483,000 in the fiscal year 2026.
Nearly 60% of illegal aliens ICE arrested across the country have criminal convictions or pending criminal charges just in the U.S.
President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences.
Illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.
text:
Immigration – and especially the White House’s focus on mass deportations – was a top issue for voters and candidates ahead of the midterm elections.

And the results are clear. Voters want a change. In exit polling published by NBC News, 59 percent of voters polled said the Trump administration’s immigration enforcement efforts had gone too far.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement say the agency arrested more than 491,000 people and deported more than 483,000 in the fiscal year 2026. That’s the most in the agency’s history – and more than last year’s record number of around 442,000.

And in a departure from the high-profile operations in urban areas that we’ve seen in the past, ICE’s presence is being felt in rural communities as well.

In September, an ICE crackdown in Kansas swept through the state’s agricultural heartland. About 110 people were arrested by ICE in southwest Kansas in the week of Sept. 22. And the economic effect was immediate – beef processing plants shortened and cancelled shifts as employees didn’t show up for work. Restaurants and hotels were unable to service guests without workers.

How did Trump’s efforts influence the election? And what will Congress do about immigration in the near future?

The Department of Homeland Security sent us this statement…

ICE is NOT backing away or slowing down. Under the leadership of President Trump and Secretary Mullin, DHS will continue to enforce our nation’s laws and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets. The results speak for themselves. Less than two years after President Trump returned to office, he has fulfilled his signature promise to secure our border, arrest, and deport illegal aliens, and Make America Safe Again. Our mission continues.

Nationwide our law enforcement is targeting public safety threats—including murderers, rapists, gang members, pedophiles, and terrorists. Nearly 60% of illegal aliens ICE arrested across the country have criminal convictions or pending criminal charges just in the U.S. This statistic doesn’t account for those wanted for violent crimes in their home country or another country, INTERPOL notices, human rights abusers, gang members, terrorists, etc. The list goes on.

President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences. Illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S.

text:
A federal appeals court has agreed to keep deportation protections frozen for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, shortly after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

The order handed down late Wednesday means the administration remains free to detain and deport Venezuelans who had previously been granted temporary protected status. Federal attorneys have said some 1,800 are in detention, and about 330 are subject to deportation proceedings.

The Supreme Court previously intervened to allow the administration to temporarily end the program for Venezuelans.

Congress created the TPS program in 1990 to protect migrants from deportation to countries experiencing natural disasters or civil unrest. The designation is granted in periods of up to 18 months.

The Trump administration argues that TPS is a temporary program and that Venezuela no longer meets the requirements for its renewal.

During President Donald Trump's second term, the Department of Homeland Security has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

However, in a shift in policy in recent months, the administration has maintained protections for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans and more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan.

TPS was first granted to Venezuelans in March 2021, under Democratic President Joe Biden. The designation was expanded in September 2023 to cover additional beneficiaries. About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections.

The Trump administration's move to end protections for Venezuelans was challenged in court, and a California-based judge ruled it unlawful. The Supreme Court twice intervened with temporary emergency orders, and later sent the case back to an appeals court after upholding the end of TPS for Haitians in a different case.

The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to rule when the administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, arguing that a temporary pause would soon expire and allow the restoration of deportation protections. Hours later, the appeals court extended its temporary freeze on protections until seven days after it hands down a full ruling.

After the Trump administration terminated TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also became invalid. Thousands faced deportation proceedings, detention and removal. Many others chose to leave the country voluntarily.

It remains unclear how many Venezuelans who previously held TPS are still living in the United States.

text:
What Is Happening With Venezuelan TPS?

The legal battle over Temporary Protected Status for Venezuelans continues.

On November 18, the federal government filed an emergency request with the U.S. Supreme Court seeking to prevent the reinstatement of TPS protections while litigation proceeds.

Later that day, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals extended its temporary stay until seven days after the court issues its forthcoming decision. As a result, the anticipated restoration of TPS protections on November 20 will not take effect as previously expected.

The court has not yet resolved the underlying dispute over the termination of these protections.

For Venezuelans affected by this uncertainty, I recommend reviewing their individual immigration circumstances to determine whether other legal options may be available.

Some may have pending asylum claims supported by substantial evidence. Others may qualify for family-based immigration petitions or have potential employment-based opportunities.

In my practice, I have encountered professionals whose employers are willing to sponsor them for permanent residence. However, an employment petition does not automatically provide lawful immigration status or guarantee eligibility for an immigrant visa.

What Does the Latest I-220A Decision Mean for Cubans?

On November 17, 2026, the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals issued its decision in Aguiar-Fernandez v. U.S. Attorney General.

The court ruled that release from immigration detention under 8 U.S.C. § 1226 does not constitute the humanitarian parole required to qualify for adjustment of status under the Cuban Adjustment Act.

This decision is particularly important for affected Cuban immigrants in Florida, Georgia, and Alabama, the states within the Eleventh Circuit.

However, the ruling does not mean that every Cuban holding an I-220A has an identical immigration case. Each person’s entry records, immigration history, and potential eligibility for other forms of relief must be examined individually.

During the interview, we also discussed the Calderon Jimenez settlement, which provides specific protections for certain immigrants with final removal orders who are married to U.S. citizens and meet additional requirements in New England.

The settlement is not a general solution for all I-220A holders. Its protections depend on strict eligibility requirements and do not automatically apply simply because someone files an I-130 petition or moves to another state.

What Immigration Options May Still Be Available?

One of the most important points I emphasized during the interview is that a setback in one immigration process does not necessarily mean every legal alternative has been exhausted.

Depending on the circumstances, options may include asylum, family petitions, employment-based immigration, consular processing, or certain immigration waivers.

However, leaving the United States can trigger serious immigration consequences, including potential three-year or ten-year unlawful-presence bars. Not everyone qualifies for a waiver, and approval of a petition alone does not guarantee permission to return.

Before leaving the country, relocating to another state, or making significant changes to an immigration case, it is essential to understand the legal consequences.

I appreciate the opportunity to discuss these important developments with the N+ Univision 24/7 team and help our community stay informed.

My recommendation remains the same: review your immigration history carefully, understand the decisions affecting your situation, and seek individualized legal guidance before taking steps that could affect your future.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senator Tim Kaine (D-VA), a member of the Senate Armed Services and Foreign Relations Committees, introduced a resolution to force the Trump-Vance Administration to provide answers to Congress about the human rights implications and other impacts of recent decisions that benefit Russia at the expense of our allies. Specifically, the resolution requests more information about how the purchase of Russian diesel, easing of sanctions, delays in the delivery of air defense munitions, and manipulation of early warning notifications of impending missile strikes has affected Russia’s ability to wage war in Ukraine and allowed it to worsen its campaign of horrific human rights abuses. It also requests an update on the current status of negotiations to end the war. The resolution is privileged under Section 502B(c) of the Foreign Assistance Act, meaning Kaine can call it up for a vote on the Senate floor soon.

“Instead of standing with our democratic allies, President Trump has cozied up to dictators like Vladimir Putin. The Administration’s recent decisions to delay deliveries of Patriot interceptors, waive certain Russian sanctions, and buy diesel from Russia—after launching an illegal, unnecessary, and costly war in Iran—are short-sighted. We should not be buying Russian fuel from Putin so that he can turn around and use American dollars to bomb and kill innocent Ukrainians, commit human rights violations, and prop up Iran,” said Kaine. “Sunlight is the best disinfectant, and this resolution would assess the consequences of this Administration’s recent actions. I urge my colleagues to support it.”

Kaine has introduced several privileged resolutions under the Foreign Assistance Act to challenge the Administration’s third-country deportation network. In May 2025, he forced a vote in the Senate to require the Administration to produce a human rights report regarding El Salvador after the Trump-Vance Administration deported Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia to El Salvador and President Trump threatened to imprison U.S. citizens there. Kaine also joined his colleagues in introducing a resolution requiring a report on the growing violence in the West Bank, including the deaths of nine Americans in recent years.

title: Senator Unveils Bill to Force More Disclosure of Deaths in ICE Custody - TIME
description:
“We cannot allow ICE and CBP to skirt accountability for their abuses at detention facilities around the country,” Kim said.
Private contractors, which run most of the ICE detention facilities, need to abide by death reporting requirements when agreeing to run detention facilities for the agency.
The number of deaths in ICE detention centers has been on the rise nationwide.
ICE has so far reported 29 detention deaths in 2026, second only to the 33 recorded in 2025.
A sizable portion of the deaths in ICE detention centers are a result of medical neglect.
text:
The Death in Detention Transparency Act put forward by Kim would beef up what Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) is required to tell Congress when a detainee dies in a detention center, hospital, or while being transported. Lawmakers and activists have complained that the Trump Administration has dragged its feet on making such notifications, and provided scant details about the conditions under which dozens of people have died.

“We cannot allow ICE and CBP to skirt accountability for their abuses at detention facilities around the country,” Kim said. “We cannot allow them to try to cover up how many people have died under their watch.”

The bill would cut the timeline from 90 days to 30 days when ICE has to make a report on a detainee death public, and would also require ICE disclose any deaths that happened during an enforcement operation, such as an arrest or a traffic stop.

Details regarding the death, including a copy of the results of an independent autopsy, and information such whether a firearm was discharged and if there is any relevant body camera footage, would also need to be included in the public report.

Private contractors, which run most of the ICE detention facilities, need to abide by death reporting requirements when agreeing to run detention facilities for the agency. Failure to comply on more than three occasions would subject a contractor to a five-year suspension of operations, along with other enforcement measures, according to the bill.

Kim’s office said the legislation is in response to the death of three detainees in less than eight months from Delaney Hall in New Jersey, a privately-owned facility run by GEO Group that was plagued with allegations of unsanitary living conditions and medical neglect. ICE has refused to disclose details of the third death, saying only that the detainee experienced a “medical emergency” and was released from ICE’s custody to a local hospital. The agency in June stopped reporting the deaths of those detainees who had been released from federal custody, claiming that it is not responsible for “monitoring or reviewing deaths that may occur.”

Kim, a member of the Senate Homeland Security Committee who has visited the Delaney Hall facility multiple times, says the bill would help to ensure no family is left in the dark about what is happening to their loved ones in the detention facilities.

The Senate bill comes on the heels of New Jersey Attorney General Jennifer Davenport suing the Department of Homeland Security on Tuesday to compel information regarding the medical care provided inside Delaney Hall and whether they were properly licensed. The state government is also seeking records of what happened when detainees sought treatment and documentation of injuries, deaths and emergency hospital visits. Davenport’s suit came after GEO Group declined to cooperate with New Jersey’s investigation into the facility, arguing that the records were federal documents and the state needed to go through the Department of Homeland Security for access.

Delaney Hall has also become a flashpoint for protests and clashes over congressional oversight. In May, Kim was pepper sprayed by federal agents outside the facility as he tried to defuse a confrontation with demonstrators. A year earlier, Rep. LaMonica McIver of New Jersey was indicted on charges of forcibly impeding and interfering with federal officers during an oversight visit. She disputed the allegations and called the prosecution politically motivated.

The number of deaths in ICE detention centers has been on the rise nationwide. ICE has so far reported 29 detention deaths in 2026, second only to the 33 recorded in 2025. A sizable portion of the deaths in ICE detention centers are a result of medical neglect. The agency’s own internal investigators said that staff members at the detention facilities “deviated from safe limits of practice” or “did not provide medical care within safe limits of practice” in at least 23 of the 33 deaths reported in 2025, according to records obtained by the San Francisco Chronicle. The investigator also said medical staff failed to perform CPR correctly or at all on immigrant detainees who then died in eight different instances.

text:
For audio listeners, you can listen to our audio version of the News Digest here. You can also join our Immigration News Digest Newsletter here.

Federal Court Invalidates Fixed Admission Rule for F-1, J-1, and I Visa Holders

DOL Proposes Major PERM Reforms Affecting Recruitment and Employer Compliance

Vietnam Expands Work Permit Eligibility and Introduces New Immigration Reforms

Federal Court Invalidates Fixed Admission Rule for F-1, J-1, and I Visa Holders

A federal district court in Massachusetts has vacated the Department of Homeland Security’s regulation that would have replaced the longstanding Duration of Status (D/S) framework with fixed admission periods for F-1 students, J-1 exchange visitors, I foreign media representatives, and their dependents.

In Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration v. DHS, U.S. District Judge Dennis Saylor granted summary judgment in favor of the plaintiffs, finding that the regulation exceeded DHS’s statutory authority and conflicted with Congress’s intent in establishing the affected nonimmigrant visa programs.

The rule would have required affected foreign nationals to comply with fixed admission expiration dates rather than generally remaining in the United States for the duration of their qualifying academic, exchange, or professional activities. Individuals needing additional time would have been required to seek extensions of stay through USCIS.

The decision follows a legal challenge filed in August 2026 by a coalition of educational organizations and labor unions. In September, the court temporarily postponed implementation of the regulation while litigation continued.

Unlike the earlier postponement, the latest ruling vacates the regulation itself, providing more substantial relief to affected foreign nationals and institutions.

For now, the existing Duration of Status framework remains in place, although students and exchange visitors must continue complying with all applicable immigration and employment authorization requirements.

The Administration is expected to appeal the decision, meaning further legal developments could affect the rule’s future.

Impact: The ruling removes the immediate threat of fixed admission periods and additional extension requirements for affected F-1, J-1, and I nonimmigrants. Employers, universities, and research institutions can continue operating under the existing D/S framework while monitoring potential appeals and further DHS guidance.

DOL Proposes Major PERM Reforms Affecting Recruitment and Employer Compliance

The Department of Labor has released a proposed rule that would significantly overhaul the PERM labor certification program, a critical step in many employment-based green card cases. Scheduled for publication in the Federal Register on November 17, 2026, the proposal introduces major changes to recruitment requirements, workforce reductions, and employer compliance obligations.

Among the most significant proposed changes are:

Elimination of Schedule A: The streamlined labor certification process for certain occupations, including registered nurses and physical therapists, would be eliminated.

Modernized recruitment: Traditional newspaper advertising requirements would be replaced with digital recruitment methods, including online job boards, employer websites, and social media.

Stricter layoff restrictions: Employers could face a two-year restriction on PERM filings following qualifying layoffs, along with additional obligations involving affected U.S. workers.

Expanded compliance requirements: New provisions would address remote and hybrid work arrangements, employer attestations, recordkeeping, and electronic filing procedures.

The proposal could also introduce additional considerations for employers undergoing workforce reductions while PERM applications or I-140 immigrant petitions are pending.

Importantly, the proposed changes are not yet in effect. Employers must continue following existing PERM regulations while DOL completes the rulemaking process. A 60-day public comment period is expected following publication.

Impact: If finalized, the reforms could substantially reshape employer-sponsored green card strategies, particularly for healthcare organizations, employers conducting layoffs, and businesses with remote or geographically dispersed workforces. Employers should review recruitment procedures, evaluate potential impacts on pending sponsorship cases, and coordinate workforce planning with immigration counsel.

Vietnam Expands Work Permit Eligibility and Introduces New Immigration Reforms

Vietnam has announced significant changes to its foreign worker regulations under Decree 393, scheduled to take effect December 5, 2026. The new framework will replace Decree 219 and introduce broader eligibility for foreign professionals, expanded work permit exemptions, and streamlined application procedures.

One of the most significant changes expands eligibility for foreign experts. Individuals with at least five years of relevant professional experience may qualify for expert classification without meeting the previous academic qualification requirement, potentially opening additional opportunities for international talent.

Other key reforms include:

Expanded work permit exemptions: New exemptions for certain technology and artificial intelligence professionals, researchers, educators, and other qualifying foreign workers.

Simplified health requirements: Medical certificates issued by eligible overseas facilities will be accepted, while standard work permit renewals will no longer require new health certificates.

Revised intracompany transfers: Technical workers will no longer qualify under the intracompany transfer category, which will be limited to managers, executives, and experts.

Faster renewals: Renewal applications may be submitted up to 90 days before expiration, with government processing times reduced from 10 to five business days.

text:
Federal auditors warned Thursday that Immigration and Customs Enforcement is spending billions of dollars to expand immigration detention without "determining the cost effectiveness" of new initiatives or keeping its spending plan up to date.

A new report released by the Government Accountability Office examined how ICE has managed the $45 billion in detention funding provided under the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

"A January 2025 Executive Order directed DHS to increase efforts to detain individuals apprehended for violations of immigration law and to allocate all available resources for ICE detention," according to the report. "ICE received significant funding in July 2025 to operate and expand detention facilities."

According to GAO, ICE acquired 11 warehouses to be converted into immigration detention centers for about $1.07 billion before scaling back the initiative and planning to sell seven of them. The facilities ranged in cost from $35 million and $145 million.

For nine of the warehouses, ICE paid at least 50% more than the state or local government assessment of taxable value, auditors found. In one example, the agency purchased a warehouse in Social Circle, Georgia, for about $128.6 million after a previous buyer purchased it in 2023 for about $29.4 million.

"Our analysis of ICE documentation and public records showed that ICE potentially overpaid for many of the warehouses it purchased," auditors wrote. "Moreover, given ICE's plans to sell seven of the warehouses -- six for which it paid at least double the assessed value -- there is risk that these sales could result in financial losses to the federal government."

In July and August 2026, ICE also bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion total.

A spokesperson for the Department of Homeland Security did not immediately respond to a request for comment from ABC News.

Auditors also pointed to high-cost detention operations on military bases. ICE has obligated more than $1 billion to Camp East Montana on the grounds of Texas' Fort Bliss.

"ICE obligated over $1 billion to one facility, Camp East Montana, representing 36 percent of total obligations to detention facilities in the first three quarters of fiscal year 2026," auditors wrote. "We previously reported on cost efficiency concerns related to contract design and administration at Camp East Montana."

At the Guantanamo Bay Naval Base in Cuba, ICE and the Defense Department obligated roughly $111 million for two facilities despite an average daily population of fewer than 30 detainees. ICE previously said it would use Guantanamo Bay to hold "high-threat noncitizens" but has held "multiple noncitizens who had no criminal convictions or pending charges," auditors wrote.

According to the report, ICE plans to continue using Guantanamo Bay "based on direction from senior leadership and the White House."

GAO recommended that "ICE update its spending plan for detention funding in accordance with internal guidance, and develop life-cycle cost estimates, in coordination with DHS, before making new detention investments."

According to GAO, DHS concurred with the recommendations.
