text:
I

n a major escalation of efforts to curb irregular migration, five European Union member states have unveiled formal plans to establish an offshore deportation and return hub in Rwanda. The proposed scheme, announced in Vienna, marks a significant shift in European migration policy as centrist governments seek tougher measures to deter unauthorized arrivals and counter rising far-right political momentum.

Under the framework currently under negotiation, Germany, Austria, Greece, Denmark, and the Netherlands plan to transfer rejected asylum seekers—individuals who have exhausted all legal avenues to remain within the EU—to a dedicated center in Rwanda. According to Rwandan officials, migrants housed at the facility would be given options to voluntarily return to their countries of origin, integrate into Rwandan society, or seek relocation to another nation where they possess a legal right to reside.

Proponents of the agreement argue that establishing an external return mechanism will serve as a vital deterrent. Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen hailed the initiative at a joint press conference as a potential “game changer” for confronting systemic migration challenges, asserting that it will help dismantle the business models of human smuggling networks and restore tighter control over European borders.

A pilot approach and scale

Unlike previous controversial proposals—such as the United Kingdom’s former, now-scrapped deportation scheme which targeted asylum seekers while their legal claims were still being processed—the new five-nation EU initiative strictly applies only to individuals whose claims have already been definitively rejected.

While discussions are ongoing and a finalized agreement is targeted for early 2027, participating officials indicated that the initial phase will operate on a modest scale. The proposed pilot center is expected to accommodate approximately 100 people at any given time—roughly 20 individuals per participating country. Proponents describe the limited capacity as a calculated test phase designed to prove the operational viability of third-country returns under the framework of the European Union’s newly adopted Return Regulation.

Rwanda has signaled its willingness to host the initiative without demanding direct service payments, though participating European nations will cover the financial costs associated with relocation and local integration. Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta emphasized that his country aims to offer a constructive solution to a global challenge rather than acting merely on a transactional basis.

Human rights condemnation

The announcement has triggered swift and severe backlash from international human rights organizations, humanitarian groups, and trade unions. In a joint statement, 47 advocacy organizations—including Amnesty International, the International Rescue Committee, and various national refugee councils—urged the five governments to abandon the project.

Critics argue that outsourcing migration management to Rwanda exposes vulnerable individuals to severe human rights violations. Human rights advocates point to persistent concerns regarding Rwanda’s domestic political freedoms, suppression of dissent, and allegations of regional instability, warning that externalized return hubs lack adequate oversight and independent scrutiny.

Despite these intense criticisms, the participating European governments remain committed to finalizing the framework. As negotiations proceed toward a formal rollout, the initiative is being closely watched across the continent as a precedent-setting test case for European immigration enforcement.

(Source: CNN)

text:
More asylum hotels have closed as the government accelerates plans to end their use entirely and continues to restore fairness and control to Britain’s immigration system.

From Bournemouth to Falkirk, 8 further asylum hotels have been returned to communities across the UK since the summer.

This means a total of 52 hotels have closed so far this year, leaving around 140 open – down from 400 at the 2023 peak and 213 at the 2024 election. The number of people in asylum hotels has halved in just a year to 16,000, down 71% from a peak of 56,000 under the previous government.

The closures announced today are expected to reduce asylum costs by around £16 million – building on more than £1 billion already saved since the election.

This is possible because of system-wide immigration reforms made under this government, including a significant drop in small boat arrivals, a fourfold increase in asylum decision making, a 21% reduction in asylum claims, and the highest level of removals in nearly a decade.

Alongside this, the Home Secretary is going further through new legislation to stop migrants from exploiting the system. The Immigration and Asylum Bill, which passed third reading in Parliament earlier this week, will discourage unfounded, late and repeated asylum claims, strengthen decision making, and bring cases to a conclusion quicker.

This action forms part of the government’s drive to deliver a fairer, more controlled asylum system across the UK, which reduces the burden on local communities.

Border Security and Asylum Minister, Anna Turley, said:

This government is restoring fairness and control to an immigration system that had spiralled out of control, with hundreds of expensive asylum hotels opened up across the country.

Thanks to our reforms, small boat arrivals and asylum claims are down while processing and removals are up, meaning thousands fewer asylum seekers are relying on taxpayer-funded support.

That is why more hotels are closing and we won’t stop until they are all shut for good.

While asylum hotels continue to close, the overall asylum population is also falling. 13,800 fewer people are now in taxpayer funded accommodation compared to last year, marking a 13% reduction.

More efficient processes mean those who have their asylum claims approved are swiftly moved on from the asylum estate, while those who are refused are removed from the country wherever possible.

While claims are considered, rather than staying in costly hotels, asylum seekers are being moved to alternative and more basic forms of accommodation. This includes former military barracks.

Unlike hotels, large sites provide greater control and are self-contained, with essential on-site services and 24/7 CCTV and security.

These hotel closures follow on from the government announcing yesterday that asylum seekers who are caught working illegally could now be stripped of their support payments and accommodation, removing another pull factor driving illegal migration to the UK.

Taken together, these reforms are fixing an asylum system left under extraordinary pressure.

description:

U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney excoriated top Colorado ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials in a 15-page ruling.

Sweeney wrote on Wednesday that that testimony saved the federal government from greater consequences.
text:
A Colorado federal judge on Wednesday held Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials in contempt of court for repeatedly violating judicial orders by re-detaining immigrants after they had been ordered to be released from detention.

U.S. District Court Judge Charlotte Sweeney excoriated top Colorado ICE and Department of Homeland Security officials in a 15-page ruling. The contempt amounts to a stern warning that they better start reading and complying with judicial orders in relation to immigrants in detention.

Or, they potentially will face greater punishment.

“ICE’s new ‘policy’ of immediately re-detaining petitioners following release made a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release,” Sweeney wrote. “Lest there be any confusion: All orders and judgments of courts must be complied with promptly … This is neither a novel nor complex statement to comprehend.”

At least 18 people in Colorado, and immigration attorneys estimate it’s higher given immigrants who represent themselves, have been held in detention longer than they should have or have been re-arrested within minutes of their judge-ordered release in the past six weeks.

“Sometimes, behavior stuns and renders a listener speechless,” Sweeney wrote in her contempt ruling. “To the extent any reader may be lost for words as to what ICE and (the federal government) did in this case and others in this judicial district like it — and the ridiculous nature of the justification for their behavior — turn to what the Supreme Court has said repeatedly over the course of our nation’s history. The government of the United States has been emphatically termed a government of laws and not of men.”

Judges have broad powers when holding people in contempt, which can include fines or ordering behavior stopped. Wednesday’s ruling by Sweeney stopped short of any of those sanctions and mostly amounted to a scolding by an equal, but separate, branch of the federal government.

Sweeney’s strong words on Wednesday, though, which were laced with maxims from the Constitution and dozens of court cases rendered over decades, indicated that if there were any more violations of judicial orders she wouldn’t hesitate to open this back up.

“Our system of jurisprudence rests on the assumption that all individuals, whatever their position in government, are subject to federal law,” she said, citing a 1979 case. “No man is above the law.”

The case at issue in front of Judge Sweeney was the illegal detention of Ramon Quintero Alvarez, who was born in Mexico and entered the United States with his mother between 1993 and 1994. Alvarez has not left the United States since arriving more than 30 years ago. Alvarez told the judge that he has lived in Wyoming for 12 years with his two American-born sons.

The respondents, represented by the U.S. Attorney’s Office, didn’t challenge any of these facts in an October hearing in which Alvarez was seeking a writ of habeas corpus, which essentially means he could be released from detention while fighting his immigration case.

The Colorado U.S. Attorney’s Office, led by Peter McNeilly, failed to show cause as to why Alvarez should not be let out of detention by Oct. 27. Alvarez was then released from immigration custody, but was immediately re-detained after he took a few steps in freedom.

This, Sweeney said, was unlawful.

During a series of hearings held about this and other similar cases in front of other Colorado federal judges, ICE officials, under oath, seemed like they didn’t know about who was in charge and about what rules they should be following.

Nichole Black, the assistant field office director for ICE’s Enforcement and Removal Operations, told Sweeney that she “received a direct order” from her supervisor that she could “re-detain” immigrants “that had some type of criminality.”

“Ms. Black said in her own words that she believed it was permissible to simply escort someone to a public area and immediately re-detain them despite a court order to the contrary,” Sweeney wrote. “This should — and in the court’s opinion, must — shock any reader.”

Black’s supervisor, Nathan Rasper, told Sweeney that he thought he was under the obligation to “make lawful arrests” and that he heard he could re-arrest people based on a policy in Minnesota.

Rasper did tell a visibly frustrated Sweeney at the hearing earlier this month that he had stopped re-arresting people who were ordered released from detention.

Sweeney wrote on Wednesday that that testimony saved the federal government from greater consequences.

“Given the (government) cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue, the court declines to take any further action,” she wrote.

U.S. Attorney McNeilly, who attended at least one of the hearings before irate federal judges in recent weeks as a spectator in the bench seats, had no comment Wednesday on Sweeney’s order.

Prominent Cambodian activist monk But Buntenh has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to the agency’s online detainee database and members of the Cambodian community in the United States.

Buntenh was taken into custody Sunday, according to a community member, and is being held at the Pine Prairie ICE Processing Center in Louisiana, according to the database. The reason for his arrest and where it took place were not immediately clear.

ICE did not immediately respond to an emailed request for comment sent after business hours. It was not clear whether Buntenh faces deportation to Cambodia.

Buntenh, 46, founded the Independent Monk Network for Social Justice and is known for his environmental advocacy and his criticism of the Cambodian government. He fled to the U.S. in 2017 after facing criminal charges in Cambodia that human rights groups widely condemned as politically motivated. A Cambodian court convicted him in absentia in 2020 and sentenced him to 20 months in prison for incitement. He has been based in Massachusetts in recent years, according to Radio Free Asia.

Muong Nareth, a former Radio Free Asia reporter who lives in California and hosts a popular YouTube channel on Cambodian affairs, said in a video Thursday that Buntenh was arrested while traveling. Nareth said the detention was “discriminatory” and that Buntenh holds valid documents to remain in the U.S. Nareth did not immediately respond to a message sent through Facebook.

Am Sam Ath, operations director at the Cambodian rights group Licadho, said Buntenh’s activism and criticism of the government could put him at risk if he is returned to Cambodia.

“If he is deported back, it truly will be a risk and concern for his safety,” he said. He added that Buntenh’s legal status and his role at a pagoda in the U.S. might help him avoid deportation.

Since U.S. President Donald Trump returned to office in January 2025, his administration has pursued a sweeping immigration crackdown that it says targets people living in the country illegally.

text:
Congress Must Provide Lasting Solutions to Mitigate Ongoing ‘Delegalization’ Campaign

Washington DC, Nov. 19 2026 – A new report provides the most complete account to date of one of the defining trends of the second Trump administration: a deliberate and ongoing effort to strip protections away from people who are living and working here legally, creating a new population of people vulnerable to detention and deportation. The report finds that since Trump has taken office, more people have been “delegalized” than deported.

Released by the American Immigration Council, the report is titled Mass Delegalization: How the Trump Administration Took Away Legal Protections from Millions of Immigrants Following the Rules. It provides a definition and framework for understanding the Trump administration’s “delegalization” efforts – a term which, along with “de-documentation,” has been used to refer to the federal government’s systematic stripping of executive-branch protections from immigrants who had been authorized to live or work in the United States.

As a new majority sets its priorities for the coming Congress, the Council’s report identifies how the legislative branch is fundamentally responsible for creating the conditions that have allowed “delegalization” to occur – and calls on them to solve the problem, by passing bills to protect these newly-undocumented populations in the next two years.

“Mass delegalization is happening because of a lack of action from Congress. The failure to deliver solutions means that the executive branch has had to rely on these temporary fixes, so changes in administration can lead the pendulum to swing back the other way. Temporary fixes aren’t a substitute for an immigration system that actually works. Congress needs to deliver on lasting solutions, so that people who’ve followed the rules and built their lives here don’t have to worry that a new president could suddenly take away their ability to stay and work legally,” said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council.

READ THE REPORT HERE

Many of those affected followed the government’s rules, paid fees, and maintained their legal protections for years and even decades. Over a million people have lost protections under the humanitarian program Temporary Protected Status (TPS), while another 300,000 have lost protections under the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program (DACA) and the Cuban, Haitian, Nicaraguan and Venezuelan parole program (CHNV). The full number of people affected by the Trump administration’s broader delegalization policies are unknown.

The report identifies two main ways the administration is carrying out mass delegalization:

Ending legal protections for entire groups of people living in the United States. This is what happened with many TPS designations and the humanitarian parole protections that benefitted Venezuelans, Haitians, and Cubans, among other countries. Some people have had these protections for decades, including Hondurans and Nicaraguans who’ve held TPS since 1998.

Making it harder for certain groups of immigrants to keep their protections. This includes Dreamers, people who came here as vulnerable migrant children, and victims of crime and trafficking.

The report found that thanks in part to this ongoing mass delegalization campaign, the number of Dreamers protected from deportation under DACA has dropped sharply. When Trump took office in January 2025, more than 530,000 people were enrolled in DACA. By June 2026, that number had fallen to 436,000, after the administration made several policy changes that made it harder for Dreamers to maintain their status. This is the steepest drop in the number of Dreamers since the government stopped accepting new applicants in 2018.

The report argues that the Trump administration’s ability to carry out mass delegalization exposes a problem that has been exacerbating for decades: Congress’s failure to create options so that people who’ve immigrated and who have lived and worked in the United States for years can apply for permanent legal status.

The report calls on the incoming Congress to expand oversight into the Trump administration’s delegalization campaign and take action to create accessible pathways to permanent legal status for immigrants who have lived and worked in the United States for years.

“The point of the rule of law is supposed to be to encourage compliance. It undermines the whole point when people spend years making an effort to follow all the rules set out for them, only to have the protections they had yanked away,” said Dara Lind, senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. “These people have been relying on the government for protection, and their employers, families and neighbors have come to rely on them in turn. You can’t just remove these people from the workforce without destabilizing entire American communities.”

READ THE REPORT HERE

The American Immigration Council works to create a more welcoming and fair immigration system. Through litigation, research, and programs that expand access to legal assistance, the Council helps ensure immigrants are embraced, communities are enriched, and justice prevails for all. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization.
Civil rights advocates fear Cair’s targeting is only the beginning of Florida exploiting its power to cripple all kinds of lawful advocacy, especially the pro-Palestinian movement.
Aside from Cair, Florida also applied the domestic terrorist designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and “antifa” – a vague umbrella term for far-left-leaning and anarchist anti-fascist groups and individuals.

He dreams of attending law school and working at a civil rights non-profit; he interned at Cair-Florida this summer.
text:
Omar Soboh, a student at the University of Florida, was organizing a campus panel about Islamophobia when he found out one of the groups being represented had suddenly been blacklisted by the state. Under a new process, Florida had designated the Council on American-Islamic Relations (Cair), the nation’s largest Muslim civil rights group, a domestic terrorist organization. The university’s Arab Students’ Association decided to cancel the event, and Soboh, who is Palestinian American, was disheartened.

“Our existence itself is political,” he said.

In July, Governor Ron DeSantis approved legislation giving five state officials the power to designate groups as “domestic terrorist” organizations. Once the designation goes into effect, as it did on 5 November for Cair and its Florida chapter, it can trigger debilitating penalties for the group and its supporters under state law.

The threat of these punishments effectively forces designated groups to shut down, said Cair. In turn, the group has sued Florida officials, including DeSantis, in federal court with the help of the American Civil Liberties Union, alleging violations of free speech and due process. Cair-Florida’s website homepage is now pitch black, except for a note stating that staff has suspended operations because of the “baseless and unconstitutional enforcement” of Florida’s law.

“For the first time in over 20 years, Florida Muslims cannot call their community’s leading civil rights organization for help if they experience a hate crime at their mosque, illegal discrimination in the workplace, violent bullying in school, or any other acts of bigotry,” said Edward Ahmed Mitchell, national deputy director at Cair, in a press release.

The shutdown has already affected Muslims in the community, as Cair-Florida can no longer provide pro bono legal services for discrimination and immigration cases, leaving local attorneys scrambling to pick up the pieces. Civil rights advocates fear Cair’s targeting is only the beginning of Florida exploiting its power to cripple all kinds of lawful advocacy, especially the pro-Palestinian movement.

“It’s entirely unprecedented for state governments to attempt to shut down organizations by branding them as terror organizations,” said Shirin Sinnar, a law professor at Stanford University who co-authored an amicus brief for Cair in a related case. “This sends a message to the Muslim American community, as a whole, that this organization, which has defended your civil rights, is no longer able to do that.”

The effects of the shutdown amid a rise in Islamophobia

Cair and its Florida chapter are the main civil rights organization for Muslims in the state, focusing on immigration, discrimination and free speech cases, know-your-rights workshops, voter mobilization and Islamophobia research. Cair-Florida, which employed about 12 staff members and eight contractors, has fought for prisoners’ access to halal meals and pro-Palestinian students’ right to protest. Cair’s national division took Muslim Americans’ grievances about federal “no-fly lists” to the supreme court – and won.

State officials have argued in legal filings, without clear evidence, that Cair and its Florida chapter have been operating as a front for Hamas and the Muslim Brotherhood, “all while masquerading as run-of-the-mill civil rights organizations”.

Cair denies these claims and has never been charged with or convicted of any crime. The group has been outspoken against extremist violence by groups like the Islamic State. Instead, Cair says, Florida is using the new law to “punish their perceived political enemies” and that the organization is being targeted for its religious missions and advocacy.

Aside from Cair, Florida also applied the domestic terrorist designation to the Muslim Brotherhood and “antifa” – a vague umbrella term for far-left-leaning and anarchist anti-fascist groups and individuals. This aligns with the Trump administration labeling “antifa” and certain branches of “the Muslim Brotherhood” as terrorist groups, alongside its targeting of leftist and pro-Palestinian activists.

Tactically, Florida’s focus on Cair reflects an attempt to go after one of the most marginalized groups first, said Sinnar: “The whole point is to establish a precedent with the most disfavored of organizations – the one that few people in the state will rally to defend.” Then, that power can be weaponized against other groups, she added.

Florida’s targeting of Cair comes amid rising Islamophobia in the US – and the pushback against it. That includes a growing crackdown on pro-Palestinian activism, felt most sharply by students facing discipline and immigrants threatened with deportation. Islamophobic attacks also colored the Michigan Democrat Abdul El-Sayed’s run for Senate – with Trump referring to him as a “jihadi” and his Republican opponent falsely linking him with the Muslim Brotherhood.

But El-Sayed’s victory, after leaning in to his Muslim identity and pro-Palestinian values, reflected that Muslims are building electoral power, regardless.

In January, El-Sayed will become the first Muslim US senator, joining a record-breaking seven newly elected Muslims in Congress. Civil rights advocates argue that electing progressive and Muslim lawmakers at the state level can help fight back against Republican-led legislatures and governors enforcing terrorism laws.

This has already happened in Texas, which flipped blue on election night. Governor Greg Abbott, who issued a proclamation last year declaring Cair a terrorist organization, and the attorney general, Ken Paxton, who sued Cair in an attempt to shut down the organization, both lost their seats to Democrats. Incoming governor Gina Hinojosa said she will reverse Abbott’s designation in an interview with the Washington Post last week and Paxton recently dropped his lawsuit against Cair. The Muslim Legal Fund of America, which is representing Cair in its Texas lawsuit against Abbott’s designation, said that “it’s pretty clear this case is probably not going to go much further”.

However, it may be too late for an electoral solution in Florida, said Abdullah Sheikh, a community activist who tried to rally opposition to the state’s domestic terrorism program before the legislation hit the governor’s desk. While he’s typically an optimist, he now worries: “The legislature has zero incentive to do anything at this point.” A repeal would need to win over both chambers and the governor, all of which Republicans control.

Florida serves as a “cautionary tale for other states”, he said, to squash these measures before they become law.

The chilling effect sets in

In a normal year, Cair-Florida would have scheduled meetings with elected officials right after the midterms, but that didn’t happen this year.

Before the designation even kicked in, Cair and its Florida chapter had already restricted activity in the state by pausing donor outreach, cancelling active recurring donations and suspending plans for its three annual “life-sustaining” fundraising galas. A Florida-based IT company that Cair was relying on to relaunch a website tracking Islamophobia terminated its relationship with the group. Cair-Florida’s lawyers had already been turning away new prospective clients.

Earlier this month, a federal court rejected Cair-Florida’s request to operate while litigation continues; the organization has since appealed to the US court of appeals. In the meantime, Muslims across the state are feeling a chilling effect. “The mosques now are scared of their own shadow,” said Sheikh.

He has spoken with board members at more than a dozen mosques across central Florida, many of whom are now wary of programming, outside of prayers, that could be perceived as political. Some mosque leadership have told Sheikh they don’t believe Florida will designate them as terror organizations, though they’re wary that growing anti-Muslim hysteria means the government will “look for any excuse” to take away their non-profit status.

In Cair’s absence, individual lawyers are trying to help Muslims and pro-Palestinian advocates who need legal help. But “the void left behind by Cair-Florida’s absence is far too large to be filled by the good-hearted local attorneys that are trying to help the community”, said Jalal Shehadeh, a Palestinian American lawyer who serves on the boards of many legal organizations, including the Florida Muslim Bar Association. “We can only do so much.”

Shehadeh, who frequently fights cases related to the pro-Palestine movement, is anticipating a higher caseload because of Cair-Florida’s suspension. He pointed out that Cair lawyers who were focused on civil rights cases cannot be replaced with private attorneys, who may lack the time and not be able to front the legal costs that Cair does. “Most often the people that need help are the ones without resources,” Shehadeh said. “These individuals don’t have the ability to fork up $10,000 to hire a good attorney.”

Salma Khan, a Muslim American, reached out to Cair-Florida three years ago after a video of a man verbally harassing her went viral. It was the obvious choice, she said, explaining that she grew up in Fort Lauderdale and was familiar with Cair’s presence at mosques and schools; they helped students request Eid off and encouraged fundraising during Ramadan. Cair provided Khan with attorneys after she was harassed, as well as advocacy staff who raised awareness about her case online. Learning that Florida had designated Cair a domestic terrorist organization has made her wonder what will happen to Muslims who rely on the organization to protect them as they speak out against the government.

“Who else is going to be labeled that?” she said. “What will happen to our community?”

Soboh, at the University of Florida, felt hopeful about Muslims breaking ground in the midterms and believes the courts will ultimately rule in Cair’s favor. But he’s worried about the void left by Cair’s absence, and even his own career path.

He dreams of attending law school and working at a civil rights non-profit; he interned at Cair-Florida this summer. “I just want to protect my community and people,” he said. It’s still important for him to “fight for what he believes in”, he said, but he’s feeling more cautious since the designation went into effect.

“It’s made me associate doing work for the Muslim community as being something that is controversial,” he said.

title: ICE Flights Are the Air Travel Crisis No One's Talking About - The Intercept
description:
As one flight attendant working on ICE Air flights told ProPublica last year, it’s “only a matter of time” before one of these deportation flights ends in disaster.
According to Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, since Trump’s second inauguration, there have been almost 20,000 individual flights chartered by ICE.
But an unsafe plane can put anyone at risk, and ICE flights regularly violate FAA safety standards.
At the Northeast Alabama Regional Airport in Gadsden, Alabama, for example, over 300 ICE flights have gone in and out since September 2025.
Reports that ICE used tools to shield deportation flights from public scrutiny and congressional oversight have only compounded these safety concerns.
text:
It’s finally time to talk about air travel safety. High-profile crashes, equipment failures, and last week’s rare nationwide ground stop have thrust a long-overdue conversation about flying to the fore. But the chatter has largely omitted a major factor exacerbating the risk of airline catastrophes: the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement policies.

With slapdash and violent immigration enforcement as arguably its defining feature, the second Trump administration has mobilized and redirected vast federal resources to hit impossibly high detention and deportation targets. The administration has bent and broken laws, ignored proper vetting processes for new Immigration and Customs Enforcement recruits, and slashed mandatory training hours. The results of these dangerous shortcuts have been deadly: 2025 saw the highest number of deaths for people in ICE custody in decades. At the urging of Stephen Miller, now the White House chief of staff, the detention and deportation quotas have pushed ever higher. To meet them has required the rapid transportation of migrants, often via flights.

In the air, as on the ground, speed kills.

Traditionally, the federal government has not owned and operated its own airline, instead chartering flights from private airlines. Reliance on private contractors is not atypical, but in December 2025, the Trump administration broke with past practice and began to acquire its own fleet to complement the private charters.

In less than two years, ICE’s air operation has quietly transformed into a full-fledged domestic airline, adding more traffic to the already crowded skies. Just as the Federal Aviation Administration has failed to keep up with flight capacity at major airports, this shadow network of detention shuffle flights has been operating with a reckless attitude toward safety that befits ICE’s overall reputation. As one flight attendant working on ICE Air flights told ProPublica last year, it’s “only a matter of time” before one of these deportation flights ends in disaster.

According to Human Rights First’s ICE Flight Monitor, since Trump’s second inauguration, there have been almost 20,000 individual flights chartered by ICE. Between January 2025 and January 2026, the number of flights inside the U.S. quadrupled. Most of these flights are not actually deportations, but trips shuffling detainees around the country between the hundreds of county jails, state prisons, and privately owned detention centers. Vulnerable migrants are locked in handcuffs, waist chains, and leg irons for the entire trip, unable to unbuckle themselves, violating a federal standard that says a full plane must be evacuated in 90 seconds. ICE Air has quietly removed three safety layers at once — the passenger, the crew, and the airport — and every flight risks triggering an emergency that no one on board could survive.

There was little mention of these risks after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop last week, which Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy blamed on technological upgrades and aging infrastructure.

But an unsafe plane can put anyone at risk, and ICE flights regularly violate FAA safety standards. On ICE’s airliner-size jets, shackled detainees land at one of more than 100 airports in ICE’s expanding network, usually not at major hubs but at small regional airports and airfields. Many of these small, regional airports are not certified by the FAA for planes that size, and some have no fire-and-rescue crews on the ground.

If you live near a small airport in the U.S. and began noticing increased jet noise in the last year and a half, you were probably not imagining things. Your local airfield may be one of the nodes in this network. At the Northeast Alabama Regional Airport in Gadsden, Alabama, for example, over 300 ICE flights have gone in and out since September 2025. The airport, together with the nearby Etowah County detention center, has developed into a transfer node, feeding migrants who were arrested in Alabama, Georgia, and Eastern Tennessee into the major deportation removal hubs centered in Louisiana.

At least five airports in the ICE flight network, including Northeast Alabama, lack FAA Part 139 safety certification, which mandates basic standards like on-the-ground aircraft rescue and firefighting capability. Dozens of other airports have hosted immigration-related aircraft that are sized beyond what their certification index anticipates.

When a small airport falls short of fire and rescue safety minimums, local departments often wait at the airport on standby, further stretching local municipalities’ abilities to keep everyone, even those not flying, safe. As illustrated by numerous videos of federal agents using excessive force or arrest, every encounter between ICE agents and ordinary people brings its own risk of harm. Each chartered flight also brings with it another chance for something to go wrong, and the number of flights keeps climbing. When it does, it could happen at an airport, like Gadsden, with no federal fire-and-rescue requirement and no certification.

Reports that ICE used tools to shield deportation flights from public scrutiny and congressional oversight have only compounded these safety concerns. In May, several Democratic members of Congress sent a letter to FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford raising the alarm about ICE’s reported misuse of “Limiting Aircraft Data Displayed,” a program that allows private aircraft to request that the FAA withhold registration numbers and other identifiable data to block public flight trackers. “ICE’s use of this program to obscure routine government operations and suppress information about deportation flights is out of the scope of this program, and therefore inappropriate and dangerous,” the lawmakers wrote.

For the last 18 months, as this network of flights and airports ramped up, supercharged by windfalls from the so-called “Big Beautiful Bill,” congressional Republicans exercised little to no oversight. Come January, once Democrats take the gavel, a new opportunity for accountability will open up. One legislative option includes closing the loophole that lets ICE’s charter contractors operate airliner-size jets out of smaller regional airports that have no FAA Part 139 safety certification, either by amending the negotiated-charter exemption in federal law, or by demanding that the FAA explain — and if necessary enforce — the rules that appear to require certification for flights of this size.

With the power to legislate comes the power to investigate, and congressional Democrats should make full use of the subpoena. Mullen, Bedford, former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem, and representatives from CSI Aviation and the other private airlines making millions off of these flights should answer questions in public, at congressional hearings. In addition to Trump administration officials and those profiting from the flights, the American people also need to hear from those on the ground who run these small airports, and the local municipalities all across the country who have been assuming increased public safety risks, both in the skies and on the ground.

In pursuit of its draconian immigration policy, the Trump administration has pushed the immigration system beyond its ability to function safely, which puts all Americans at risk, with migrants at the most vulnerable end of the spectrum. Failing to mention how immigration enforcement contributes to the crisis plaguing air travel only risks prolonging it.

title: Hundreds of Oregon families could lose rent help under new Trump administration rule
description:
The change could affect U.S.-citizen children living with a parent who does not qualify for federal housing help.
Under the new rule, the household could lose that assistance if the parent remains in the home after a final eligibility determination.
Housing agencies may need additional documents, another verification step or a correction to a tenant’s record.
Home Forward told KATU it is looking to the courts as families face uncertainty about their housing assistance.
Housing agencies must notify current tenants who still need to submit evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status by Jan. 11, 2027.
text:
Up to 259 households served by Home Forward could lose eligibility for federal housing assistance under a new Trump administration rule requiring everyone in a household to prove U.S. citizenship or an immigration status that qualifies for the program.

Home Forward, the public housing agency serving Multnomah County, confirmed the estimate to KATU. The agency told KATU it has no clear solution for affected families right now and is looking to the courts as the rule faces a legal challenge.

The change could affect U.S.-citizen children living with a parent who does not qualify for federal housing help.

ALSO READ: Portland renters share housing struggles at City Council feedback forum

Under existing rules, those families can receive a smaller rent subsidy calculated using only eligible household members. The new rule generally limits that reduced assistance to the time needed to verify everyone’s eligibility, with limited exceptions.

HUD Secretary Scott Turner described the change as closing a “decades-old loophole” in an interview with FOX Business.

“So you may have one that’s eligible or legal and then others living inside the house that are not legal,” Turner said. “And so we’re closing this loophole, Larry, because American taxpayers work hard and earn taxpayer money.”

What would change for families?

A household with two U.S.-citizen children and a parent whose immigration status does not qualify can currently receive reduced rent assistance based on the children’s eligibility.

Under the new rule, the household could lose that assistance if the parent remains in the home after a final eligibility determination. Missing required proof by the deadline, including an approved extension, can also trigger termination procedures.

The rule protects current tenants during timely verification and a requested informal hearing. It also provides an exception if the household member whose status cannot be verified moves out. Limited continued-assistance and temporary-deferral provisions remain.

Turner said the administration wants assistance to reach people waiting for housing.

“We have, you know, myriads of people in our country that are on waiting lists for our public housing authorities to receive housing,” he said. “You have elderly people, you have veterans that are homeless, you have people that are escaping from domestic violence, you know.”

What HUD says its audit found

HUD announced the results of a nationwide review with the Department of Homeland Security in January. According to HUD, the review identified nearly 200,000 tenants requiring more eligibility verification, nearly 25,000 deceased tenants and nearly 6,000 noncitizens it classified as ineligible for assistance.

The agencies compared housing records with information in the federal Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements, or SAVE, system.

The nearly 200,000 figure represents records requiring further eligibility checks. HUD’s November announcement describes those tenants as having incomplete or unknown eligibility verification.

HUD’s accompanying instructions explain that the matching report can include people a local housing agency already classified as eligible citizens when federal records suggest a discrepancy. Housing agencies may need additional documents, another verification step or a correction to a tenant’s record.

The letter also says people already classified by their housing agency as ineligible noncitizens are excluded from that matching report.

HUD directed agencies to review the report and begin corrective action within 30 days. It said it would recover funding for payments made on behalf of ineligible and deceased tenants.

Housing agencies face potential funding penalties

HUD’s letter warns that agencies failing to follow its reporting requirements could face corrective orders, reimbursement from sources outside HUD, or withheld or reduced funding.

Whether assistance must end depends on the household and the applicable verification, hearing and family-preservation requirements.

The letter gives local agencies responsibility for checking the records, documenting eligibility and correcting inaccurate information.

The federal law behind the dispute

HUD cites Section 214 of the Housing and Community Development Act of 1980, codified at 42 U.S.C. 1436a. The law restricts covered federal housing assistance to U.S. citizens and specified categories of eligible noncitizens, including qualifying permanent residents, refugees and people granted asylum.

Turner said he views the new rule as enforcing that law.

“The Housing and Community Development Act says for the Secretary of HUD, which for this season of time, that’s who I am, that’s my job, that you may not provide assistance for those that are here illegally,” he said. “And so we’re enforcing this law.”

For decades, HUD’s regulations have allowed mixed-status households to live together while reducing their subsidy to account for ineligible members. The legal dispute includes whether HUD can end that longstanding arrangement under the statute.

HUD says a person without eligible status benefits from living in a subsidized home even when the subsidy is calculated using only eligible residents.

The department proposed the change in February and announced the final rule in November.

Families and tenant groups ask a court to intervene

Public Counsel, along with other law firms, filed a lawsuit Nov. 16 in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California.

They represent three Los Angeles County residents and tenant organizations People Organized for Westside Renewal and Union de Vecinos.

The plaintiffs argue the rule unlawfully threatens housing for mixed-status families, including U.S.-citizen children. Their attorneys say households could be forced to separate or lose their assistance.

The complaint asks the court to postpone the Dec. 14 effective date and prevent enforcement in the Central District of California while the case proceeds.

The effect of any court order on Oregon households would depend on what the judge orders and the scope of that relief.

Home Forward told KATU it is looking to the courts as families face uncertainty about their housing assistance.

When the rule would take effect

The final rule is scheduled to take effect Dec. 14.

Housing agencies must notify current tenants who still need to submit evidence of citizenship or eligible immigration status by Jan. 11, 2027.

Affected mixed-status households generally have 90 days from Dec. 14 to submit the missing evidence. Extensions of up to 60 days are available in qualifying circumstances.

Other current tenants who still need to provide proof generally submit it at their next annual or interim eligibility review.

title: Appeals court grants Trump request to halt order restoring Venezuelan TPS
description:
A federal appeals court has agreed to keep deportation protections frozen for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, shortly after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.
The Trump administration argues that TPS is a temporary program and that Venezuela no longer meets the requirements for its renewal.
The Supreme Court twice intervened with temporary emergency orders, and later sent the case back to an appeals court after upholding the end of TPS for Haitians in a different case.

After the Trump administration terminated TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also became invalid.
text:
A federal appeals court has agreed to keep deportation protections frozen for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, shortly after the Trump administration filed an emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

The order handed down late Wednesday means the administration remains free to detain and deport Venezuelans who had previously been granted temporary protected status. Federal attorneys have said some 1,800 are in detention, and about 330 are subject to deportation proceedings.

The Supreme Court previously intervened to allow the administration to temporarily end the program for Venezuelans.

Congress created the TPS program in 1990 to protect migrants from deportation to countries experiencing natural disasters or civil unrest. The designation is granted in periods of up to 18 months.

The Trump administration argues that TPS is a temporary program and that Venezuela no longer meets the requirements for its renewal.

During President Donald Trump's second term, the Department of Homeland Security has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria.

However, in a shift in policy in recent months, the administration has maintained protections for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans and more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan.

TPS was first granted to Venezuelans in March 2021, under Democratic President Joe Biden. The designation was expanded in September 2023 to cover additional beneficiaries. About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections.

The Trump administration's move to end protections for Venezuelans was challenged in court, and a California-based judge ruled it unlawful. The Supreme Court twice intervened with temporary emergency orders, and later sent the case back to an appeals court after upholding the end of TPS for Haitians in a different case.

The U.S. 9th Circuit Court of Appeals had yet to rule when the administration returned to the Supreme Court on Wednesday, arguing that a temporary pause would soon expire and allow the restoration of deportation protections. Hours later, the appeals court extended its temporary freeze on protections until seven days after it hands down a full ruling.

After the Trump administration terminated TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also became invalid. Thousands faced deportation proceedings, detention and removal. Many others chose to leave the country voluntarily.

It remains unclear how many Venezuelans who previously held TPS are still living in the United States.

text:
On Monday (November 16), five European Union member states -- Germany, Denmark, Greece, the Netherlands, and Austria -- announced concrete plans to establish a joint migrant deportation hub in Rwanda, marking the first such facility created outside the bloc.

The five EU nations reportedly aim to have the pilot facility in the East African country operational as early as next year.

The initiative targets individuals who have no legal right to remain in Europe but cannot be returned directly to their countries of origin, representing a significant shift in European migration policy.

The proposed "return hubs" would receive non-EU nationals who have been issued with enforceable departure orders but cannot be repatriated directly to their origin countries. Data for the number of migrants issued with notices to leave but who don't actually leave varies from country to country across the bloc. However, in June this year, a post on the European Parliament website indicated that in 2025, those who were asked to leave but did not do so was roughly one in four, or between 20 and 28 percent. This state of affairs was what pushed some, like the center-right Dutch politician Malik Azmani from the VVD party to argue for the measures included in the new European pact on asylum and migration thaat was introduced in June this year.

According to preliminary details, the facility in Rwanda will initially operate as a pilot hosting around 100 individuals, with each of the five participating states contributing roughly 20 returnees.

Defending the initiative, prominent migration expert Gerald Knaus told news agency KNA that he believed the arrangement could act as an effective deterrent.

Knaus argued that establishing clear signals -- that crossing the Mediterranean irregularly would not lead to European residence -- could ultimately save lives. "A moral catastrophe is that thousands of people drown in the Mediterranean every year -- in 2025, the number exceeded 2,000," Knaus emphasized, noting that ending sea deaths while upholding protection standards constitutes a moral victory.

He insisted deportees would not face persecution in Rwanda, highlighting that the UN Refugee Agency (UNHCR) has relocated over 3,000 vulnerable migrants from Libya to Rwanda since 2019 without issue.

Read Also

Brussels proposes turning Frontex into the EU’s central returns agency

UN, Rwandan politicians, rights groups voice criticism

However, the plan has encountered fierce resistance from international human rights bodies. UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Türk voiced serious concerns regarding Rwanda's human rights record, news agency dpa reported.

"The solution does not lie in single measures -- often very costly -- of finding countries far away to deal with one aspect of migration governance, or in externalizing human rights obligations," Türk is quoted in a press release published on Wednesday (November 18).

Türk urged European leaders to address the root causes of displacement, such as global inequality and violent conflict, while pointing out that managed migration offers economic benefits for aging European societies facing labor shortages.

Domestic opposition inside Rwanda has also spoken out forcefully against hosting European return centers, as news agency dpa reported.

Frank Habineza, leader of the Democratic Green Party of Rwanda, rejected the concept of receiving migrants forcibly relocated from Europe.

"What we fundamentally reject is bringing these people here against their will," Habineza reportedly stated to reporters. Questioning why migrants who reached Europe should be sent to East Africa, he added that European nations "should not shirk their responsibilities" and expressed concern that the proposal would strain Rwanda's already scarce public resources.

German refugee advocacy organizations and church representatives have joined the chorus of criticism, news agency epd reported. Karl Kopp, executive director of Pro Asyl, labeled the plan a failure and pledged legal assistance to affected individuals.

"Rwanda is not a model democracy. Opposition members are detained there and, in some cases, tortured," Kopp cautioned, casting doubt on whether human rights standards there can be guaranteed.

'Inhuman, inefficient and costly'

Similarly, Bishop Christian Stäblein of the Protestant Church in Germany warned that the EU risks destabilizing fragile partner states and creating political dependency on authoritarian regimes.

Humanitarian organizations have voiced similar ethical concerns regarding externalized facilities, news agency KNA reported.

German Catholic welfare organization Caritas warned of arbitrary detentions, inadequate healthcare, and potential degrading treatment in off-shore return centers. Meanwhile, Gesine Ames of the Catholic aid organization Misereor argued that outsourcing responsibility is "inhumane, inefficient and costly."

Political pushback has also emerged within Germany's governing coalition, with Development Minister Reem Alabali Radovan expressing skepticism over unanswered legal and operational questions.

Read Also

Europe’s externalized migration policies face a human rights test

Rwanda seen as efficient partner

Despite these concerns, European governments view Rwanda as an efficient partner capable of swift implementation, news agency AP reported.

Under President Paul Kagame, Rwanda's government has built a reputation for bureaucratic efficiency and low tolerance for petty corruption.

Rwandan Interior Minister Vincent Biruta defended the proposal, stating it will "save lives by helping to stop criminal human smugglers who profit from migrants making desperate, dangerous journeys," and reiterated that Rwanda remains a welcoming nation for displaced persons.

The current deal follows years of European efforts to tighten border controls and explore off-shore processing schemes, news agency AFP reported. Previous externalization attempts have faced severe legal and political hurdles.

A prominent bilateral deal signed between the United Kingdom and Rwanda in 2022 was struck down by the UK Supreme Court in 2023 on safety grounds before being formally scrapped in 2024. Similarly, Italy's initiatives to process male migrants in centers in Albania have faced continuous judicial challenges and delays in Italian courts.

Nevertheless, broader legislative changes across the European Union have paved the way for the current proposal. Following gains by far-right and anti-immigration parties across member states, EU lawmakers voted to ease regulations governing third-country detention centers.

Under newly established EU rules, individual member states or coalitions are empowered to negotiate bilateral agreements to deport non-citizens to external return hubs, setting the stage for the five-nation agreement with Rwanda.

text:
Leads coalition of 20 AGs in recommending inquiries into accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and DHS waste and corruption

Encourages Congress to include the voices and experiences of community members, advocates, and AGs who are fighting for the rule of law

November 19, 2026 (SAINT PAUL) — Minnesota Attorney General Keith Ellison today led a coalition of 20 attorneys general in encouraging leaders of the incoming majorities in Congress to hold hearings on Trump Administration abuses in immigration enforcement. In a letter to congressional leadership — including the incoming chairs of House and Senate committees with responsibility over the judiciary, homeland security, and government oversight and accountability — Attorney General Ellison and the coalition encourage Congress to hold hearings on the accountability of immigration officers, detention practices, and waste and corruption in the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition also encourage the incoming chairs of these committees to feature testimony at the hearings from Americans directly harmed by immigration enforcement abuse, advocates for immigrant communities, and from state Attorneys General who have been using the tools at their disposal to fight against this abuse and for the rule of law. State officials and community leaders have important insights to share gathered through truth councils, accountability commissions, and other community engagement.

“I led this coalition of attorneys general in encouraging incoming Congressional leaders to hold hearings on abuses in immigration enforcement because we are supposed to be a nation of laws — but DHS has acted like an agency that answers to no one, and it must be held accountable,” Attorney General Ellison said. “It is critically important to take a clear, hard look at the facts now and establish a complete public record so that we have a clear picture of the problems we need to solve. This record must include the experiences and voices of people who have been directly harmed and those, including state attorneys general, who have advocated for them and fought for the rule of law. As the chief legal officers of our states, we attorneys general have sworn oaths to uphold the Constitution — and we recognize no exception to the Constitution for immigration agents. We look forward to working with the new majorities in Congress to make sure the Constitution applies to all Americans and protects all Americans from the abuses of the lawless Trump Administration.“

Trump abuses in immigration enforcement, corruption

Donald Trump’s DHS and its agencies, including Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and Customs and Border Protection (CBP), have operated as if they are exempt from accountability and the rule of law. In 2025, DHS began a months-long campaign of terror across multiple American cities. Since the beginning of Trump’s second term, DHS agents have shot at least 25 people across the United States. In Minnesota, they include Renee Good and Alex Pretti, whom DHS agents killed, and Julio Sosa-Celis, whom they injured when they shot him through the door of a house where children were present.

Use of force by immigration agents has also increased dramatically. In just the first three months of the current administration, there was a nearly fourfold increase in reported ICE use-of-force incidents. Independent researchers have subsequently documented more than 400 incidents of misuse of crowd-control weapons in sixteen cities across the country in just 12 months, resulting in over 200 injuries to demonstrators, bystanders, and journalists attempting to cover the events.

Attorney General Ellison and the coalition write to Congressional leaders, “In the face of immigration enforcement conduct that is both immoral and unlawful, the outgoing House and Senate majorities were content to look the other way. The incoming majorities need to confront this head-on. The American people voted for real, serious oversight — with teeth and consequences for any agency or individual who would ignore the rule of law.”

Immigration detention practices are in dire need of reform and oversight as well. By ICE’s own accounting, close to 60 people have died in ICE custody in the past two years, enough to make 2025 the deadliest year in immigration detention in over two decades.

DHS has already wasted significant sums in its rushed and ill-conceived efforts to rapidly expand immigration detention. DHS spent approximately $1 billion purchasing warehouses in a grossly inhumane effort to house people in them before shifting course. Now DHS has purchased four prisons from CoreCivic, a significant donor to President Trump’s inaugural committee and his PACs, for the extraordinary sum of $2.2 billion. DHS paid CoreCivic $495 million for a prison in Minnesota that CoreCivic offered to the State of Minnesota for just $75 million in 2025. Americans deserve to know whether DHS is inflating the purchase price of these facilities and diverting their tax dollars into the coffers of the President’s supporters.

Attorney General Ellison has used the power of his office to halt abuses in immigration enforcement and draw attention to waste and corruption by, among other things, suing to have Operation Metro Surge declared illegal and unconstitutional, which is still ongoing; suing the Trump Administration for access to the evidence in the shootings of Renee Good, Julio Sosa-Celis, and Alex Pretti, which is also still ongoing; suing outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott to compel the return of the ICE officer criminally charged in Minnesota in the shooting of Alex Pretti to face the charges laid against him; and calling for a congressional investigation into DHS’s purchase of the Appleton prison from CoreCivic at a wildly inflated price. The Minnesota Truth Council, in which Attorney General Ellison’s Office actively participated, also recently released its preliminary report and will issue its final report and recommendations on December 1.

text:
The leaders of Russia, China and the United States — Presidents Vladimir Putin, Xi Jinping and Donald Trump — have wrapped up an unprecedented trilateral summit in Shenzhen, China, with what Chinese media is calling a landmark “peace declaration.” The four-point plan calls for the three nations to reduce nuclear risks, increase oil refining, promote reforms to the United Nations and limit the jurisdiction of the International Criminal Court. This is President Trump.

President Donald Trump: “In another area of potential cooperation between us, I’ll be suggesting ways to protect our nation’s sovereignty from rogue globalist organizations such as the International Criminal Court, which has gotten out of control, which I believe we all agree has really strayed far from beyond its jurisdiction.”

President Putin faces an ICC warrant seeking his arrest for war crimes committed in Ukraine, including the unlawful transfer of children from Russian-occupied areas. Neither the U.S., nor China, nor Russia is a party to the Rome Statute that established the International Criminal Court.

During the summit, President Trump lavished praise on President Xi and referred to President Putin as “my friend.” That prompted Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk to write on social media, “God, protect us from such friends.”

On Capitol Hill, House Democrats voted 251-11 on Wednesday to nominate New York Congressmember Hakeem Jeffries to be the next speaker of the House. Jeffries is poised to make history as the first African American to fill the role. The vote came during a closed-door caucus meeting. Afterward, seven incoming Democratic congressmembers issued a joint statement explaining their opposition to Jeffries. They wrote, “Whether on Medicare for All, stopping ICE terror, getting money out of politics, or ending the genocide in Gaza, our constituents sent us to Congress with a mandate on these issues.”

In Gaza, thousands of Palestinians have been forced to flee again after Israeli tanks and bulldozers pushed past the ceasefire’s “Yellow Line” on Wednesday and into Palestinian-held territory. Israeli troops operating east of the “Yellow Line” have gradually pushed the boundary westward and now occupy about two-thirds of Gaza’s territory, with 2 million Palestinians trapped in an increasingly narrow strip of land, most of them forced to live in tents. This is Salam Aql, a Palestinian woman who says she was displaced for the 15th time on Wednesday.

Salam Aql: “They ordered an evacuation, but we wanted to stay because we are exhausted from being displaced so many times. We are tired. I swear to God, we are tired. But as we were sitting there, gunfire started coming in. The boy was sitting in front of the tent and was hit in the leg. Once he was wounded, we could not stay any longer. We are scared.”

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said the military is ready to take more land and turn the newly seized areas into permanent parts of Israel’s security zones. The Palestinian Health Ministry says Israeli forces have killed over 1,600 Palestinians in Gaza since last October’s so-called ceasefire.

An Israeli court has once again extended the detention of Dr. Hussam Abu Safiya, the director of Kamal Adwan Hospital in Gaza, by six months. Dr. Abu Safiya was seized by the Israeli military along with several of the hospital’s staff and patients during a raid on Kamal Adwan in December 2024. He’s been held without charge ever since. Dr. Abu Safiya’s legal team condemned the latest extension of his imprisonment as “neither a fair nor a transparent process.” The Office of the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights has said that it has received information that Dr. Safiya “has been subjected to torture and other ill-treatment, including prolonged solitary confinement, repeated severe assaults resulting in grave injuries, and denial of medical care.”

Judges at the International Court of Justice have found that Burmese security forces committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims during military operations nearly a decade ago. It’s the first time the court has held a nation accountable for violating the 1948 Genocide Convention. The ruling follows the 2017 military crackdown by government forces and ethnic Rakhine mobs that killed about 10,000 people and drove more than 730,000 Rohingya into Bangladesh. Ahead of today’s verdict, survivors hoped the ICJ would deliver justice and pave the way for them to return to their homeland. Hasina Khatun is a Rohingya refugee who was forced to flee her home when a mob burned her village to the ground.

Hasina Khatun: “To save our lives, we fled into the jungle, where we spent five days. Our children suffered from the cold, as we had no warm clothes, blankets or tarps. We endured immense hardship. Later, as the Myanmar military continued its attacks, we left the jungle and returned to the village before moving to the riverbank for shelter. But even there, we were not safe. We witnessed Myanmar soldiers taking away my husband and other men from the area right before our eyes.”

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth made a surprise visit to Caracas on Wednesday, where he announced the U.S. and Venezuela have signed an agreement to restore military ties. Under the deal, the two countries will work together on areas such as joint training, intelligence sharing and border security. It’s Hegseth’s first visit to Venezuela since U.S. forces violently abducted former President Nicolás Maduro and his wife, National Assembly deputy Cilia Flores, back in January. The deal comes after months in which Washington has effectively controlled Venezuela’s oil sales. This is Defense Secretary Hegseth.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth: “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China from rigs built by Americans and Venezuelans has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States through the Department of War that is bringing energy dominance for the benefit of Americans and for Venezuelans for decades to come. In fact, this makes the Strait of Hormuz a nonfactor for the Western Hemisphere.”

Hegseth also traveled to Colombia Wednesday, where Colombia’s Trump-backed right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella, turned down a U.S. plan for joint operations against drug cartels.

Anthropic has become the first major AI lab to become a publicly traded corporation, after completing what’s become the largest initial public offering in history. On Wednesday, Anthropic said it had raised a record $107.3 billion, giving it a valuation of more than $1.5 trillion. This comes after Anthropic warned in its IPO filings that, without proper safeguards, its technology poses “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity.”

New research has shown that advanced AI models repeatedly flagged civilians and civilian infrastructure as military targets in simulated scenarios. Anthropic’s models performed worst overall, according to the study by the independent evaluation company Vals AI. In tests using real satellite imagery of southern Iran, Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 misidentified the school in Minab — which was hit by a U.S.-Israeli attack in February, killing more than 120 children — as a military target in most hypothetical runs. The Pentagon has touted its heavy reliance on AI models in its war with Iran.

The U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency is urging users of the computer language Java to immediately patch a serious security flaw, which could allow hackers to take over a server without needing a password or login. The bug was discovered by the cybersecurity startup Calif on Tuesday, using advanced AI tools. Java has been described as the “backbone of the internet”; it runs on billions of devices across government agencies and is used by the majority of Fortune 500 companies.

title: Attorney General James Sues Over Forced Labor and Trafficking at Rochester Holiday Inn
description:

Attorney General James alleges that Petrik routinely delayed and withheld wages, leaving some workers with little or no compensation for months of work.
Attorney General James additionally alleges that Patel and Petrik subjected workers and their families, including children, to dangerous living conditions inside the hotel.
Attorney General James is seeking unpaid wages, restitution, damages, and penalties for the workers, as well as disgorgement of the profits each defendant made from their labor.
