text:
What GAO Found

Within the Department of Homeland Security (DHS), U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) received $45 billion in immigration detention funding in July 2025 through Public Law 119-21, commonly known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, available through fiscal year 2029. In addition to maintaining existing facilities with these funds, ICE began implementing an initiative to buy and renovate a collection of warehouses to use as new detention facilities. However, after acquiring 11 warehouses for about $1.07 billion, ICE scaled down the initiative significantly and plans to sell seven of them. In July and August 2026, ICE also bought four existing detention facilities for about $2.2 billion total. However, the scope, time frames, and estimated costs for further acquisitions remain undetermined. In addition, ICE did not update its spending plan for detention funding to reflect the shifting status of the warehouse initiative or other planned acquisitions, as required by its internal guidance. As a result, the spending plan includes an inflated estimate of planned obligations, which affects oversight efforts and ICE’s ability to assess long-term budget needs.

Examples of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement Warehouse Facilities

ICE obligated about $2.8 billion for detention in fiscal year 2025, an increase of about 41 percent from the prior year, amid expanded enforcement activity. Daily costs per detained noncitizen varied by facility type. The nine Federal Bureau of Prisons facilities ICE used charged a median daily rate of $180 per noncitizen, the highest of any facility type. Privately operated facilities had a median rate of $151, while those operated through agreements with the U.S. Marshals Service or state and local governments ranged from $85 to $103. ICE officials said that services provided, detention standards used, and location also influence rates.

ICE employs various processes to manage and oversee facility costs, but some were affected by the rapid expansion of new facilities. For example, the workload of staff who provide oversight and validate invoices for these facilities increased significantly, and ICE is working to fill 55 of the 87 allocated positions nationwide. Further, ICE did not manage detention facility investments in accordance with DHS acquisition practices, which include the development of life-cycle cost estimates. Developing such estimates before making further acquisitions would position ICE to better assess these investments, reduce potential waste, and help ensure the cost effective use of taxpayer dollars.

Why GAO Did This Study

A January 2025 Executive Order directed DHS to increase efforts to detain individuals apprehended for violations of immigration law and to allocate all available resources for ICE detention. ICE received significant funding in July 2025 to operate and expand detention facilities.

GAO was asked to review the costs of ICE’s detention facilities. This report examines (1) the extent to which ICE has planned to use available funds to expand detention capacity; (2) the costs of detention facilities over time and by facility type; and (3) the extent to which ICE has developed processes and procedures for managing and overseeing these costs.

GAO reviewed documentation on detention expansion efforts, agency spending plans, and facility costs from October 2022 through various points in 2026. GAO interviewed headquarters and field officials at four ICE field offices, including site visits to multiple existing and planned detention facilities. GAO selected these locations, in part, because they were the sites of multiple detention expansion efforts. GAO reviewed available cost estimates and compared spending plans to ICE guidance. GAO also analyzed information on the Department of Defense’s and Federal Emergency Management Agency’s costs for supporting immigration detention.

text:
A perceived escalation of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement activity in the Roanoke Valley is being monitored by involved groups this week, community members said.

Roanoke City Council member-elect Danny Clawson and current city council member Vivian Sanchez-Jones, who were monitoring the situation on Wednesday, both said 30 people have been detained since Monday — from worksites in Daleville, a trailer park, a gas station and while driving, they said. ICE has not confirmed any detainments or other information yet.

Kiesha Preston, a volunteer taking media requests for Los Ayudantes Southwest Virginia on Wednesday, said the number is likely higher than 32. She said the group feels “pretty confident” that local ICE agents have received outside support, “so basically more manpower.”

Los Ayudantes Southwest Virginia is a social media page which was constantly updated with videos and information this week. On Facebook, the group says it is an all-volunteer collective “dedicated to mutual aid, rapid response and community care.”

Preston said pickups are happening all over the region, with many in the city of Roanoke. In 2025, the number of ICE detainees in the Roanoke City Adult Detention Center more than tripled from the year before.

Jaime McGuire, an attorney with Amaryllis Law, an immigration firm based in Salem, said in an email Wednesday night that the firm has been receiving “a surge of calls.”

“Many individuals detained and it doesn’t seem to have a clear pattern or reasoning,” she said. “It seems to be planned and expanded enforcement but there is not a specific policy change that would have caused this. There is an increase in the number of officers present beyond the officers that were previosuly handling the cases.”

McGuire said she could not comment on whether proceedings are happening legally. She said she was told that 40 people were detained but is “sure it may be more by now.”

Sanchez-Jones, a longtime advocate for the Hispanic community, also said Wednesday that she knows of two people picked up by ICE at a gas station and that one person was stopped and later released outside of El Costeno restaurant on Peters Creek Road. She said the restaurant locked its doors but remained open after that.

Sanchez-Jones said new and old videos are circulating, and some rumors that have circulated are not true. She said she believes everything Los Ayudantes is posting is verified.

At the Salem ICE Office on West Main Street Wednesday afternoon, the fenced-in parking lot was full of vehicles, and unmarked black SUVs were parked around the facility. At one point, when pulling a large white van out of the lot, one agent pulled on a hoodie and therefore could not be seen, and another led the van out of the parking lot with a hood up, sunglasses on and wearing industrial gloves.

An observer yelled insults at that officer, and the officer yelled back. A Department of Homeland Security vehicle periodically parked outside of the building for periods of time before circling back out. Protesters screamed as vans and black SUVs entered or left the facility’s lot.

Clawson said Los Ayudantes is in direct communication with family members of those who have been detained, as well as witnesses or those with “close personal associations” with the detainees to confirm the incidents.

Katie Elmore was outside observing what was happening on Wednesday at the Salem facility. Elmore said multiple groups, including Roanoke Indivisible and Roanoke ICE Watch, have been concerned about “neighbors being taken, often illegally, without the correct warrants that they need to take them.”

“Often the citizens are very vulnerable, and they don’t know their rights. They’re being taken and they’re brought here into this building.” The building, leased out by ICE, has no signage indicating what it is used for.

“They then take them to the Farmville detention center, but often they disappear in the system,” she said. “Their families have absolutely no way of knowing where they are. So we’re here as peaceful observers, just to see how we could help.”

McGuire confirmed that to her knowledge, ICE is detaining individuals within the local ICE office for initial processing and “quickly” moving individuals to larger facilities “sometimes within the same day.”

Elmore said she saw about four vans coming into the fenced gate through the back door of the facility just after noon on Wednesday, with ICE agents “fully masked with hoodies on.” Vans and SUVs continued in and out of the facility consistently throughout the afternoon.

Cardinal News reached out on Wednesday to ICE’s media contact, who did not respond to inquiries.

In a news release earlier this week, the U.S. Department of Homeland Security said that “America is safer because we are enforcing the rule of law, keeping threats out of our communities, and putting the security of the American people first.”

Clark Ruhland, communications specialist with the city of Salem, said in a phone interview Wednesday that police are monitoring the West Main Street area and that all protesting has been “peaceful and calm.”

Clawson said those who know someone who was detained should reach out to Amaryllis Law, a Salem-based immigration firm which conducts free intakes, for legal counsel. They said once detainees are removed from Roanoke, they are harder to track.

Preston said typos and misspelled names are also making it harder to track those who have been detained.

“It looks like a lot of clerical errors are happening,” she said.

Preston said members of the community are afraid to leave their homes, even with legal status, and that Los Ayudantes is helping those individuals put together emergency plans and bringing groceries to them.

She said that she has not heard of any deportations yet from the area since Monday but that “anyone who is picked up and sent to Farmville … is not there very long.”

Government has deported nearly 39 000 undocumented foreign nationals over a seven-month period, as law enforcement intensifies immigration enforcement within the bounds of the law.

Between 1 April and 31 October 2026, some 38 982 deportations were carried out, comprising 31 878 from the Lindela Repatriation Centre and 7 104 cumulatively from the provinces.

During an Inter-Ministerial Committee (IMC) on Migration media briefing on Thursday, committee chairperson and Justice and Constitutional Development Minister, Mmamoloko Kubayi, reiterated that all enforcement and deportation processes remain strictly governed by immigration legislation and legal safeguards.

“The Department of Home Affairs, working with law enforcement agencies and relevant foreign missions, continues coordinating deportation and repatriation processes. These interventions form an important component of restoring the credibility of immigration enforcement.

“Government will continue strengthening cooperation with countries of origin to facilitate the identification, documentation and return of their nationals. The effectiveness of immigration enforcement must ultimately be measured not only by arrests, but also by the lawful conclusion of immigration processes,” the Minister said.

Furthermore, through Operation Shanela, police and partner agencies continue to “target immigration-related offences alongside other criminal activities”.

“These interventions support the identification and apprehension of persons suspected of contravening immigration legislation, subject to appropriate verification and legal processes.

“The IMC emphasises that enforcement operations must produce measurable outcomes, including arrests, successful prosecutions and lawful deportations,” Kubayi emphasised.

She reported that:

Between 26 October and 8 November 2026, 2 593 suspects were arrested for contravening the Immigration Act across multiple provinces.

Between 9 and 15 November 2026, 1 777 suspects were arrested for contravening the Immigration Act across multiple provinces.

“Government will continue to strengthen operational coordination to ensure that immigration enforcement is sustained and produces demonstrable results,” the Minister said.

Maintaining public order and curbing vigilantism

At the same time, Kubayi said the IMC welcomed the ongoing implementation of coordinated public order policing interventions to “prevent violence, intimidation, unlawful protests and attacks against individuals and businesses”.

She noted that through the National Joint Operational and Intelligence Structure (NATJOINTS), police and other law enforcement agencies continue to track emerging threats and coordinate responses.

“We must also add that these operations remain focused on protecting life and property, preventing criminal activity, maintaining public order and restoring stability. All interventions must comply with constitutional requirements, applicable legislation and human rights standards.

“The objective is to protect communities and restore public safety, not to militarise communities,” Kubayi emphasised.

She said although government recognises legitimate concerns regarding irregular migration, unemployment, crime and pressure on public services, lawlessness will not be tolerated.

The Minister said these concerns do not “justify vigilantism, unlawful identity checks, intimidation or attacks against foreign nationals”.

“No individual, organisation or community formation has the authority to assume the immigration enforcement responsibilities of the State.

“The IMC reiterates that peaceful protest is constitutionally protected, but violence, criminal intimidation and incitement will be dealt with decisively.

LIVERMORE FALLS, Maine (WGME) -- A judge is ordering ICE to explain the legality of an allegedly warrantless arrest in Livermore Falls earlier this week.

According to the Portland Press Herald, ICE agents arrested six people during a traffic stop Monday.

Also read: Maine ICE agent accused of killing man in Biddeford sent racist emails to sister: report

Among those detained was an 18-year-old from Ecuador who has Special Immigrant Juvenile status.

That classification is available to certain immigrants under 21 who have experienced abuse, abandonment or neglect by a parent.

The 18-year-old's brother, who says he was on the phone during the arrest, claims an ICE agent was aware of his brother's special immigration status but said he would detain him anyway.

A judge ordered ICE to explain the legality of the arrest and prohibited the 18-year-old from being removed from Maine.

However, ICE claims the teen was already on his way to a detention facility in Rhode Island when agents received the order.

Also read: Maine farm, construction workers brace for potential ICE raids

An attorney representing ICE and Border Patrol argues that the legality of the initial arrest is irrelevant because a valid warrant was issued after the 18-year-old was detained.

The teen's name has not been released.

According to the report, he has no criminal history and allegedly came to the United States alone at age 16 to escape his father.

description:

We’ve even seen ICE operating with impunity inside airports, sowing chaos and fear, and further disrupting Nevada’s tourism economy,” said Senator Rosen.

text:
WASHINGTON, D.C. — Today, U.S. Senators Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), Ranking Member of the Senate Judiciary Committee’s Immigration Subcommittee, and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) introduced the Travel Without Fear Act, a bill to limit the ability of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to broadly conduct civil immigration operations at or near airports without a judicial warrant related to a felony criminal conviction. The bill would also ban information sharing between ICE and the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) for civil immigration enforcement actions unless they have a judicial warrant for a specific target or is for the purposes of maintaining trusted traveler programs.

In the last year, there has been an increase in violent ICE civil enforcement operations at airports across America. This includes a recent incident in which a student at UC Berkeley was arrested at San Francisco International Airport (SFO) and detained in an ICE facility in California City for more than a week. According to their own reports, ICE recorded the highest number of administrative arrests in ICE’s history. Earlier this year, Padilla conducted an oversight visit to the California City facility to learn firsthand of the concerns surrounding the condition of detained individuals at this facility amid the Trump Administration’s mass detention and deportation campaign.

“ICE is out of control, and these are bare minimum standards for reining it in: officers who are visibly identifiable, as my VISIBLE Act requires, protections for travelers’ personal information, and a check for pending applications before arrests,” said Senator Padilla. “These safeguards protect everyone involved – travelers, officers, and the public. It’s commonsense and responsible.”

“ICE should not be allowed to operate recklessly and aggressively in our communities – putting lives and livelihoods at risk. We’ve even seen ICE operating with impunity inside airports, sowing chaos and fear, and further disrupting Nevada’s tourism economy,” said Senator Rosen. “That’s why I’m introducing this bill to prohibit ICE from conducting civil enforcement operations at airports without a judicial warrant, and to set clear guidelines for their conduct when they have one.”

The legislation would further require ICE officers to ensure that targets for arrest or detention are not within a period of authorized stay, prohibit ICE from accessing passenger data without a warrant, require ICE to notify airports and airlines in advance of any enforcement action, and require updates to the online database that tracks detainee locations for their families and attorneys within six hours of a detainee’s change in custody.

In addition to Padilla and Rosen, the bill is cosponsored by Senator Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.).

Padilla has been a leader in holding the Trump Administration accountable for its cruel and reckless mass deportation agenda. Last week, Padilla and Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) demanded answers over the detention of an eight-year-old Haitian child who lost Temporary Protected Status during a routine immigration check in. Last month, Padilla pressed Department of Homeland Security (DHS) officials over reports of increased ICE enforcement activity in Mendota and across California. In September, Padilla called on DHS to end immigration enforcement activity around San Diego County schools and educational institutions. In August, Padilla called out the Trump Administration’s continued abuses of power and demanded accountability. In June, Padilla sounded the alarm over the significant increase in deaths among detainees in ICE custody since January 2025. In April, Padilla and Schiff launched an inquiry into data sharing by TSA and ICE officials relating to the arrest and removal of Angelina Lopez-Jimenez and her child at SFO.

Padilla has also repeatedly conducted oversight visits to immigration detention facilities and holding centers across California to examine conditions firsthand and demand accountability from federal officials. His visits include facilities in California City, Otay Mesa, San Francisco International Airport, Downtown Los Angeles, Sacramento, San Diego, and McFarland.

text:
Cantwell & Colleagues Push CTFC To Reverse Ban on Geofencing by Prediction Markets

WASHINGTON, D.C. –U.S. Senator Maria Cantwell (D-WA), ranking member of the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation and senior member of the Senate Finance Committee, joined Senate colleagues in calling out Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig for the agency’s decision to prohibit prediction markets from geofencing, effectively requiring prediction markets to offer contracts in all 50 states and tribal lands. The Senators note Selig’s action directly conflicts with active court orders in California, Michigan, Nevada, and Washington – and demand that he reverse it.

“Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws…. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation,” the Senators wrote.

“We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws… The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved,” the Senators continued.

Joining Cantwell are all Senators representing California, Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-NV), Jacky Rosen (D-NV), Patty Murray (D-WA), Elissa Slotkin (D-MI), Gary Peters (D-MI), Adam Schiff (D-CA), and Alex Padilla (D-CA), as well as the ranking member of the Senate Agriculture Committee Amy Klobuchar (D-MN).

The full text of the letter can be found here and below:

Dear Chairman Selig:

We write to express our opposition to the Commodity Futures Trading Commission’s November 5 interpretation ordering Designated Contract Markets (DCMs) to end access criteria that restrict access to certain event contract markets based on prospective traders’ location or residence (e.g., geofencing) within 30 days. Your unilateral decision directly conflicts with active court orders, undermines state and tribal law, and must be reversed.

Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws. Your novel interpretation of the impartial access requirements effectively requires DCMs to offer improperly regulated gambling products in all fifty states without regard to state and tribal gaming laws and these state and federal court decisions. There is no basis or precedent under 17 CFR 38.151(b)’s impartial access requirements for this interpretation and indeed this argument has been made in several of the active cases—and rejected.

The Sixth and Ninth Circuits have ruled that states retain the authority to apply state gaming laws to prediction markets. The Ninth Circuit has also ruled that sports event contracts on Tribal lands constitute unauthorized Class III gaming under the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act in the preliminary-injunction context. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation.

We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws.

The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved. At minimum, the Commission must expressly state that the following do not violate Regulation 38.151(b): geographic restrictions imposed by court order, those adopted to comply with the Indian Gaming Regulatory Act or tribal-state compacts, and those an exchange adopts voluntarily.

We further request that the Commission preserve all records and communications relating to the topics addressed in this letter, from January 1, 2025, to the present and continue preserving existing and future materials on an ongoing basis. This preservation hold applies to all relevant records within the Commission’s possession and any person or entity representing or purporting to be acting on its behalf. This includes, but is not limited to, records and communications via email, whether official or personal; mobile devices; encrypted or disappearing messaging applications; social media; calendar entries; meeting notes; and voicemail and text messages. To the extent that the Commission uses any auto-delete functions, it should immediately suspend auto-delete functions and notify persons with control over potentially relevant records of similar preservation obligations.

Thank you for your attention to this matter. We look forward to your prompt response by November 23, 2026, including a written confirmation that the Commission is preserving all records related to this Congressional inquiry.

Mullin defends ground stop response Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.
Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

A look at some of the highlights:

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.

Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.

Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.

Mullin defends ground stop response

Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. text:
A federal judge in Massachusetts has temporarily blocked the Trump administration's restrictions on internships for international students, finding that immigration officials abruptly reversed a 35-year-old policy without explaining the change or considering its impact on universities.

U.S. District Judge Julia E. Kobick issued the ruling Tuesday, November 17, 2026, suspending two Department of Homeland Security (DHS) directives that prevented foreign students from receiving academic credit for certain elective internships. The order allows colleges and universities to resume authorizing qualifying training opportunities while the lawsuit proceeds.

The decision follows a separate ruling a day earlier that struck down the administration's restrictions on how long international students could remain in the United States. Both challenges were brought by higher education organizations and concerned federal immigration policies affecting foreign students.

The latest ruling addresses Curricular Practical Training (CPT), which allows international students holding F-1 visas to participate in internships, cooperative education, and other work experience tied to their studies. Since 1991, federal authorities had permitted students to receive authorization for elective internships that earned academic credit.

That changed in August when the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, part of U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), issued directives requiring internships to be mandatory for every student pursuing the same degree. Under the new interpretation, an international law student could participate in an externship with a federal judge only if the experience was required for graduation.

Federal officials also warned universities that improperly authorizing internships could expose administrators to civil or criminal penalties and potentially cost institutions their certification to enroll international students.

The restrictions prompted colleges to cancel internship authorizations, revise academic programs and withdraw previously approved training opportunities. Columbia University denied authorization to more than 120 international students, while at least 13 students at Grinnell College lost fall internship opportunities. Cornell University and Michigan State University reported that the loss of training opportunities contributed to students leaving academic programs.

Four higher education organizations challenged the directives in federal court on October 5, arguing that the administration had unlawfully departed from decades of established immigration policy. The lawsuit was brought by the Association of American Universities, Presidents' Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, and NAFSA: Association of International Educators.

Government attorneys argued that the directives merely clarified existing regulations and that the organizations lacked grounds to challenge them. Kobick disagreed, citing federal rules adopted in 1991 and immigration guidance issued over subsequent decades that expressly permitted elective internships for academic credit.

The judge found that the administration had adopted a new interpretation without acknowledging the change, providing a reasoned explanation or considering the universities and students who had relied on the established policy.

Under the Administrative Procedure Act, federal agencies may change existing policies but must explain their decisions and account for significant reliance on previous rules. Kobick concluded that the organizations were likely to succeed in showing that the government's reversal was arbitrary and capricious.

The court also found that universities faced substantial harm from disrupted academic programs and the possibility of losing authorization to enroll foreign students. Those findings supported a preliminary injunctionA preliminary injunction is a temporary court order issued before a case is finally decided that requires a party to take or stop an action while the litigation continues. Federal courts generally consider the likelihood of success, irreparable harm, the balance of equities, and the public interest before granting one.Read more → suspending enforcement of both August directives pending further judicial review.

The order also bars federal officials from applying the new interpretation against the organizations that sued, their member institutions, employees and students, including in connection with training approvals issued before the restrictions took effect.

Universities have begun restoring access to qualifying internships. On November 18, the University of California, Berkeley announced that its international office would resume processing applications for elective internships taken for academic credit.

US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked the Supreme Court to issue an emergency order allowing officials to strip legal protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, marking the third time it has appealed to the nation’s top judicial body over the issue.

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to put on hold a federal judge’s ruling that officials lacked the authority to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) granted to the migrants under former President Joe Biden.

San Francisco-based US District Judge Edward Chen’s ruling is due to take effect on Friday unless a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court moves to suspend it. The Supreme Court previously paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorisation. It also argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm”.

If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The plaintiffs who challenged the administration’s actions, including TPS holders and an advocacy group, said that since the previous Supreme Court intervention in the case, Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, separated from children who are US citizens, deported to Venezuela, and even sent to so-called “third countries” where they have no ties.

The Supreme Court in June backed the administration’s separate actions ending TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians, giving a boost to the Republican president’s hardline approach towards immigration.

Trump clamps down on TPS

TPS is a designation that lets migrants from countries stricken by war, natural disaster or other catastrophes live and work in the US while it is unsafe for them to return to their home countries.

A person granted TPS cannot be deported, can obtain an employment authorisation document, and may be given travel authorisation. A TPS holder cannot be detained by the US over their immigration status.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire by September 9, and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan in October.

Millions of people have fled Venezuela in recent years due to political repression and a crippling economic crisis spurred in part by US sanctions against the government of President Nicolas Maduro.

Before leaving office, the Biden administration had extended TPS for about 600,000 Venezuelans through October 2026.

The State Department currently warns people to reconsider travel to Venezuela due to the risk of crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure, among other issues.

WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

A look at some of the highlights:

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.

It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee is laying the groundwork for long-promised investigations of the Trump administration that will launch with the new Congress in January.

Rep. Robert Garcia of California, who is expected to lead the committee when Democrats take control, sent letters directing members of President Donald Trump’s family and top administration officials to preserve documents. It’s an early step toward undertaking investigations of the Republican president and his administration.

The letters released Wednesday cover a wide range of potential investigations, including alleged financial conflicts involving Trump’s family, misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security and the administration’s handling of files related to Jeffrey Epstein.

“Oversight Democrats are fighting to put an end to this Administration’s self-dealing, misconduct, and abuse,” Garcia said in a statement. “These investigations will lay the groundwork for legislation which helps all Americans. This is just the beginning.”

Targets of the letters include two of Trump’s sons, Vice President JD Vance, White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, Attorney General Todd Blanche and Jared Kushner, the president’s son-in-law.

The White House has repeatedly pushed back at the investigative ambitions outlined by Democrats, with officials saying they are willing to engage on oversight inquiries that they see as legitimate but not ones assessed as politically motivated.

The president is “willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said. “If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people.”

Later Wednesday, White House counsel Will Scharf wrote a letter addressed to Democratic lawmakers, effectively dismissing requests for information from them for the remainder of the year because Democrats are currently not in the majority.

Scharf said he was citing a position that the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden took in 2022, and that while “some of you may (or may not) become a chair in the 120th Congress, that does not mean that requests from the 119th Congress carry over.”

The letters that the White House has gotten from Democrats in recent days, Scharf wrote, “drip with an animus or pettiness revealing that the purpose of these letters is not legitimate oversight but to harass and aggrandize.” The latest White House letter was first reported by Politico.

Still, the letters from Democrats offer an early glimpse of how they plan to use their newly won congressional majority to scrutinize Trump and his administration. As favorable election results rolled in for Democrats on election night, Garcia posted a two-word warning on social media: “Lawyer up.”

The preservation notices do not compel recipients to turn over documents, but they signal the investigations that Democrats intend to pursue once they gain control of the committee and its subpoena power in January.

Before the midterms, Garcia outlined several areas Democrats would scrutinize, including the administration’s handling of the Epstein investigation, U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations and potential financial conflicts involving Trump’s family.

The letters to Kushner and Trump’s sons Eric and Donald Jr. seek to preserve documents related to alleged conflicts of interest and their business dealings. Garcia also sent notices to Kimberly Guilfoyle, the former U.S. ambassador to Greece, and former Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem over separate allegations of misconduct and financial conflicts.

The letters to Vance and Blanche focus on the administration’s handling of files related to Epstein, including allegations by Democrats that White House officials sought to conceal information and manage the political fallout from the investigation.

The White House has warned Garcia and other Democrats that their planned investigations into the Trump administration may open them up to investigations from the Justice Department.

Last week, Scharf said in a letter to Garcia that “threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality.”

The investigative powers of Congress are well established, inherent in its constitutional authority as a check on the other branches of government. Modern U.S. history is filled with congressional investigations and their aftermath, from the Watergate investigation to the 9/11 attacks to Republicans’ more recent look into Biden’s family.

text:
In October 2026, the Department of Justice (DOJ) made several announcements that it had charged aliens in multiple states with election-related federal crimes, including unlawfully casting votes in U.S. elections in violation of 18 U.S.C. § 611 (Section 611). This statute makes it "unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate" in federal elections. Those indicted by the government included unlawfully present aliens and aliens admitted for lawful permanent residence.

DOJ also cited Section 611 as the basis for a complaint it filed against the State of California on October 15, 2026, in which it alleged that the state failed to take action to address a list of persons that the federal government "believes are likely noncitizens who were sent a vote-by-mail ballot from California to participate in the federal election." According to the federal government, California's failure to act amounted to "knowingly imposing an obstacle on the United States' ability to enforce 18 U.S.C. § 611 by facilitating unlawful voting rather than working with the Federal Government to prevent it," in violation of the Supremacy Clause of the U.S. Constitution. In denying the United States' request for a temporary restraining order requiring California to take action, the district court found, among other things, that the United States failed to show sufficiently that (1) it had standing to bring suit against the state, (2) Section 611 preempts California election law, and (3) the actions demanded by the United States were consistent with federal law. A majority of a panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit then determined on appeal that the district court had not abused its discretion and upheld the denial of the temporary restraining order. The United States applied to the Supreme Court for an injunction against California pending its appeal of the lower court orders, but that application was denied without noted dissent. DOJ voluntarily dismissed that case on November 6, 2026.

On October 1, 2026, a district judge in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Florida issued an opinion in United States v. Cox concluding, as a matter of nationwide first impression, that Congress did not have the constitutional authority to enact Section 611. The government has appealed that decision, and its appeal is pending before the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. After the district court's decision issued, a magistrate judge in the Western District of Wisconsin reached the same conclusion in dismissing two other criminal cases, using much the same reasoning as the district court. Those dismissals have been appealed to the relevant district court. Additionally, a district court judge in the Northern District of Texas summarily rejected the Cox opinion as a basis for a similar challenge made on the eve of a trial for violation of Section 611.

The decisions concluding that Section 611 is unconstitutional are particularly notable in light of DOJ's recent enforcement efforts. The question of the statute's constitutionality may therefore play a prominent role in the federal government's current and future enforcement of the statute and related litigation. Because of the depth of the district court's opinion in Cox and the prospect of it yielding the first appellate court opinion on this question, this Legal Sidebar outlines its reasoning in finding Section 611 to be outside of the scope of congressional authority.

The Federal Bar on Alien Voting

As the district court in Cox recounted, "since our earliest days as a republic," states have had different legal regimes "allowing (or forbidding) non-citizen voting," but states have "largely prohibited non-citizen voting since 1926." Congress enacted Section 611 in 1996; under Section 611(a), it is "unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President, Presidential elector, Member of the Senate, Member of the House of Representatives, Delegate from the District of Columbia, or Resident Commissioner." This prohibition does not apply if an election "is held partly for some other purpose" and "aliens are authorized to vote for such other purpose under a state constitution or statute or a local ordinance." Some jurisdictions do afford aliens voting opportunities in local elections. In such circumstances, Section 611(a)(3) mandates that the method of voting must be such that "an alien . . . [does] not [have] an opportunity to vote for a candidate for any one or more of" the listed federal offices. Section 611(c) additionally provides that an alien is not subject to its prohibition if, among other criteria, the alien "reasonably believed at the time of voting . . . that he or she was a citizen of the United States."

An alien found to have violated the statute may be fined and imprisoned for up to one year. There are also potential immigration consequences for violation of the statute.

Constitutional Authorities

Elections for federal office in the United States are governed by various constitutional provisions that allocate specific authorities between the states and the federal government. As detailed below, these authorities address the qualifications necessary for voting in federal elections and the way in which federal elections are carried out. Congress also has independent constitutional authority over immigration in the United States, and, in the exercise of this authority, it may preempt state laws related to aliens.

Constitutional Authorities of the States Regarding Elections

Three provisions of the Constitution set forth state authorities for establishing the qualifications of voters in elections for Congress and the President. Article I, Section 2, clause 1, of the U.S. Constitution provides that, for elections to the House of Representatives, voters "shall have the Qualifications requisite for Electors of the most numerous Branch of the State Legislature." Voters in Senate elections, under the Seventeenth Amendment to the Constitution, "shall have the qualifications requisite for electors of the most numerous branch of the State legislatures." With respect to the President, electors are, under Article II, Section 1, clause 2, appointed by each state "in such Manner as the Legislature thereof may direct."

Constitutional Authorities of Congress Related to Elections and Immigration

Congress has two primary constitutional authorities that the United States has urged in litigation pertain to the prohibition against aliens voting in federal elections. First, the Elections Clause of the Constitution provides that "[t]he Times, Places and Manner of holding Elections for Senators and Representatives, shall be prescribed in each State by the Legislature thereof; but the Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such Regulations, except as to the Places of chusing Senators." This authority permits states (or Congress, if it chooses to act) "to enact the numerous requirements as to procedure and safeguards which experience shows are necessary in order to enforce the fundamental right involved."

Second, Congress has "plenary power" to regulate immigration, powers that the Supreme Court has identified as deriving from both certain constitutional provisions and the nature of the sovereignty of the government.

United States v. Cox (S.D. Fl.)

In Cox, the United States charged, through a one-count information, an alien with "knowingly voting in a federal election" in 2020 while "fully aware that she was not a United States citizen," in violation of Section 611. The defendant moved to dismiss the information on the ground that Section 611 is an unconstitutional attempt by Congress to pass a voter qualification law for federal elections, a power that the defendant argued the Constitution instead reserves for states by conferring on them the sole authority to set qualifications for such elections under the provisions discussed above.

The district court concluded that "the text, structure, and original public meaning of the Constitution show that Congress does not have the constitutional power to enact" Section 611. In doing so, the court (1) rejected the government's contention that Supreme Court precedent required it to uphold the statute, (2) held that only states are empowered by the Constitution to set voter qualifications, including qualifications related to citizenship status, and (3) further held that no other provision of the Constitution empowered Congress to pass Section 611. As part of its analysis, it noted that there was little dispute from the parties that Section 611 functions as a voter qualification law, insofar as it "dictates who may vote in federal elections."

Applicability of Supreme Court Precedent

The government argued in Cox that the Supreme Court's decision in Oregon v. Mitchell, which upheld a law setting the minimum voting age to 18 in federal elections, demonstrated that Congress was empowered to set voter qualifications in federal elections, including on the basis of citizenship.

The district court acknowledged that, to the extent Mitchell was binding, Section 611 would be constitutional. It did not consider application of Mitchell so straightforward, however. The district court explained that, in Mitchell, the Justices agreed on a result—Congress could set an age-based voter qualification in federal elections—but could not agree on what constitutional authority lay behind that result. The district court pointed out that five Justices "rejected the view that the Elections Clause empowered Congress to regulate voter qualifications in federal elections." It also pointed out that five Justices "also rejected the view that the Fourteenth Amendment empowered Congress to lower the voting age." Faced with this set of divergent rationales, the district court concluded that it was bound by Supreme Court and circuit precedent to view Mitchell as establishing only that "Congress can regulate voting-age qualifications in federal elections," and therefore could not control questions concerning other types of voting qualifications. It further found that subsequent precedent "further diminish[ed] Mitchell's force." In particular, the district court recited the Supreme Court's statement in Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona (ITCA), that "the Elections Clause empowers Congress to regulate how federal elections are held, but not who may vote in them." The district court conceded that this statement was dicta, but "the kind of dicta that merits careful attention from the lower courts," and, when considered alongside other precedent, further reason to believe that Mitchell did not control.

Scope of State Authority over Voter Qualifications

Having identified no binding Supreme Court precedent resolving the case, the district court in Cox then held that "[t]he Constitution commits to the States, and the States alone, the general power to set voter qualifications in federal elections" as a matter of both its text and history. The court examined the clauses of the Constitution addressing election of Representatives, Senators, and the President, and concluded that they all reflected the same principle: "The States have sole authority to set voter qualifications." According to the court, the constitutional provisions addressing congressional elections establish that "voters' qualifications are a function of each State's rules" and the provision addressing presidential elections provides that "the States have the prerogative to establish whatever rules for selecting electors they see fit." This reading reflected a "foundational principle of our constitutional order," namely, a federal government of limited powers.

The district court identified further support for this reading of the text of the Constitution in the history surrounding its adoption and the adoption of subsequent amendments. As to the former, the court recounted that the framers of the Constitution considered and rejected "a proposal . . . that would have assigned the federal government the power to set voter qualifications for federal elections." As to the latter, the court recounted the rejection of a similar proposal during consideration of the Reconstruction Amendments and noted further that subsequent amendments addressing voting "[did] not alter the Framers' original design."

Scope of Congressional Authority over Voter Qualifications

The district court in Cox then rejected both congressional plenary power over immigration and congressional authority under the Elections Clause as adequate bases for Section 611.

The government characterized Section 611 as a means to address foreign interference in elections, placing it well within congressional authority over immigration and foreign affairs. The court in Cox agreed that congressional authority in this respect is "broad indeed," but was not convinced that Section 611 was a means of "legislat[ing] against foreign interference in federal elections." Textually, the district court focused on the statute's exception for state and local elections, finding that "[i]f Congress really intended the statute as an exercise of its plenary authority over aliens, there's no reason it would have cleaved off non-federal elections." It also found the generalized nature of congressional power over immigration and foreign affairs to cut against the ability of Congress to override the specific authorities concerning voting qualifications in federal elections that the Constitution textually commits to the states. It explained that these latter specific clauses reflected "a foundational limit on federal authority," and such "[f]oundational constitutional limits do not give way, even to capacious general provisions of enumerated congressional power."

The government also characterized Section 611 as a means to ensure the integrity of federal elections, thereby making it a legitimate exercise of congressional authority under the Elections Clause. Relying largely on ITCA, the district court held that Section 611 fell outside of that authority because the Elections Clause reflects "[t]he power to regulate the 'mechanics' of federal elections" and not "the power to decide who may vote" in federal elections. The court further determined that the government had offered no evidence that Section 611 was "designed to further" the purpose of preventing voter fraud.

Enforcement Consequences

In light of the exclusive authorities to set voter qualifications given by the Constitution to the states, and the concomitant lack of congressional authority to independently set voter qualifications, the district court in Cox held that Section 611 was unconstitutional as applied to the defendant. "To hold otherwise," it reasoned, "would allow Congress to establish and modify the parameters of its own special electorate, entirely divorced from what . . . any . . . State may decide," a "result [that] is precisely what our federal constitutional republic does not allow."

The district noted three further points related to its holding. First, it explained that the state in which the defendant voted "can and does" punish the same conduct. Second, it made clear that its opinion did not "address the Government's power to remove a non-U.S. citizen who engages in the same conduct." Third, while disclaiming any definitive conclusion, it suggested that a federal statute criminalizing voting in federal elections in violation of state law would present "very different" legal considerations.

Considerations for Congress

Because the district court in Cox considered only an as-applied challenge to Section 611 in the posture of a motion to dismiss, the effect of its constitutional holding is limited to the defendant. If, in the appeal to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit, that court rejects the government's position and upholds the district court's decision, similarly situated aliens in that circuit may be able to rely on this precedent to claim that the statute is also unconstitutional as applied to them. Should that court or other appellate courts reach broadly applicable determinations that the statute is unconstitutional, several paths are available to Congress, including waiting for a definitive Supreme Court decision; repealing the statute in favor of state enforcement of state voter qualification laws; or amending the statute, as contemplated by the district court, to criminalize voting in federal elections in violation of state voter qualification laws.

description:
About this Report This report examines the Trump administration’s campaign of “delegalization,” the process by which people who lawfully obtained temporary immigration protections lose those protections through broad policy decisions rather than any individual wrongdoing.
Key Findings The Trump administration is carrying out the largest delegalization campaign in modern U.S. history, with a conservative estimate showing that more than 1.3 million — and likely far more — immigrants have lost legal protections since January 2025.
Why it Matters For decades, Congress has failed to create lasting pathways to permanent legal status for many immigrants who live and work in the United States.
In the absence of legislative solutions, successive administrations relied on temporary protections to allow millions of people to remain legally present and participate in American communities.
True stability requires permanent solutions that allow long-term residents who have followed the rules and built their lives in the United States to obtain lasting legal status.
text:
About this Report

This report examines the Trump administration’s campaign of “delegalization,” the process by which people who lawfully obtained temporary immigration protections lose those protections through broad policy decisions rather than any individual wrongdoing. Many of those affected followed every rule the government established. They registered with federal agencies, submitted biometric information, paid application fees, renewed their status on time, and built lives around the promise that compliance would allow them to remain in the country legally.

By documenting the administration’s efforts and their consequences, this report shows how millions of immigrants, along with the families, employers, and communities that depend on them, are being pushed into uncertainty.

Key Findings

The Trump administration is carrying out the largest delegalization campaign in modern U.S. history, with a conservative estimate showing that more than 1.3 million — and likely far more — immigrants have lost legal protections since January 2025.

More than 1 million people have lost status through the termination of Temporary Protected Status (TPS) programs.

Humanitarian parole programs have been dismantled or restricted, affecting hundreds of thousands more.

Dreamers, immigrant youth, survivors of crime and trafficking, and other immigrants with pending applications for legal status are increasingly vulnerable to arrest, detention, and deportation, even when they are pursuing pathways specifically created by U.S. law.

The consequences extend beyond immigrants themselves. Employers are losing experienced workers, industries are facing workforce disruptions, families are losing income, and local communities are experiencing growing instability and fear.

Why it Matters

For decades, Congress has failed to create lasting pathways to permanent legal status for many immigrants who live and work in the United States. In the absence of legislative solutions, successive administrations relied on temporary protections to allow millions of people to remain legally present and participate in American communities. As a result, the legal security of entire populations now depends on decisions that can change from one administration to the next.

The current delegalization campaign reveals the limits of that approach. People who followed government rules, maintained their status, and built their lives in the United States are now finding that those protections can be withdrawn with little warning. The consequences reach far beyond affected immigrants, creating uncertainty for employers, local economies, schools, and communities across the country.

Without congressional action, the cycle is likely to repeat itself every time political control changes. True stability requires permanent solutions that allow long-term residents who have followed the rules and built their lives in the United States to obtain lasting legal status. Until then, millions of people will remain vulnerable to abrupt policy shifts that can upend families, businesses, and communities overnight.

text:
Earlier this week, One Nation’s migration policy disappeared from its website, only to be replaced by an updated platform announced via press conference on Wednesday morning.

By my count, this is the third iteration of One Nation’s immigration policy – if you factor in Pauline Hanson’s Press Club address in June and her later announcement of a 130,000 yearly arrival target, amid internal disagreements and contradictions.

The latest announcement involves an end to permanent parent migration, with an estimated $1bn in visa fees to be refunded to applicants, and parents already in the country to be rounded up and deported at taxpayers’ expense. Another plank involves the reduction of humanitarian intake to 2,000.

At this point, it has become trite to observe that One Nation’s immigration policies are as cruel as they are unworkable. Abruptly closing parent visas would permanently separate families who have been waiting decades to be reunited. It would mean that future generations would not have the chance to live with their Nonna or Nonno, their Dadi or Dada, the way so many of us did.

Slashing humanitarian numbers will leave thousands of people – including the victims of wars that Australia has waged – stranded both overseas and on our shores. It would involve, for instance, abandoning communities like the Yazidis who were systematically targeted by the Islamic State. One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce has previously expressed his personal solidarity with Yazidi refugees and actively encouraged them to settle in his electorate during the Morrison era.

Applied onshore, a rigid humanitarian cap wouldn’t block people from applying for asylum. Instead, it would mean that people entitled to refugee status would have to wait in a decades-long queue to be granted a permanent visa. During that time, they would be locked out of permanent jobs, prevented from setting down roots and making a home for themselves in Australia.

Hanson says the proposals would save the government $141bn over 10 years but admits they haven’t been costed. The absence of critical details and evidence is to be expected if we accept, as we should at this point, that One Nation’s migration policy has nothing to do with immigration at all. Rather, it is about providing thin populist cover to a political program shaped by billionaire interests and hostile to working people across the country.

Just as its net migration targets were said to be about protecting “Australian jobs,” Wednesday’s announcements were sold to the public as a tough but fair attempt to “look after Australians first”. But if we look beyond the talking points, it’s clear that the party selling itself to the battlers is, in fact, committed to selling out working people – wherever they are from.

What will these “Australian jobs” look like, in a future society where One Nation has successfully deported 75,000 people (and perhaps even managed to exclude some of the rest of us who were born overseas)? One Nation’s voting record provides the answer.

In federal parliament, One Nation has consistently voted against measures that would improve the lives of working people. One Nation voted against measures that would have strengthened the rights of casual workers to secure permanent jobs. It voted against a “same job, same pay” proposal that would have ensured pay parity between contractors and permanent workers. It opposed paid parental leave, on the basis that women “get themselves pregnant” to access entitlements. And when this voting record was put to Hanson at the Press Club, she said businesses had complained to her about workers being lazy and “on their phones”.

The same case can be made about any part of One Nation’s voting record. When it comes to housing affordability, One Nation wants to reintroduce investor discounts that have put home ownership out of reach for many working people. On healthcare, One Nation wants to limit abortion, shifting the physical and psychological cost on to women.

The political, social and economic grievances driving support for One Nation are real. One Nation’s solutions to those problems are not. They rely on a simple, base political assumption: that ordinary people will not look beyond their immediate patch – their family, their neighbourhood – and realise what they have in common with one another.

As we face down the dystopian proposal of rounding up and deporting grandmothers, we can show that we are better, and smarter, than that.

title: Most Americans want at least some congressional effort put into investigating the Trump ...
description:
Most Republicans, and the vast majority of MAGA Republicans, say Congress should spend no effort investigating the Trump administration.
Overall, 40% of Americans say Congress should put a lot of effort into investigating the Trump administration, and 18% say it should spend some effort doing this.
The poll asked Americans who support Congress spending at least a little effort investigating Trump an open-ended question about what they wanted Congress to investigate.
Majority support for Congress investigating the Trump administration comes as both Trump and many of his senior officials are unpopular.
Trump's net job approval of -25 is near his lowest on Economist / YouGov Polls in either term; only the other two November 2026 polls show fractionally lower net job approval.
text:
Most Democrats and Independents — and one-quarter of Republicans who aren't MAGA supporters — want Congress to spend some or a lot of effort investigating the Trump administration after Democrats take over in January, according to the latest Economist / YouGov Poll. Most Republicans, and the vast majority of MAGA Republicans, say Congress should spend no effort investigating the Trump administration.

Overall, 40% of Americans say Congress should put a lot of effort into investigating the Trump administration, and 18% say it should spend some effort doing this. 10% say Congress should spend a little effort on investigations, and 31% say it should spend none at all. Almost all Democrats (90%) and few Republicans (17%) support congressional effort toward investigations. 66% of Independents and 27% of non-MAGA Republicans support Congress spending some or a lot of effort on investigations.

The poll asked Americans who support Congress spending at least a little effort investigating Trump an open-ended question about what they wanted Congress to investigate. Corruption is mentioned most often (by 34% of those who support at least a little effort investigating Trump), followed by financial self-enrichment (29%), sexual misconduct and the Jeffrey Epstein files (19%), and war crimes (12%), based on coding of the responses by an AI model.

60% of Americans say Trump is using his office for personal gain, including 92% of Democrats, 65% of Independents, and 21% of Republicans. Only 27% of Americans disagree. 51% say "corrupt" describes Trump and only 17% say it doesn't. That's in line with "dangerous" (50% vs. 17%). Fewer say each of the other 11 traits asked about describes Trump.

Majority support for Congress investigating the Trump administration comes as both Trump and many of his senior officials are unpopular. 37% of registered voters strongly or somewhat approve of how Trump is handling his job as president, while 62% disapprove. Trump's net job approval of -25 is near his lowest on Economist / YouGov Polls in either term; only the other two November 2026 polls show fractionally lower net job approval. A three-week rolling average of Trump's job approval among registered voters is -25, which covers the entire postelection period and is the lowest average net approval he has ever received.

The Economist / YouGov Poll asked Americans whether Trump should keep or fire six of his Cabinet members. While many Americans have no opinion about firing many of the Cabinet members, those with opinions are more likely to support than oppose firing five of the six. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has more support for keeping him (54%) than firing him (46%). The other five all have majorities of those with opinions supporting firing: Scott Bessent (54%), Robert F. Kennedy Jr. (58%), Todd Blanche (61%), Pete Hegseth (62%), and Howard Lutnick (66%).

Majorities of Democrats say each of the six Cabinet officers should be fired, ranging from 53% for Bessent to 78% for Kennedy. Republicans are more likely to say Trump should keep than fire each of the six, though 53% of Republicans are unsure about firing Lutnick and 46% are unsure about firing Blanche.

A majority of Americans disagree with the statement that "presidents should govern without too much interference from Congress and the courts": 28% strongly or somewhat agree, and 57% disagree.

Almost all Democrats disagree with this statement (10% agree and 79% disagree), as do most Independents (18% vs. 61%). A majority of Republicans agree (59% vs. 30%). Most MAGA Republicans agree (68% vs. 25%), while non-MAGA Republicans are more closely divided (45% vs. 39%).

There's little partisan split about which branch of the U.S. government is most powerful. Among Democrats, Independents, and both MAGA and non-MAGA Republicans, the most common answer is that all three are equally powerful (45% of Americans, 47% of Democrats, and 49% of Republicans say this). Another 18% of Americans say the executive branch is the most powerful, 15% say the judicial branch is, and 8% say the legislative branch is.

Republicans are slightly more likely than Democrats to say the executive branch is the most powerful (23% vs. 15%). 3% of MAGA Republicans say the legislative branch is the most powerful, compared to 16% of non-MAGA Republicans.

Trump started his second term with positive ratings on his handling of immigration, but these have fallen steadily over the past two years to a -14 net approval among registered voters (42% strongly or somewhat approve and 56% disapprove). This is the lowest net approval on immigration he has received in any Economist / YouGov Poll in either of his two terms. Trump has comparatively higher approval ratings for his handling of immigration than he does for many other issues, including health care, the economy, and inflation.

During the first year of Trump's second term, Americans' approval of how Trump was handling the economy closely paralleled Trump's overall job approval. In early 2026, however, Trump's approval on handling the economy began diverging. Since then, it usually has been lower than his overall job approval. In other words, in a typical week a small share of Americans disapprove of how Trump is handling the economy but approve of his overall job performance.

Instead, approval of how Trump is handling foreign policy has been the closest match to Trump's overall job approval of all the issues regularly asked about on Economist / YouGov Polls. Before the U.S. attacked Iran on Feb. 28, 2026, net approval of how Trump handled the economy was an average of less than 1 point different from his overall job approval; after that, Trump's economic net approval has been an average of 8 points lower than his overall approval. Trump's foreign policy net approval averaged about 2 points of difference from his overall approval before the Iran war, and less than 1 point after.
