title: Lawmakers press Mullin on flight disruptions and ICE tactics | PBS News
description:
Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin said none of the incidents were tied to any attack.
Stephanie Sy: Mullin was also sharply questioned by Ranking Member Bennie Thompson over a flight he took in a private plane the morning after the grounding.
Stephanie Sy: Mullin also said he took that flight to signal to Americans that it was safe to fly again.
Stephanie Sy: That policy is likely to face further scrutiny by Congress next year as it ushers in new majorities.
Stephanie Sy: For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.
text:
Amna Nawaz:

National security officials from the Trump administration were on Capitol Hill today, and lawmakers had plenty of questions about the series of outages and cyber problems that have alarmed millions.

Markwayne Mullin, the secretary of homeland security, and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, sought to reassure Americans during their testimony before a House committee.

Stephanie Sy has that report.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino (R-NY):

Committee on Homeland Security will come to order.

Stephanie Sy:

On Capitol Hill today, lawmakers demanded answers from the Trump administration over a series of outages that have jolted Americans in the last couple of weeks, including the National Security Agency, Microsoft, banks, and the nationwide grounding of air travel.

Homeland Secretary Markwayne Mullin said none of the incidents were tied to any attack.

Markwayne Mullin:

I have said this publicly, I'm 98 percent confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems.

Stephanie Sy:

Mullin was also sharply questioned by Ranking Member Bennie Thompson over a flight he took in a private plane the morning after the grounding.

Rep. Bennie Thompson (D-MS):

While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game. For the secretary of homeland security to do that during a crisis was not only irresponsible, Mr. Secretary, but also incredibly tone-deaf.

Markwayne Mullin:

We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication, and didn't have one single incident. That in itself is a great success. And then you want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great-nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior to that, because I wanted to be a good uncle.

Stephanie Sy:

Mullin also said he took that flight to signal to Americans that it was safe to fly again.

But the recent disruptions extend well beyond the skies to other daily life, leaving many nervous Americans with questions. Lawmakers pressed for more specifics.

Rep. Michael Guest (R-MS):

We have seen Microsoft services go offline, a nationwide ground stop, disruption within our major banking institutions, disruption of U.S. national security communications infrastructure. And, earlier this week, United Airlines had a nationwide system outage.

Stephanie Sy:

While Cabinet officials didn't provide a definitive answer on the causes, Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, reassured Americans the failures were not related or coordinated.

Jay Clayton:

We have no indication that they have come from external threat actors or state-sponsored actors.

Stephanie Sy:

But Clayton did say system upgrades were being performed during some of the outages that occurred.

Jay Clayton:

I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions. These are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes.

Stephanie Sy:

Meanwhile, after their overwhelming election wins, Democrats also used the opportunity to grill Mullin on immigration enforcement and the role of ICE.

Pablo Hernandez Rivera, Resident Commissioner of Puerto Rico: When the government enters an apartment and zip-ties children and citizens, the government is the threat. When the government opens fires on our streets, and families have to bury their dead, the government is the threat.

Stephanie Sy:

Mullin defended his record.

Markwayne Mullin:

Our policy right now is to go after the worst of the worst. But every time you go after the worst of the worst, you also have what we call collateral criminals. So, when we arrest someone that's on a warrant, most of the time, they're not by themselves.

Stephanie Sy:

That policy is likely to face further scrutiny by Congress next year as it ushers in new majorities.

Rep. Andrew Garbarino:

Without objection, this committee stands adjourned.

Stephanie Sy:

For the "PBS News Hour," I'm Stephanie Sy.

text:
Three Twin Cities churches are asking a judge to order the Trump Administration to reveal the full extent of its surveillance of religious and civic groups during and after last winter’s immigration operation. The undercover activity first came to light this summer in defense filings in a criminal case against 15 anti-ICE activists.

In June, a federal grand jury charged the group with conspiracy to impede or injure federal officers by setting up blockades and staging protests around the Whipple Federal Building. The 94-page indictment does not include evidence that the defendants hurt anyone. The charges are largely based on information that undercover agents gathered while infiltrating Signal chats and meetings of activists.

A batch of documents defense attorneys received from prosecutors as part of the routine discovery process are included in a motion attorney Kevin Riach, who represents lead defendant Isaac Sant, filed on Aug. 13. Riach writes that the initial tranche of materials the Department of Justice handed over omits numerous documents and communications, as well as data from phones and laptops undercover agents used.

The documents revealed so far show Homeland Security Investigations obtained years worth of financial records from labor unions and sent undercover agents to meetings at libraries, parks, union halls and churches as part of efforts that the agency dubbed “Operation Puppet Master” and “Project Whipple Shield.”

Attorney Irina Vaynerman of the nonprofit Groundwork Legal filed a friend-of-the-court brief on Wednesday on behalf of the three churches — First Universalist Church and Hennepin Avenue United Methodist in Minneapolis and St. John the Evangelist Episcopal Church in St. Paul — in support of Riach’s motion for additional discovery.

In an interview with MPR News, Vaynerman said the public deserves to know the full extent of how and why federal agents spied on Minnesotans. She said the surveillance activities carry dark echoes of government spying on Japanese Americans during WWII and on an earlier generation of civil rights activists in the 1960s.

“History does not look fondly on the American government spying on its own people and targeting them for their beliefs and who they are, not what they do,” Vaynerman said. “There’s not criminal activity to justify the wide dragnet of surveillance that occurred here.”

A spokesperson for the Minnesota U.S. Attorney’s Office declined to comment on the brief. In a Sept. 10 filing, Assistant U.S. Attorney Tory Sailer writes the defendants’ “extraordinarily broad” request for additional information is not necessary for preparing their defense and that additional disclosure about undercover operations could endanger confidential informants and agents.

In her brief, Vaynerman notes that on Dec. 13, 2025, an agent surreptitiously attended a meeting of the Sunrise Movement social justice group at First Universalist. In a report, which is part of the public court file, the agent did not identify any crime but writes that “further attendance was determined to be necessary to rule out violations of law.”

First Universalist Senior Minister Jen Crow said in an interview with MPR News on Wednesday that the revelations have led the church to keep a close eye on unfamiliar people and that some members have stopped attending in person.

“It’s been frightening, both for myself and for members of the community, in particular for folks in our church community who are from any kind of marginalized group. They were already being targeted during the ICE occupation. They’re already at greater risk,” Crow said.

She also said that on Jan. 10, agents “openly surveilled” the church from the outside, repeatedly circling the block during a memorial service for a church member.

“It would be nice to have the full discovery and be able to see how often the government was here, what they were looking for and to have an honest record of their behavior for this period of time,” Crow said.

In late February, Homeland Security Investigations agents followed Emmett Doyle, who was later charged in the Minnesota 15 case, to Hennepin Avenue United Methodist and observed him loading “ICE Out” signs into a truck. In mid-April, an undercover agent attended a meeting of the group Direct Action Minnesota at St. John’s and ran the license plates of people parked outside.

Federal prosecutors allege Direct Action Minnesota is an “antifa affinity group.” They filed the charges after President Donald Trump in issued a national security memorandum known as NSPM-7 in September 2025 targeting people he called “anarchists and agitators.”

Friend-of-the court briefs, also known as amicus briefs, are rare in criminal cases, but this is the second filed in support of Riach’s discovery motion.

In August, three conservative and libertarian-leaning organizations — the Cato Institute, the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression and the Society for the Rule of Law — filed a similar brief.

The groups argue the surveillance and prosecution are “designed to chill participation in protest activity, quell dissent and silence critics of Trump administration policies under the guise of combating terrorism.”

text:
US President Donald Trump’s administration has asked the Supreme Court to issue an emergency order allowing officials to strip legal protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants, marking the third time it has appealed to the nation’s top judicial body over the issue.

The Department of Justice on Wednesday filed an emergency application asking the Supreme Court to put on hold a federal judge’s ruling that officials lacked the authority to end the Temporary Protected Status (TPS) granted to the migrants under former President Joe Biden.

San Francisco-based US District Judge Edward Chen’s ruling is due to take effect on Friday unless a federal appeals court or the Supreme Court moves to suspend it. The Supreme Court previously paused Chen’s ruling in October 2025.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorisation. It also argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm”.

If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The plaintiffs who challenged the administration’s actions, including TPS holders and an advocacy group, said that since the previous Supreme Court intervention in the case, Venezuelan TPS holders have been detained, separated from children who are US citizens, deported to Venezuela, and even sent to so-called “third countries” where they have no ties.

The Supreme Court in June backed the administration’s separate actions ending TPS for hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians, giving a boost to the Republican president’s hardline approach towards immigration.

Trump clamps down on TPS

TPS is a designation that lets migrants from countries stricken by war, natural disaster or other catastrophes live and work in the US while it is unsafe for them to return to their home countries.

A person granted TPS cannot be deported, can obtain an employment authorisation document, and may be given travel authorisation. A TPS holder cannot be detained by the US over their immigration status.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire by September 9, and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan in October.

Millions of people have fled Venezuela in recent years due to political repression and a crippling economic crisis spurred in part by US sanctions against the government of President Nicolas Maduro.

Before leaving office, the Biden administration had extended TPS for about 600,000 Venezuelans through October 2026.

The State Department currently warns people to reconsider travel to Venezuela due to the risk of crime, kidnapping and poor health infrastructure, among other issues.

text:
By Kanishka Singh

WASHINGTON, Nov 18 (Reuters) – A federal judge said on Wednesday the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency “made a mockery of court orders” in Colorado and that ​the court found government officials in contempt for instantly ‌re-arresting a man whom the judge had ordered released.

US District Judge Charlotte Sweeney declined to take any further action because she said the officials had “cured the contempt by ceasing the practice at issue” as sworn by ‌an ​official in court.

“ICE’s new ‘policy’ of immediately re-detaining ⁠petitioners following release made ⁠a mockery of court orders mandating petitioners’ immediate release,” the judge wrote, according to court records in the US District Court for the District of Colorado.

At least 18 people in ​Colorado have been held in detention longer than they should have been or have been re-arrested within minutes of their ⁠judge-ordered release in the past six ⁠weeks, CPR News, the news division of Colorado Public ​Radio, reported.

The report said that immigration attorneys estimated the number may ​be higher given that some immigrants represented themselves.

ICE, which ‌is part of the Department of Homeland Security, has been the face of Republican President Donald Trump’s immigration crackdown and deportation drive that rights groups say has violated free speech and due ⁠process rights.

Human rights groups also say the crackdown has created an unsafe environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial ⁠profiling.

The Trump administration ‌has maintained that its actions aim to ⁠improve domestic security and are in compliance with ​the law. ‌ICE and DHS did not immediately respond ​to a ⁠request for comment on what the judge said on Wednesday.

Democrats, who won majorities in both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections earlier this month, say they aim to hold the Trump administration accountable for its immigration policies.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing ​by Thomas Derpinghaus)

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.

The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.

It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”

President Donald Trump has moved to withdraw protections that have allowed immigrants from multiple countries to remain in the United States and work legally, some for decades.

The Supreme Court also allowed the Trump administration to end temporary legal protections for people from Haiti and Syria in June. An appeals court subsequently paused the judge's decision that kept the program in place for Venezuelans, but that pause is set to expire Friday.

The program known as TPS was created by Congress in 1990 to prevent deportations to countries suffering from natural disasters or civil strife. It is granted in increments of up to 18 months. The government argues that TPS is a temporary program that only offers short-term protections.

The Trump administration has terminated TPS for more than 1 million people from 13 countries, including Venezuela, Haiti, Honduras, Nicaragua, Afghanistan and Syria. But in a change in practice, the administration kept protections in place for nearly 200,000 Salvadorans whose TPS was set to expire Sept. 9 and for more than 100,000 people from Ukraine and Sudan, in October.

TPS for Venezuelans was first introduced in March 2021, under the administration of Democratic President Joe Biden. In September 2023, it was expanded to include more beneficiaries. About 600,000 Venezuelans have received TPS protections.

After the administration ended TPS for Venezuelans last year, their work authorizations also ceased to be valid. Thousands of people were subjected to removal proceedings, detained and deported. Many Venezuelans chose to leave the country voluntarily. It is not clear how many Venezuelans who had the protections are still living in the U.S.

Emi MacLean, an attorney for the National TPS Alliance at the American Civil Liberties Union of Northern California, said the administration has no basis for its request to the Supreme Court.

“The lower courts should be able to rule on this question, and they are taking it seriously and they’re moving expeditiously,” MacLean said. “What the government is trying to do is jump the line to get the Supreme Court to endorse their illegal actions and allow the harm inflicted on Venezuelan TPS holders to continue."

——

Salomon reported from Miami.

text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, in testimony Wednesday to Congress, defended his flight to a weekend college football game, tried to tamp down speculation about a series of recent cyber outages and found himself pressed repeatedly on training given to the country’s immigration enforcement officers.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee, a standard yearly opportunity for lawmakers to question administration officials about national security threats, covered a broad range of topics. It also gave Democrats, after their recent midterm drubbing of Republicans, a chance to confront a Cabinet member.

A look at some of the highlights:

Officials keep trying to reassure Americans over computer system disruptions

Mullin and the two other witnesses, FBI Deputy Director Christopher Raia and Jay Clayton, the director of national intelligence, insisted that the high-profile outages across the government and private sector over the past week had no connection to each other and did not result from a cyberattack or nefarious activity.

“I understand the timing of these incidents can raise questions, and it should. The American people should ask us these questions,” Clayton said. “But based on what we know today,” he said, “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack.”

Among the events were an hourslong outage in Microsoft services; a nationwide ground stop brought about by a technology upgrade on the nation’s air traffic control system that overloaded antiquated equipment and caused “intermittent” communications and radar gaps; banking problems that rippled through the financial industry; and a disruption to a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

The episodes stirred widespread public concern that they could be linked or caused by hackers. Officials said there was no evidence of that.

“I’m 98% confident that this has nothing to do with our adversaries hacking or going after our systems,” Mullin said.

Those statements of reassurance came against the backdrop of concerns about the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is part of Mullin’s Department of Homeland Security. It is tasked with working with industry to protect infrastructure, including water and electric generation, election systems, chemical facilities and cyber networks.

That agency has been without a Senate-confirmed leader since President Donald Trump took office for a second term in early 2025. Trump’s original pick withdrew his nomination earlier this year after it had languished for months in the Senate. The agency also lost staff last year during cuts aimed at reducing the size of the government.

Mullin flew to a football game as travelers were scrambling

Mullin defended his decision to fly to Louisiana on Saturday for the LSU-Texas game as travelers across the United States were still stuck at airports after the nationwide grounding of flights.

Mullin’s flight took place after the stoppage was lifted and as planes were back in the air. But thousands of flights were canceled because of the ground stop, and Mullin flew as people nationwide were forced to scramble for alternative travel options.

On Wednesday, he said canceling the trip could have sent a confusing message.

Mullin said his travel had been planned for weeks so he could take relatives to the game and there was discussion before the trip about whether to forgo it.

“If we canceled something with the airspace completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there. I was meeting other people there that would show maybe distrust that we’re not even willing to fly,” Mullin said.

Mullin reiterated that he is required to fly on government planes and that he paid for the trip.

Mullin defends ground stop response

Mullin was front and center in the Republican administration’s response to the grounding of all aircraft last week.

The administration has said the ground stop was the result of problems with newly installed routers that caused the Federal Aviation Administration’s telecommunications system to be flooded with data, forcing the agency to ground all flights while it addressed the issue.

At the hearing, Mullin pushed back on criticism that the administration wasn’t giving the public clear answers.

“We were able to put the planes back in the air safely. We landed over 4,000 planes when the ground stoppage went out because of the communication and didn’t have one single incident. That in itself is a great success,” Mullin said.

Immigration enforcement under new scrutiny

Lawmakers focused part of their scrutiny of Mullin on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters with federal officers. Also discussed was shortened training and the vetting of some newly hired agents.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement has had an unprecedented hiring spree, bringing on 12,000 new officers and special agents. The hiring rush has raised questions about whether the government lowered standards and conducted incomplete background checks. In one prominent case, an ICE officer with what his family and records say was a history of violent behavior shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine.

Mullin said every ICE officer in service now has had a full background check and that those who have not are on administrative leave. Officers who have not completed a full 13 weeks of training also have been placed on leave until they conclude their training, he said.

The deaths of U.S. citizens such as Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis led to a tense exchange when Rep. LaMonica McIver, D-N.J., asked Mullin if he had any regrets over his role in enforcing Trump’s immigration agenda.

Mullin said he had none. Then McIver pressed him about apologies for the deaths.

“You are killing people,” McIver replied.

“No ma’am. That’s your opinion,” Mullin said, ending the exchange.

Mullin took over DHS after Kristi Noem was ousted in March when the deaths of the Minnesota protesters at the hands of immigration enforcement officers forced the administration to adjust its mass deportation strategy.

Immigration arrests initially fell but then rebounded as ICE, flush with billions of dollars in new congressional funding, hired new officers and maximized cooperation from local and state law enforcement agencies.

Trump has indicated after the Nov. 3 election losses that he could work with Democrats on immigration legislation, but he has also elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his immigration crackdown, to be his chief of staff.

___

Associated Press writers Josh Funk in Omaha, Nebraska, and Valerie Gonzalez in McAllen, Texas, contributed to this report.

text:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was scheduled to testify to members of Congress during an annual hearing Wednesday on the state of worldwide threats to the U.S., hinged this year on the 25th anniversary of the September 11 attacks.

But moments into his opening statement, Mullin launched into his most extensive defense yet of his attendance at a college football game during a weekend of air travel chaos for thousands of Americans, along with growing fears of cyberattacks and critical infrastructure compromised by artificial intelligence.

Mullin, whose DHS gutted the cybersecurity agency responsible for responding to those threats, wasn't in attendance at the hearing to calm the nerves of anxious Americans. Instead, he used his opening remarks to insult Democrats on the panel and spun any criticism about his weekend trip into a personal attack against his family.

The secretary, who Trump appointed to lead the beleaguered agency after firing Kristi Noem earlier this year, spent the rest of the hearing struggling to respond to questions about deadly immigration enforcement incidents and insufficient training for thousands of ICE officers who were quickly deployed to the streets after Republicans approved billions of dollars in new funding for new recruits.

The hearing marked Mullin's first appearance before lawmakers since sweeping Democratic victories in midterm elections earlier this month, teeing up Democratic control of both chambers of Congress in January. Democrats are eager to start investigating Mullin, and other Trump administration officials, and they made clear during Wednesday's hearing that oversight is coming.

In his opening statement, the committee's top Democrat Bennie Thompson, who is poised to lead the committee in January, called Mullin's attendance at Saturday's Louisiana State University football game "tone deaf."

"While Americans were stranded in airports across the country, with many sleeping on the floor at their gates, the secretary boarded a luxury jet, flew to a college football game and visited the private suite of a company that DHS had awarded a $2.2 billion contract for the secretary of Homeland Security," said Thompson, referencing a suite owned by the CEO of Louisiana-based contractor Bollinger Shipyards.

Later in the hearing, Republican Rep. Michael McCaul even thanked Mullin because nobody died.

"Let me commend you," he said. "36,000 planes being grounded? Yes, it was chaotic, but you know what? Nobody died. I want to thank you for that."

The only thing that appeared to crash after those massive air traffic system failures was Mullin himself.

In his opening remarks, Mullin blasted "hypocrisy" from Democratic members of the committee, arguing that they would have done the same thing if they were in his shoes, even though they were not. Canceling the event, he said, would have created "confusion" and "distrust" about air safety, he said.

"You want to bring up the fact that I took my family and my great nieces to an LSU game that was scheduled for weeks prior to that, because I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece — who has never been to an LSU game, and she's a huge LSU fan — to a game," the Homeland Security chief said.

"We had deep conversations about it, and it came in that if we cancel something with the airspace that was completely open, it could bring confusion because I was meeting the governor there, I was meeting other people there," he added. "That would show maybe distrust that we're not even willing to fly."

He claimed Democrats "would have done the same thing but would've called it a campaign event," he said.

"This hypocrisy has got to stop," Mullin said. "I have nothing to keep from you. I want you to do your job, but I'm not playing games."

Mullin and other officials on the panel sought to reassure Americans that alleged threats from Iran, tech outages and air traffic closures are all separate, unrelated incidents, stopping short of calling it a coincidence.

"I understand the timings of the incidents can raise questions, and it should," Trump's intelligence director Jay Clayton told the committee. "But based on what we know today … these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state sponsored attack."

But the Trump administration has gutted the agency tasked with responding to those kinds of cybersecurity threats.

The Cybersecurity & Infrastructure Agency has been villainized by the president and his allies over the agency's past efforts to disrupt election disinformation after former director Christopher Krebs publicly assured that the 2020 presidential elections were the "most secure in American history." Trump, of course, falsely believes that the election was stolen and rigged against him, a narrative that formed the basis of his 2024 campaign and his administration's threats to seize control of midterm elections.

Since taking office, Trump has purged nearly one-third of the agency's workforce, or roughly 1,000 people — leaving the agency unprepared to respond to emerging threats from artificial intelligence and a new era of cyber warfare, experts previously told The Independent.

The administration wants to hire back 300 employees, but a fiscal 2027 budget proposal suggests eliminating another 900 positions from the agency.

A group of Democratic lawmakers are pushing for a Government Accountability Office report on the impact of those cuts — which Mullin didn't appear prepared to answer.

"Was it a mistake in 2025 for those employees … that you now need back … to have been fired and pushed out? Yes or no?" Democratic Rep. James Walkinshaw asked.

"I wasn't there," Mullin said. "I'm not going to talk about why someone was let go when I wasn't involved."

"If it wasn't a mistake, why did you tell Congress you need hundreds of them back?" Walkinshaw fired back.

"You have no information about CISA's workforce. As our cyber threat facing the American people is exploding, you don't have basic information," he said. "What work is not getting done at CISA?"

Mullin insists "we have not missed a mission" but "we need to address emerging threats."

For Mullin and other Trump administration officials, those threats are coming from inside the country, the so-called "worst of the worst" immigrants that the White House wants deported by the millions.

Immigration agents have shot at least seven people — killing two — since Mullin entered office in March. Officers have shot more than two dozen people since Trump returned to the White House, and at least 57 people have died in ICE custody in that time.

Trump himself recently conceded that his anti-immigration policy has been "too tough." On Wednesday, Mullin wouldn't say whether he agreed.

Democratic Rep. Seth Magaziner asked Mullin how many ICE agents had been on the job without having full background checks completed, like officer David Brouillette, who fatally shot Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero in Biddeford, Maine in July.

Mullin also couldn't say.

"I do think you should get comfortable because there are so many unanswered questions and next Congress, things will look a little different," Democratic Rep. Rep. Delia Ramirez told him. "I cannot wait to see you again."

text:
U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said Wednesday the United States and Venezuela have signed a deal to reestablish military ties, over 10 months after U.S. forces seized then-Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro from his home and flew him to the U.S. to face drug trafficking charges in New York. Hegseth offered few specifics on the military agreement, but it is expected to range from conducting joint training to intelligence sharing. The deal comes as the U.S. military has been expanding focus on Latin America during President Donald Trump’s second term, while uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future.

Also Wednesday, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullintestified before Congress, defending his flight to an LSU-Texas football game when travelers across the U.S. were still stuck at airports after the nationwide ground stop. Canceling his trip could’ve caused confusion, Mullin told the House Homeland Security Committee. Mullin, who oversees the agency tasked with protecting the country’s cyber infrastructure, faced lawmakers as a string of cyber and technology issues in public and private sectors have rattled Americans.

Elsewhere in Congress, Democrats nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker of the House, putting him on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker in the role. Jeffries, who ran unopposed, secured the nod during closed-door voting ahead of a full vote in January by the new House — where he faces a restive party eager for a change.

Trump, meanwhile, landed in China, where he hopes to reinforce the U.S. status as the world’s leading technological power. That posture is complicated by the recent outages, putting Trump on the defensive ahead of a potentially complicated trilateral meeting on Thursday with the presidents of China and Russia, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.

Here's the latest:

Hegseth uses Venezuela speech to boast about operation that captured former leader

Hegseth called the operation that seized Maduro “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America” that “lasted just 48 minutes.”

“America’s best and bravest warfighters solved a 27-year problem for this hemisphere in a matter of hours,” he added.

But Venezuela’s ruling party, which has held onto power since 1999, still continues to lead the nation, just now with Rodríguez in charge.

Hegseth also turned a Maduro catchphrase from last year back on him, saying that as the ousted leader “predicted,” the operation ended with “no war, yes, peace.”

Uncertainty remains about Venezuela’s political future

Hegseth’s visit comes at a time of uncertainty for Venezuelans regarding who will lead the nation in the coming months and years.

Acting President Delcy Rodríguez, a Maduro ally, took over in Venezuela after Maduro’s capture and despite the fact that her court-allowed term expired in July, she has continued to function as Venezuela’s head of state.

Hegseth praised her leadership and thanked her for “working closely and pragmatically and diligently with the United States to stabilize Venezuela.”

Meanwhile, opposition leader María Corina Machado recently returned to Venezuela from exile following seven failed attempts that opposition activists claimed were thwarted by the government.

U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has said the “safe” return of the politician was the result of “reconciliation talks” supported by the U.S., which he considered “the best opportunity” Venezuela has had in three decades to achieve free and fair elections and a lasting democracy.

The lack of a date for the next presidential election has left many Venezuelans conflicted on their sentiment toward Trump. While relieved that Maduro is no longer president, many believe that the White House’s decision to prioritize reviving Venezuela’s oil industry over pro-democracy steps was the wrong approach for meaningful changes in their country.

▶ Read more

Fishermen from Ecuador sue Trump administration over boat strike

A group of Ecuadorian fishermen has sued the Trump administration over allegations that the U.S. military attacked their fishing vessel and kidnapped them after mistakenly identifying them as drug smugglers.

The fishermen allege American drones struck their boat in the eastern Pacific Ocean off the coast of Ecuador in March, according to a federal lawsuit filed Monday.

The vessel was engulfed in flames, with two of the men suffering serious burns, the lawsuit says. The men allege they were held against their will by the U.S. for around 24 hours and treated in cruel and inhumane ways.

The lawsuit is the second against the Trump administration over U.S. military attacks on alleged drug-smuggling boats in Latin America. It was filed under a U.S. admiralty law that allows for claims for severe injuries inflicted on the high seas as well as unlawful attacks, kidnapping and torture.

Trump administration appeals to Supreme Court over legal protections for Venezuelan migrants

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court on Wednesday to halt an order that would restore deportation protections for hundreds of thousands of Venezuelan migrants.

The emergency appeal comes after a California-based judge found it was unlawful to end their temporary protected status.

The Supreme Court allowed the administration to strip protections from Venezuelans when the case was at an earlier stage last year. If the justices do not intervene again before Friday, the administration could be required to release about 1,800 Venezuelans from detention, federal attorneys wrote.

The Trump administration argued that reinstating TPS for Venezuelans would prevent the administration from carrying out up to 332 removal orders and require it to provide them with work authorization.

It argued that reinstating the protections would cause “severe and immediate harm.”

▶ Read more

Acting International Criminal Court prosecutor tells UN the tribunal is achieving results despite US sanctions

Mame Mandiaye Niang said those trying to undermine the ICC should know they are trying to undermine justice for victims of the world’s worst atrocities — war, crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide.

He told a U.N. Security Council meeting Wednesday that “despite the coercive measures and despite the attacks, the ICC and its partners continue obtaining concrete results for the victims in Libya” — and for victims elsewhere.

The Senegalese prosecutor addressed the council by video because of Trump administration sanctions against the court itself and 13 current and former staff members — including himself. The U.S. opposes any investigation into American citizens or allies such as Israel.

Last week, ICC judges ended part of its investigation into Afghanistan that could have involved U.S. military personnel.

U.S. deputy ambassador Jeff Bartos stressed to the council “our ongoing, unequivocal opposition” to the ICC.

Misinformation about a FEMA test leveraged distrust in Spanish-speaking communities

Ahead of a simulated emergency alert from the Federal Emergency Management Agency was a spate of outages that disabled Outlook and other Microsoft programs, grounded thousands of flights, blocked access to JPMorgan Chase, and halted internal communications at the National Security Agency.

The test, scheduled every three years to identify issues in the system, has previously become a lightning rod for conspiracy theories and misinformation.

Online, false and misleading claims questioned the cause of the outages. The worries especially hit Latino or Spanish-language communities.

Experts warned that these online conversations show how growing distrust in elites and institutions uniquely influences Latino media consumption.

“This sense of general distrust within many communities, but especially including the Latino community in the United States, will then feed into and be amplified by the online discourse around it,” said Dr. Arthur Soto-Vásquez, who teaches ethnic and equity studies at the University of Nevada, Las Vegas.

▶ Read more

Incoming class of House Democrats meets with Obama

Former President Barack Obama is meeting with the incoming class of House Democrats in Washington on Wednesday, according to two people familiar with the private gathering who spoke on condition of anonymity.

The meeting, convened by House Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries, comes just hours after House Democrats overwhelmingly nominated Jeffries to become speaker, putting him on track to make history as the nation’s first Black lawmaker to hold the gavel.

Obama, the nation’s first Black president, remains one of the Democratic Party’s most prominent figures nearly a decade after leaving office, though those close to him have emphasized that he now plays a more advisory role.

US military down to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East

The U.S. military is down to two aircraft carriers in the Middle East with the departure of the USS George Washington from the region.

A spokesperson for the U.S. Pacific Fleet confirmed that the Japan-based USS George Washington was now under their control and “conducting routine operations” in the area.

The development comes just two days after the USS Theodore Roosevelt arrived in the Middle East, briefly bringing the number of carriers in the waters off Iran to three. The USS George H.W. Bush, which arrived in the region in April, remains in the area.

US and Venezuela sign military agreement, Hegseth says

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, speaking in Venezuela, said the two countries have signed an agreement to reestablish military ties, from training to intelligence sharing.

Hegseth also said that following the January capture of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro by the U.S. military, the country “has gone from our most aggressive regional threat to a compliant security partner.”

Hegseth also praised the “close cooperation” with interim President Delcy Rodríguez that allowed officials “to stabilize Venezuela and rid it of narco-terrorists once and for all.”

The Pentagon did not immediately offer further details on the new partnership.

Rodríguez separately lauded the opportunity to strengthen the military partnership.

“I hope that this technical-military cooperation … can be brought to its highest possible level, so that … we may address common threats,” she said.

▶ Read more

Black lawmakers reflect on Jeffries vote

The vote to nominate Hakeem Jeffries as the next speaker of the House was a particularly emotional moment for longtime Black members of Congress.

Rep. Maxine Waters of California called it perhaps the most significant vote she has ever cast and a day that she never thought she would see.

Rep. Gregory Meeks of New York said he thought back to the 13 original members of the Congressional Black Caucus. “Could they have even dreamt of this day?”

Rep. Kweisi Mfume of Maryland said he flashed back to being sworn in with the late John Lewis back in 1987.

“It was very emotional. You could feel a sense of presence of so many people who have worked and toiled to try and find a way to create a Congress and create a government that reflects the best of America,” Mfume said.

House hearing on worldwide threats ends

The hearing included testimony from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, FBI deputy director Christopher Raia and Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.

The hearing before the House Homeland Security Committee was aimed at assessing threats 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks.

‘We are not killing people,’ Mullin says under immigration crackdown scrutiny

House members scrutinized DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin during Wednesday’s hearing on immigration enforcement actions that have led to fatal encounters, shortened training, and incomplete background checks for officers in the field. U. S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement had an unprecedented hiring spree — 12,000 new officers and special agents to double its force. In one prominent case, an ICE agent with a troubled mental health history shot and killed a Colombian man in Maine. Mullin said some agents who haven’t completed training or background checks are placed on administrative leave until they are completed. Tense exchanges centered on the deaths caused by ICE agents including those of Renee Good, Alex Pretti and Lorenzo Araujo Salgado. “We are not killing people,” Mullin responded to Rep. LaMonica McIver. “You are killing people,” McIver replied. “No m’am. That’s your opinion,” he said, ending the exchange.

Nike to give valedictorians custom sneakers after Mississippi’s Colom asked

The sneaker giant announced Tuesday it would be gifting custom Air Force 1s to every high school valedictorian in the country.

Democrat Scott Colom, who is poised to become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction, had called on Nike to honor his historic election by gifting every high school valedictorian in his state a pair of his favorite sneakers.

Nike responded and said it would expand the giveaway to top students across the country.

Colom suggested the sneaker design give a nod to Hiram Revels, a fellow Mississippi senator who was the first African American to serve in Congress.

Mullin, Puerto Rico representative Hernandez spar over killings by immigration officers

A testy exchange between Mullin and Pablo Jose Hernandez, Puerto Rico’s representative in Congress, erupted over investigations into the deaths caused by Homeland Security Department law enforcement agents.

Hernandez asked Mullin for an update on the status of investigations into the deaths of Renee Good and Alex Pretti, who were killed by Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol officers in January amid the administration’s immigration crackdown. He also inquired about Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, who was killed in July in Maine as well as Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, fatally shot by an immigration officer shortly after Guerrero in Texas.

“I cannot talk about ongoing investigations, but I can talk about the angel families,” Mullin said.

Does that justify the killings? Hernandez asked.

Mullin began responding, saying that it never justifies it, when Hernandez asked: “Why do you have to bring up that comparison? That is very disrespectful to those people.”

Mullin went on, referring to angel families — a term frequently used by the Trump administration to refer those whose family members were killed by someone in the country illegally — saying Hernandez should talk about them.

Newsom unveils proposals to crack down on AI

California Gov. Gavin Newsom warned the influence of artificial intelligence is spurring a “national crisis of confidence.”

The potential 2028 presidential candidate, who is leaving the governor’s office in January, issued a proposal on Wednesday calling on California to expand AI oversight. It calls on the industry to submit to mandatory independent testing, stronger requirements for reporting safety incidents and limits on systems improving themselves.

He proposes giving the state power to order an AI company to immediately shut down a model if officials determine it poses a potential catastrophic threat. He vetoed a so-called kill switch bill in 2024.

Newsom said he plans to speak to his successor, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra, about his proposal later Wednesday.

Newsom said there’s an urgency for governments to address threats posed by AI. He blasted the Trump administration’s response to a series of tech outages that have surfaced over the past week.

“I don’t think there’s much trust in this administration on these issues,” Newsom said. “Too many times, we’ve been lied to by this administration.”

In Senate farewell address, Ohio’s Jon Husted says ’selfishness must be forsaken for selflessness'

The Republican, who lost his retention bid Nov. 3 to Democrat Sherrod Brown, suggested “the algorithm that we might be trapped in” has caused Washington’s elected representatives to lose perspective on “what this place is supposed to be about.”

Reflecting on his 25 years in public service, Husted observed that the national debt has exploded in his 59 years of life, as “the collective ‘we’ stopped sacrificing for the future and started taking from it.”

“From this Capitol, the harvest that was supposed to be planted for the future has been devoured,” he said.

Husted was tapped last year to fill the seat vacated by JD Vance as the latter ascended to the vice presidency.

His appointment expires Dec. 15, when Brown — a former three-term senator who lost his seat to Sen. Bernie Moreno in 2024 — will finish out Vance’s final two years.

Sen. Sanders welcomes working with MAHA on issues such as food labeling, junk food ads

Sen. Bernie Sanders said Wednesday that he can find common ground with Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement, even though he has “profound disagreements” with Kennedy on vaccines.

The Vermont independent who caucuses with Democrats said in a call with reporters that he “can work with the MAHA people” on areas of shared interest such as improving food labeling and getting junk food advertisements off the airwaves.

Sanders, who is likely to chair the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee next year, also said he thinks his newly announced plan to use the role for a “ Medicare for All push ” is aligned with the MAHA mission.

“We want to keep people out of hospitals, out of emergency rooms, by keeping them healthy,” he said.

On the same call, Sanders teased plans to investigate Kennedy’s leadership, saying the health secretary is “into conspiracy theories.”

Mullin says he wasn’t involved in export controls of Nvidia chip sales to China

Mullin disavowed involvement during the House Homeland Security Committee worldwide threats hearing.

Asked by Democratic Rep. Seth Magaziner whether he was concerned Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had resisted implementing export controls on certain chips sold by Nvidia to China that others in the administration supported, Mullin denied any knowledge.

“This wasn’t something I’m dealing with. It’s outside of my lane,” he said.

Mullin also said he did not learn that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy until the news had broken publicly.

“The way that I understand it is because this is a spy outside of just our network, and they were handling it in different agencies. If it was a direct threat to the homeland, I would have been read in on it.”

Hegseth is in Venezuela to meet with interim authorities

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is visiting Venezuela to meet with interim authorities Wednesday, underscoring efforts by the Trump administration to deepen its influence in the Latin American country since U.S. forces ousted then-President Nicolás Maduro in January.

Hegseth is the latest member of President Donald Trump’s Cabinet to travel to Venezuela following visits this year by the Interior and Energy secretaries, who have focused on efforts to tap the South American nation’s oil reserves and critical minerals. It comes after Trump said in August that Hegseth helped broker a sweeping deal for the U.S. to take control of some Venezuelan oil reserves.

Venezuelan state television broadcast footage of Hegseth at the presidential palace in Caracas, alongside acting President Delcy Rodríguez. The Pentagon chief is there months after U.S. forces carried out a surprise nighttime raid in the Venezuelan capital to capture Maduro and whisk him to New York to face drug trafficking charges.

Intelligence director: Service disruptions are not part of a coordinated cyberattack

The Trump administration’s director of national intelligence, Jay Clayton, says recent computer systems service disruptions in the government and private sector are “not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee the outages instead appear to be separate and “associated with maintenance and technical changes.”

The testimony was the latest effort by the Trump administration to offer reassurances after technical outages that have affected everything from Microsoft to the Federal Aviation Administration, the banking industry to United Airlines and a classified internal communications network at the National Security Agency.

Clayton said in interviews Tuesday that the outages appeared to be connected to recent efforts to upgrade systems and patch vulnerabilities.

text:
A federal judge in Charlotte heard arguments Wednesday over whether U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement must publish the agency's full memo expanding electronic monitoring of immigrants.

Carolina Migrant Network and the Amica Center for Immigrant Rights requested the memo through the Freedom of Information Act in October 2025 and sued in January after ICE did not respond. ICE later published a version with portions blacked out, which the groups argue hides information that should be public.

The June 2025 memo involves immigrants enrolled in ICE’s Alternatives to Detention program, which monitors people living outside detention centers while their immigration cases proceed. The memo directs officers to increase required check-ins and use GPS ankle monitors on immigrants, even on pregnant women.

Government attorneys said ICE mistakenly released the memo without redacting it. They argued that a copy made public in a Pennsylvania court case makes the lawsuit moot. But Carolina Migrant Network says it still hasn’t officially received the full memo.

Amica Center attorney Evan Benz said after the hearing that the groups are seeking publication of the document on ICE’s website.

“The remaining issue is whether the judge will order ICE to publish the memo in an unredacted version on their website and we’re hopeful that he will do so,” Benz said.

The judge gave the nonprofits 10 days to explain in writing why they believe ICE should publish the full memo. The government will then have 10 days to respond.

text:
The U.S. Department of Homeland Security said Tuesday that after consideration, a ship used for training maritime students in Vallejo will not be part of deportation efforts.

In a letter to U.S. Rep. John Garamendi, D-Fairfield, and U.S. Rep. Salud Carbajal, D-Santa Barbara, David Venturella, a senior DHS official, wrote that Training Ship Golden Bear, a ship for Cal Poly Maritime Academy students, will not be used to carry out deportations by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.

“DHS has determined it will not use ships, including training vessels or private foreign ships, for removals. Removal efforts will continue using air and ground transportation,” Venturella wrote.

The response came after Garamendi and Carbajal sent a letter to DHS in October condemning reports that the agency considered using the “floating classroom” for ICE deportations.

“DHS has determined it will not use ships, including training vessels or private foreign ships, for removals. Removal efforts will continue using air and ground transportation.”

David Venturella, senior DHS official

The letter noted that possible deportations by sea raised safety and legal issues.

“This plan recalls catastrophic historical examples of deportations by sea that violated human rights and resulted in deadly consequences,” the representatives wrote. “The insensitivity of this plan alone should have stopped it from being evaluated to this reported stage.”

According to the college, after a final voyage with several hundred cadets in July, the Golden Bear was retired following 30 years of service.

Following DHS’ confirmation, Carbajal told constituents that the work is not over.

“While this commitment from DHS is a major victory for the Central Coast and congressional oversight, our work is not done. We must continue to hold the Trump Administration accountable for its extreme immigration enforcement and mass deportation agenda,” said Carbajal.

text:
House Democrats will introduce legislation on Thursday that would provide relief to some immigrants who have final orders of removal but no criminal record, and create a pathway for them to obtain legal permanent residency.

This comes after President Trump told CBS News’ “60 Minutes” that he would “love to do something on immigration” with Democrats, who will take control of both houses of Congress in January after their wins in the midterm elections.

A final order of removal is issued by an immigration judge or immigration authorities and requires a noncitizen to leave the country or be deported. It becomes final once the person’s administrative appeals are exhausted or the deadline to appeal has passed.

The bill, titled the “Protect Our Neighbors Act," was shared first with ABC News and will be introduced by California Democratic Rep. Lateefah Simon.

Under this proposal, final orders of removal would expire 10 years after they were issued for individuals who have been continuously present in the U.S. and have not been convicted of a crime. As of now, there is no expiration on final orders of removal.

The bill would allow an immigration judge to renew an expired final order of removal if it was established by "clear and convincing evidence" that there was significant cause for the delay in executing a final order unrelated to administrative or funding delays and renewal of the order is in the public interest based on new evidence, according to the bill's text.

While a final removal order gives Immigration and Customs Enforcement the legal authority to deport an individual, it does not mean deportation happens instantly or automatically -- removal can be delayed or suspended through the government deferring action, a stay of removal, ongoing litigation or other circumstances.

Former acting ICE Director Todd Lyons told lawmakers in February that there were about 1.6 million people in the U.S. who have final deportation orders.

The legislation would also create a pathway to lawful permanent residency for individuals with expired orders of removal. It's co-sponsored by California Democratic Reps. John Garamendi, Zoe Lofgren and Juan Vargas.

While Democrats are introducing the bill during the lame-duck session, it is unlikely that this bill will be taken up before the end of the year. But it could reemerge on the agenda next year after Democrats take control and are empowered to send legislation to the floor for votes.

Trump’s openness to an immigration deal, however, doesn’t guarantee he would back this measure.

The bill was inspired by the case of Harjit Kaur, a 73-year-old grandmother who had lived in the San Francisco Bay Area for three decades before she was deported to India.

In September 2025, Kaur was unexpectedly detained during a routine check-in with ICE. Her attorney said then that she had been checking in with ICE regularly while under a final order of removal and had received authorization to work legally in the U.S.

ICE has said that an immigration judge ordered her removed in 2005.

Kaur worked as a seamstress in Simon's district. In an interview with ABC News, the freshman congresswoman expressed optimism in bipartisan support for her bill and said she has spoken to Democratic leadership about it.

"If you have deportation orders that have been in place for over 10 years, and you continue to do everything right, those deportation orders need to be again turned off, and you need to be able to be in line with other folks to get your green card to continue being a hardworking resident of these communities and hopefully a citizen," Simon said.

Garamendi worked on Kaur's case when she was detained, and after she was deported to India, he dedicated his guest seat to her at Trump's State of the Union address last February and left it empty in protest.

"President Trump promised to go after the 'worst of the worst' in his immigration policy. Yet his administration has repeatedly decided to cruelly deport residents who have been working, paying taxes, and raising families in their communities for decades," Garamendi told ABC News in a statement.

The Department of Homeland Security and ICE have expanded enforcement in Trump's second administration against individuals with final orders of removal, including through deportations to third countries. Individuals who have routinely appeared for required immigration check-ins now face renewed risk of detention and deportation.

Kaur's family told ABC News in a statement, "The pain that we still feel today remains with the knowledge that Harjit is one of thousands who've experienced the same situation. We thank the members of Congress for their continued advocacy, and we hope that some good could come from Harjit's story with this bill and others like it."

text:
University of Maryland student Maria Flores Garcia and her mom are back home Wednesday after being released from a federal detention facility in Lousiana.

Flores Garcia and her mom, Mirna Aracely Garcia Cabrera, were immediatley embraced by family members when they arrived at their home in Maryland.

"I want to say thank you guys so much for the coverage that you guys brought to my story. Thank you for bringing awareness to the injustices," Flores Garcia told reporters.

"But overall, and the most important thing, I want to thank you guys for the prayers. This would not have been possible without God. So I want to thank you guys for ... whatever time you took of your day to pray for me and my family," she said. "Miracles do happen. And now I'm happy and, like — I can't even explain it in words — to be back with my family."

Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained Flores Garcia and her mom when they went to a scheduled immigration check-in in Baltimore in early November.

The Prince George’s County residents were then taken to a detention center in Louisiana under threat of deportation to Mexico, a country where they have never lived.

University of Maryland President Darryll J. Pines announced Flores Garcia's release in a letter to students Wednesday morning, saying the school was "overjoyed and relieved to learn this news."

Pines thanked students, organizations and lawmakers who rallied for the pair to be let go since ICE agents took them into custody.

"Terps advocated for Maria, and students held rallies, information sessions and meetings with Student Affairs leaders ... Latine student organization leaders worked tirelessly, and we are grateful for Student Government Association leadership advocacy," Pines' letter said in part. "So many members of our community stepped up, and I couldn’t be prouder."

A number of lawmakers joined the call for Flores Garcia's release.

Congressman Glenn Ivey told News4 that "major pushback" helped in getting her out of ICE custody.

"I just thought it was, you know, a bad look for the administration, especially since they said the focus was going to be going after the worst of the worst," Ivey said.

"We'll see what happens with the process. The MO of the Trump administration is to, you know, throw everything but the kitchen sink at these folks, but I'm hoping that the lessons of the Kilmar case will be applied here," Ivey said, referring to Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland man mistakenly deported to El Salvador last year. Abrego Garcia's case became a focal point in the immigration debate.

“Maria Flores Garcia ... never should’ve been detained," Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., said in a statement Wednesday. "This action by Trump’s ICE put a clear lie to their claim that they’re going after ‘the worst of the worst.’ But over the last two weeks, we saw our community stand up and rally around her. We immediately called out her senseless detention and worked to get her released. Today, I am relieved that she and her mother are no longer detained and will be reunited with their family.”

Flores Garcia came to the U.S. when she was 9 years old. She was valedictorian at Parkdale High School just last May.

"Congratulations, class of 2026, and remember that dreams don't have limits or borders," she said in her speech.

Flores Garcia illegally entered the U.S. in 2016, She was placed in removal proceedings and released.

In 2021, an immigration judge issued a final order of removal, according to a statement from the Department of Homeland Security.

Flores Garcia’s long-term boyfriend spearheaded efforts to bring attention to her case, raising more than $35,000 for her defense fund and securing legal representation.

“A top student of her class shouldn’t be detained from ICE or from anyone, and yeah, we’re just hoping that it reaches out to the most people,” he said.

At the University of Maryland, where Flores Garcia is studying public health, classmates organized to support the fight for her release.

“The Latino community is not very highly represented here at the University of Maryland. So for me, I really wanted to take the time and kind of respond,” one UMD student told News4. “Like, it’s important for us to stand as a united front, and I think for me, responding as quickly as possible. Because ultimately, people are the most vulnerable whenever they are detained. We've seen that as Maria has been moved to Louisiana, which, what is she doing over there, right?”

text:
LOS ANGELES — It all happened in what felt like seconds.

Elvis, a 26-year-old originally from Peru, was arrested Nov. 12 during a scheduled appointment with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) at the federal building in Los Angeles.

Before he knew it, he was being sent to the detention center in Adelanto, three hours east.

“It is completely inhumane,” said Elvis’ husband, Nicholas Green, a U.S. citizen. “They require you to come to ICE’s offices. If you don’t come, it’s a problem. If you do come, you’re arrested. Whatever you do, you lose. There’s no way out.”

Green, who is originally from Baltimore, Maryland, said his husband (who he asked to be identified only by his first name fearing potential reprisals) had complied with all U.S. Customs and Immigration Services (USCIS) requirements, including having his fingerprints taken just a few weeks earlier. He also has no criminal record, Green stressed.

The pair got married a year ago. Last summer, they submitted a petition seeking permanent residency for Elvis, who first entered the US in 2022 and was granted temporary “parole” status by the Biden administration. He was one of tens of thousands to be granted such status during Biden’s tenure.

President Trump abruptly ended parole protections after returning to the White House in 2025. Since then, unauthorized crossings at the U.S. southern border have fallen to unprecedently low levels, while arrests of immigrants in the interior of the country have spiked dramatically.

According to ICE, the agency carried out nearly half a million arrests this year, with a similarly record-high number of deportations. In Southern California, some 15,000 people arrested by ICE since 2025 have been deported, according to the UCLA–UC Berkeley Deportation Data Project.

A growing number of those arrests, meanwhile, are happening in and around immigration court houses nationwide and during routine field-office appointments like the one Elvis attended.

An analysis by the San Francisco-based news outlet, Mission Local found that of more than 1000 ICE arrests in the city last year, at least half were made during such appointments.

“He is more than just a number,” insisted Green, referring to his husband, with whom he’s been able to speak by phone since his detention. “He’s a human being going through something no one deserves to experience.”

Green added that during their conversation, Elvis “was crying. He’s scared.”

Numerous reports point to especially harsh conditions for members of the LGBTQ+ community in ICE detention centers, including verbal and physical harassment by center staff.

“Many of these individuals came to the US fleeing violence and persecution because of who they are, only to face the same cruelty at the hands of our government,” Ramiro Sarmiento, National Press Secretary for the Human Rights Campaign, told LGBTQ Nation in October.

For Green, who works as a cosmetologist in Studio City, the experience has been traumatizing. He’s fallen into a deep depression and says there are moments in the day where he just breaks into sobs.

“I’m completely broken. I’ve never felt like this before,” he said. “It’s as if everything I ever cared about was being taken from me, and I have no control over it.”

Green also faults the lawyer Elvis initially hired to assist with his residency petition.

“I asked her numerous times before he was arrested whether she was sure things were ok. Whether there was anything we should do,” he explained. “And she assured me things would be fine. And now I feel like all she did was take our money without doing anything.”

According to Green, the couple paid $4000 prior to Elvis’ arrest. They still owe an additional $3000. “Now, after his arrest, we’re looking at another $10,000 to $20,000 we’ll have to spend for a new lawyer.”

Green has launched a GoFundMe campaign hoping to cover some of the expenses.

Elvis’ next scheduled court date, meanwhile, is Nov. 23. Green says they are actively looking for a new lawyer who he hopes can present a habeas petition on Elvis’ behalf prior to the next hearing.

There are approximately 100,000 habeas cases now wending their way through immigration courts nationwide as more detainees are relying on the legal strategy to fight their detentions.

“They told us, ‘Follow these rules, attend appointments, submit applications, pay fees,” said an exasperated Green. “They assured us that if we complied with all of that and had a legitimate marriage, we would have a viable path.”

Instead, he said they were betrayed by a system both put their trust in. Which is why he’s now speaking out.

“People are still being taken, families continue to suffer,” he said, noting he’s since been in touch with families of other detainees, some of whose relatives have spent months in detention. It’s something he says deepens his own sense of anxiety, and resolve.

“At first, I stayed silent,” said Green, “but later, I realized that is precisely why they get away with it, because too many people stay quiet.”

text:
Sign up for TPR Today, Texas Public Radio's newsletter that brings our top stories to your inbox each morning.

The City of San Antonio is moving to expand public reporting on interactions between local police and federal immigration authorities, the latest in a series of efforts by local officials to push back against an expanding federal immigration enforcement presence in the region.

In January, City Council directed the San Antonio Police Department to begin tracking requests for assistance from U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, with monthly reporting beginning in March. On Wednesday, the council's Governance Committee advanced a proposal to expand those requirements to capture a broader range of interactions between SAPD and federal immigration authorities.

The proposal, introduced by District 2 Councilman Jalen McKee-Rodriguez in August, seeks greater transparency about when police contact immigration authorities, participate in joint operations and use city resources to assist federal immigration enforcement.

Under the expanded reporting framework, SAPD would begin documenting police responses to ICE-related incidents and immigration detainers issued after arrests each month, alongside quarterly reports of incidents referencing ICE or immigration.

The additional reporting is intended to address concerns from residents about the extent of SAPD's cooperation with ICE and whether contacting local police could put people at risk of immigration enforcement.

Police Chief Jesse Salame stressed Wednesday that SAPD does not enforce federal immigration laws but must comply with state laws and federal grant requirements governing cooperation with federal authorities.

McKee-Rodriguez said the existing reports have done little to ease residents' concerns, particularly when they report seeing SAPD officers alongside immigration authorities despite months with no recorded requests for assistance from ICE.

"If it is true that SAPD is not expending resources on immigration at the scale the public believes, it should be easy to communicate and prove," McKee-Rodriguez said. “As this dashboard and report progresses and evolves, that is what it needs to demonstrate, with as much information as possible.”

Salame presented figures showing limited documented interactions with ICE. Of more than 42,000 SAPD arrests between January and October, ICE issued immigration detainers for 54 individuals. The department also recorded five requests for assistance from ICE between March and October.

A broader review identified 312 police reports mentioning ICE or immigration during the first nine months of 2026, although about two-thirds involved no federal immigration enforcement activity.

Salame also addressed concerns surrounding SAPD's role in a large immigration raid near San Pedro Avenue in November 2025, where residents saw SAPD officers at an operation that resulted in mass immigration-related detentions.

According to Salame, SAPD had been assisting the FBI and Texas Department of Public Safety with a narcotics and weapons investigation and was not informed beforehand that the operation would lead to immigration detentions. He said SAPD officers did not participate in any of those detentions.

District 9 Councilwoman Misty Spears pointed to those figures as showing limited involvement with ICE in her opposition to the proposal, she argued that additional reporting could unnecessarily undermine public confidence in the department.

Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones, however, said the expanded reporting could help address fears among residents who might otherwise avoid calling police, including victims of domestic violence and other crimes, concerned about potential immigration consequences.

The proposal heads to the full City Council for consideration Dec. 3, although Salame said SAPD plans to begin the expanded monthly reporting Dec. 1.

The reporting requirements are among several measures city and county officials have pursued this year in response to the federal government's expanding immigration enforcement operations in the San Antonio region.

City challenges detention facility, federal office leases

The city's most significant challenge has been its federal lawsuit over plans to convert a nearly 640,000-square-foot warehouse on the East Side into an immigration detention facility capable of holding up to 1,500 people.

Earlier this year, City Council began pursuing legal and administrative options to oppose the facility, including a moratorium on new private detention facilities and requests for information about the project. After sending five letters to the Department of Homeland Security and ICE seeking details about the federal government's plans and receiving little response, the city filed a lawsuit Oct. 13 alleging that federal officials failed to conduct an environmental review required under the National Environmental Policy Act.

Mayor Ortiz Jones said earlier this month that DHS had agreed to conduct the review, but the City Attorney's Office subsequently clarified that negotiations remain ongoing over a proposed agreement to pause the lawsuit while environmental reviews are completed.

Under the proposed terms, work to convert the warehouse would not proceed during that process. No final agreement has been filed in federal court, and both sides are expected to provide a status update to a federal judge by Nov. 30.

Following the suit, the city expanded its opposition with an expanded resolution calling for additional legal and administrative challenges to be explored for two federal leases worth approximately $51 million for immigration-related legal offices at Brooks on the Southeast Side. The Brooks Development Authority has stated that they were not involved in the leasing of those office spaces.

The development authority has since issued a formal notice of default to the company who leases the offices from Brooks, Dallas-based Preston Hollow Community Capital, alleging subleasing the space to the federal government is a violation of their lease agreement.

Preston Hollow Community Capital disputes the allegations and was given 60 days to address the alleged violation.

The November election results have also emboldened some council members to pursue changes to SAPD's cooperation with ICE, drawing inspiration from a policy recently adopted in Houston.

On Nov. 6, City Council members Teri Castillo, Jalen McKee-Rodriguez and Ric Galvan requested a special meeting to consider an ordinance modeled on Houston's new policy, which limits when police can notify ICE about individuals with administrative immigration warrants.

The three council members subsequently withdrew their request to revise and strengthen the proposal. Meanwhile, outgoing Attorney General Ken Paxton sued Houston on Tuesday over the policy that inspired their effort.

Bexar County plays a supporting role

While San Antonio has pursued legal challenges, Bexar County's response has largely consisted of resolutions expressing opposition to federal immigration enforcement projects and support for the city's efforts.

Commissioners first approved a resolution opposing the proposed East Side detention facility in March.

On Tuesday, Commissioners Court expanded that opposition to include the federal office leases at Brooks, an existing ICE lease on Crosspoint Drive and a $382 million GardaWorld contract to transport people in federal immigration custody.

The resolution, introduced by Precinct 4 Commissioner Tommy Calvert, also supports San Antonio's lawsuit and encourages outside legal organizations to pursue challenges to the federal projects.

However, the measure does not authorize the county to pursue litigation of its own. County attorneys said they have been coordinating with the city's legal team, but any legal action would need to be brought before Commissioners Court for approval.

Precinct 3 Commissioner Grant Moody opposed the resolution, arguing that the county has limited authority over federal immigration operations and cannot cancel legally compliant federal contracts.
