text:
Monroe County commissioners have sued to invalidate Stinesville's immigration enforcement agreement with federal authorities.

The lawsuit questions whether local police chiefs can enter such agreements without approval from elected officials.

Commissioners argue the dispute is about procedural authority, not immigration policy.

Monroe County commissioners have filed a lawsuit seeking to invalidate Stinesville's agreement with federal immigration authorities, alleging local officers have already exercised powers granted under what they contend is an invalid agreement, including transporting individuals from the Monroe County Jail.

In the lawsuit, filed Nov. 10, 2026, in Monroe Circuit Court, commissioners asked that a judge declare as void Stinesville’s agreement with Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and prohibit Stinesville’s law enforcement officers from exercising powers granted under the agreement.

The case could have implications far beyond Stinesville. Across Indiana and other states, local law enforcement agencies have increasingly entered agreements allowing officers to assist federal immigration authorities. Commissioners are asking a judge to determine whether police chiefs and town marshals can enter those agreements on their own or whether they first require approval from elected officials, a ruling that could affect how similar agreements are authorized elsewhere.

County commissioners have filed the suit against Stinesville; its town marshal, Shane Pittman, who signed the agreement on behalf of the town; and Todd Rokita, Indiana's attorney general, who concluded that police chiefs and town marshals may enter such agreements without approval from city councils or town boards. The lawsuit asks a judge to reject that interpretation and follows warnings from Rokita's office that local officials who discourage participation in the program could face penalties under state law.

Commissioners contend the dispute is about process, not immigration policy. They argue that requiring approval from elected officials “does not prohibit participation” in the federal program but simply determines who has authority to enter such agreements on behalf of a municipality.

The lawsuit alleges that Pittman signed the agreement, called a 287(g), when he was deputy marshal on Jan. 30, 2026, without authorization from or a vote of the Stinesville Town Council. The U.S. Department of Homeland Security signed the agreement Feb. 10.

"Stinesville officers have conducted stops under the agreement in unincorporated Monroe County and transported individuals from the Monroe County jail," commissioners said in the suit. "These activities affect County jail operations, territorial law-enforcement interests, financial exposure, interlocal, and insurance interests."

The lawsuit also states that on Oct. 6 Rokita sent the Stinesville Town Council an advisory letter concluding Stinesville’s police chief could execute the agreement with ICE without town council approval. Rokita in the letter also warned that "county action discouraging continued participation" would violate state law and that his office could pursue civil penalties of up to $10,000 per violation.

Commissioners pointed out that other Indiana towns, including Waterloo and Andrews, publicly approved agreements before their police officials signed them, and that the Claypool Town Council suspended its marshal on July 21 after he entered an agreement with federal immigration officials without town council approval.

While the Stinesville Town Council voted Nov. 10 to ratify the agreement, commissioners plan to argue in an amended filing that the vote did not cure what they contend was a defective approval process because the agreement had already been signed and implemented. They maintain the dispute is about whether elected officials, not police officials acting alone, have authority to commit municipalities to such partnerships.

A spokeswoman for Rokita's office said via email Friday that the attorney general had not yet been served with the lawsuit.

"We will evaluate it when we receive it, and we will continue to oppose and fight any, and all efforts by Monroe County to interfere with immigration enforcement activities in Indiana," the statement read.

Pittman and Stinesville Town Board President Scott McGlocklin did not reply to emailed inquiries. They had not filed a response to the lawsuit. No hearing has been set.

text:
Coalition calls on UC leadership to protect immigrant patients and health care workers through strong, enforceable systemwide policies

SAN FRANCISCO, CA — Today, resident physicians and nurses from across the University of California, alongside community members, rallied outside the Board of Regents Meeting. The coalition is demanding that UC get Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) out of its hospitals and establish clear, systemwide protections for patients and health care workers.

The rally coincides with hundreds of emails that were sent to the Board of Regents and UC President Milliken reiterating the need for a comprehensive policy and protocol. The email action is cosponsored by CIR/SEIU, the California Immigrant Policy Center, California Nurses Association, and UAW 4811.

These actions are part of a growing campaign to ensure UC hospitals remain places of healing, dignity, and confidential medical care for everyone, regardless of immigration or custody status.

Currently, the lack of clear, consistent protocols and staff training for situations involving patients in immigration enforcement custody at UC Health facilities creates confusion, safety risks, and the potential for violations of patients’ rights. Health care workers need clear guidance to protect patient privacy, uphold legal rights, and provide appropriate medical care.

“As doctors, the well-being of the people we serve is our utmost priority. The presence of immigration enforcement in our hospitals undermines our ability to provide care and impedes patients from receiving proper, dignified treatment. UC must take action now to protect patients and staff,” said Dr. SatKartar Khalsa, CIR-SEIU regional vice president.

The presence of immigration enforcement officers in health care settings can interfere with medical examinations and treatment, compromise patient confidentiality, and undermine trust between patients and providers. Patients in immigration custody may face barriers to contacting family, accessing support services, and participating in decisions about their care. health care workers also report fears of unsafe working conditions, racial profiling, and retaliation for advocating for their patients.

"Nurses demand that our hospitals must be places of healing and safety and completely off limits to any sort of ICE or federal immigration agent presence," said Jamile Cabacungan, a medical-surgical-telemetry RN at UCSF Stanyan Hospital. "From the start of this cruel and unnecessary deportation program, nurses have been educating ourselves and our patients to know and exercise our rights, and we even sponsored state legislation to keep ICE out of our hospitals. Our employer UC must step up and proactively do everything possible to support us and our ability to provide safe care to our patients and communities."

The coalition has specific demands which essentially call on UC leadership to:

Protect patient privacy and dignity by limiting ICE access to patient care areas and safeguarding confidential patient communications.

Uphold patients’ rights and continuity of care, including access to certified medical interpreters, family notification, surrogate decision-makers, social services, legal support, and safe disposition planning.

Protect health care workers from racial profiling and retaliation for advocating for immigrant patients.

Establish clear protocols and staff training for responding to immigration enforcement activity in hospitals.

Ensure transparency and accountability, including information about federal immigration agents’ visits to UC hospitals over the past year.

Meet with union representatives to address health care workers’ concerns and develop effective protections.

At a minimum, the coalition is urging UC to adopt the updated California attorney general guidelines, with stronger protections modeled on comprehensive immigrant rights policies. These protections must include practical protocols, staff training, clear lines of responsibility, and accountability for implementation.

The coalition will also deliver formal public testimony at the UC Board of Regents meeting on Nov. 18, urging UC leadership to address these concerns and commit to systemwide protections. The rally follows coordinated phone and email actions calling on the university to take immediate action.

UC RNs also detail problems with staffing and A.I.

In addition to their concerns about immigration, UC nurses on Nov. 17 also detailed problems they are experiencing within the UC medical system over chronic understaffing and inappropriate staffing, as well as encroachment of artificial intelligence (A.I.) on their nursing practice.

At many of its facilities, including the UCLA campuses and UCSF, management’s failure to staff enough nurses routinely leads to extremely long emergency department wait times, holding patients in emergency department spaces, such as hallways, where they should not be placed, and unsafely reassigning nurses outside their units of expertise -- a practice known as “floating.”

UC nurses also oppose the giant health system’s rollout of untested and unregulated artificial intelligence into their workplaces without their input or agreement. “Nurses are not inherently against new technology, but we know when our employers are actually using technology to deskill, displace, and override our judgment,” said Lee Reinerston, an emergency department RN at Benioff Children’s Hospital Oakland. “Hospitals want to remove real human nurses from the bedside because it ultimately cuts costs and boosts their profits. Some of this A.I. is untested or tested unreliably, it is unregulated and not verified to be effective. What has been proven time and time again to be effective is safe RN staffing. Nurses provide the skills, experience, intuition, judgment, and hands-on care that can never be replaced by an algorithm, software, or robots.”

California Nurses Association is the largest and fastest-growing union and professional association of registered nurses in California, representing more than 100,000 members in hundreds of facilities statewide.

The Committee of Interns and Residents (CIR) is the largest house staff union in the United States. A local of the Service Employees International Union (SEIU), representing over 40,000 resident physicians and fellows. Our members are dedicated to improving residency training and education, advancing patient care, and expanding health care access for our communities.

Former boxing world champion Jorge Linares has been detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), according to the president of the World Boxing Association (WBA).

On Monday, Gilberto Mendoza took to X to announce the news, saying: “I can confirm that my friend Jorge Linares, former WBA world champion, is in ICE custody.

“Immigration attorneys are handling his case, and I am in constant contact with his family.

“As WBA President, I will always support our champions, in and out of the ring. Stay strong, Jorge.”

Venezuela’s Linares is a former three-weight world champion, having reigned at super-featherweight, featherweight and lightweight in a career that ended with a 47-9 record.

The 41-year-old fought Vasiliy Lomachenko, Devin Haney, Luke Campbell and Anthony Crolla among others, before retiring after losing to Jack Catterall in 2023.

ICE has proven particularly controversial since the start of Donald Trump’s second term as US President.

Several fatal shootings by ICE agents this year have sparked protests across the country, also increasing scrutiny of the body’s recruitment process.

Jim Kambosos, father and manager of former world champion George Kambosos Jr, claimed that Linares “held a P1 Athlete visa to allow you to enter and compete freely”.

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has renewed a lawsuit against the city of Houston over Mayor John Whitmire's recent executive order limiting how police interact with federal immigration authorities, but the mayor vowed to fight the state in court.

Attorneys in Paxton's office on Friday filed a motion for summary judgement in a case originally brought earlier this year in Fort Bend County, arguing Whitmire's Nov. 6 executive order violated Senate Bill 4, which prohibits cities and counties from declining to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement operations.

"The good news is that with the election results, with the governor-elect, the attorney general - SB 4 is not their priority," Whitmire said after a Tuesday morning groundbreaking on a new adoption center for the city animal shelter.

Joe Jaworski, an attorney and former Democratic candidate for attorney general, said he couldn't see any path for Paxton to win the case before his time is office is up. It would take 21 days to set a hearing for the motion and, in all likelihood, incoming Attorney General Nathan Johnson would dismiss the case on his first day in office, Jaworski said.

Paxton is proceeding with the case against Houston despite having dropped other high-profile cases since the election, Jaworski noted.

"It feels like some of the MAGA warriors are undaunted and, while they can, sending out signals to the base to see who's still there," he said.

Travis Fife, an attorney for the Texas Civil Rights Project, echoed that.

"Paxton should enjoy his vacation to Fiji and leave Houston to the clear will of its voters," Fife said.

The city's policies on immigration have become a central conflict at City Hall ever since President Donald Trump's administration added 700,000 civil "administrative" ICE warrants to a national police database last year at the outset of his immigration crackdown.

Whitmire for months turned back calls to restrict the police department's interactions with ICE, citing the risk of angering Gov. Greg Abbott, Paxton and other state leaders. Then, in April, the city council passed an ordinance limiting HPD's cooperation with ICE – only to quickly rescind it after Abbott threatened to pull $114 million in public safety grants from the city.

Paxton also sued the city. That case had sat dormant since late April until Paxton's new court filing Friday.

"These repeat violations show that both branches of Houston's municipal government seek to curtail HPD's cooperation with ICE and handcuff the freedom of individual officers to assist federal authorities," state attorneys wrote in Friday's court filing.

READ MORE: Whitmire orders HPD to limit ICE contacts after Democrats’ midterm election sweep

While the state's new Democratic leaders don't take office until January, Whitmire in announcing his executive order this month said he'd be willing to take the risk now of angering the outgoing Republican leadership.

The order says HPD will contact ICE "only if that person is already going to jail on new charges or other warrants." Previously, officers were instructed to call ICE anytime they came across someone with an administrative warrant and wait "a reasonable amount of time" for an ICE agent to reach the scene – a directive that sometimes led officers to wait more than an hour.

That policy had been negotiated with Abbott's office after the council showdown in April. Under that policy, Houston police handed 17 people to immigration authorities from July through September, according to city data.

Another 13 people were charged with crimes and transferred to the Harris County jail, where they are likely to be released to ICE. That group would not be affected by Whitmire’s executive order.

READ MORE:Inside the collapse of Houston’s ICE policy

Immigration advocates have questioned whether that policy violated the U.S. Constitution by directing officers to detain people based solely upon civil warrants and not criminal charges.

Three council members in the days after Whitmire's executive order proposed codifying his changes into city laws. The mayor said Tuesday he is concerned that effort would violate Senate Bill 4, the same measure on which Paxton's lawsuit is based.

The council members as of Tuesday morning had not heard back from the city legal department on whether or not the measure was "lawful" and could progress toward a council vote.

One of the authors of that ordinance, Council Member Alejandra Salinas urged the mayor to fight Paxton's office in court.

"Ken Paxton is yet again trying to bully Houston into abandoning protections for our immigrant neighbors and families," she said. "Earlier this year, we urged the city to defend our original immigration ordinance in court, and now we have another opportunity to get this right."

text:
Former world championship boxer Jorge Luis Linares Palencia is being held in ICE custody in El Paso, the boxer said.

Linares, 41, of Venezuela, posted on X, formerly Twitter, that he was detained by the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and is being held in El Paso.

"Me tiene el ICE en El Paso Texas. Que locura," the boxer posted on X. In English, it translates to "ICE has me in El Paso, Texas. What a crazy situation."

TEXAS — Walking on a well-used hiking trail of what is considered the “crown jewel” of the National Wildlife Refuge System, Denisse Carreon recalls visiting the same path with her grandfather decades ago.

“I would come here when I was young with my grandpa,” Carreon said.

On the U.S.-Mexico border near the city of Alamo, the Santa Ana National Wildlife Refuge is a 2,088-acre federal preserve — long considered sacred and protected ground.

“When I was in high school as part of the National Honor Society, we actually built a trail,” Carreon said.

Established in 1943, the natural refuge offered protection of migratory birds, butterflies and other wildlife species native to the Rio Grande Valley. Now, recently placed orange ribbon survey stakes inside the federal preserve signal that Carreon’s special place as a child will be torn down in the name of border security.

Spectrum News has learned through attorneys representing contractors that new U.S. Customs and Border Protection (CBP) wall plans will spare a levee where border wall was initially planned, but wall construction will continue as marked by new stakes parallel to the levee.

“We’re following the judge’s order,“ said Spencer Construction attorney Ruben Pena. “The judge ordered us to stop so we agreed. CBP said you can stop but there is more wall to be built.”

In July, a lawsuit filed by the Hidalgo County Irrigation District tried to stop the building of border wall through the preserve. Before the lawsuit was filed this summer, wall construction through the preserve began. U.S. Magistrate Judge Juan Alanis issued a restraining order for Spencer Construction, LLC and Royal Concrete Products, LLC to halt further work and damage to the levee owned by Hidalgo County.

The construction companies and CBP then decided to establish a new path off the levee to continue construction.

Staring at the new stakes planted about 50 feet below the levee, Carreon said, “there’s no need for a border wall.”

The latest CBP data released earlier this month shows more than 90 miles of new border walls have been built during President Donald Trump's second term. CBP reports that 388.2 miles of wall barrier on the border is planned, and 90 miles of new wall is slated for the RGV.

Carreon says the new Congress must work together to stop the Trump administration’s promise to erect as much wall as possible.

“We need all of congress, republicans and democrats and independents to all protect Santa Anna. Enough is enough. Ya basta,” Carreon said.

text:
East Lansing could soon accept a large federal grant to upgrade its security cameras, but the grant appears to come with conditions that conflict with East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and diversity, equity and inclusion programming.

The city has been awarded and could accept a $472,000 grant from the U.S. Department of Justice, or DOJ, that pays for upgrades for up to 350 security cameras. The city’s cameras are a decade old and the new cameras will have better image quality and motion detection, according to the staff report.

However, the grant comes with a series of conditions. One condition states recipients “may not prohibit, or in any way restrict, any government entity or official from sending to, receiving from, maintaining, or exchanging information regarding citizenship or immigration status, lawful or unlawful, of any individual with components of the U.S. Department of Homeland Security or any other federal, state or local government entity.”

Another condition says that by accepting the grant, recipients certify they do not operate diversity, equity and inclusion programs. The grant also stipulates recipients must comply with all presidential memoranda and executive orders.

The East Lansing City Council could accept the grant funding by approving the consent agenda at its meeting Tuesday night, a possibility that has some residents concerned about East Lansing’s sanctuary city status and other stances. East Lansing officials say accepting the grant would not force any policy changes and the city is asking the DOJ to remove the conditions. East Lansing’s mayor said if the federal government tries to challenge or revoke the funding, the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed.

Residents are concerned that accepting the grant contradicts the city’s current sanctuary city status. The resolution declaring East Lansing a sanctuary city states that in a manner consistent with state and federal law, city officials will not actively collaborate with federal agents solely for the purpose of enforcing federal immigration law.

Further, East Lansing employs a DEI director.

“I have grave concerns that by accepting this grant money, that the city is committing to cooperating with the U.S. Department of Justice when it comes to immigration enforcement,” said Karen Hoene, chair of the city’s Human Rights Commission. “This is very concerning considering the fact that we are a sanctuary city and we have City Council members that have committed to remaining a sanctuary city.”

Hoene said that the City Council placing the resolution to accept the grant funding on the consent agenda, which is usually passed without discussion, is “sneaky” and feels like a “MAGA move.”

But city officials say the grant does not force it to change any of its operations. Councilmember Mark Meadows said the city’s policy is that officials do not communicate with federal officials on immigration enforcement, except in cases where federal law requires it. He said this will continue to be how the city operates.

Meadows said conditions the grant places are illegal and courts have ruled cities don’t have to comply with these regulations. He said the federal government cannot force municipalities to assist in federal immigration enforcement.

“It’s just another example of Trump’s administration trying to, I guess, create law that doesn’t exist,” Meadows said. “That’s how we’ve approached it.

“If they want to yank the grant, then they’ll have the opportunity to yank the grant. But we haven’t changed anything,” he continued. “We’re accepting it. If we get the money, they can order us to return the money. We’ll deal with that at that point in time.”

Mayor Erik Altmann said in a call on Tuesday that the city believes the conditions are unenforceable due to injunctions and court rulings. He pointed to a two-page memorandum that was added to the City Council agenda at some point on Tuesday after residents had reached out to East Lansing Info about the grant conditions.

The memorandum from Interim City Manager Annette Irwin, dated Nov. 18 – which is tomorrow – asks that the conditions referencing DEI, immigration enforcement and executive orders be removed. The memo argues that the conditions are not enforceable.

Altmann said accepting the grant does not change the city’s policies and the plan is to continue operating in the same way. He said he does not know how the federal government will respond.

“The problem is that we are in completely uncharted territory here,” Altmann said. “I have no idea because nobody can predict what the Trump administration is going to do on a given day.”

If the federal government does seek to challenge or revoke the funding, Altmann said the community should have conversations about the best way to proceed.

“That is a conversation we will have to have, not just at the council level but at the community level if we get to that point,” he said.

“We have a bunch of people writing to us at the City Council account saying basically ‘don’t take a half-million-dollar grant,’” Altmann continued. “There’s probably a lot of other people in the community who say ‘You better take a half-million-dollar grant.’”

text:
Washington, D.C. – U.S. Senators Catherine Cortez Masto (D-Nev.) and Jacky Rosen (D-Nev.) joined Senator Adam Schiff (D-Calif) in calling out Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Michael Selig for the agency’s decision to prohibit prediction markets from geofencing, allowing prediction markets to continue operating in all 50 states and on Tribal lands.

This CFTC decision undermines Nevada’s state gaming laws applicable to sports event contracts listed on prediction markets, which were upheld by the 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in August, and similar state and Tribal restrictions in Michigan, California, and Washington. Both Senators from each of these states joined the letter.

“Numerous courts have held that sports-related event contracts are not swaps and instead are indistinguishable from sports bets subject to state and tribal gaming laws…. The courts have ordered platforms to cease offering various prediction contracts in Michigan, Nevada, and Washington, and on the land of two California tribes, and imposed geofencing requirements. The Commission now appears to be encouraging prediction markets to offer prohibited contracts in contempt of these court orders during active litigation,” wrote the Senators.

“We are particularly troubled that this action came just hours after the Northern District of California issued its latest court order in Blue Lake Rancheria v. Kalshi requiring Kalshi to geofence around the plaintiff’s tribal lands. This interpretation raises concerns that the Commission may be coordinating with platforms currently engaged in litigation and encouraging them to violate state and tribal gaming laws… The Commission must withdraw the interpretation or freeze all efforts to implement until litigation is resolved,” they continued.

Senators Cortez Masto, Schiff, and Rosen were joined by Maria Cantwell (D-Wash.), Patty Murray (D-Wash.), Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), Gary Peters (D-Mich.), Alex Padilla (D-Calif.), and Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.).

The full text of the letter can be found here.

Senators Cortez Masto and Rosen have repeatedly called for more stringent oversight of prediction markets. The Senators have previously called on the CFTC to prohibit prediction markets incentivizing physical injury, death, or war; raised the alarm about offshore prediction markets allowing people to bet on wildfires; and pushed the CFTC to do more to combat insider trading in prediction markets. They have also urged Selig to abstain from intervening in pending litigation involving prediction markets. Cortez Masto is a co-sponsor of the Prediction Markets Are Gambling Act, which would prohibit CFTC-registered entities – like Polymarket and Kalshi – from listing any prediction contracts that resemble a sports bet or casino-style game.

NOTE: The above video is a livestream of WIS featuring current newscasts, Soda City Living and Gray Media’s Local News Live.

ATLANTA (WIS) - A new federal lawsuit is challenging what the plaintiffs say is an ICE policy that allows agents to detain immigrants again after they’ve been released, even when nothing significant has changed in their cases.

The American Civil Liberties Union organizations in Georgia, North Carolina and South Carolina are among the attorneys representing the plaintiffs, who are suing the Department of Homeland Security, ICE and several federal officials.

The plaintiffs allege the policy change is part of the federal government’s campaign to expand immigration detention and accelerate deportations.

The lawsuit was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia. It asks the court to declare the policy unlawful, set it aside and temporarily stop it while the case proceeds.

The proposed class could include eligible people in all three states, which are covered by ICE’s Atlanta field office.

The four plaintiffs with pending immigration relief applications are Livinton Sosa Martinez of Greensboro, North Carolina; Raquel Mariona Ebora of Dunn, North Carolina; Alvaro Ibañez Cardenas of Athens, Georgia; and Ambrosio Trujillo Zavaleta of Savannah, Georgia.

The lawsuit alleges that Sosa Martinez was re-detained at an ICE check-in in March, then released on bond after a federal judge ordered a bond hearing. It also alleges that a woman suffered a miscarriage as a result of trauma, stress and physical violence during her re-arrest and re-detention in South Carolina. The complaint provides few additional details about the incident.

The suit names DHS, ICE, DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin, acting ICE Director David Venturella and acting Atlanta Field Office Director Kristen Sullivan as defendants. It challenges the policy change under the Administrative Procedure Act.

The complaint cites a California federal court that found the re-detention policy likely violated federal law and temporarily stayed its use within the San Francisco ICE field office’s jurisdiction. The plaintiffs say that the court found the agency departed from longstanding practice without adequate justification.

_______________ 1 See our May 18, 2026, client alert “Litigation Under the Antiterrorism Act: Updates From Early 2026” (May 2026 client alert) and January 21, 2026, client alert “Litigation Under the Antiterrorism Act: 2025 Year in Review” (January 2026 client alert).
text:
Executive Summary

What’s new: Plaintiffs filed a wave of new ATA actions arising from attacks that took place prior to September 2016 to avoid a potential statutory deadline; pending matters continue to present important merits and jurisdictional issues.

Why it matters: Multinational corporations — particularly those that operate in high-risk or unstable regions — continue to face expanding risks of potential civil liability arising from alleged connections to international terrorist activity.

What to do next: Corporations with significant non-U.S. touchpoints should consider taking steps to assess, address and mitigate potential risk exposure under the ATA, while also monitoring further developments.

__________

The past few months featured a flurry of new civil actions brought under the Antiterrorism Act of 1990 (ATA), as amended by the 2016 Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA). Most were filed in advance of a potential deadline for asserting certain claims arising from “historical” terrorist attacks committed more than ten years ago. The passing of that date should mark a shift toward actions that arise from more recent terrorist activity abroad.

Recent months have also brought further developments relevant to civil ATA litigation, including additional foreign terrorist organization (FTO) designations and rulings concerning the scope of personal jurisdiction.

New Lawsuits

The past few months brought a significant uptick in newly filed ATA actions. The influx of new cases, as anticipated, was driven largely by some plaintiffs’ perception that the ten-year anniversary of JASTA — September 28, 2026 — serves as a deadline to bring secondary liability claims arising from events that took place before the statute was enacted in September 2016.1 Some courts have permitted plaintiffs to bring such claims to recover for injuries that arose as far back as September 11, 2001. Under that permissive (and potentially controversial) interpretation — which has yet to be tested at the appellate level — September 28, 2026, was the last day for filing such “historical” ATA claims.

Of the 28 ATA actions initiated so far this year, 23 were filed after June 1, 2026, and most of those were filed in the 10 days leading up to September 28, 2026. Notably, 18 of the 23 actions filed after June 1, 2026, were brought against corporate defendants. Many newly filed actions assert claims that relate to previously filed ATA actions pending against the same corporate defendants.

Among the wave of new ATA actions, two merit particular mention:

Connolly v. UniCredit Bank GmbH (D.D.C.).2 On September 2, 2026, victims of terrorist attacks in Iraq from 2008 to 2011 filed suit against a German bank, its Italian parent company and an Austrian subsidiary, alleging that the defendants aided and abetted those attacks through their business relationship with an Iranian maritime cargo carrier integral to Iran’s shipment of weapons to terrorist proxies in the Middle East. The plaintiffs allege that the bank processed the carrier’s financial transactions — notwithstanding global restrictions and despite known risks regarding the carrier’s links to terrorist actors — and thereby facilitated Iran’s supply network to terrorist actors that perpetrated the attacks.

As is common in ATA actions, these allegations draw on stipulated facts from the bank’s 2019 resolution of related U.S. government enforcement actions.3 Connolly is the latest case that should offer clarity on how district courts will apply a recent decision issued by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit,4 discussed below, that arguably embraced a comparatively flexible construction of the aiding-and-abetting standard.

Ben-Yishai v. Agrium Asia Pacific Ltd. (S.D.N.Y.).5 On September 27, 2026, victims of Palestinian terrorist attacks in Israel from 2001 to 2002 brought aiding-and-abetting claims against two Australian companies arising from their participation in Iraq’s United Nations-sponsored Oil-for-Food Program. The plaintiffs allege that from 1999 to 2003, the defendants evaded the program’s carefully monitored escrow mechanism to funnel more than $224 million in unapproved kickback or “protection” payments to the Saddam Hussein regime, which diverted the funds for illicit purposes — including to fund “martyr” payments to the families of Palestinian terrorist operatives who perpetrated the attacks that injured the plaintiffs.

The plaintiffs’ theory implicates timely questions regarding the “nexus” and “culpability” components of the aiding-and-abetting standard set forth in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit’s recent decision in Ashley v. Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft.6

Notable Developments

Beyond the new cases, the past few months featured a number of developments applicable to current and future ATA litigation:

Pending petition for a writ of certiorari. On January 23, 2026, the D.C. Circuit issued its decision in Atchley, an ATA case alleging that medical supply and manufacturing companies are subject to primary and secondary liability for providing funds and medical supplies to the Iraqi Ministry of Health, an entity that the plaintiffs allege was controlled by terrorist organizations. In that decision, the D.C. Circuit held that the plaintiffs had sufficiently alleged their ATA claims and allowed the case to proceed to discovery.7

On August 21, 2026, the Atchley defendants petitioned the U.S. Supreme Court for a writ of certiorari, requesting that the Court review the case and overturn the D.C. Circuit’s decision.8 The defendants asked the Supreme Court to review questions concerning the proper bounds of aiding-and-abetting liability and the proximate cause requirement for primary liability claims. On November 9, 2026, the Court requested the views of the U.S. Solicitor General regarding defendants’ petition, which could indicate an interest in the questions presented. If the Supreme Court grants the petition and hears the case, its resulting decision could have significant implications for those two issues, which are central to the scope of corporate liability under the ATA.

Personal jurisdiction in ATA cases. Although it remains unclear whether a recent Supreme Court decision portends a sea change for personal jurisdiction defenses in ATA cases, recent developments suggest that a drastic shift is unlikely.

In Fuld v. Palestine Liberation Organization, the Supreme Court upheld the constitutionality of a 2019 amendment to the ATA that codifies federal personal jurisdiction over the Palestinian Authority and the Palestine Liberation Organization in ATA actions under certain circumstances. In so doing, the Court held that the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment — which applies to ATA cases filed in federal court — permits a federal jurisdictional inquiry that is more flexible than the “minimum contacts” standard applicable under the Fourteenth Amendment.9 The Court declined to define the outer bounds of that inquiry but suggested that the ultimate analysis might entail an “inquiry into the reasonableness of the assertion of jurisdiction in the particular case.”10

While courts generally have been hesitant to conclude that Fuld relieves plaintiffs of the burden to show a meaningful relationship between defendants and the United States, at least one court applying Fuld concluded that it had personal jurisdiction to hear ATA claims against non-U.S. corporate defendants irrespective of the defendants’ contacts with the United States. Until additional courts (including appellate courts) address Fuld’s application to ATA claims with greater clarity, that jurisdictional landscape will remain uncertain.

In contexts beyond the ATA, however, appellate courts have minimized the effect of Fuld. In Rodriguez v. Imperial Brands, PLC, for example, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit applied Fuld in an action against two British corporations under the federal Helms-Burton Act.11 Although the court adopted the general “reasonableness” standard from Fuld, it applied that standard relatively rigidly, ultimately affirming the district court’s dismissal of the case for lack of personal jurisdiction. Among other things, the court observed that — unlike the idiosyncratic statute at issue in Fuld — the Helms-Burton Act did not “g[iv]e [defendants] clear notice that [their] alleged actions would expose [them] to suit in U.S. courts” without any “meaningful relationship with the United States.”12

The D.C. Circuit has likewise taken a restricted approach. In July 2026, the court issued a decision holding that Fuld does not affect personal jurisdiction standards in D.C. local courts; in dicta, the court also cautioned against a sweeping application of Fuld, observing that “[a]ny seemingly broad statements” contained therein should be read only to reach circumstances “similar to” those before the Supreme Court in that particular case.13 The following month, the D.C. Circuit again encountered Fuld, this time affirming the dismissal of federal civil RICO claims against foreign corporate defendants for lack of personal jurisdiction.14 The court found minimal interests associated with litigating the RICO claims in U.S. court, and (like the Eleventh Circuit) distinguished Fuld on the ground that the statute at issue in Fuld expressly authorized personal jurisdiction over specific, identifiable defendants.15

Additional FTO designations in Latin America. The Trump administration has continued to expand the universe of entities designated by the U.S. government as “Foreign Terrorist Organizations.” Since February 2025, 34 organizations have been designated as FTOs, more than the combined number across the previous decade.16 Most of the designated entities are drug cartels operating in Mexico, Central America and South America, a trend consistent with the administration’s broader emphasis on strengthening U.S. border security and reducing cartel violence. The pace has maintained in recent months — since June 1, 2026, the U.S. government has designated additional criminal organizations based in Brazil, Mexico, Ecuador and Guatemala as FTOs.17 Because JASTA limits claims for aiding and abetting or conspiracy to injuries stemming from attacks perpetrated by FTOs, these designations both expand the scope of ATA liability and increase civil, criminal and government enforcement risks for companies operating in these regions.

Restrictions on secondary liability claims under other statutes. Litigation exposure for corporations operating in high-risk jurisdictions is not confined to the ATA. Plaintiffs may seek to recover for injuries suffered abroad under various other federal, state or foreign laws. Notably, however, two recent decisions sharply restrict these plaintiffs’ ability to assert secondary liability theories under certain other federal statutes.

In Cisco Systems, Inc. v. Doe I, the U.S. Supreme Court held that neither the Alien Tort Statute (ATS) nor the Torture Victim Protection Act (TVPA) permits aiding-and-abetting claims.18 The decision further confirms that the ATS — which allows foreign nationals to bring suit in U.S. court for injury arising from torts committed in violation of international law or treaty — is a jurisdictional statute that does not create new causes of action (beyond a handful of narrow, historical common law claims). Moreover, Cisco’s rejection of aiding-and-abetting claims under the TVPA — which contains a cause of action against individuals for torture or extrajudicial killing under the actual or apparent authority of foreign law — removes a potential alternative for putative ATA plaintiffs who seek to recover in connection with certain types of conduct perpetrated abroad.

Similarly, in Mueller v. Deutsche Bank Aktiengesellschaft, the Second Circuit narrowly construed the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act (TVPRA), a federal statute that allows victims of human trafficking and similar offenses to sue direct perpetrators as well as anyone who “knowingly benefit[ted], or attempt[ed] or conspire[d] to benefit, financially or by receiving anything of value from participation in a venture which that person knew or should have known has engaged in” the principal violation.19 The court held that the phrase “participation in a venture” requires that a defendant affirmatively take part in a venture involving “elements of risk, potential gain, or both.”20 Applying that standard, the court concluded that allegations that the bank provided services to certain terrorist-affiliated banks — absent any shared common purpose or interest with the other alleged venture participants — were insufficient to state a TVPRA claim.21

‘Material support’ under the INA. The Supreme Court recently agreed to interpret a provision of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), and the resulting decision could apply to ATA actions as well. In Ozurumba v. Bondi, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit held that an individual’s preparation of meals served to leaders of a Nigerian terrorist organization did not constitute “material support to a terrorist organization” as defined in the INA because the assistance “was not sufficiently substantial standing alone to help the [organization] accomplish their terrorist activities.”22 On October 13, 2026, the Supreme Court granted review to determine whether alleged support must advance an organization’s actual commission of terrorism to qualify as “material” under the INA. Given that a plaintiff can pursue a primary liability claim under the ATA by likewise establishing that the defendant provided “material support” to a terrorist organization, the Supreme Court’s interpretation of the term as used in the INA could inform the scope of primary liability under the ATA.

Multinational corporations — particularly those that operate in high-risk or unstable regions — continue to face expanding risks of potential civil liability arising from alleged connections to international terrorist activity. text:
In his interview with “60 Minutes” a week ago, President Donald Trump seemed to extend an olive branch to Democrats, acknowledging his deportation policies may have been “too rough” and floating the possibility of bipartisan immigration reform, calling it “doable.”

That gesture of goodwill was called into question the same day the interview aired, when Trump elevated Stephen Miller, the architect of his administration’s violent immigration crackdown, to White House chief of staff.

On the one hand, the Trump White House recognizes that most Americans are not on board with the aggressive removal of immigrant workers with strong community ties and no criminal history. But by promoting Miller, Trump is indulging his worst impulses and sending mixed signals to the incoming Congress.

There is still a chance for Trump to rise above a broken legacy on immigration that includes the killings of Americans and immigrants on his watch. He could be the president who not only fixed the crisis at the southern border but also found a bipartisan path forward for broader immigration reform.

A united Congress can bring momentum to this issue. Voters punished Republicans down the ballot for Trump’s immigration excesses. Republicans had said before that a secure border was necessary before they would entertain a comprehensive immigration bill. Well, we have a secure border now.

Meanwhile, it’s up to Democrats taking their seats in Congress to stand by their pro-border control stances from this midterm election season.

Americans’ broad support for stronger border control never equated to indiscriminate, unnecessarily cruel immigration enforcement. Republicans now face an important choice: Continue a divisive approach that deepens public distrust, or work toward meaningful reforms that fix America’s broken immigration system.

Reforms should focus on temporary guest workers in industries where there is a shortage of labor, such as agriculture, as well as visa programs for skilled workers. Congress should also secure a permanent pathway for recipients of DACA, or Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals.

The Obama-era program offered temporary protection from deportation to undocumented immigrants who had been brought into the U.S. illegally as children. But DACA recipients have been stuck in limbo, caught between lawsuits challenging the program and Congress’ inaction. Yet 81% of Americans support a legal pathway for DACA holders as long as they meet certain requirements, according to a recent Gallup poll.

This editorial page has also raised concerns about the reshaping of immigration courts reviewing asylum cases. We’ve swung between a permissive asylum system to one that seems unfairly biased against immigrants. Congress should review these courts.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — The Chairs of the Congressional Tri-Caucus — Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus (CAPAC) Chair Grace Meng, Congressional Hispanic Caucus (CHC) Chair Adriano Espaillat, and Congressional Black Caucus (CBC) Chair Yvette Clarke — strongly condemn the Trump Administration’s intent to expel families with mixed immigration statuses, including tens of thousands of American children, from public housing.

The Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) is moving forward with a rule(link is external)that would force all residents of public housing to prove their immigration status to live in subsidized public housing.

“In the midst of a housing crisis, the Trump administration is implementing a new rule that would kick thousands of families out of their homes and put children on the streets. We urge HUD to reverse this harmful rule, protect families currently receiving assistance, and ensure that federal housing policy does not create unnecessary hardship for eligible residents, including American citizens and children. No family should be pushed closer to homelessness because of the immigration status of a loved one. HUD's mandate is to provide fair housing opportunities, and we will use every available congressional avenue to hold this administration accountable and protect access to safe, stable, and affordable housing,” said Tri-Caucus Chairs Grace Meng, Adriano Espaillat, and Yvette Clarke.

Currently, mixed-status families are permitted to live together in public housing though subsidies only cover eligible residents. Because ineligible residents are not covered by subsidies, mixed-status families often pay higher rent, contributing to HUD's financial stability.

HUD is moving forward with the rule despite widespread opposition from Members of Congress and housing advocates. According to the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities(link is external), approximately 80,000 people in mixed-status households could be affected, including nearly 37,000 children, most of whom are U.S. citizens.

For decades, federal policy has recognized that families should not have to choose between maintaining a roof over their heads and remaining together. Under the existing framework, mixed-status households may receive prorated housing assistance covering only eligible family members. The Trump Administration is now dismantling that framework, creating new barriers to housing stability and putting HUD's finances at risk.

WASHINGTON, D.C. (November 17, 2026) — Today, Congresswoman Valerie Foushee (NC-04), Congresswoman Deborah Ross (NC-02), and Congresswoman Alma Adams (NC-12) sent a letter to the U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin demanding answers regarding the imminent reopening of the Rivers Correctional Institution (RCI) in Winton, North Carolina in partnership with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE).

On July 29th, The GEO Group, Inc. announced that it had entered into a five-year contract with ICE to operate a federal immigration processing center at the GEO-owned Rivers Correctional Institution.

“The facility would open during the deadliest period for people in ICE custody in more than two decades, at a site with a documented history of violence and medical neglect, run by a contractor whose facilities are currently under state investigation,” the lawmakers wrote.

“At a time when North Carolina families are struggling with the rising cost of housing, health care, and groceries, private prison companies are receiving billions of dollars in federal funds. North Carolinians deserve robust investment in needed infrastructure and economic opportunities, not federal subsidization of a new detention facility,” the lawmakers continued.

"At least 10 people died in GEO-operated facilities in 2025, and deaths have continued in 2026. At Delaney Hall in Newark, New Jersey, Jovanny Lopez Cornejo died in August. His mother said he was not receiving his daily medication for diabetes and high blood pressure and had complained of numbness in his face and hand. When New Jersey health inspectors arrived at Delaney Hall in May, they were barred from the medical unit,” the lawmakers concluded. “A company that blocks state health inspectors from auditing their facilities should not be entrusted with more lives in North Carolina.”

The letter includes the following questions for U.S. Department of Homeland Security Secretary Mullin relating to facility operations, legal access and immigration court, medical and mental healthcare, and community impacts:

What is the current status of ICE's contract with GEO Group for the Winton facility, and when will it begin receiving detainees?

Will the facility open at full capacity or phase in its detained population? If phased, what is the anticipated timeline for reaching full operational capacity?

Please provide a copy of the contract, including its term, per-diem rate, and any guaranteed minimum occupancy provision.

How many full-time and part-time correctional staff will be employed at Rivers?

What population will Rivers house (men, women, children)?

Are there any categories of detained individuals that Rivers will not be equipped or authorized to house? (ex. Pregnant people, people living with disabilities, unaccompanied minors, people with certain security-classifications, etc.)

What ICE AOR (Area of Responsibility) and ERO (Enforcement Removal Operations) field office will be in control of this facility?

Does ICE anticipate that Rivers will operate as a regional facility? If so, serving which state populations?

Which detention standards (NDS 2025, PBNDS 2011, or other) will govern the facility, and will ICE or an independent body complete a pre-occupancy inspection? If such an inspection was already completed, please provide the results.

How many private attorney-client visitation rooms will be available?

Will Rivers participate in ICE’s Virtual Attorney Visitation program? If so, how many confidential video stations will be available?

In what immigration court will cases for individuals detained in this facility take place?

Will immigration hearings for individuals detained at Rivers occur in person, by video teleconference, or both?

Will legal organizations be permitted to conduct Know Your Rights presentations?

What medical staffing levels are required under the contract, including physicians, nurses, and mental health professionals?

Will Rivers be contracting with an outside provider for medical or mental health services? If so, who?

Will medical personnel be physically present on-site 24/7 for medical emergencies?

What are the nearest hospitals capable of emergency and specialty care, what are the transport times, and what protocols govern emergency transfers?

How many mental health beds will be available?

How many restrictive-housing or solitary confinement beds will be available?

Did ICE evaluate the 2016 DOJ findings and the 2007 medical care litigation at Rivers when deciding to contract for this site?

What, if any, corrective measures has GEO Group committed to?

What steps has ICE taken to review GEO Group's medical care practices in light of deaths at Delaney Hall and Adelanto?

Given the state of New Jersey's litigation over access to Delaney Hall, will ICE require GEO Group to permit unannounced inspections by state and local health authorities at Winton?

Will any inspections as to facility fitness/safety be conducted prior to opening?

Have any evaluations been made regarding the impact that the re-opening of Rivers will have on the infrastructure of Winton and the surrounding area (e.g. traffic, emergency services, hospital capacity)?

What agreement, if any, has ICE or GEO reached with local entities regarding services associated with Rivers? (ex. EMS providers, local law enforcement, hospitals, local government)

Will local government or service providers receive federal reimbursement for costs associated with Rivers?

text:
WASHINGTON—The National Association of Immigration Judges (NAIJ), represented by the Knight First Amendment Institute at Columbia University, today asked the U.S. Supreme Court to let the association’s members go directly to federal court to challenge a Justice Department policy that imposes a sweeping gag order on what immigration judges can say publicly.

“This case is about whether the government can gag its own employees and then make it nearly impossible for them to challenge that gag in court,” said Ramya Krishnan, a senior staff attorney with the Knight First Amendment Institute. “No one should have to put their job on the line to defend their right to speak. With immigration at the center of national debate, Americans should be able to hear what immigration judges have to say.”

In 2020, the Knight Institute filed this lawsuit on behalf of NAIJ, challenging an Executive Office for Immigration Review (EOIR) policy that prohibits immigration judges from speaking publicly in their personal capacities about immigration or the agency that employs them. A district court dismissed the case in 2023, holding that the Civil Service Reform Act (CSRA) of 1978 requires such claims to go through an administrative process rather than federal court.

In June 2025, the Fourth Circuit revived the case, expressing concern that Trump administration actions may have undermined the agencies charged with hearing federal employee claims—the Office of Special Counsel and the Merit Systems Protection Board. It sent the case back to the district court to determine whether that administrative system was still functioning as Congress intended. The court also held, though, that if the system was functioning as intended immigration judges would have to pursue their challenge through that administrative process.

Earlier this year, the Supreme Court summarily reversed that decision on procedural grounds and declined to review NAIJ’s separate argument that federal employees should be able to go directly to court to challenge broad restrictions on their speech. It returned the case to the Fourth Circuit, which affirmed the district court’s dismissal in August without ruling on whether the policy violates the First Amendment.

“Judges do not turn in their right to free speech when they put on the robe,” said Holly A. D’Andrea, president of the National Association of Immigration Judges. “Our country was designed to be governed by public reason, not private silence. Silencing judges deprives the public of a key perspective on the rule of law.”

Because the Supreme Court reversed the earlier Fourth Circuit ruling about the CSRA’s functioning, today’s petition presents a more focused question: whether immigration judges must pursue their challenge through an administrative process that does not guarantee any—let alone meaningful—judicial review of their time-sensitive constitutional claims. Under the Fourth Circuit’s ruling, the only guaranteed pathway for an immigration judge to challenge EOIR’s policy in federal court is to violate the policy, get punished, and then challenge that punishment.

The petition warns that this ruling threatens to create “a First Amendment black hole”: “The federal government could categorically forbid federal employees from engaging in even private speech about gun rights, health care, vaccines, university admissions, or the war in Gaza—and judicial review of these brazenly unconstitutional policies would come only with the blessing of an agency official, and only after protracted and futile administrative proceedings.”

Even eventual judicial review would come too late to remedy the harm, the petition argues: “The ability of federal employees to contribute to currently unfolding debates cannot be regained once lost.”

Read the cert petition here.

Read more about the case here.

Attorneys on the case include Ramya Krishnan, Alex Abdo, Xiangnong (George) Wang, Zoe Rubin, and Jameel Jaffer for the Knight First Amendment Institute, and Victor M. Glasberg of Victor M. Glasberg & Associates in Alexandria, VA.

Attorney General Jennifer Davenport and the Division on Civil Rights (DCR) announced today the filing of a lawsuit in federal court against the U.S. Department of Homeland Security (DHS) over its months-long failure to respond to lawful subpoenas seeking information about the treatment of detainees at Delaney Hall, the private immigration-detention facility in Newark owned and operated by The GEO Group, Inc.

View Complaint

In the wake of reports of alarming conditions and recent deaths of detainees held at the facility, Attorney General Davenport and DCR issued an investigative subpoena to GEO Group in August. The investigation focuses on whether GEO Group employees violated the civil rights of people detained at the facility. GEO Group has claimed that it cannot respond to the subpoena without DHS’s permission.

Today’s lawsuit asks the court to find that DHS has unreasonably delayed its response in violation of the Administrative Procedure Act. It also asks the court to set a firm deadline by which DHS must communicate its decision.

“There are far too many reports of inhumane treatment of the people held at Delaney Hall. But what we have received for months from both GEO Group and DHS is plain stonewalling,” said Attorney General Davenport. "We will continue to do all we can to ensure that these civil detainees are treated with the dignity and decency that all people are entitled to under the law.”

“Individuals housed in an immigration detention facility do not waive their constitutional and legal right to receive adequate medical care or to be protected from violence,” said Yolanda N. Melville, Director of the Division on Civil Rights. “People who have been held at Delaney Hall have shared extremely troubling accounts—as have the families of those who died. The federal government’s silence in response to our lawful requests for information speaks volumes.”

On August 7, 2026, the Attorney General and DCR opened an investigation into potential violations of detainees' civil and constitutional rights under the New Jersey Civil Rights Act and the New Jersey Law Against Discrimination. As part of that investigation, DCR issued a subpoena to GEO Group seeking records related to the provision of medical care to detainees.

DCR issued a subpoena to GEO Group after at least three individuals died while in GEO Group's custody at Delaney Hall. Public reports have alleged inadequate medical care, the rapid spread of communicable diseases, abuse by staff, unreasonable exposure to violence, and other harms.

As the complaint details, GEO Group declined to comply with the subpoena, asserting that it required authorization from DHS under DHS’s internal regulations. GEO Group claimed that pursuant to those DHS regulations, it had promptly forwarded the subpoena to DHS’s general counsel to provide GEO Group authorization to comply.

While the State maintains that GEO Group, as a private business operating on its own property within New Jersey’s borders, is mistaken in thinking it needs DHS authorization to comply with the subpoenas, it nonetheless began following up on its requests with DHS directly as an alternative pathway to obtain the necessary information. For over three months, and despite multiple follow-up inquiries from Attorney General Davenport’s office to DHS, DHS has failed to respond. DHS has not authorized production of any information, nor has it stated whether it will or will not do so.

The State's ongoing investigation has identified reports of serious deficiencies in medical intake and screening, failures to provide medications for chronic conditions, inadequate responses to medical emergencies, failures to protect individuals from physical and sexual harm, denial of accommodations for individuals with disabilities, and routine denial of language interpretation services.

Attorney General Davenport and DCR believe that based on the reports gathered so far, there is a serious risk of further harm to those housed at Delaney Hall, including additional death and disease.

DHS’s failure to respond to DCR’s subpoena is part of a pattern of stonewalling any efforts to examine conditions inside Delaney Hall. Litigation in a separate lawsuit over GEO Group’s refusal to allow a full health inspection is ongoing.

The State argues that DHS's prolonged silence, combined with a pattern of obstructing State and municipal oversight, has unreasonably delayed the investigation and prolonged risks to detainees' health and welfare.

In today’s lawsuit, New Jersey is asking the court to compel DHS to communicate a decision regarding compliance with the subpoena.

text:
GENEVA – UN rights chief Volker Turk voiced concern on Nov 17 about a plan by five EU countries to set up a migrant deportation centre in Rwanda, saying it raised human rights risks.

Germany, Denmark, Austria, Greece and the Netherlands on Nov 1 6 unveiled plans for the first such facility outside the European Union.

The centre is expected to host migrants whose asylum applications have been rejected and who have exhausted all avenues of appeal in one of the five countries.

“We know how difficult, politicised and polarising migration issues have become,” Turk said in a statement.

“While we are not privy to the text of the proposal, we are concerned about the human rights risks raised by the proposed transfer of people from five EU countries to Rwanda, where they have no genuine connection and which has its own set of human rights challenges.”

Turk said the solution was not finding faraway countries or in externalising human rights obligations.

“The response lies in a deeper analysis of the drivers behind migration,” he said, including inequalities, geopolitical tensions and economic disadvantages.

Turk called for a comprehensive approach anchored in human rights, “including through the expansion of regular migration pathways and with recognition of the enormous contributions of migrants to European societies and economies”.

Arrivals of asylum seekers have steadily declined over the past three years, as the EU struck deals with a host of countries in Africa and the Middle East to stem departures.

UN refugees chief Barham Salih took part in a meeting in Vienna with the five EU countries and Rwanda.

He called for “preserving the integrity of asylum systems, ensuring respect for international refugee and human rights law, and reinforcing international responsibility-sharing”, a statement said.

The UN’s International Organisation for Migration (IOM) said it had received a request from Rwanda for operational support, which it could offer, provided international standards are upheld.

“IOM’s assistance would begin only once individuals have arrived,” the UN migration agency said.

“It would focus on access to essential services, potentially including healthcare, mental health and psychosocial support, information and counselling, protection screening and referral, and support for access to the local labour market for those integrating locally.”

The five EU countries have expressed hope to have a centre up and running in 2027.

Diplomatic sources say the Rwanda hub will be initially run as a pilot, hosting about 100 people. AFP

text:
Outgoing Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton is attempting to force the Houston Police Department to cooperate with U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), after Mayor John Whitmire ordered officers to sharply limit contact with the agency.

Paxton's effort continues a battle between the state and city that stretches back to April, when Whitmire and the city council first attempted to curb HPD's cooperation with ICE. After Texas Gov. Greg Abbott threatened to revoke more than $110 million in public safety funding, Houston police officers resumed detaining people while waiting for ICE to respond to civil immigration warrants.

On Nov. 6 — days after Texas voters elected Democrats to all open statewide offices — Whitmire announced HPD would stop contacting ICE about civil immigration warrants, except when arresting someone on a jailable offense.

Sign up for the Hello, Houston! daily newsletter to get local reports like this delivered directly to your inbox.

Related: Houston Mayor John Whitmire directs HPD to reduce cooperation with ICE after midterm results

On Friday, Paxton's office filed a motion in a Fort Bend County District Court seeking to block the policy.

The state’s argument centered on Senate Bill 4, a state law passed in 2017 that requires local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement. In the filing, Paxton's office argued "a municipality may not undermine or subvert local law enforcement cooperation and communication with federal immigration enforcement, whether by decree or by legislation."

In a statement to Houston Public Media, City Attorney Arturo Michel indicated the city may attempt to run out the clock on Paxton, who leaves office in January.

"It will be difficult for the Attorney General to obtain a court ruling before the new administration takes over, which has indicated it will not pursue SB4 enforcement of this nature," Michel said in an email.

The development was first reported by the Houston Chronicle.

Paxton's office did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

City ordinance to enshrine executive order stalls

Before Paxton's filing, Houston City Council members Alejandra Salinas, Edward Pollard and Tiffany Thomas sought to codify Whitmire's executive order as a city ordinance approved by the council. Whitmire opposed the effort, arguing it could run afoul of state law.

On Tuesday, City Attorney Arturo Michel — who reports to Whitmire — was expected to deem the proposed ordinance unlawful in a memo to city council members.

Related: Houston police responded to a man in a mental health crisis. ICE arrested him

From April through September, officers contacted ICE nearly 200 times — including during traffic stops and while responding to people who requested emergency assistance — and handed over at least 36 people directly to ICE.

With Republicans maintaining control of statewide offices until January, it's unclear why Whitmire was willing to issue an executive order that could draw their ire but unwilling to support an ordinance enshrining his own directive. The campaign for incoming Texas Attorney General Nathan Johnson, a Democrat, did not immediately respond to a question about whether he would allow Houston to implement Whitmire's policy.

Related: Houston Mayor Whitmire opposes effort to enshrine HPD-ICE executive order as an ordinance

In a written statement on Tuesday, Salinas urged Whitmire's administration to defend the executive order in court.

"Ken Paxton is yet again trying to bully Houston into abandoning protections for our immigrant neighbors and families," Salinas wrote. "Earlier this year, we urged the City to defend our original immigration ordinance in court, and now we have another opportunity to get this right. I once again urge the Administration to fight this lawsuit in court. We cannot continue bowing down to state officials attempting to bulldoze over lawful City policies and constitutional rights.”

text:
Editor's Note: This is an excerpt from WBUR's daily morning newsletter, WBUR Today. If you like what you read and want it in your inbox, sign up here.

The audit isn't the only unresolved 2024 ballot question. Many local Uber and Lyft drivers are expected to take a break at noon today to rally for a collective bargaining deal, after they won the right to unionize in 2024.

But first, let's get to the news:

House rules: The Trump administration is planning to implement a new rule next month requiring all people who live in federally subsidized housing to prove their U.S. citizenship or legal residency. Families in Massachusetts with mixed-immigration statuses are bracing for the effects, WBUR's Rachell Sanchez-Smith reports. Advocates say the new rules will displace or split up hundreds of households in the state, including legal residents and children. You can read Rachell's full story here. Here's a quick breakdown:

Catch up: Undocumented immigrants are not eligible for federal rental vouchers or public housing. But since 1995, they've been allowed to live in subsidized housing with family members who are legal residents. Trump administration officials characterize that as a "loophole." The Department of Housing and Urban Development tried to make the change during Trump's first term, but ran into opposition from landlords and the proposal was later withdrawn under former President Biden. But Trump's HUD revived the policy this year and finalized it last week.

By the numbers: The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning think tank, estimated last year that 79,600 people in mixed-status households receiving federal rental assistance would be affected by the change. Roughly two-thirds of those people are U.S. citizens, and nearly half of them are children. According to the center, there are 910 mixed-status households in Massachusetts that would be affected.

The case for the change: There are long waitlists for federally funded public housing. The Trump administration says only a quarter of people eligible federal rental assistance get it, leaving many legal residents — including vulnerable groups like homeless veterans and elderly individuals — on long waitlists.

The case against it: Local advocates say the change will throw low-income residents into the state's expensive private rental market and lead to more people experiencing homelessness.

What's next: The new rule is slated to take effect on Dec. 14.

Meanwhile: A federal judge in Boston is blocking the Trump administration's attempt to limit the number of years international students can study in the U.S. The Department of Homeland Security had announced rules this summer that would cap most foreign students' stays at four years and require them to pay a fee for an extension. (International students are currently allowed to stay in the country as long as they are making progress on their degrees.) But in a ruling yesterday, U.S. District Court Judge F. Dennis Saylor overturned the new rules.

Why? Saylor said limits were an overstep of DHS's authority on a congressionally approved visa program and that the Trump administration failed to consider less burdensome ways to combat suspected overstays.

In court: The Lindsay Clancy case is headed to a retrial. Judge William Sullivan set a March 29 start date yesterday for the new trial of the Duxbury woman accused of killing her three children in 2023. Clancy's first trial ended in a deadlocked jury in September.

Reading between the lines: Prosecutors didn't specify if they intend to pursue the same or lesser charges. However, Clancy's defense attorney Kevin Reddington said he expects they will pursue first-degree murder charges again based on a prosecutor's comment that it will "require a jury trial."

Now approaching: The MBTA wrapped up its nine-day Green Line closure over the weekend, but two more substantial line disruptions are headed toward us next month. The T announced yesterday that a similar chunk of the Green Line will be closed for four days, Dec. 4-7. After that, more than half of the Blue Line will be suspended for nine days, Dec. 12-20. (Plan ahead if you're flying in or out of Logan Airport early for the holidays.)

description:
VIENNA — Rwanda’s interior minister has rebuked criticism of a plan by five European Union countries to deport failed asylum-seekers to his country.
Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands on Monday announced a partnership with Rwanda to set up a deportation hub.
The announcement led to a storm of protest from civil society and human rights groups, which said the fundamental rights of people sent to Rwanda cannot be guaranteed.
Human rights groups don’t believe the countries can come up with a framework that will guarantee migrants’ rights are respected.
Rwanda has an abysmal human rights record, is responsible for serious abuses and war crimes in eastern Congo and engages in transnational repression, Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO.
text:
VIENNA — Rwanda’s interior minister has rebuked criticism of a plan by five European Union countries to deport failed asylum-seekers to his country.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands on Monday announced a partnership with Rwanda to set up a deportation hub. They aim to send the first asylum-seekers to the African country in 2027.

The plan comes after the EU adopted legislation that allows countries to negotiate deals to build such “return hubs” outside the bloc — as long as they meet human rights standards. The announcement led to a storm of protest from civil society and human rights groups, which said the fundamental rights of people sent to Rwanda cannot be guaranteed.

Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, disagreed.

“Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country,” Biruta said Tuesday, speaking on a panel at a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

He argued his country’s migration policies are among the “most progressive” as they allow refugees to work and start a business.

In a joint warning against the plan Monday, 47 organizations pointed to a 2023 court decision that slapped down the United Kingdom’s plans to process asylum seekers’ claims in Rwanda. It cited “substantial grounds” to believe that people sent to the African nation would be exposed “to a real risk of ill-treatment by reason of refoulement” — referring to a practice whereby people are forcibly moved to countries where they face real threats. Under a 2013 deal with Israel, people sent to Rwanda “were routinely moved clandestinely to Uganda,” the court added.

Biruta said he was “not surprised” by NGOs’ warnings and said the government faced “the same issue” when it was making plans with the U.K. Those plans “didn’t work but … helped to improve our asylum system,” he added.

NGOs “always … say that nothing is working, that our human rights record is bad,” Biruta said, “but I’d like them to come forward with an alternative solution.”

EU ministers repeatedly stressed Monday that their partnership with Rwanda would meet international and European standards. Biruta said his country would put in place an independent monitoring mechanism and that it wants to involve the International Organization for Migration and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.

Details about such mechanisms and cooperation, as well as how the EU countries and Rwanda will divide responsibilities for the refugees’ wellbeing, have not yet been revealed.

“There are still some technical things that have to be solved, including where [the responsibility of ] Europe ends and where Rwanda starts,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told POLITICO after the plan’s announcement.

Human rights groups don’t believe the countries can come up with a framework that will guarantee migrants’ rights are respected.

Rwanda has an abysmal human rights record, is responsible for serious abuses and war crimes in eastern Congo and engages in transnational repression, Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO.

“No amount of nominal safeguards will be sufficient to mitigate the risks of serious human rights violations, particularly as there is unlikely to be any way to implement effective monitoring or seek accountability,” she said. “Given its track record, the fact that Rwanda was even considered, much less chosen, justifies deep skepticism about EU rhetoric about respecting people’s rights.”

Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting.
