text:
An 8-year-old Haitian boy who was detained by ICE earlier this month during an immigration check-in, prompting concerns from Democratic lawmakers, has been released from government custody, a Haitian immigration advocacy group said Monday evening.

The third grader, who is among tens of thousands of Haitians who earlier this year lost temporary protected status as part of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown, has been living with his uncle since his father was deported to Mexico last year.

"An eight-year-old child belongs in a classroom, on a playground, and surrounded by love -- not in immigration detention," said Guerline Jozef, the executive director of Haitian Bridge Alliance, in announcing the boy's release. "We welcome his release, but his freedom should never have required a public outcry. No child should endure the trauma of detention because of their immigration status."

An ICE spokesperson said earlier this month that during the boy's routine immigration check-in, the agency was unable to determine legal guardianship of his uncle, and out of an abundance of caution "determined it was best to remove the child from the household and place him in the care of the Office of Refugee Resettlement."

The child was in government custody for 11 days.

In a statement, a DHS spokesperson said the boy was returned to the custody of his uncle once the uncle could establish guardianship under the Trafficking Victims Protection Reauthorization Act. DHS says the boy was initially brought to the country illegally "with a man who alleged to be his father."

"His father has never been in ICE custody and was previously removed to Mexico by CBP," the spokesperson said.

A spokesperson for the Department of Health & Human Services, which oversees the Office of Refugee Resettlement, said in a statement that ORR's responsibility "is the care and welfare of the children referred to it. By law, a foreign national child who is not in the care of a parent or legal guardian becomes the responsibility of ORR."

"Family reunification is the goal for every child," the HHS spokesperson said. "Placement decisions are based on each child’s safety and best interests and sponsor vetting protects children from trafficking and exploitation."

Jozef told ABC News that the child will continue living with his uncle.

"This is a victory for humanity, but our work is far from over," Jozef said. "We will continue fighting until every immigrant child is treated with the dignity, compassion, and protection they deserve."

text:
MIAMI — The Southern Poverty Law Center (SPLC) and Americans for Immigrant Justice (AI Justice) filed a complaint today with the Department of Homeland Security’s (DHS) Office of Inspector General, its Office for Civil Rights and Civil Liberties, and Immigration and Customs Enforcement’s (ICE) Office of Professional Responsibility calling for an immediate investigation into reports of severe abuse, prolonged detention, medical neglect and coercion at the Miramar ICE sub field office.

“DHS’ oversight offices must step in now,” said A.J. Hernandez Anderson, deputy legal director for immigrant justice, SPLC. “No one should be forced to endure the appalling conditions and mistreatment that detained people have experienced at Miramar, in violation of ICE’s own rules. These are not isolated incidents; they are a pattern that must end today.”

The complaint draws on accounts from people held at Miramar, including sworn declarations filed in federal court, which describe an alarming pattern of mistreatment. Beginning in October 2025, ICE used the Miramar facility to hold people for days at a time — far beyond the 12-hour limit set by ICE’s own holding facility policy. Detained people are packed so tightly into holding cells, a garage and offices that they could not lie down, forcing them to sleep in shifts and on office desks. The only toilets available are in open view of surveillance cameras and other detained people, denying any bodily privacy. Detained people also have been denied adequate food and water for extended periods of time. No known ICE inspection of Miramar has occurred since the facility began operating as a multiday detention site.

“People facing consequential immigration decisions need a meaningful opportunity to understand their options and speak privately with a lawyer. Reports of delayed, limited or monitored calls at Miramar raise serious concerns about whether people can protect their rights while in custody,” said Jennifer Smith, senior litigation attorney, Americans for Immigrant Justice.

The accounts also describe widespread medical neglect. Detained people have been denied prescribed medication, including insulin and medications for HIV and high blood pressure, while others have collapsed or had seizures while waiting for care. One family reported that their daughters were told they could receive their medication only if they signed documents agreeing to deportation. Sanitation and hygiene were reported to be equally dire, with people going over a week without a shower, receiving sink water that smelled and tasted foul and being served expired microwaved meals that left many people ill. Many described daily pressure to sign documents agreeing to voluntarily depart the United States, or that offered false promises of quick release or threats of years in detention.

In July, Rep. Debbie Wasserman Schultz made an unannounced oversight visit and found roughly 150 people held in crowded rooms, sleeping shoulder-to-shoulder on the floor next to exposed toilets. These consistently clogged toilets have led to urine and feces overflowing onto the floor of the holding cell in the facility. Representatives Robert Garcia, Bennie Thompson and Maxwell Frost have separately demanded answers from ICE regarding dangerous conditions at Florida immigration facilities, including Miramar, where they described people being shackled in an unventilated garage entrance and that ICE was attempting to conceal these conditions from members of Congress.

“No one should have to endure the horrific conditions and cruel policies that people are experiencing at the Miramar ICE facility,” said Guadalupe De la Cruz, Florida program director, American Friends Service Committee. “For months, we have been hearing disturbing reports of people held for long periods of time packed into overcrowded spaces without basic sanitation or bedding. We are calling on DHS to bring an end to these abuses immediately.”

The SPLC and AI Justice are urging all three oversight offices that have received the complaint to act without delay and ensure that the allegations receive a thorough investigation.

The complaint is available here.

The Southern Poverty Law Center is a catalyst for racial justice in the South and beyond, working in partnership with communities to dismantle white supremacy, strengthen intersectional movements and advance the human rights of all people. For more information, visit www.splcenter.org.

text:
Updated Nov. 16 on 7:09 p.m.

Barnard will not authorize Curricular Practical Training for the spring 2027 semester, pausing the program that allows international students to work off-campus internships during college.

Akilah Rosado, interim dean of the college and vice president for inclusion and belonging, announced the decision in a Monday email to F-1 international students.

The announcement extends a pause on CPT approvals that Barnard quietly put in place in August. That pause followed two messages from the Student and Exchange Visitor Program, the branch of Immigration and Customs Enforcement that oversees international students, which sharply narrowed when colleges may authorize CPT.

“This is not a decision we take lightly, but one we believe is necessary in light of current guidance from the United States Student and Exchange Visitor Program,” Rosado wrote.

In the email, Rosado also wrote that the SEVP sent messages to designated school officials on Aug. 12 and 24, instructing schools that internships for both domestic and international students must be “an essential and required part of an established academic curriculum” rather than an elective experience. The memos warned that colleges and universities could be cut off from enrolling international students if they did not comply.

The federal guidance also requires CPT to be carried out through formal cooperative agreements between colleges and employers.

In a Sept. 1 email, Rosado told international students that CPT authorizations granted on or before Aug. 24 for summer or fall 2026 would not be rescinded, and that all pending and new requests were on hold while Barnard reviewed its protocols. Barnard said it would update students on that review by Nov. 16.

Columbia Provost Angela Olinto announced in August that its International Students and Scholars Office reviewed international students’ work authorizations following the memos.

Brown University announced earlier this month that it would no longer issue CPT authorizations for undergraduate students.

The email also referred to a federal lawsuit challenging the guidance. On Oct. 5, a group of organizations—including the Association of American Universities, the Presidents’ Alliance on Higher Education and Immigration, the Association of Independent Colleges and Universities in Massachusetts, and NAFSA: Association of International Educators— sued the Department of Homeland Security, ICE, and the Department of Justice in the Massachusetts Federal District Court. The lawsuit seeks to restore CPT and protect students and institutions from retroactive penalties.

“While this litigation is ongoing, the August guidance remains in effect. We will continue to monitor developments and their implications for CPT opportunities at Barnard,” Rosado wrote.

Barnard is “exploring curricular opportunities in specific majors” that would comply with the guidance, according to the email. The college hopes to update students on possible offerings for summer 2027 and the 2027–28 academic year by March 1, 2027.

The email also pointed students to pre-completion Optional Practical Training as a possible alternative to internships, and directed those interested to Barnard’s International Student Services office.

Rosado warned students not to start or continue any off-campus work or internships until there are further updates on the litigation. Working without authorization “even for a single day” could jeopardize their visa status and ability to remain in the United States, she wrote.

text:
A pregnant Modesto woman who says she was pepper-sprayed, forced to the ground and arrested by federal immigration agents outside the Stanislaus County Jail is demanding answers about the encounter.

Lizbeth Vargas Andrade, who says she is a U.S. citizen, was among several people protesting an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) detention in the jail's parking lot when the incident occurred on Sunday.

CBS News Sacramento confirmed that video of the encounter was recorded outside the jail. The footage shows Andrade on the ground as agents handcuff her, at one point with her stomach against the pavement.

Andrade said the confrontation began when an agent backed into her.

"He backed up into me. We bumped. 'She hit me! She hit me!' We bumped," Andrade said. "That's when everything started. They started holding my hands with my phone in my hand. I was trying to still go around. That's when another agent maced me and dropped me to the floor."

Andrade said the situation escalated when federal immigration agents attempted to detain her sister-in-law, who she said had given someone a ride.

Andrade's husband recorded the encounter in the parking lot near the jail and the Stanislaus County Sheriff's Office headquarters.

A spokesperson for the sheriff's office referred CBS News Sacramento to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) for questions about the incident.

CBS News Sacramento sent questions to both DHS and ICE regarding the incident. Neither agency has responded.

Andrade said she remained in ICE custody for several hours before being taken to a hospital. She said her sister called emergency medical responders to check on her.

"They took me. My sugar was super high. My blood pressure was super high. They told me, 'You have no choice. You're going to the hospital,' " Andrade said.

Andrade returned to the parking lot with her husband and attorney on Monday to discuss the incident and call for accountability.

Her attorney, Patrick Kolasinski, criticized the number of agents involved and questioned their handling of the encounter, as well as the sheriff's office response.

"What I see is too many, too close. It's clear ICE isn't trained. It's clear if the sheriff is seeing this scenario, some deputies should've come out and controlled the situation," the attorney said.

text:
SAN ANTONIO — The American Civil Liberties Union of Texas and the ACLU conducted polling prior to the midterm election that revealed widespread opposition to a U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) proposal to open a new detention warehouse in San Antonio.

Respondents said they are most concerned about the cost to taxpayers and the treatment of the people detained.

In the survey, registered Texas voters oppose detention facilities in their communities and want local residents to make decisions about detention centers, not the federal government.

48% of respondents oppose the Eastside ICE detention center, compared to just 35% who support it.

65% of respondents are concerned about the $83 million cost to taxpayers. ICE paid $66 million to purchase the building and signed a $17.3 million contract with GardaWorld Federal Services to renovate the facility.

59% of respondents are concerned about the treatment of people detained. 58% are concerned about the living and sanitary conditions that detainees will face.

58% of respondents are concerned that ICE could skip normal permit and regulatory processes to get approval.

text:
Why It Matters

The Trump administration can keep removing immigrants to third countries for now while the Supreme Court reviews the policy, according to a new Congressional Research Service (CRS) report. However, Congress has options to expand or constrain the Department of Homeland Security's (DHS) authority over these removals. ​

The Immigration and Nationality Act lets the DHS secretary remove people to countries willing to accept them when removal to a designated country or a country with ties to the person would be "impracticable, inadvisable, or impossible." CRS says withholding of removal and Convention Against Torture protections may constrain those options.

The Big Picture

A February 2025 DHS guidance memo identified groups of people with final removal orders to consider for third-country removal. They include people who won protection from removal to their home countries and people earlier released from detention because removal was not reasonably foreseeable.

A class action followed. A federal district court issued a preliminary injunction requiring written notice and a "meaningful opportunity" to raise torture claims, and the Supreme Court stayed it in June 2025. In February, the district court dissolved its injunction and vacated the policy, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the First Circuit largely affirmed that judgment. The Supreme Court then granted the government's petition and stayed the district court's ruling.

Under a July 2025 Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) memorandum, the U.S. Department of State first checks whether the destination country gave credible assurances against persecution or torture. Without them, ICE serves a Notice of Removal and waits 24 hours, or six hours in undefined "exigent circumstances." ICE does not ask whether the person fears removal, so the person must say so.

CRS says the administration calls the removals a national security and enforcement tool that also deters unlawful migration. Critics say people lack "meaningful notice or an opportunity to challenge the removal." The report cites reported abuses at the CECOT prison in El Salvador and life-threatening conflict in South Sudan.

Advertisement

DHS has not published totals. Refugees International and Human Rights First estimate that, as of September, more than 25,000 people had been removed under agreements with more than 30 countries, with Mexico receiving the most. The executive order "Securing Our Borders" directs the secretary of state to pursue such agreements.

The Bottom Line

The Supreme Court docket in DHS v. D.V.D., No. 26-426, lists oral argument for Dec. 9. The respondents' brief was submitted Nov. 16.

Congress could clarify that DHS may remove people to any designated third country, or codify the July 2025 ICE memorandum. It could also require added procedures, let people contest removal before an immigration judge, or require reporting on third-country agreements.

text:
An immigration rule drafted by the Trump administration to plug an alleged gap in the visa system has met its end at the hands of a federal judge appointed by former President George W. Bush.

District Judge F. Dennis Saylor IV of Massachusetts ruled Monday that the Department of Homeland Security overstepped its authority by promulgating a rule that placed greater restrictions on visas for international students, exchange visitors and foreign journalists. His ruling represents a victory for the labor unions and university presidents that challenged the rule, and another loss in the Trump administration’s legal crusade to crack down on immigration.

The DHS rule would have replaced a longstanding policy by only allowing international students to study in America for a fixed timeframe, generally capped at four years, requiring them to apply for an extension if they wish to continue their studies. Previously, there was no fixed time limit for international students so long as they remained enrolled in a university and otherwise maintained legal status. The rule also would have imposed new restrictions on transferring schools, changing academic programs and pursuing additional degrees, while subjecting students to additional immigration reviews intended to combat fraud and national security threats.

TRUMP ADMIN SUED OVER VISA TIME RESTRICTIONS FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS, JOURNALISTS

"DHS acknowledges that there are legitimate reasons why a student may pursue another academic degree at the same or lower level as the one he or she has completed — for example, pursuing an M.B.A. after a J.D.," the judge wrote. "But the Final Rule would effectively prohibit such a student from entering the United States to pursue those studies. And the purported reasons given by DHS for doing so — protecting national security and preventing fraud — are not reasonably related to the nature and purpose of the F-1 visa program."

"Put bluntly, DHS is seeking to prevent or discourage the very activity — providing educational opportunities for foreign students in the United States — that Congress sought to permit and encourage," Saylor continued. "The statute simply does not grant DHS such broad and open-ended authority to undermine the F-1 visa program."

US STATE DEPARTMENT HAS YANKED MORE THAN 175K VISAS UNDER TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SO FAR

Saylor had already blocked the rule from taking effect in September, but Monday's ruling went further by striking it down entirely after finding that DHS violated federal administrative law.

Lawyers representing the department disagreed with the judge’s characterization, arguing that indefinite admission periods prevent immigration officials from periodically reassessing whether foreign nationals are complying with the conditions of their visas. Mandatory extensions, in the telling of the agency, would create additional opportunities to identify fraud, security risks and immigration violations — risks it says are substantiated by past cases of fraud and abuse in the student visa system.

"The performative outrage is incredible. Where was the outrage when foreign nationals were abusing the system, violating the terms of their student visas, and making a mockery of our immigration laws? If the media really cared about legitimate international students, they would be thanking President Trump for cracking down on the rampant fraud to ensure only those truly intending to study in the United States are given the privilege," a DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

Saylor, however, further argued that DHS failed to establish how its new rule would constitute an improvement over existing systems meant to catch visa fraud.

"But DHS has not adequately explained how implementing an unreviewable, completely discretionary renewal system — after a foreign student has already been in the country for four years — meaningfully enhances the ability of DHS to root out cases of fraud, or how the benefits of such a system outweigh the immense costs of abandoning the existing system," he wrote.

DHS PROPOSES MASSIVE $70K FEE FOR FOREIGN STUDENTS SEEKING WORK AUTHORIZATION

Currently, DHS relies on the Student and Exchange Visitor Information System (SEVIS) to monitor student visa fraud. SEVIS is a federal database that monitors international students and exchange visitors, tracking their enrollment, immigration status and compliance with visa requirements through information reported by schools and program sponsors. The agency argued that the system is a "data-reporting system for schools" that is "not designed for performing all relevant fraud and security screening."

Saylor was identified as a Republican in a 2014 profile piece. The same piece noted Saylor had close ties to former Massachusetts Gov. Mitt Romney and that he was reportedly considered for a position in the Bush administration. He was confirmed by a bipartisan vote in the Senate, even winning the support of Democratic Sen. Ted Kennedy, a noted liberal, who praised him for his fair-mindedness and independence.
